case_summary.text: Sum paid to 'Deloitte' for use of brand name in order to attract more business was allowable as deduction

INCOME TAX: Where assessee paid DTT subscription to use 'Deloitte' brand which helped in developing brand image and, consequently, getting more business, since subscription so paid was to run assessee's business activity more effectively, same was to be allowed as deduction under section 37(1)

INCOME TAX : Where payment in question not only permitted use of TATA name but also gave an opportunity to assessee to inform business world that it was having back up of excellence, with a code of conduct and a promise of quality and by making such a contribution, assessee-company was benefitted in its day-to-day business, said expenditure was a revenue expenditure

IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where by virtue of non compete agreement, assessee had acquired right to carry on business unfettered by any competition which resulted in protection for business as a whole and would help appreciate whole of capital assets, since non compete fees was held as capital expenditure, assessee would be entitled for depreciation under section 32 (1)(ii)

INCOME TAX: Where assessee paid a non-compete fee to restrain another party from operating in same business segment, such payment merely protected or enhanced assessee’s business profitability and facilitated more efficient conduct of business, and though it could confer an enduring advantage, same was not in capital field and did not result in creation of any new asset or accretion to profit-earning apparatus; therefore, non-compete fee was allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1)

INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect against High Court ruling that where assessee made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Exp. incurred for use of goodwill attached to name of another firm is allowable u/s 37: HC

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made payment to 'S' and said payment had not been made for acquiring a brand name, but for facilitating acquisition of brand name, which in turn, made substantial improvement in earning capacity of assessee's business, expenditure incurred by assessee company for payment made to 'S' was a revenue expenditure
Non-compete fee paid to protect business is capital exp.; Claim of dep. is to be allowed: ITAT
Sum incurred by coaching institute on scholarship to attract more students allowed as revenue exp.

IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Non-compete fee paid to holding co. to do chit fund business in northern Telangana was a revenue exp.

IT : Where non-compete fee paid by assessee was for purpose of its business and it did not entail any enduring benefit to assessee in its business, payment of such fee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where non-compete fees was paid to individuals who had experience in business of consultancy for not to engage themselves in similar kind of business activities for a period of 3 years and such consideration was independent and not part of cost of acquisition of business paid to shareholders, payment of such fee was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where employees of assessee-company participated in management and technical development programmes, workshops and seminars conducted by IICM with a view to improve their skills and expertise and Assessing Officer observed that contribution to IICM was sum paid by assessee as an employer which was not allowable under section 40A(9), since amount paid represented fee for participation in training programmes, organised by IICM and contribution made by assessee-company towards training had direct nexus with nature of business of assessee, said sum was allowable as expenditure wholly and exclusively for purpose of business of assessee

IT : Where assessee at time of acquiring an undertaking, paid certain amount under head 'Techno Commercial Agreement' and 'Brand Licensing Agreement', amounts so paid were deductible as it was essential for assessee to make such payments on account of nature of its business and on account of procuring knowledge for setting up systems as well as other procedures

INCOME TAX : Where assessee paid non-compete fees to a company on termination of agreement, since by paying said fees, assessee acquired rights which not only gave it enduring benefit but also protected assessee's business against competition, impugned non-compete fees paid by assessee would be capital in nature, however, it would be an intangible asset on which assessee was entitled to claim depreciation

INCOME TAX : Where in view of non-compete agreement entered into by assessee with a company from which it acquired business, non-compete fee paid by assessee would form part of initial outlay on acquisition of business, Assessing Officer was justified in treating said non-compete fee as capital expenditure and disallowing same under section 37(1)
Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under sec. 37(1): SC

IT : Where assessee made payment to its partner to ward-off competition, rights acquired by assessee under said agreement would not only give enduring benefit, but protected assessee's business against competition, and fell under expression 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' used in Explanation 3 to sub-section 32(1)(ii) and, thus, assessee was eligible for depreciation

IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee on advertisement to bring public awareness regarding change in its name, could not be said to bring into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, thus, same was to be allowed as deduction under section 37(1)

License fee for use of goodwill of another firm allowable as deduction u/s 37(1) incurred for business: HC
Non-compete fee was allowable as deduction as it facilitated earning more profit in business ; SLP dismissed

IT : Expenditure on training of employees would be revenue expense
Sum paid to IFA to create awareness of 'Vaish Associates' by constructing meeting hall in its name is business exp.
X. INCOME TAX : Recruitment and training expenses have to be treated as revenue expenditure and cannot be seen as leading to enduring benefit warranting any disallowance

IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Non-compete fee paid to directors to restrain them from engaging in same business was allowable deduction
IT : Training expense on new manufacturing unit which was extension of existing business were allowable as revenue expenditure

IT-I : Where assessee, engaged in manufacturing of pharmaceutical products, paid certain amount as trademark and patent registration fee, in view of fact that said expenditure was incurred for protection of its running business without generating any new asset, same was to be allowed as deduction
Employees training exp. to run an extended unit of an existing business is an allowable expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, manufacturer of sports products, claimed an expenditure towards establishing a pace foundation for giving training to pace bowlers, since assessee got huge publicity by training of bowlers through said foundation and it promoted assessee's brand thereby helping in sale of products, impugned expenditure was to be allowed under secion 37(1)

INCOME TAX : Where assessee company, engaged in business of production and telecasting of TV serials, entered into non-compete agreement with two firms belonging to same person for a period of 5 years wherein it acquired copyrights of number of movies owned by two firms and paid certain amount as non-compete fee, since entire business was transferred as a going concern concept, then, nothing was left with transferee firms to carry on business and what was held by them was a copyright
IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee on coaching of its IPL team was to be allowed as deduction
HC allows business exp. as assessee was doing new business with retained employees after transfer of old business

CL : Where brand name 'Vardhaman' was already registered trade mark of respondent-company and both appellant and respondent companies were doing same business, appellant was to be directed to delete word 'Vardhaman' from its existing name
Exp. incurred by MRF on establishing foundation to give training to pace bowlers allowable as business exp.: HC

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made a payment as donation to CCI and as part of research programme under which employees of assessee would undergo training in theory of disruptive innovation, though amount was paid under head 'donation', actual nature of payment was towards research programme which would benefit assessee in long-term and, thus, same should be allowed as a deduction under section 37(1)

IT: Where for assessment year 1996-97 under an agreement, assessee transferred one of its business to other company but continued its business using its own logo, trade name, licenses and permits, no part of non-compete fee received by assessee under aforesaid agreement could be treated as considerations for goodwill and it was not taxable as income
Non-compete fee can’t be treated as intangible asset; Depreciation claim on it to be disallowed: ITAT

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: IV. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

HELD: It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11] Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company offering training courses in field of financial services took over business of ‘W’, who was also carrying on similar activities, for a consideration which was claimed by assessee-company as revenue expenditure - Revenue, however, treated it as of capital nature - Whether essence of agreement being taking over of business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, said expenditure fell in category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

-compete agreement is to enhance assessee’s profitability or not - Held, yes - Whether since benefit to be derived by assessee in consequence upon incurring expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to enhancement of assessee’s profitability in business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals, it could be said that said expenditure was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure - Held, yes FACT: The assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate. The assessee had acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores. The industry/plant so purchased was to include entire business undertaking situated at Ponada including movable and immovable properties and all other tangible and intangible assets relating to the business of manufacturing of aforesaid chemicals. The assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them. The said agreement provided forrestriction on ‘V’ and ‘M’ to engage in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate directly or indirectly for a period of 5 years for a cash consideration of Rs. 6 crores to be paid upfront. In the books of account, the assessee wrote off one-fifth of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores because the period during which agreement was to remain in force was 5 years but in the computation of income furnished along with return, the assessee claimed whole of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that the expenditure was not incurred for improving the profitability, as there was no existing business and the assessee had acquired the business of chemicals for the first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to the company and disallowed the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores claimed as revenue expenditure and treated it as capital expenditure. The Assessing Officer also disallowed the alternative claim made by the assessee that if the expenditure in question was not considered as revenue expenditure, then the assessee by having entered into non-compete agreement as per which ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ were not to carry on either manufacturing or trading business in the two chemicals for a period of five years, the assessee had acquired commercial/business rights for a period of 5 years to carry on manufacturing and trading activities in both the chemicals undisturbed and freely for a period of five years, which were of intangible nature entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the assessee might be allowed depreciation. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not acquired any specific intellectual right by making payment of Rs. 6 crores, which was eligible for depreciation under section 32.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. He held that no doubt the assessee earlier was doing only some trading business in the chemicals but it was not much; another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India; by making a payment of Rs. 6 crores to ‘V’ the advantage had accrued to the assessee and that too of enduring nature and, accordingly, the expenditure was capital in nature and; the impugned expenditure could not be considered as deferred revenue expenditure and, accordingly, could not be allowed proportionately in five years as contended by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the non-compete fees of Rs. 6 crores paid by the assessee to ‘V’ did not bring in any asset as mentioned in section 32(1)(ii) so as to qualify for depreciation.

On second appeal :

HELD: The Commissioner (Appeals) had specifically admitted that the assessee was carrying on trading business in the chemicals, though he further observed that it was not much. Further, the Commissioner (Appeals) had accepted that another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India, but in the central eastern part of India ‘D’ did not have any hold worth the name.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(ix) of the Indian Income-tax 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1938-39 - Assessee-company incurred expenses in connection with a suit which it had brought against ‘B’ to restrain it from making use of a trade mark to which assessee had acquired exclusive right by long user - Assessee-company claimed deduction of that amount under section 10(2)(ix) of 1922 Act - ITO disallowed assessee’s claim - Tribunal upheld ITO’s order - Whether since expenditure in question did not make any addition to capital of company or bring any additional advantage but only removed an impediment in way of earning legitimate profits by sale of goods produced by assessee, it was a revenue expenditure and, thus, deductible in computing taxable income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company incurred expenses in the year of account in connection with a suit which it had brought against ‘B’ Ltd., to restrain it from using a trade-mark to which the assessee had acquired exclusive right by long user. The assessee claimed deduction of expenditure so incurred under section 10(2)(ix) of 1922 Act. The ITO wrote back the amount without assigning any particular reason for doing so. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO holding that it was capital expenditure, being a non-recurring outlay for retaining a valuable asset of the company. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the trade-mark was a capital asset of the assessee consequently, the legal expense incurred for protecting it against infringement was capital expenditure

On reference:

HELD: The question, how far the expenses incurred in litigation were permissible deductions under the law of Income-tax, was not free from difficulty as the law of Income-tax in British India makes no express provision in that behalf. The 1922 Act no doubt gives certain positive directions in section 10 (2) as regards the deductions that are allowed in computing profits or gains of business, profession or vocation, but the item of legal expenses is not included among those enumerated in that section.

It is indeed difficult to draw a line of demarcation between what is capital expenditure and what is revenue expenditure. The question assumes ostensibly the form of a question of fact. But since the decision of the question turns upon a principle which the legislature has left it to the judiciary to evolve and apply, it must be treated as involving a point of law. That is how the matter has been regarded in the numerous decisions relevant to the issue. It must be noticed that though the provisions of the Income-tax Act may in their terms appear to be different from those in the English Act the question, whether legal expenses should be treated as capital expenditure or revenue expenditure, is one that arises in both countries and in respect of which the law has made no specific provision. The matter therefore has to be considered on some principle of general application. Whether that principle is evolved by the British or by the Indian Courts is immaterial. If it is found to answer a judicial purpose it cannot be rejected for the simple reason that the letter of the laws in the two countries is different.

In the instant case, the assessee had to displace a counterfeit trade-mark which prejudicially affected the sale of its goods. The threat was not directed against the capital of the company but against its trade. The capital is concerned with production, while the trade is concerned with selling, with a view to profit, the goods which the assessee has manufactured. The counterfeit trade-mark introduced into the market by the assessee's unscrupulous rival must be deemed to have had serious effect on the volume of the sale of the goods manufactured by the assessee. The object of launching legal proceedings against the competitor was to restore the trade to its original standard. It was not merely a voluntary act intended to improve the sales but an act necessary to prevent actual loss in the sales. The drop in the sales impaired directly the dividend-earning power of the company not to speak of its status or reputation, and had nothing to do with its capacity to manufacture them and had no bearing on the capital. The assessee was hit not as an industrialist but as a trader; the expulsion of the counterfeit trade-mark from the market by means of litigation in Court did not make any addition to the capital of the company or bring any additional advantage but only removed an impediment in the way of earning legitimate profits by sale of the goods produced by the assessee.

In view of the forgoing discussion, the legal expense incurred was a revenue expenditure and was a proper deduction in computing the taxable income of the assessee from the business.

Concurrent view

(Per Digby, J)

see's apprentices. Trained personnel were necessary for the purpose of the assessee's business. It was necessary because a condition of the agency agreement with Telco required the assessee to have trained personnel. It was necessary also because the staff of trained personnel obviously induced better sales. There was no question here of the assessee acquiring any asset or advantage of an enduring nature. There was nothing to show that the personnel so trained were under bond to serve the assessee for a long term of years. There was no question of the assessee acquiring any "know-how" from Telco which would become it property subsequently. The assessee had entered into an agreement to sell vehicles manufactured by Telco, and for the purpose of ensuring compliance with the agreement requiring the assessee to maintain a staff of trained personnel, it secured the training of its personnel form Telco and made payment thereof to it. It was open to the assessee to have its personnel trained from any other suitable center. There was nothing in the agreement binding the assessee to have its personnel trained by Telco. If it selected Telco for that purpose it was obviously persuaded by the circumstance that the vehicles in which it dealt were manufactured by Telco.

The payment made by the assessee to Telco was payment made wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business and it was not of a capital nature. The payment should have been allowed as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1976-77 - Assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business by an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that assessee would pay vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages - Whether aforesaid payment made by assessee to vendors could be claimed as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business, under an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that the assessee would pay to the vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages as also the value of assets over the liabilities taken over. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee-firm paid certain amount to the vendors under the said agreement and claimed deduction of the same as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground of the payment being a capital expenditure. On appeals, both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

HELD: No test of universal application can be laid down to determine the question whether an expenditure made by the assessee is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure. The question whether an expenditure is on account of revenue or capital has to be decided by looking at the facts and circumstances of the case from the point of view of a practical and prudent businessman rather than from the viewpoint of a tax-gatherer upon strict juristic classification of the legal rights, if any, secured in the proceeds. In order to arrive at a just and proper conclusion one must look at the true nature and character of advantage in a commercial sense without giving undue emphasis to the form thereof or the terminology used in the light of the surrounding circumstances and in the larger context of necessity and expediency. If the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-making process and not for acquisition of an asset, or a right of permanent character, the expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future.

Admittedly, in the instant case, the said payment was made for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages. These rights so acquired evidently facilitated the day-to-day trading operations of the assessee and were intended to increase profits. No asset or right of permanent nature was acquired thereby. It was not even a case where the advantage would endure for indefinite future. Considering the nature and advantages flowing from obtaining the user of the rights in question in the commercial sense, the aforesaid payment was a revenue expenditure, and allowable as a deduction in computing taxable income of the assessee.

is similar to the business being acquired, from directly or indirectly soliciting or influencing clients or customers of the existing business or any other person either not to do business with the person who has acquired the business and paid the non-compete fee or to do business with the person receiving the non-compete fee to do business with a person who is directly or indirectly in competition with the business which is being acquired. The right to acquired for carrying on the business and, therefore, it is a business right. The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, productions or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and commerce and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The term 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' has to be interpreted in such a way that it would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

When once the expenditure incurred for acquiring the said right is held to be capital in nature, consequently the depreciation provided under section 32(1)(ii) is attracted and the assessee would be entitled to the deduction as provided in the said provision i.e., precisely what the Tribunal has held. [Para 8]

FACT: • The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

HELD: Nature of expenditure incurred by assessee

• In the present case, the assessee is a joint venture between 'S' corporation and L&T. Apparently, the agreement entered into with the L&T in view of the changed relationship ensures that the latter does not enter into the same business. Although it is contended that the advantage is only by way of facilitation of the assessee's business and ensuring greater efficiency as well as profitability, on the other side, what can be seen is that the arrangement was to endure for a substantial period, i.e. 7 years coupled with the fact that the L&T had its own presence in consumer goods sector and would be able to put up an effective competition for business engaged in by the assessee, there is no doubt that the amount is to ensure a certain position in the market by keeping-out L&T. In such circumstances, it is opined that the deduction cannot be claimed as a revenue expenditure, it clearly falls within the capital field. [Para 10]

Depreciation in case of intangible asset

• The question arises as to whether a non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for seven years amounts to a depreciable intangible asset. Each of the species of rights spelt-out in section 32(1)(ii), i.e. know-how, patent, copyright, trademark, license or franchise as or any other right of a similar kind which confers a business or commercial or any other business or commercial right of similar nature has to be 'intangible asset'. The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the ownership. In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance 'in rem'.

• However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity. The right can be asserted in the present instance only against L&T and in a sense, the right 'in personam'.

HEADNOTE: I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 - Assessee-company acquired brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement - Under a separate non-compete agreement, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company as consideration for restraining it from competing in business of products similar to Lacto Calamine for a period of ten years - Amount paid as non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure by assessee - Whether in cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and benefit of restrain acquired by assessee for period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit - Held, yes - Whether therefore, by paying non-compete fee, it could be said that assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by assessee was in nature of capital expenditure and not revenue in character as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company, engaged in the business of manufacture of medicines and Lacto Calamine, purchased the brand name ‘Lacto Calamine’ from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement. Subsequently, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company under a non-compete agreement for restraining it from competing directly or indirectly in the business activities carried on by the assessee. The payment so made for the purchase of brand name was accounted for by the assessee as an item of capital expenditure but the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs paid as non-compete fee was claimed as a deduction being revenue in nature under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer, however, rejected the assessee’s said claim by holding that non-compete fee paid by it to ‘D’ was a capital expenditure inasmuch as by making said payment the assessee had acquired an advantage of an enduring nature by way of freedom from competition that would have been induced by ‘D’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

HELD: The assessee-company had acquired the brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs. That acquisition was carried out on the basis of an agreement. In addition to the said agreement, the assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement. In terms of the non-compete agreement, the assessee had paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to ‘D’ as consideration for restraining ‘D’ from competing in the business of products similar to Lacto Calamine, for a period of ten years. Regarding the first agreement and the amount of Rs. 85 lakhs, the assessee itself admitted that the expenditure was capital in nature. It was in respect of the second payment of Rs. 40 lakhs that the claim of the assessee was that payment was revenue in character. The most important and direct feature to be seen, in the instant case, was that the agreement of acquisition as well as non-compete agreement, both were executed contemporaneously. The assessee was, in fact, acquiring a new branded product in its sole right from ‘D’. The product, namely, Lacto Calamine is a valuable brand in the cosmetic industry and the assessee acquired the brand right from ‘D’. Once the assessee had acquired the brand right of Lacto Calamine with all the attendant rights and privileges from ‘D’, the assessee had become the owner of that brand against the entire world. The assessee brought in a new profit making apparatus in the form of a brand name in its possession. It was for the purpose of expansion into new line of product. It was also necessary for the assessee to see that the demand for the new product in the hands of the assessee should not be adversely affected by any possible competition from ‘D’. Therefore, it had entered into another non-compete agreement. Non-compete agreement had imposed restrain on ‘D’ from indulging in competition with the assessee for a period of ten years. [Para 22]

In the cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and the benefit of restrain acquired by the assessee for the period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit. By paying non-compete fee, the assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with the acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product. [Para 23]

The another observation of the Assessing Officer for holding the expenditure in question to be capital expenditure was that there was no fear of competition from ‘V’ or that ‘V’ would not have been able to compete within a period of 5 years and that the assessee was to continue to get the benefit, even after 5 years, which was of ‘enduring nature’. Consequently, the revenue authorities’ observation that the benefit to be derived by the assessee was of ‘enduring nature’ because ‘V’ was not in a position to compete during the period of 5 years because it could not start manufacturing these chemicals within 5 years and by that the assessee would get established itself so well in the market that it would be difficult to dislodge was misplaced, without any basis or reasoning and devoid of any merit. In that case, the assessee would have got depreciation on whole of the amount, i.e., including payment of Rs. 6 crores and in that situation nobody was going to question the assessee’s bona fide and, therefore, to term the expenditure as of capital nature, only because the assessee had claimed the payments separately, was not justified.

HEADNOTE: section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-capital or revenue expenditure-assessee, carrying on business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in licensed public cinema theatres, paid rs. 1,50,000 to a rival to induce the latter not to compete with it for nine years-whether payment was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1)-held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

On reference, the assessee-company contended that since the expenditure was incurred for acquiring the film shorts, it should be taken to have been expended for acquiring stock-in-trade of the assessee's business :

HELD: The agreement entered into by the assessee-company with B does not indicate that the film shorts as stock-in-trade were the subject-matter of the bargain. In substance and effect, the agreement involved a transfer of the B's business to the assessee-company for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. It cannot be said that the said sum was paid for acquiring the stock-in-trade. The assessee-company has not only warded off the business rivalry but also acquired the business of the rival for a period of nine years in a specified area. By this agreement, the assessee-company has in fact derived an advantage by eliminating the competition and acquired a business which actually generated income. Any amount expended for acquiring a business or asset which generated income or for avoiding competition in business has to be treated as capital in nature.

In that case, the assessee would have got depreciation on whole of the amount, i.e., including payment of Rs. 6 crores and in that situation nobody was going to question the assessee’s bona fide and, therefore, to term the expenditure as of capital nature, only because the assessee had claimed the payments separately, was not justified. It was found that the assessee already carried on the trading business in the relevant two chemicals. The scale of business was not relevant so far as the fruits of non-competition agreement were concerned. After having purchased the manufacturing unit, the assessee was to sell these two chemicals in central and eastern parts of India where ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ had been selling the chemicals, though not under any special brand, for the last 8-10 years and had definitely earned a good rapport, relationship and name with the consumers of these chemicals, consequently, they could be a potential threat by entering into the trading of same chemicals of other manufacturers. By entering into the agreement, the assessee had not only prevented the potential threat but had derived a benefit/right as a result of which prospects of the assessee’s sale/profitability of these two chemicals, which were not branded, was bound to increase. Even if it was assumed that the assessee was not carrying on the business in these two chemicals at all, even then the purchase of manufacturing unit was itself relevant and sufficient to support the assessee’s claim that subsequent agreement was only to enhance the assessee’s sales of these two chemicals in central and eastern parts of India which in turn was bound to enhance the profitability. So far as the revenue’s view that ‘V’ was not able to compete after sale of manufacturing unit because it would have taken about five or more years to install such a plant and by that time, the assessee might have established itself well in the market. The said theory could not be subscribed to firstly, because the authorities had not pointed out as to how the installation of such a plant was to take five or more years and, secondly, the authorities had not considered the fact that agreement was with two parties, namely, ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ in his individual capacity and was for both manufacturing and trading activities. Since not only these two chemicals but all such type of chemicals are normally sold without any brand because manufacturing of these chemicals does not require any secret formula or secret know-how and even if, sold under a brand, then also, it is not of such importance because in case of goods whose quality is dependent on secret formula or secret skill or secret know-how, it is the ‘brand’ which matters. For example, Nitric Acid is always sold as Nitric Acid—it has neither secret formula nor secret know-how. Similarly, Ammonium Nitrate is always sold as Ammonium Nitrate—again does not require any secret formula or secret know-how, and, since there were other manufacturers (manufacturing on large scale) of these two chemicals in the field, there was an existing cut-throat competition from these manufacturers and since ‘V’ as well as its founder ‘M’ had been in this business for the last 8-10 years, they were definitely a potential/substantial threat in marketing of these two chemicals by the assessee. They could easily get trading rights for sale of these two chemicals from the aforesaid two manufacturers.

Therefore, the findings of the revenue authorities were only on the basis of fictional thinking without there being any cogent material on record, whereas the assessee’s apprehension of future threat was real and supported by the facts already existing.

So far as the ‘enduring nature’ is concerned, there cannot be any hard and fast rules which may prescribe time limitation, i.e., period during which the benefit survives is not uniform in every case. It may differ from case to case and it bears on the facts of the individual case and future probabilities. In some case, it may be a period of one year, and in other case, it may be five years or in other may be 15 years which may not bring benefit of ‘enduring nature’. The only point to be considered is that can the threat, which is perceived at the time of agreement/incurring of the expenditure cease to exist after expiry of the period or will re-occur. If the threat has the potential of re-occurring after the expiry of period, then the benefit derived cannot be said to be of ‘enduring nature’.

So far as the instant case was concerned ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ both being well in a position financially, as well as otherwise, to compete with the assessee even after a period of five years, the threat which was perceived at the time of agreement still subsisted and was liable to re-occur at the expiry of period of five years, and benefit derived could not be said to be of enduring nature.

Further, the benefit to be derived by the assessee in consequence upon incurring the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores by entering into a non-competition agreement with ‘V’ and ‘M’ was directly related to the enhancement of the assessee’s profitability in the business of manufacturing and trading of these two chemicals and, therefore, the same was of revenue nature and was liable to be allowed as business expenditure.

On second appeal: HELD: There was no dispute about the fact that L&T was having well-established country-wide network in developing, manufacturing, marketing, distributing and selling various electronic equipments and products in India. The joint venture i.e., assessee would have faced tough competition if L&T had set up any undertaking or assisted in setting up any undertaking carrying on business of selling/marketing and trading of electronic office products in India. To ward off that competition, the assessee company had paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T. Therefore, by payment of non-compete fee to L&T the competition for a period of 7 years had been eliminated. The period of 7 years is quite long during which any new company can establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would had been acquired. Therefore, the payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase the profitability, but to establish itself in the market and acquire market share. By keeping away L&T from the same business, the assessee had visualized to acquire a good market share. The contention of the assessee that after a period of 7 years L&T Ltd. would have entered in the same trade and, therefore, the expenditure should be treated as revenue in nature, could not be accepted. The payment had been made to ward off the competition for a period of 7 years during which any company could have set up its products and reputation in the market. Therefore, the expenditure could not be treated to have been incurred in revenue field. [Para 11]

The next contention of the assessee was that the payment of non-compete fee had not created any asset or advantage in the capital field and, therefore, it should be revenue in nature. [Para 12]

In the instant case the expenditure was incurred to ward off the competition for a period of 7 years at the start of the business and hence, would form part of initial outlay of the business. For said reason also, the expenditure by way of non-compete fee had to be treated capital in nature. [Para 14]

The provisions of section 28(va ) were inserted in the statute by the Finance Act, 2002 with effect from 1-4-2003 according to which any sum, whether received or receivable, in cash or kind, under an agreement for not carrying out any activity in relation to any business will be chargeable to tax under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession'. In the instant case, the assessment year involved was 2001-02. It was not the case of the assessee that L&T had treated the payments received by it as business income and, hence, as a corollary to the amended provisions of section 28(va ) the payment made would be treated as revenue expenditure. Hence, it was not possible to treat the payment of non-compete fee as revenue expenditure in the hand of the assessee for the assessment year under consideration. [Para 15]

In view of the above, it was to be held that the non-compete fee paid by the assessee to ward off competition from L&T was capital in nature and as such, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure. Accordingly, the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) confirming the addition made by the Assessing Officer was to be upheld. [Para 16]

Alternatively, it had been argued that in case the expenditure was treated as capital in nature, depreciation should be allowed as non-compete fee was an intangible asset. From a plain reading of language of section 32(1)(ii) it is clear that (i) the asset should intangible asset; (ii) should be wholly or partly owned by the assessee; (iii) and used for the purposes of business or profession. All three conditions are cumulative and non fulfilment of any of the condition would disentitle the assessee for depreciation allowance. Admittedly, the non-compete fee was not in the nature of know-how, patents, copy-right, trade-marks, licenses or franchises. Now, it was to be seen whether non-compete fee would fall under residuary part of the definition 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature'. The intangible asset falling in expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' should belong to same genus to which know-how, patents, copy rights, trademarks, licenses/franchises belong. Therefore, the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' would mean that the business or commercial right should be in the nature of know-how, patents, copy-rights, trade-marks, licenses or franchises. By no stretch of imagination, the non-compete fee could be treated to have belonged to the same genus to which know-how, patents, copyrights, trademarks, licences/franchises belong. [Para 17]

As per the agreement, an amount of Rs. 10 crores was given to their promoters for the restrictive covenant not to compete with the assessee for 10 years with a view to facilitate its profits by eliminating competition from the promoters. The Assessing Officer observed that there were limits to the price of shares of a company determined by market forces and in the instant case it was difficult to imagine that such limits would not have been operative and the assessee was left with no option but to pay the cost of acquisition over and above the price paid for the acquisition of the shares of these companies to their promoters; that, in order to claim the payments as allowable deduction, the transaction was given the colour of payments as non-competition fees, but, in fact, the real purpose of those payments was to compensate the promoters of the companies owning the two distilleries for the cost of the distilleries; that it was not the case of the assessee that the payments were made to any distillery owner or business rival and it was also not the case of the assessee that the persons who were paid the said amounts possessed special expertise and skill so as to threaten the business of the assessee; and that the circumstance that these persons’ companies/ distilleries did not produce any brand of liquor with national market presence, did not support the case of the assessee as to the real purpose or motive of the said payments. He, therefore, held that the claim of the assessee for allowability of Rs. 10 crores as business expenditure was nothing but part of the cost of distilleries and added it to the income of the assessee. On appeal, it was submitted that agreement for non-competition fees was for 5 years and based on certain decisions, it was claimed that where the benefit was not of enduring nature but was to exhaust in a short period, the expenditure was of revenue nature. The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the payment could not be taken as the revenue expenditure because the agreements were to run for a long duration of 10 years unfettered by any stipulation of termination; that payment of non-competition fees could have some rationale if the competition was between equals producing the same commodity and that the promoters of the two distilleries taken over were no match for the assessee who had monopoly of manufacturing and marketing its own brand names. He, therefore, held that there was no business necessity for making the non-competition fees of Rs. 10 crores and upheld the disallowance.

On further appeal :

HELD: The expenditure incurred in violation of a provision of the Act would not be an allowable deduction, as held by the Supreme Court in Maddi Venkataraman & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1998] 229 ITR 534 / 96 Taxman 643 and as held by the Karnataka High Court in CIT v. Bangalore Arrack Co. [1993] 201 ITR 25 payment to ward off competition being against a public policy will not be an allowable deduction. [Para 5.5]

In view of the above, the payment made by the assessee to ward off competition for the period of 10 years would be a payment for acquiring an enduring benefit which could not be allowed as deduction in view of the later decision of the Madras High Court in the case of Chelpark Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1991] 191 ITR 249 / 56 Taxman 29 and those of Calcutta and Madhya Pradesh High Courts. The disallowance was, accordingly, to be upheld. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: SECTION 37(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BUSINESS EXPENDITURE-
WHETHER EXPENDITURE INCURRED BY ASSESSEE-FIRM ON TRAINING OF 
PARTNER IN BUSINESS MANAGEMENT WAS ALLOWABLE EXPENDITURE-HELD, 
YES

FACT: The assessee-firm claimed as business expenditure the amount spent by it on sending one of its partners to the United States for training in busi- ness management. The ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that the training had nothing to do with the business of manufacture and sale of hosiery goods carried on by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

HELD: Training in modern business management would definitely be beneficial to the carrying on of any business. The mere fact that the said training is beneficial to any business does not, in any way, obliterate the fact that it is beneficial to the particular business carried on by the assessee-firm. Further, the mere fact that it has incidentally benefited the partner him- self, was immaterial. The knowledge that the partner was gaining was such that it would definitely benefit the business carried on by the assessee-firm and so, the expenditure in acquiring that knowledge had a direct nexus with the business carried on by the firm, as would be evident from the increase in sales in the succeeding year. The expenditure incurred for such training in this case had been definitely incurred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the assessee's business.

In order to be capital expenditure, that expenditure should not only bring into existence a benefit of enduring advantage or benefit but the same should also be in the capital field. In the instant case, so assuming that the benefit even if considered to be enduring in nature, was not in the capital field of the assessee-firm and so it could not be said to be capital in nature.

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA' - Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into Indian compressor market - In said process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh facilities - In accordance with terms of MoU, both parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through assessee-company agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility - Total amount paid by assessee to Whirlpool India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores paid towards non-compete fee - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee being revenue expenditure by separating said amount from main agreement - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether, when an expenditure is made for initial outlay or for expansion of business or for a substantial replacement of equipment, then it would fall under capital expenditure - Held, yes - Whether since, in instant case, it was apparent from records that non-compete agreement was part and parcel of whole transaction (i.e., main agreement entered into between assessee and Whirlpool), it could be concluded that non-compete fee was paid as a part of initial outlay, and, therefore, it was to be disallowed being in nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether an expenditure incurred on warding off competition in business from a rival dealer will constitute a capital expenditure and to hold it as capital expenditure, it is not necessary that non-compete fee is paid to create monopoly rights - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a wholly-owned subsidiary of 'Tecumseh-USA'. Tecumseh-USA being a global compressor manufacturer was interested in entering into the Indian compressor market. In the process, Tecumseh-USA entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Whirlpool India Ltd. through which Whirlpool-India had decided to sell the compressors and related operations owned by it at Faridabad and Ballabgarh. In accordance with the terms of the MoU, both the parties entered into an 'asset purchase agreement', whereby Tecumseh-USA through its 'to be an established local Indian entity' agreed to purchase all compressor machineries, equipments and tooling located at Whirlpool-India's Faridabad facility as well as related compressor component assets located at Whirlpool-India's Ballabgarh facility including laminations, wire drawings, centralized tool room, overload protectors and relays. The total amount paid by the assessee to Whirlpool-India was an amount of Rs. 52.50 crores which was the total sum agreed to be paid by the assessee for whole of the transaction as per the MoU. The said amount of Rs. 52.50 crores included a sum of Rs. 2.65 crores towards non-compete fee. As per terms of non-compete agreement against the receipt of full consideration specified therein, Whirlpool India was to sign and deliver to the assessee an undertaking not to compete with it in the manufacture, sale or repair of compressors in India, except that Whirlpool would be entitled to sell and install compressors purchased from the assessee to the persons under its service arrangements, subject to the provisions of the supply agreements. It was the amount of Rs. 2.65 crores which was claimed by the assessee to be the non-compete fees or revenue expenditure by separating the said amount from the main agreement. The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

On second appeal :

In view of the forgoing discussion, the legal expense incurred was a revenue expenditure and was a proper deduction in computing the taxable income of the assessee from the business.

Concurrent view

(Per Digby, J) A trade-mark is a capital asset, but an attack on a trade-mark made by infringement is to be regarded not as an attack on a capital asset but rather as an attack on existing and future trade and on the value of stock-in-trade, existing and in course of manufacture and to be manufactured in the future.

The word ‘solely’ in Section 10 (2) (ix) of 1922 Act under construction is related to the object of expenditure, the earning of profits and gains, and not to the profits and gains of the particular year in which the expenditure is made and deducted. For, obviously, expenditure of one year, not of a capital nature, may often be intended to have a favourable effect on the next year's profits. A good example would be the ordinary expenses of advertisement. Hence, the expenditure was not in the nature of capital expenditure.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.
