Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee company was incorporated in pursuance of joint venture agreement by and between LT Ltd. and 'S' Corporation, Japan - Prior to joint venture agreement, LT was engaged in business of developing, manufacturing, marketing, distributing and selling various electric equipments and products in India and it had a well established country-wide sales network in India - LT and 'S' Corporation, Japan established assessee company with limited liability for purpose of importing, marketing and selling in India certain electric and electronic office products - During relevant assessment year assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to LT in lieu of latter, not setting up undertaking/assisting in setting up any undertaking carrying on business of selling, marketing and trading of electronic office product for a period of 7 years in India - Assessee claimed deduction of non-compete fee paid to LT under section 37(1) - Assessing Officer took a view that expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, therefore, amount so paid was to be treated as capital in nature - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer - Whether since payment had been made to ward off competition for a period of 7 years during which assessee company could have set up its products and reputation in market, expenditure in question could not be treated to have been incurred in revenue field - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, authorities below were justified in rejecting assessee's claim - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of [Training expenses] - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether expenditure incurred on training of employees after business was set up and production had commenced would be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Para 3] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee-company claimed deduction of Rs. 10.80 lakhs paid to one 'GCL' for imparting training to its employees - Assessing Officer disallowed claim of assessee on ground that those were ad hoc charges levied by 'GCL' without any basis whatsoever; that since assessee neither furnished any details/evidence of services rendered by 'GCL' to assessee nor established genuineness of expenditure - Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed order passed by Assessing Officer - Tribunal held that not an iota of evidence had been brought to notice that expenditure by way of reimbursement to 'GCL' was towards training of employees of assessee - Whether two revenue authorities and Tribunal having concurrently found on facts that claim was not acceptable, same needed no interference - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

SECTION 37(1) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-BUSINESS EXPENDITURE-
WHETHER EXPENDITURE INCURRED BY ASSESSEE-FIRM ON TRAINING OF 
PARTNER IN BUSINESS MANAGEMENT WAS ALLOWABLE EXPENDITURE-HELD, 
YES

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2002-03 - Assessee-company spent certain amount on training of its employees and claimed same as revenue expenditure deductible under section 37(1) on ground that same was incurred for increasing employees' efficiency in day-to-day working - Whether since expenditure in question was incurred wholly and exclusively for purpose of assessee's business, same was entirely deductible in year under consideration - Held, yes

I. Section  37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business expenditure  -  Allowability of  (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year  2001-02  - Assessee, a company, was engaged in business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipment in India - It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and L & T - During year, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L &T as consideration for latter not setting up or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years - Said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in return of income filed by assessee as non-compete fee paid to L &T - Assessing Officer held that such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, hence, treated payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure - Whether non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance profitability of business, thereby facilitating carrying on of business more efficiently and profitably and, thus, such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to profit earning apparatus of payer - Held, yes - Whether, further, on facts, assessee had not acquired any new business and there was no addition to profit making apparatus of assessee, assets remained same and expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of same business and, thus, non-compete fee paid by assessee was an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes [Paras 26, 28 and 29] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-Capital or revenue expenditure-Whether payments made for obtaining technical knowledge, advice and information, and for providing training facilities for assessee's employees, to bring assessee-company into effective and efficient operation are of revenue nature-Held, yes

I. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment years 2004-05 to 2009-10 - Assessee purchased one division of 'N' chemicals by way of slump sale - Assessee paid certain amount as non-compete fee which represented difference in value of tangible and intangible assets and lump sum amount paid for taking over business - It was found that on account of payment of non-compete fee, seller was restrained from carrying on similar type of business for three years - Whether since payment of non-compete fee resulted in enduring benefit to assessee, it could not be allowed as revenue expenditure; it was capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee purchased business division of another concern which also included payment to non-compete fee restraining seller from carrying on similar business for three years, said payment was to be regarded as capital expenditure  IT : Payment made for taking legal and professional advice in connection with purchase of business division, was to be treated as capital expenditure  IT : Where assessee made payment to its holding company for using its trade mark and to obtain expertise in field of commerce, finance, manufacturing etc. for smooth running of business, amount so paid was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where assessee paid commission on export sales at same rate at which it had been paid by seller of business earlier, disallowance made by Assessing Officer taking a view that a part of commission payment was excessive, was to be deleted  IT : Foreign exchange fluctuation loss incurred by assessee in respect of outstanding foreign currency term loan was to be allowed as business loss  IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee in connection to transfer of business such as legal notice charges, performance incentive etc., was to be allowed as revenue expenditure  IT : Where in order to give effect to business transfer agreement, assessee purchased shares of management staff, since impugned amount was non-recoverable and was a loss on account of business transfer, it was required to be deducted from capital gain in respect of slump sale of trading business  IT : Where Assessing Officer made disallowance in respect of dividend income by relying upon Rule 8D of Income-tax Rules, 1962, since said rule was applicable for assessment year 2008-09 while assessment year under consideration was 2007-08, impugned disallowance was to be deleted

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 - Assessee-company acquired brand ownership of Lacto Calamine from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement - Under a separate non-compete agreement, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company as consideration for restraining it from competing in business of products similar to Lacto Calamine for a period of ten years - Amount paid as non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure by assessee - Whether in cosmetic industry, where fashion and technology are fast changing, a ten year period is a sufficiently long period and benefit of restrain acquired by assessee for period of ten years was definitely an enduring benefit - Held, yes - Whether therefore, by paying non-compete fee, it could be said that assessee had acquired enduring benefit along with acquisition of brand right of a familiar cosmetic product - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by assessee was in nature of capital expenditure and not revenue in character as claimed by assessee - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-Compete fee) - Assessee-company, engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors - Assessee's claim for deduction of said expenditure was rejected by Assessing Officer on ground that it was in nature of capital expenditure - Tribunal upheld order passed by Assessing Officer - Whether since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 15] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee engaged in business of manufacture, marketing and distribution of ice cream and dairy based frozen products, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

III. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Year in which deductible - Assessment year 2002-03 - Whether since expenditure incurred on training of employees is a revenue expenditure, same cannot be spread over number of years and can be allowed in year of incurrence - Held, yes

I - Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Employees' welfare expenses - Assessee-company, which was principally in area of manufacturing plastic pouches, incurred expenditure for sponsoring a trainee for overseas education in computer software development and accounting - Whether such expenditure could not be allowed - Held, yes [Para 30] [In favour of revenue]

section 37(1) of the income-tax act, 1961-capital or revenue expenditure-assessee, carrying on business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in licensed public cinema theatres, paid rs. 1,50,000 to a rival to induce the latter not to compete with it for nine years-whether payment was allowable as a revenue expenditure under section 37(1)-held, no

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1951 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 1999-2000 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns, engaged in similar business as going concern, for certain consideration - In addition, assessee undertook to pay certain amount per month to said concerns for a period of 15 years in consideration of non-compete obligation undertaken by them and claimed said payments as revenue expenditure - Whether said payments, having been made for eliminating competition in same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years, were of capital nature and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Non-compete fee - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one on revenue account - Held, yes - Assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with one 'U' for a period of 5 years - It paid a certain sum as non-compete fee to 'U' and claimed same as revenue expenditure - 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to clientele and pricing of products; as a business proposition, assessee entered into non-compete agreement - Whether payment was in respect of performing of business of assessee and, thus, expenditure was on revenue account and not on capital account - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where assessee made payment as non-compete fee for purpose of business of assessee, expenditure was on revenue count

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowable as - Assessment years 1964-65 and 1965-66 - Assessee-company, engaged in manufacture and sale of pharmaceutical goods, had set up during year under consideration a plant for manufacturing additional pharmaceutical goods - Assessee incurred travelling expenses on account of visit of a foreigner to impart training to assessee's staff - Whether Tribunal was justified in holding that such expenditure on travelling was of capital nature - Held, yes

IX. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Brand building expenditure) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee had paid a certain amount to Tata towards Tata Brand Equity  Designs Promotion as per agreement entered into between Tata and assessee and it was allowed to use Tata brand name and logo - Assessing Officer called on assessee to justify as to why payment made to Tata should be treated as revenue expenditure - Assessee submitted that under agreement entered into with Tata assessee was under contractual obligation to make payment towards subscription fee and in consideration of subscription fees a whole lot of shareable resources of Tata group was made available to assessee and it provided assistance in accessing network of domestic and international business contracts using business name and that TDS under section 194J was made on payments made to Tata - Assessing Officer held that payment was for overall brand building of assessee-company and accordingly, same was in nature of capital expenditure which was an intangible asset - It was noted that payment in question not only permitted use of TATA name but also gave an opportunity to assessee to inform business world that it was having back up of excellence, with a code of conduct and a promise of quality and by making such a contribution, assessee-company was benefitted in its day-to-day business - Whether, on facts, said expenditure was a revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Para 58] [In favour of assessee]

IV. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Where assessee purchased merchant banking division of other company and paid non-compete fee for restricting transferor from carrying out similar business for 36 months, same would be capital in nature [In favour of revenue]   As per transfer of business agreement, the assessee had purchased the merchant banking division from IGFL. The assessee in terms of agreement had also paid non-compete fee of Rs. one crore to the transferor and Rs. 70 lakhs to one S who was the managing director as well as shareholder of the transferor company for restricting the above persons from carrying out similar business and for preventing them from doing certain other actions. The assessee claimed said expenditure as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed expenditure as capital expenditure. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, held that the expenditure had only facilitated higher efficiency and profitability of the assessee there being no changes in the fixed assets of the assessee. He, therefore, allowed expenditure as revenue expenditure.  Held that non-compete expenditure had been incurred in connection with setting up of the new business. Therefore, the expenditure had to be considered as capital in nature. Further, the non-compete agreement was valid for a period of three years which has to be considered as sufficient length of time to treat the expenditure as capital in nature. The protection acquired by the assessee from competition was not part of the working of the business and went on to appreciate the whole of the capital amount. Accordingly, the addition made by the Assessing Officer was confirmed.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of – Assessee was engaged in business of holding race meetings on commercial scale - For popularity of races run by assessee and to make its business profitable it was necessary that there were jockeys of requisite skill and experience in sufficient numbers who would be available to owners and trainers and for this purpose assessee started a school for training Indian jockeys – Assessee claimed deduction of expenditure incurred in running said school – Whether if there were not sufficient number of efficient Indian jockeys to ride horses assessee's interest would have suffered, and it might have had to abandon its business if it did not take steps to make jockeys of necessary calibre available, therefore, any expenditure which was incurred by assessee for preventing extinction of its business would be expenditure wholly and exclusively laid out by it for purpose of business and would be an allowable deduction – Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-Compete fee) - Assessee-company, made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors - Assessee's claim for deduction of said expenditure was rejected by Assessing Officer on ground that it was in nature of capital expenditure - Tribunal upheld order passed by Assessing Officer - High Court by impugned order held that since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Whether special leave petition filed against impugned order was to be dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect - Held, yes [Paras 12 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : SLP dismissed as withdrawn due to low tax effect against High Court ruling that where assessee made payment of non-compete fee to two of its directors, since advantage of restraining individuals from engaging in competition was in field of facilitating assessee's own business and rendering it more profitable and there was no increase in fixed capital, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2005-06 - Assessee was engaged in business of wholesale trading, selling and marketing of hi-tech documents and providing maintenance and after sales services of its products - Assessee-company acquired mailing business from 'KOAL' as a going concern on a slump sale basis pursuant to Business Transfer Agreement entered into by assessee with latter - Consideration for such transfer included certain non-compete fee which was limited for a period of five years - For assessment year 2005-06, assessee filed its return of income wherein deduction of non-compete fee was claimed as business/revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer, however, disallowed same on ground that payment of non-compete fee was a capital outlay - Commissioner (Appeals) held that expenditure incurred on non-compete fee by assessee was to be allowed on deferred revenue basis, i.e., in five years as period of non-compete fee agreement was for five years - On second appeal, Tribunal held that non-compete fee paid by assessee was capital in nature, as such disallowed claim - It was noted that assessee itself treated expenditure as capital in books of account - Likewise, in schedule 2 to balance sheet disclosing 'fixed assets', payment of non-compete fee was treated as 'intangible assets' - This also showed that assessee treated this as asset acquired, which was intangible in nature - Whether in view of above, Tribunal rightly held expenditure as capital in nature - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

X. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Recruitment and training expenses) - Assessment year 2005-06 - Whether recruitment and training expenses have to be treated as revenue expenditure and cannot be seen as leading to enduring benefit warranting any disallowance - Held, yes [Para 78] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1994-95 - Whether payment made by assessee to ward off competition for period of 10 years is a payment for acquiring an enduring benefit and cannot be allowed as deduction - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2008-09 - Non-compete fee paid to director of company whose services were terminated when new management took over company, restricting him from exercising competitive activities within specified territories for one year would be allowed as revenue expenditure [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 32,  read with section 28(va), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/Rate of (Intangible assets) - Assessee-company had made payments to his partner to ward-off competition and to protect its existing business - Assessee capitalized such expenditure arguing that such payment was for acquiring commercial rights and claimed depreciation on same as applicable to intangible assets - Whether since rights acquired by assessee under said agreement would not only give enduring benefit, but protected assessee's business against competition, it could be covered under expression 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' used in Explanation 3 to sub-section 32(1)(ii) and, thus, assessee was eligible for depreciation - Held, yes [Paras 10 to 11] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether payment made to ward off competition in business would constitute capital expenditure if object of making that payment is to derive an advantage by eliminating competition over some length of time; however, same result would not follow if there is no certainty of duration of advantage and same can be put on an end any time - Held, yes - Whether payment made by assessee-company to purchaser of its insecticides plant for restricting from selling and distribution of fast selling major products i.e. Thimet, Malathion and Abate, and for parting with specialized knowledge and expertise in relation to those products for a specific period of time, was required to be considered as capital in nature - Held, yes [Para 3.3] [In favour of revenue]

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company had a collaboration agreement with 'GIC' which trained its personnel in operation and maintenance of float glass plant - That training was given before plant was set-up by assessee - Amounts payable for imparting training was claimed during relevant previous year on ground that invoice was received from 'GIC' during relevant previous year, and that it had deducted TDS and deposited same during relevant previous year - Whether since expenditure was, admittedly, incurred prior to setting-up of plant, it was to be capitalized as part of plant and machinery - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of Income-tax Act, 1961
Where a partner of firm of Chartered Accountants was sent abroad for higher studies in line of profession and his services were to be available to firm for a minimum period of five years, after completion of studies expenditure incurred by firm on his education was an allowable business expenditure
Eleventh ITO v. Argade Shyam & Co. [1988] 32 TTJ (Bom.) 17
Under an agreement, one of the partners of the assessee-firm was sent abroad to prosecute higher studies where he studied for the course of MBA. The assessees agreed to bear the expenditure on his studies and the partner in turn undertook to serve the firm for five years after completing the course. The assessee claimed deduction in respect of the aforesaid expenditure which was disallowed by the ITO :
Held that the assessee ensured for itself services of a better qualified partner to atleast for a period of 5 years. The partner had not only got a permission from the Reserve Bank but had also obtained admission in the University for MBA course and the Reserve Bank of India had sanctioned foreign exchange for his study. He had secured admission in the University even prior to entering into agreement with the two firms. In these circumstances, the expenditure incurred by the assessee’s firm on his education was allowable as deduction.

The assessee-company was engaged in the manufacture and sale of asbestos sheet and allied products. It sent 'P', son of its managing director, to USA for higher education and training. After completing said training, 'P' joined the assessee as director. The assessing authority held that the expenditure incurred on the studies and training of 'P' was not a business expenditure, hence added in the overall income of the assessee.

II. Section 32 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Depreciation - Allowance/rate of - Assessment year 2001-02 - Depreciation would be allowable on non-compete expenditure incurred by assessee [In favour of assessee]   As per transfer of business agreement, the assessee had purchased the merchant banking division from IGFL. The assessee, in terms of agreement, had also paid non-compete fee of Rs. one crore to the transferor and Rs. 70 lakhs to one S who was the managing director as well as shareholder of the transferor-company for restricting the above persons from carrying out similar business and for preventing them from doing certain other actions. As the revenue authorities treated said expenditure as capital expenditure, the assessee claimed that it should be allowed depreciation on same.  Held that the Tribunal, in case of Asstt. CIT v. Real Image Tech. (P.) Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 80 (Chennai)(Mag.), observed that by obtaining non-compete right on payment of non-compete fee, the assessee can run his business without bothering about competition and, therefore, non-compete right is an intangible asset falling in the category of any other business or commercial right under section 32(1)(ii). Following said decision, depreciation would be allowed to the assessee on the non-compete expenditure incurred by it.

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non compete fee) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged in business as Registrar and Transfer Agent licensed by SEBI - It entered into a non-compete agreement with a person - Tenor of agreement was only 18 months - Whether it could not be stated that assessee derived any enduring benefit due to payment effected by it to said person for obtaining certain commitments and restricting himself from indulging in any competition with business of assessee or from weaving away employees - Held, yes - Whether therefore, non compete fee had to be treated as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1986-87 - Two former employees of assessee-company having access to secret formula were retained in service even after their retirement to ensure that would not be any competition from them by setting up rival ink manufacturing concerns - Whether payment to such retired personnel was made only to protect company’s existing asset for smooth running of its business without apprehending competition from its own retired personnel and, therefore, same could be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Non-compete fee) - Assessment year 2001-02 - During relevant year, assessee-company acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid (NA)  Ammonium Nitrite (AN) belonging to another company styled as 'VBC' Ltd. - In addition to payment made for purchase of so-called Industry/Plant Manufacturing Unit, assessee entered into another 'Non Compete Agreement' with 'VBC' and its founder as a result of which assessee paid a lumpsum of Rs. 6 crores to them - Assessee filed its return wherein non-compete fee was claimed as revenue expenditure - Assessing Officer rejected assessee's claim - Tribunal, however, allowed claim raised by assessee - High Court took a view that expenditure incurred primarily and essentially related to non-competition of transferor company against assessee in same business, which constituted profit-earning apparatus of assessee - High Court thus upheld order passed by Tribunal - Whether, on facts, SLP filed against decision of High Court was to be granted - Held, yes [Para 1] [In favour of revenue]IT: Where High Court upheld Tribunal's order holding that non-compete fee paid by assessee to founder of transferor company constituted business expenditure, SLP filed against said decision of High Court was to be granted

Section  40(a)(ia),  read with section  194C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Business disallowance  -  Interest, etc., paid to a resident without deduction of tax at source  (Training expenses) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company, a dealer for Mahindra cars, incurred training expenses relating to sales and workshop staff - It submitted ledger accounts and explained that payments of Rs. 2.45 lakhs to Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd. were reimbursements for training without any separate contract, contending no TDS obligation under section 194C - AO disallowed Rs. 0.74 lakhs under section 40(a)(ia), being 30% of Rs. 2.45 lakhs, for non-deduction of tax at source on said training expense reimbursements - Whether since expenses incurred related to training of sales and workshop staff of assessee-company was a part and parcel of said business itself, disallowance under section 40(a)(ia) was not justified - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1997-98 to 2000-01 - Assessee-company had purchased shipping agency business from a vendor/seller 
through certain agreement - It had purchased said business for 
a consideration of Rs. 43,47,000, comprising of cost of goodwill at 
Rs. 5 lakhs and non-competition covenant fees of Rs. 38,47,000 - Assessee claimed that it had paid non-competition covenant fees to vendor for 
a period of 5 years and same was to be allowed as revenue expenditure 
in year of payment or in alternative same should be spread over 
 a period of 5 years - Lower authorities treated said expenditure as capital expenditure and, accordingly, disallowed assessee’s claim - Whether since assessee had made payment of non-competition fees on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down itself in a new acquired business of shipping and benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability, and was for a limited period of 5 years; and that too only in Indian territory, in such circumstances, payment of non-competition fees was allowable as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes - Whether further since assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, said expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and corresponding expenditure was to be allowed in every year - Held, yes

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of [Training expenses] - Assessment year 2000-01 - Assessee-firm debited a sum to its profit and loss account on account of indirect payroll overheads payable to 'EPS', a Dutch entity, on which no tax had been deducted - It had been claimed as expenditure on ground that amount was not chargeable to tax in India because same was in nature of reimbursement of cost, therefore, no tax was to be deducted at source under section 195 - Assessing Officer, however, disallowed expenditure for want of supporting evidence - Whether since assessee had neither produced any agreement between assessee and 'EBS', as to what kind of training and service had been provided to employees of assessee, nor provided details of employees or technicians to whom training was given and even failed to prove that it pertained to employees whose salaries had been debited in profit and loss account by assessee, disallowance was justified - Held, yes [Para 19] [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of [Extension of business, expense for] - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-company claimed deduction of certain expenditure incurred on training given to technical and non-technical persons - Assessing Officer held that expenditure had resulted in enduring benefit to assessee and allowed only one-sixth of expenditure amortizing same over period of six years - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) disallowed entire expenditure holding that it related to training given before commencement of business of manufacturing which started from 17-6-1997 - On second appeal, Tribunal allowed training expenses holding that expenditure was essentially for purpose of carrying on existing business, for which commercial operations had started in 1996-97, and new manufacturing unit was an extension of existing business - Whether on facts, Tribunal rightly allowed assessee's claim for deduction of training expenses - Held, yes [Paras 3 and 5] [In favour of assessee]IT : Training expense on new manufacturing unit which was extension of existing business were allowable as revenue expenditure

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Non-compete fee - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether amount paid for non-compete fees is capital outlay and same cannot be allowed as revenue expenditure under section 37(1) - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since amount is not in nature of revenue expenditure, a part of it cannot be considered as deferred revenue expenditure so as to allow over period of non-compete agreement - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

VI. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company paid certain amount of non-compete fee to 'H' Ltd. and claimed same as business expenses - However, Assessing Officer disallowed same holding it as capital expenditure - Whether following decision in case of Tecumseh India (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT [2010] 12 7 ITD 1 (Delhi) (SB), disallowance was to be confirmed - Held, yes [In favour of revenue]

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2000-01 - Whether where non-compete fee paid by assessee gives enduring benefit to assessee in its business, payment of such fee falls within capital field which is not an allowable expenditure - Held, yes

I. Section 37(1), read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee enjoyed income from export of spare parts and also commission from Indian and Foreign authorities - He claimed deduction of commission paid to 'GFC' which had helped assessee in getting better price - Commission was paid to ‘GFC’ according to memorandum of understanding between assessee and 'GFC' - Tribunal found that assessee received repeated orders for detergent on which he earned commission but commission was not paid to 'GFC' in respect of every contract and that both assessee and 'GFC' were free to compete with each other - Tribunal thus held expenditure related to ward off competition in individual transaction and leaving competitor surviving in field and, therefore, it was revenue expenditure - Whether finding recorded by Tribunal was purely of fact and, therefore, no referable question of law arose from its order - Held, yes

The assessee-company, engaged in the business of manufacture of medicines and Lacto Calamine, purchased the brand name ‘Lacto Calamine’ from a company ‘D’ for Rs. 85 lakhs under an agreement. Subsequently, it paid another Rs. 40 lakhs to said company under a non-compete agreement for restraining it from competing directly or indirectly in the business activities carried on by the assessee. The payment so made for the purchase of brand name was accounted for by the assessee as an item of capital expenditure but the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs paid as non-compete fee was claimed as a deduction being revenue in nature under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer, however, rejected the assessee’s said claim by holding that non-compete fee paid by it to ‘D’ was a capital expenditure inasmuch as by making said payment the assessee had acquired an advantage of an enduring nature by way of freedom from competition that would have been induced by ‘D’. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On second appeal :

The assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business, under an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that the assessee would pay to the vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages as also the value of assets over the liabilities taken over. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee-firm paid certain amount to the vendors under the said agreement and claimed deduction of the same as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground of the payment being a capital expenditure. On appeals, both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of manufacturing of terry towels and other textile materials. In its board meeting the assessee had resolved that in the textile industry, there was stiff competition in terry toweling because of emergence of cheaper material from other countries. It was also noticed by the board of directors that a UK-based company was doing digital transfer image printing on the towels exported by the assessee. The board noticed that this was a good opportunity and resolved to take the assistance of a UK-based company in further developing markets for the towels and its printing.

Therefore, it was resolved that one ‘NK’, who was working with the company should be sent for training in computer related study in printing. The board resolved that the company would bear all his travelling, maintenance and training expenses.

The assessee claimed deduction of a sum spent towards expenses of boarding and lodging and studying abroad of ‘NK’ under the head ‘Staff training expenses’ and another sum towards monthly salary paid to ‘NK’. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim for deduction. According to the Assessing Officer, the business of the assessee was manufacturing and export and trading of towels and textiles and ‘NK’ was sent for training and studies in computer related studies in printing at Rochester Institute of Technology, U.S.A. According to the Assessing Officer, there was no connection between the business of the assessee and the training of ‘NK’, as those expenses related to the computer science. It was unconnected with the business of the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the agreement with ‘NK’ by the assessee was a device to give a colour of commercial expediency to claim as expenses, the personal expenses of 99 per cent of shareholder of the assessee. The Assessing Officer had also observed that the details regarding course to be pursued by ‘NK’ had not been furnished and, therefore, it was not possible to ascertain relationship between expenditure and business of the assessee. Since the expenditure was not wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee, the same was disallowed by the Assessing Officer. The action of the Assessing Officer was confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal :

The assessee-company was carrying on the business of arranging exhibition of advertisement and film shorts in the licensed public cinema theatres in the four southern States of Madras, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Mysore. B, another company, was also carrying on the business of exhibition of film shorts on behalf of X & Y in the aforesaid States. The assessee-company felt that it would be commercially profitable to it, if it could eliminate B from the business. The assessee-company, therefore, entered into an agreement with B whereby the latter not only agreed to part with its business of exhibition of film shorts but also agreed not to compete with the assessee-company in the business for a period of nine years for a consideration of Rs. 1,50,000. The assessee paid the said sum as per the terms of the agreement and claimed the same as a business expenditure. The ITO held that payment was made by the assessee-company for obtaining the right to exhibit advertisement and film shorts and not for the purpose of purchasing any stock-in-trade or raw material and, therefore, the expenditure was of a capital nature. The ITO accordingly disallowed the claim. The AAC upheld the ITO's order. The Tribunal held that the expenditure was not incurred to carry on the business of the exhibiting of film shorts but was incurred to acquire an asset or a right of a permanent character for a period of nine years and, therefore, it could not be regarded as a revenue expenditure.

During the year under consideration, a sum of Rs. 66,13,440 was spent by the assessee on training of its employees and the same was claimed as revenue expenditure deductible under section 37(1) on the ground that it was incurred in order to increase the efficiency of the employees in the day-to-day working. According to the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals), the benefit of the said expenditure incurred on employees' training, however, accrued to the assessee at least over a period of two years and, therefore, relying on the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802/ 91 Taxman 340, the expenses incurred by the assessee were disallowed by them to the extent of 50 per cent.

On second appeal :

The assessee-AOP was carrying on business of holding race meetings on a commercial basis. The assessee did not own any horses and therefore, did not employ jockeys. Because it was of the opinion that there was a risk of the jockeys becoming unavailable and that such unavailability would seriously affect its business which might result in its closing down the business, the assessee in order to remedy that defect established a school for the training of Indian boys as jockeys so that after their training they might be available for purposes of race meetings held under its auspices. The assessee claimed deduction of expenditure incurred on the running of the school. The ITO disallowed the deduction. On appeal, the AAC as well as the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO. On reference, the High Court allowed the deduction.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee entered into agreements with two foreign companies for obtaining technical knowledge and information, training of Indian employees abroad and for use of trade name. In one case, the assessee was to establish a factory for the manufacture of trucks and other automotive products. For this, the payment was to be a percentage of net sales prices and net profits of the assessee's particular products. In the other case the foreign company's assistance was sought to start the operation of assessee-company's steel foundry for bringing it into effective commission. In the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee had paid towards fees Rs. 29,59,608 as share of profits to one company and Rs. 2,99,158 as lump sum fees to the other company. The assessee also incurred Rs. 1,69,925 as expenses on training its employees abroad by the foreign companies. All the three items were claimed as revenue expenditure but the ITO treated them as capital expenditure. On appeal, the AAC accepted the assessee's claim and allowed the appeal. On Department's appeal, the Tribunal considered the terms of the two agreements and found that, under one agreement, the assessee only got technical assistance and knowledge in regard to truck manufacture and the right to use its trade name for a specific period. It was thus really a case of fees being paid for user of technical know-how and trade name. Under the other agreement, it was the right to trade for purposes of carrying on its business upon the technical knowledge of the foreign company in regard to foundry business. In both the cases, the Tribunal opined that these items of expenditure had not resulted in acquisition or bringing into existence an asset or capital of enduring nature. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the payments were deafly revenue expenditure. Similarly, the expenditure on training was for running the business more efficiently so as to earn higher profits and was revenue in nature.

On reference :

The assessee-company was in the business of serving of ready to serve food and beverages (tea and coffee) to the hotels and clubs. It appointed 'TK', i.e., son of one of the directors, as a management trainee. Subsequently, 'TK' was sent abroad for training and education. The assessee had entered into an agreement with 'TK', wherein it was made mandatory for the sponsored employee that after training and returning to India, he would serve the assessee for a minimum period of three years. The assessee claimed expenditure incurred on education and training of 'TK' abroad as a revenue expenditure allowable under section 37(1). The Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's claim.

(4) Special knowledge, or technical knowledge, or a patent, or a trade mark, is an asset and if it is acquired by payment for use and exploitation for a limited period, and what is acquired is not an asset or advantage of an enduring nature and at the end of the agreed period that advantage or asset reverts back intact to the giver of that special knowledge or the owner of the patents or trade marks, it would be expenditure of revenue nature. (5) If it is intrinsically a capital asset, it is immaterial whether the price for it is paid once and for all, or periodically, or whether it is paid out of capital or income, or linked up with net sales, the outgoing, in such a case, would be of the nature of capital expenditure.

(6) If the amount paid for the acquisition of an asset of an enduring nature is settled and the mere fact that the amount so settled is chalked out into various small amounts or periodic instalments, the capital nature of expenditure would not cease to be so or alter into the nature of a revenue expenditure.

(7) A lump sum amount for liquidating recurring claims would not cease to be revenue expenditure or get converted into capital expenditure merely because its payment is spread over a number of years. It is the intention and object with which the asset is acquired, that determines the nature of the expenditure incurred over it, and not the method or the manner in which the payment is made, or the source of such payment.

(8) If the expenditure is recurring and is incurred during the course of business or manufacture, it would be revenue expenditure.

(9) An asset or advantage of an enduring nature does not mean that it should last for ever. If the capital asset is, in its nature, a short-lived one, the expenditure incurred over it does not, for that reason, cease to be a capital expenditure.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]

Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. • The assessee company used to import, market and sell electronic office products and equipment in India. At the relevant time, it was incorporated as a joint venture of 'S' Corporation, Japan, and L&T.

• During the year under consideration, the assessee paid Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting-up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up or undertaking any business in India, of selling, marketing and trade of electronic office products for seven years. This amount was treated as deferred revenue expenditure in the assessee's books of account and written off over corresponding period of seven years. However, in the return filed, assessee claimed entire sum as revenue deduction.

• The assessee claimed that the amount paid facilitated its business and did not enhance or alter the fixed capital and ought to be treated as revenue expenditure.

• The Assessing Officer, however, disallowed the deduction on account of non-compete fee holding that it conferred a capital advantage of enduring value.

• The appellate authorities upheld the order of Assessing Officer. They also rejected the alternative claim of depreciation in respect of non-compete fee paid by the assessee.

Assessee's contentions

• Assessee's contention was that non-compete fee did not create any capital asset and that expenditure merely facilitated the efficiency, profitability and conduct of the assessee's business; it was, therefore, deductible under section 37(1).

• Alternatively, assessee contended that once the Tribunal concluded that the assessee had acquired an advantage in the capital field, denial of depreciation under section 32(1) amounted to inconsistent approach and clear error of law.

Revenue's contentions

• According to revenue, payment of non-compete fee did not merely facilitate conduct of business but in fact ensured that the assessee's market position and customer base was not threatened by competition from its erstwhile partner. This undoubtedly amounted to capital expenditure and had to be treated as such.

• It was argued next that the question of permissibility of depreciation did not arise at all in this case because the business or commercial rights of similar nature referred to in section 32(1)(ii) could not be said to arise overnight on account of payment of non-competing fee.

Issue involved

Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in holding that non-compete fee was not allowable revenue deduction.

Without prejudice, whether the Tribunal erred in denying depreciation on the non-compete fee paid, consistent with the finding that the same represented expenditure of capital nature.

The assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading of Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate. The assessee had acquired an industry/plant manufacturing Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate belonging to another company ‘V’ for a total consideration of Rs. 29 crores. The industry/plant so purchased was to include entire business undertaking situated at Ponada including movable and immovable properties and all other tangible and intangible assets relating to the business of manufacturing of aforesaid chemicals. The assessee had also entered into another non-compete agreement with ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ and paid a lump sum amount of Rs. 6 crores to them. The said agreement provided forrestriction on ‘V’ and ‘M’ to engage in manufacturing, trading or dealing in any manner with Nitric Acid and Ammonium Nitrate directly or indirectly for a period of 5 years for a cash consideration of Rs. 6 crores to be paid upfront. In the books of account, the assessee wrote off one-fifth of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores because the period during which agreement was to remain in force was 5 years but in the computation of income furnished along with return, the assessee claimed whole of the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, inter alia, held that the expenditure was not incurred for improving the profitability, as there was no existing business and the assessee had acquired the business of chemicals for the first time; and warding-off of competition for five years would result in enduring benefit to the company and disallowed the expenditure of Rs. 6 crores claimed as revenue expenditure and treated it as capital expenditure. The Assessing Officer also disallowed the alternative claim made by the assessee that if the expenditure in question was not considered as revenue expenditure, then the assessee by having entered into non-compete agreement as per which ‘V’ and its founder ‘M’ were not to carry on either manufacturing or trading business in the two chemicals for a period of five years, the assessee had acquired commercial/business rights for a period of 5 years to carry on manufacturing and trading activities in both the chemicals undisturbed and freely for a period of five years, which were of intangible nature entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the assessee might be allowed depreciation. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee had not acquired any specific intellectual right by making payment of Rs. 6 crores, which was eligible for depreciation under section 32.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. He held that no doubt the assessee earlier was doing only some trading business in the chemicals but it was not much; another group concern ‘D’ was manufacturing and selling the two chemicals in western India; by making a payment of Rs. 6 crores to ‘V’ the advantage had accrued to the assessee and that too of enduring nature and, accordingly, the expenditure was capital in nature and; the impugned expenditure could not be considered as deferred revenue expenditure and, accordingly, could not be allowed proportionately in five years as contended by the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) further held that the non-compete fees of Rs. 6 crores paid by the assessee to ‘V’ did not bring in any asset as mentioned in section 32(1)(ii) so as to qualify for depreciation.

On second appeal :

The assessee purchased one division of 'N' Chemicals which was transferred to the assessee by way of slump sales. The assessee treated the same as capital expenditure in the books of account and claimed depreciation on said amount. For the purpose of computing total income under the Act, the assessee treated Rs. 6.80 crores as non-compete fee on the basis of the value of the intangibles determined by the valuers.

The Assessing Officer treated the said amount as capital expenditure by holding that the amount claimed as fee for non-compete was nothing but goodwill of the business.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, took a view that by entering into a restrictive covenant the assessee had warded off a potential competition from the transferor. He thus held that amount paid as non-compete fee was to be regarded as revenue expenditure.

On revenue's appeal:

During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

The assessee had claimed certain amount as expenses incurred under the head 'education and training expenses'. These expenses had been incurred by the assessee on higher education of one 'D', an employee of the company, who happened to be the son of a director, for undertaking an MBA course in the UK.

The assessee explained that 'D' was working with the assessee. Since he was a brilliant student and the company was in need of manager (marketing) who could study the mood of the investment market and the prospectus and take decision with respect to it, the Board of Directors in the meeting took a decision to send 'D' for pursuing the course of MBA from UK and to incur the expenditure. It was further stated that 'D' signed a bond that he would serve the assessee company at least for 5 years and in the breach of bond he would return the money spent.

The Assessing Officer, however, refused to accept the assessee's contentions and rejected the deduction under section 37.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the disallowance in the appellate proceedings.

On appeal to the High Court:

■

The assessee was a company which was engaged in the business of importing, marketing and selling electronic office products and equipments in India. It was incorporated as a joint venture of Sharp Corporation, Japan and Larsen and Toubro Limited (L&T). During the assessment year 2001-02, assessee paid a sum of Rs. 3 crores to L&T as consideration for the latter not setting up or undertaking or assisting in the setting up of or undertaking any business in India of selling, marketing and trading in electronic office products for 7 years. The said amount of Rs. 3 crores was claimed as a deductible revenue expenditure in the return of income filed by the assessee as non-compete fee paid to L&T.

■

The Assessing Officer held that by making payment of Rs. 3 crores to L&T, assessee could ward off competition in business. The object of making such payment to L&T was to derive an advantage by eliminating competition for a period of 7 years. According to the Assessing Officer, such an expenditure had brought into existence an advantage of enduring nature and hence treated the payment of Rs. 3 crores as capital expenditure. Therefore, the said amount was added to the income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that such expenditure was not in the nature of revenue expenditure. In so far the alternative ground was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that there was no apparent justification for the assessee to enter into a non-compete agreement with L&T for a sum of Rs. 3 crores since L&T was not a competitor of the assessee and that the business interest of the assessee would not have suffered for want of such an agreement. Since the true purport of the expenditure remained unproved, the same was disallowed being regarded as non-revenue expenditure, not for the purpose of business of the assessee. Accordingly, the assessee was held to be not entitled to depreciation. Consequently, appeal of the assessee was dismissed by Commissioner (Appeals).

■

On appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee by paying a non-compete fee of Rs. 3 crores to L&T had eliminated competition for a period of 7 years which is a duration long enough to establish its reputation and a reasonable market share would have been acquired by the assessee. Payment made by the assessee to L&T was not to increase its profitability. Thus, the non-compete fee could not be treated as revenue expenditure but it was in the nature of a capital expenditure. Further, the Tribunal held that the non-compete fee would not create intangible asset eligible for depreciation under the provisions of section 32(1)(ii). Thus, depreciation was not allowable on the expenditure made by the assessee as non-compete fee. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal of the assessee as being devoid of any merit. The High Court opined that expenditure incurred by the assessee by way of non-compete fee paid to L&T could not be claimed as a revenue expenditure as it was clearly a capital expenditure. Despite holding the expenditure to be capital in nature, the High Court was of the further view that the non-compete right of the kind acquired by the assessee against L&T for 7 years did not result in depreciable intangible asset. It was held that the right acquired by the assessee by payment of non-compete fee was a right in personam only against L&T for a period of 7 years. It was not a right in rem.

■

Adverting to the expression 'similar business or commercial rights' appearing in section 32(1)(ii), the High Court opined that it has to necessarily result in an intangible asset against the entire world to qualify for depreciation under the said provision. The High Court therefore dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee was carrying on business as ferry contractors plying launches across the river. The right to ferry was auctioned for a year and the petitioners were the highest bidders. The assessee paid certain amount to sixteen individuals who were prospective bidders at the auction in order to prevent them from competing with the petitioners at the auction. In their return for the assessment year 1964-65, the assessee claimed said amount as a deduction on the ground that the amount was paid for shutting out the other bidders. The ITO held that this deduction was not admissible. This view was confirmed by the AAC on appeal.

On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the said sum could be deducted in computing the assessee's income as it was a revenue expenditure.

On reference :

The assessee-milk co-operative society, paid compensation to another milk co-operative society for acquiring their assets, goodwill as well as to avoid competition in trade. The Tribunal held the expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the same.

On reference :

The assessee claimed deduction for a sum of Rs. 15.44 lakh towards training expenses of its employees. The training was, in fact, imparted to the employees of the assessee by two trainers who were arranged by the assessee's holding company.

The Assessing Officer invoking the provisions of section 40(a)(ia), made the disallowance for the failure of the assessee to deduct tax at source from such payment.

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company, engaged in manufacturing and trading of textile chemicals, acquired the proprietary businesses of its two sister concerns engaged in same business as going concerns for certain consideration. In addition thereto, the assessee under- took to pay Rs. 3.5 lakh and Rs. 2 lakh per month to the two concerns, respectively, for a period of 15 years in consideration of the non-compete obligation undertaken by the said concerns. In the assessment, the assessee claimed that the said payment made to dissuade the said proprietary concerns from continuing independent business, which would be detrimental to it, was to be allowed as the revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim, holding that the expenditure was clearly capital in nature, as the same was incurred by the assessee to ward off competition over a long period of time. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee’s said claim.

On revenue’s appeal :

During the relevant assessment year, the assessee purchased goodwill along with the running business from a firm for Rs. 10 lakhs. The assessee further paid a sum of Rs. 5 lakhs as non-compete charges to one of the partners of said firm for not carrying on same line of business and other related fields for 5 years. In the computation of income, the assessee claimed the expenditure of Rs. 5 lakhs as revenue expenditure. However, the Assessing Officer treated the said expenditure as capital expenditure and disallowed the assessee's claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee-company paid its ex-directors and ex-works manager, at Rs. 50,000 each. The Assessing Officer found that the assessee-company entered into an agreement with them by which their services were retained in order to avoid competition as they had access to the ink formula which was the trade secret of the assessee-company alone. The Assessing Officer held that in lieu of the payments, the assessee-company got a benefit of an enduring nature in the form of eliminating competition from these persons in case they did similar business. He further held that the payment was made by way of compensation for loss of office. He, therefore, disallowed same as capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessees were person who used to try for and frequently obtain contracts from a large tea-growing company for the cartage of their tea. The contracts were made at a flat rate which varied from year to year. There was rival contractor ‘X’ who was regarded as likely to be a competitor for the contract and in order to induce him not to compete, the assessees paid him down a sum. The result was that as ‘X’ did not compete, the assessees had the whole field to themselves; they got the whole contract and were able by screwing up the figures in former years to make more profits than they would have done in those former years. On reference :

held.text:
In essence, the agreements in question were for acquiring technical knowledge regarding methods of production and in addition, in the case of one company, payment was for use of trade name. Acquiring technical know-how and technical advice cannot in these days of technological and scientific development and consequent change in production technique, be treated as a capital asset. Mere length of period of agreement is not of much consequence if the nature of advice made available is such that it cannot be called a capital asset. Technical know-how made available by a party to such an agreement does not stand on the same footing as rights under a registered patent.

The expenditure incurred on training of employees was with a view to give training to persons so as to achieve maximum and efficient production. This was undoubtedly closely related to the profit earning process.

The expenditure in question was, therefore, held to be of a revenue nature deductible in computing taxable income.

It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

The amount in question was paid only to those members whose trucks were not booked. But for this payment, they would have otherwise competed in the business with the assessee. The object of the payment was to eliminate those competitors and to carry on the business unfettered by competition. The assessee made the payment to acquire this right of these persons. This led to enhance the value of its existing assets to make them more profit-yielding. The expense, therefore, could not be a revenue expense but was of a capital nature. The Tribunal was therefore right, in holding that amount so paid was not a permissible deduction for the purpose of income-tax.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

The assessee was saddled with the duty to establish that the expended amount fell in the revenue field. Admittedly the payment was for the purpose of business of the assessee. The payment was expended to ward off the competition in the field of the assessee’s business. Admittedly this restriction to compete or, in other words, the non-compete fee was paid by the assessee to retrain payee from the competitive business for a definite period of five years. The non-compete fee payment made by the assessee to ‘S’ gave enduring benefit to the assessee in its business. Thus, the payment of non-compete fee fell within the capital field which was not an allowable expenditure. [Para 10]

In view of ratio laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Coal Shipments (P.) Ltd. [1971] 82 ITR 902 and after examining the facts of the instant case, it was more than evident that the assessee wanted to outbid his competitor and wanted that those two partners should not enter into the same business for the period of 15 years giving a sole monopoly in manufacturing of soap in the name and style as 'NS'. Therefore, that kind of expenditure was only for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and hence that kind of expenditure incurred by the assessee could be treated to be a capital expenditure and not a revenue expenditure. Section 37 only contemplates that the expenditure which is incurred exclusively for the business shall be allowed for computing the income chargeable under the head of 'Profit and gains'. Therefore, that expenditure incurred by the assessee could be taken to be a revenue expenditure, but it was for the purpose of outbidding the competitor and it should be treated a capital expenditure. In that view of the matter, the view taken by the Tribunal appeared to be justified.

Training in modern business management would definitely be beneficial to the carrying on of any business. The knowledge that the partner was gaining was such that it would definitely benefit the business carried on by the assessee-firm and so, the expenditure in acquiring that knowledge had a direct nexus with the business carried on by the firm, as would be evident from the increase in sales in the succeeding year. In order to be capital expenditure, that expenditure should not only bring into existence a benefit of enduring advantage or benefit but the same should also be in the capital field.
