Introduction

Advertisement, Marketing & Promotional (AMP) expenditure is an expenditure incurred by the company in order to increase the sales of the company by creating awareness of the company and its products/services among the numerous customers. AMP expenditure covers various components as mentioned below :—

(1)

Sales Expenditure like discounts, salesman commissions etc.

(2)

Advertisement expenditure like banners, brand ambassador expenses etc.

However, from transfer pricing perspective where AMP expenditure is incurred by associated enterprise of a foreign company, such AMP expenditure has been a matter of long time litigation as Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) considers AMP as an international transaction by invoking Section 92CA(2A) of the Income Tax Act,1961 and make adjustment on account of AMP expenditure in the hands of AE.

Cause of Litigation

AMP expenditure by AE in order to increase sales is recharacterized by TPO as amount incurred by India AE toward creation of marketing intangible (brand) of foreign company in India i.e, Indian entity has rendered services of brand creation to foreign company , therefore such Indian company shall be compensated from foreign company on Cost plus mark-up basis.

Computation of Adjustment by TPO

There are two approaches followed by TPO in order to compute adjustment amount on account of AMP expenditure :-

(1) Substantive Approach

Under substantive approach, TPO simply computes total amount of AMP expenditure and add mark-up upon that , resultant figure is the amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian AE.

(2) Protective Approach

Under protective approach, TPO applies Bright Line Test (BLT) method. Under BLT method, Indian companies belong to same industry of AE are identified and excess AMP expenditure incurred by AE is computed [ (AMP of AE/Sales of AE) – (Avg AMP of Indian comparable/Sales of Comparable). Such excess AMP expenditure along with mark-up is the adjustment amount in the hands of AE.

Adjustment amount as per substantive approach is always more in comparison to adjustment amount as per protective approach.

Contention of Taxpayer against AMP adjustment

(1)

There is no such agreement between Indian AE and foreign entity to create brand and incur AMP expenditure for foreign entity, therefore, in absence of any agreement , such transaction shall not be considered as an international transaction.

(2)

Bright Line Test method adopted by TPO is neither a permissible method under Indian Tax Laws nor prescribed under section 92C of the Income Tax Act,1961 read with Rule 10B of the Income Tax Rule, 1962.

(3)

Economic owner of such brand is AE.

(4)

AMP expenditure incurred to increase sales and therefore it is a domestic transaction and TPO has no jurisdiction over non international transaction

(5)

While computing AMP adjustment, Selling expenditure and amount reimburse from foreign AE shall be reduced from the amount of AMP expenditure incurred.

Landmark Judicial Judgements

(1) Sony Mobile Communications (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 312 (Delhi - Trib.)

The Hon'ble ITAT New Delhi Bench, I-2 in the aforementioned case held that assessee was a subsidiary of Sony Ericsson incorporated under the laws of Sweden . It was primarily engaged in business of importing, buying, selling and distribution of wide range of mobile phones in India and providing related post sale support services. During relevant year, assessee incurred huge cost on Advertisement Marketing and Sales Promotion of its mobile phones, TPO opined that expenditure on AMP incurred by assessee was exclusively to promote brand name 'Sony Ericssion' which was owned by AE, TPO thus took a view that expenditure incurred by assessee company was for advantage of its AE and it should have been suitably compensated by AE. He applied bright line test and made certain addition to assessee's ALP. It was undisputed that Sony Ericssion being a new entrant in mobile segment in year under consideration, assessee had to incur huge advertisement expenses to remind general public of its existence in domestic market. Thus, it could be concluded that AMP expenditure was incurred mainly for purpose of increase in sales of mobile phones in India and not for brand building of AE. Moreover, net profit margin declared by assessee was much higher than comparables and, looking from that angle also, there was no merit in transfer pricing adjustment.

(2) Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT (ITA 110/2014)

Amongst many controversial issues involving transfer pricing, the adjustment on account of marketing intangibles is certainly one of the most litigated and controversial, with enormous stakes involved at either side. As a brief recap, in January 2013 the Special Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("SB"), in the case of LG India Electronics (P)Ltd.1 ("LG SB Ruling") had adjudicated that the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ("AMP") expenditure incurred by the Indian AE is an international transaction, to the extent such AMP expense, as a percentage of turnover, exceeds that of the comparable companies (The concept of pegging AMP to industry standard is typically referred to as 'Bright Line Test'or "BLT"). While so concluding, the SB observed that the incurring of non-routine or excess AMP by the Indian taxpayer is in the nature of providing brand building service to the brand owners i.e. AE and consequently up-held adjustment for such excess AMP expenditure to the Indian taxpayer along with an arm's length mark-up. The LG SB ruling, was hailed as one of the most significant wins of the revenue in a transfer pricing matter, and the principles of the ruling were followed in a plethora of cases involving marketing intangibles resulting in billions of dollars of transfer pricing adjustments. Apparently, the issue, per se, travelled to the High Court against the decision of the division benches who had merely applied the ratio of the ruling of the Special Bench, being at the detriment of the appellant taxpayers.

Recently, the Delhi High Court ("Delhi HC" or "HC") in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communication Private Limited2, and several other connected matters3, adjudicated on the issue of marketing intangibles and upheld the transfer pricing officer's jurisdiction to AMP expenditure, as an international transaction. Further, ruling in favour of the taxpayer, the High Court held that the legal principles, commercial logic and methodology relied and accepted by the tribunal in LG SB Ruling (Supra) as erroneous and unacceptable. The 142 page HC ruling is a pleasure to read, as it paves its way into intricate details of various aspects of AMP adjustments and discusses the principles of brand building versus AMP, economic ownership, aggregated versus segregated approach of benchmarking, OECD guidelines, Indian law and the methodologies adopted for determination of ALP in relation to marketing intangibles. Enumerated below are some of the key findings of the Delhi HC.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the Revenue

TPO can adjudicate on international transactions which are not reported in Form 3CEB

Pursuant to retrospective amendment4 by the Finance Act, 2012, the TPO is empowered to adjudicate on the transactions which have not been reported by the taxpayer in the Form 3CEB. No specific reference by the Assessing Officer (AO) is required for the same.

AMP expense constitute an international transaction

The HC rejected the contention of the taxpayer that AMP is not an international transaction and is outside the scope of transfer pricing provisions. In this regard, the HC observed that dispute pertains to adequacy of the compensation received by the Indian taxpayer for incurring and performing marketing and 'non-routine' AMP expense in India. By virtue of application of the TP provisions, the TPO seeks to determine an arm's length compensation for the marketing and distribution functions performed by the taxpayer towards related parties. In summary, the AMP expense is an international transaction which is covered under the realms of transfer pricing.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the taxpayers

Aggregation of transactions and application of Transactional Net Margin Method

The HC held that the usage of words "an international transaction" in section 92(1) should not be read restrictively rather its interpretation should be gathered from other section and the Rules, whereby it would be amply clear that the legislative intent was to allow clubbing of closely linked transactions, which includes continuous transactions. However, close linkage of transactions is a pre-condition for aggregation. On the same logic, the HC held that distribution and marketing are intertwined and may be examined as bundled/inter-connected transactions. The HC also observed that in case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no prohibition in applying Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) on an entity wide basis, which follows that AMP function can be looked as closely linked to and a part of overall marketing and distribution activity, whereof it can be aggregated under the realms of TNMM.

30.5.2-3 "Ownership of assets" - Depreciation shall be allowed only on the assets owned by the assessee, partly or wholly. The following points are noteworthy:

Ownership does not mean legal ownership.

If the assessee has possession of immovable property purchased by him but sale the sale deed is not registered in the assessee's name, the assessee can be considered owner under section 32.

In a landmark judgment in Mysore Minerals Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 106 Taxman 166 (SC), the Supreme Court held that to claim de-preciation, the assessee doesn't need to be the registered owner of the assets. Exclusive possession rights, to exclude others from enjoyment of assets, right to retain possession and defend the same are some of the characteristics of ownership which would entitle the assessee to depreciation under section 32 (so long as it was used for carrying on business or profession).

In Tata Electric Companies (AOP) v. Jt. CIT [ITA No. 2330/Mum./2001] (17-10-2006) (unreported), the Tribunal consid­ered the issue of 'ownership' of asset for claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Act in the light of various Apex Court decisions on the subject and beautifully extracted the law in this regard at para 21 of the Order : "... the substantial de facto ownership of an asset is to be looked into, rather than examining the religious de jure owner­ship of the asset.......... In a case where the transfer of property was contemplated by an agreement and thereafter, the physical delivery of the property was handed over and the property was used for the business of the assessee and thereafter, even if delayed, the transaction was concluded by executing the rele­vant conveyance and documents, then in such circumstances, the ownership of the asset must be considered as having been trans­ferred from the date of actual delivery of the asset. ..... in such circumstances, where the contract has been lawfully executed, ....the validity of the registered documents go back to the date of de facto transfer of ownership of the asset. This liberal principle has been upheld by the Supreme Court ...".

Sub-stantial de facto ownership is sufficient. De jure ownership (or legal ownership) is not required. This definition of ownership perfectly accords with the accounting definition of asset which stresses on 'Control' rather than legal ownership.

Thus, depreciation is available to the lessee in respect of assets acquired under a finance lease/hire-purchase.

Training charges to customer

12.8-1 Training charges to customer will be includible if they are in connection with sale or by reason of sale. If the transaction of providing training to employees of customer is an independent transaction, it may be 'in relation to sale', but not 'in connection with sale'.

Training charges are not includible in assessable value - CCE v. Real Time Systems (2009) 237 ELT 289 (CESTAT).

Training or training aids for use of missiles is post-sales activity and is not includible in assessable value - Brahmos Aerospace P Ltd. v. CCE (2014) 307 ELT 795 (CESTAT).

CCE - 1996 (88) ELT 181 (CEGAT), it was held that consultancy charges for training of customer's staff in relation to the product are not includible. - followed in Gallium Equipment P Ltd. v. Liquidated damages for late delivery or breach of contract payable/receivable

12.8-2 Liquidated damages may be either payable or receivable by assessee.

Liquidated damages payable - Some contracts make provision for liquidated damages where an amount is deducted if delivery is not effected in time or some other condition of contract is violated. 'Transaction Value' means the price actually paid or payable for goods. It includes any amount payable by buyer at the time of the sale or at any other time. Thus since the amount of 'liquidated damages' is not 'payable' by buyer to assessee at all, it can be argued that 'transaction value' should be calculated only after deducting the liquidated damages, i.e. it should be allowed as deduction. Counter argument can be that 'full amount' is 'payable' though actual amount paid is less on account of deduction by way of penalty. Thus, effectively, full amount is 'paid' and deduction has nothing to do with value of goods.

In United Telecom Ltd. v. CCE (2006) 204 ELT 626 (CESTAT), price was reduced by customer for late delivery of goods. It was held that such compensation paid to buyer is liquidated damages and not in nature of penalty. It will be allowable as deduction and duty paid in excess is refundable. It was held that ratio of decisions under old section 4 cannot be made applicable to new section 4 which has come into effect from 1-7-2000 - followed in CCE v. HFCL (2008) 231 ELT 307 (CESTAT).

This view has been confirmed in CCE v. Victory Electricals Ltd. (2014) 43 GST 649 = 42 taxmann.com 215 = 298 ELT 534 (CESTAT LB), where it was held that after such liquidated damages (even if termed as penalty), the transaction value is reduced. Excise duty is payable on such lower value only - followed in CCE v. HFCL (Wireless Division) (2014) 46 GST 664 = 47 taxmann.com 171 (CESTAT).

“Goodwill is that component of the total value of the undertaking which is attributable to the ability of the concern to earn profits over a course of years or in excess of normal amounts because of its reputation, location and other features : Trego v. Hunt [1896] AC 7 (HL). Goodwill of an undertaking therefore is the value of the attraction to customers arising from the name and reputation for skill, integrity, efficient business management, or efficient service.”

In CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294 (SC), it was observed as follows (p. 298) :

“Goodwill denotes the benefit arising from connection and reputation. A variety of elements goes into its making, and its composition varies in different trades and in different business in the same trade, and while one element many preponderate in one business, another may dominate in another business.

Its value may fluctuate from one moment to another depending on changes in the reputation of the business. It is affected by everything relating to the business, the personality and business rectitude of the owners, the nature and character of the business, its name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio-economic ecology, introduction to old customers and agreed absence of competition. There can be no account in value of the factors producing it”.

In CED v. Kanta Devi Taneja [1981] 132 ITR 437(Gau.) it was held as follows:

“Broadly speaking, it is the magnetic quality of a particular trade or business which attracts customers to it as a matter of course. This quality springs from and is developed by various contributing factors that earn a reputation for honest dealing, quality and standard. Goodwill is founded on the belief and faith of the customer. It is commonly built up in relation to a particular type of manufacture or production of articles identified by a trademark which becomes widely known to the public and by which the customers take it for granted that it represents what they wish for. No trademark gains reputation overnight. Naturally, the standing of the business is necessarily one of the contributing factors. The personalities who are engaged in the business, the location in which it is carried on and the like are other features which go into the goodwill. Where a business involves no distinguishable features and deals in standard articles manufactured by someone else which one can get from anywhere, not merely from a particular dealer, there is hardly any possibility of there being a goodwill attached to such business”.

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

In Permanent Edition of Words and Phrases, it is mentioned that ◆ A ‘trade-mark’ symbolizes business goodwill.

◆ A ‘trade-mark’ and ‘goodwill’ are similar and analogous and indicate favour which community holds for a certain commodity.

From the above, it appears that it cannot be generalised that goodwill is similar to the other intangible assets. For example, if the predominant element of goodwill is location or contacts with customers then these elements not being similar to the preceding assets in the definition of block of assets, it may not be possible to claim that goodwill is covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’. On the other hand, if the predominant element of goodwill is trademark then it could be argued that goodwill is covered by the expression.

2.2-10b Non-compete payment-whether covered by the definition - Another type of payment made is ‘non-compete payment’, that is, payment to another person in consideration of his agreeing not to compete with the payer. Having regard to the nature of the payment, it is perhaps not in the nature of the acquisition of an asset which is a precondition for grant of depreciation. In any case it may increase the value of goodwill (see definition of ‘goodwill’ as explained in Srinivasa Setty’s case, reproduced above) and if goodwill itself cannot be considered as an intangible asset, the non-compete payment also cannot be considered so.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

The scope of the words "Other similar business or commercial rights" also fell for consideration before the Delhi High Court in Sharp Business System v. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 50/211 Taxman 576 (Delhi). The issue before the Court was whether non-compete fee paid to ex-JV partner under a non-compete agreement for 7 years was 'intangible asset' eligible for depreciation. The Court held that in personam rights such as non-compete fees are not depreciable intangible assets u/s 32(1)(ii). Depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) is admissible only to those intangible assets which give exclusive rights to the owner, which can be asserted against the world at large - i.e. in rem. A non-compete agreement can be asserted only in personam against the other party to the non-compete agreement. Hence, non-compete fee is not a depreciable intangible asset u/s 32(1)(ii). The Court analysed section 32(1)(ii) as under:

As would be evident from section 32(1)(ii), depreciation can be allowed in respect of intangible assets.

Par-liament has spelled out the nature of such assets by express reference to "know-how," "patents," "copyrights," "trademarks," "licenses," and "franchises."

So far as patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses and franchises are concerned, though they are intangible assets, the law recognises through various enactments that specific intellectual property rights flow from them.

Li-censes are derivative and often confer such intellectual property rights. The enjoyment of such intellectual property rights implies the exclusion of others who do not own or have a license to such rights from using them in any manner whatsoever.

Similarly, in the matter of franchises and know-how, the primary brand or intellectual process owner owns the exclusive right to produce, retail and distribute the products and the advantages flowing from such brand or intellectual process owner, but for the grant of such know-how rights or franchises.

The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the owner-ship.

In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance "in rem".

However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity.

The right can be asserted in the present instance only against ex-JV partner and in a sense, the right "in personam".

In-deed, the 7 years period spelt-out by the non-competing covenant brings the advantage within the public policy embedded in section 27 of the Contract Act, which enjoins a contract in restraint of trade would otherwise be void.

An-other way of looking at the issue is whether such rights can be treated or transferred – a proposition fully supported by the controlling object clause, i.e. intangible asset.

Every species of right spelt out expressly by the Statute—i.e., intellectual property rights and other advantages such as know-how, franchise, license, etc., and even those considered by the Courts, such as goodwill—can be said to be alienable. Such is not the case with an agreement not to compete, which is purely personal.

The words "similar business or commercial rights" necessarily have to result in an intangible asset against the entire world, which can be asserted as such to qualify for depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) of the Act.

Thus, "Other similar business or commercial rights" would not cover rights of a person's nature. The expression would cover only alienable rights in rem.

Advertisement expenses when incurred to increase sales of products are usually treated as a revenue expenditure since the memory of purchasers or customers is short. Advertisements are issued from time to time and the expenditure is incurred periodically so that the customers remain attracted and do not forget the product and its qualities. The advertisements published/displayed may not be of relevance or significance after lapse of time in a highly competitive market, wherein the products of different companies compete and are available in abundance. Advertisements and sales promotion are conducted to increase sale and their impact is limited and felt for a short duration. No permanent character or advantage is achieved and is palpable, unless special or specific factors are brought on record. Expenses for advertising consumer products generally are a part of the process of profit earning and not in the nature of capital outlay—CIT v. Monto Motors Ltd. [2012] 206 Taxman 43/19 taxmann.com 57 (Delhi). The expenses, in the present case, were not incurred once and for all, but were a periodical expenses which had to be incurred continuously in view of the nature of the business. It was an on-going expense. Given the factual matrix, it is difficult to hold that the expenses were incurred for setting the profit earning machinery in motion or not for earning profits.

Mere fact that assessee was permitted to use brand name 'Valvoline' of its AE, it would not automatically lead to an inference that any expense incurred towards AMP was only to enhance brand 'Valvoline' particularly when there was no international transaction between assessee and its AE—Valvoline Cummins (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2017] 84 taxmann.com 191 (Delhi).

AMP expenses incurred by assessee could not be termed as an international transaction particularly when there was nothing on record to show that assessee by incurring AMP expenses wanted to promote brand of its AE and there was no agreement for sharing AMP expenses—PCIT v. Amadeus India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 145 taxmann.com 578 (Del.); PCIT v. Amadeus India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 145 taxmann.com 311/[2023] 290 Taxman 201 (Del.).

Where assessee charged royalty from foreign entity by allowing it to use its brand name, in such a case, even though assessee acquired entire shareholding of said company subsequently, yet unless at entity level there was a complete re-organization so as to result in a complete identity of two concerns, royalty arising out of use of brand name had to be treated as an 'international transaction'—Dabur India Ltd. v. PCIT [2018] 89 taxmann.com 78/253 Taxman 129 (Delhi).

Applying 'bright line test' on the basis of certain prescribed parameters would be adding and writing words in the statute and the Rules and introducing a new concept which has not been recognised and accepted in any of the international commentaries or as per the general principles of international taxation accepted and applied universally—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

Research and development - Where assessee, engaged in business of design, development, manufacture and maintenance of aircrafts and avionics systems, incurred expenditure towards R&D for manufacture of aircrafts which were to be sold, since expenditure was incurred for purpose of business of assessee and, hence, allowed as deduction [Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. The advance of technology and the widespread use of the internet has provided a very powerful medium to companies to publicise their activities to a larger spectrum of people at a much lower cost. Websites enable companies to do what printed brochures did earlier, but in a much more efficient manner as well as in a much shorter period of time and covering a much larger set of people worldwide. Hence expenditure incurred by the assessee on developing a website was allowable as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Indian Visit.com (P.) Ltd. [2009] 176 Taxman 164 (Delhi)].

An employer can restrain an employee from using the data or trade secrets of the employer in his next employment. However, he cannot be restrained from joining other employment - Krishnan Murgai v. Superintendence Co. of India AIR 1979 Del 232.

However, in Weller International Electronics v. P V Somasundaram 2003 LLR 357 (Bom HC), it was held that employer cannot enforce secrecy clause after the employee has left the job, when no time was prescribed for the period of secrecy. Employee cannot be prevented from joining other employment. Employee has right to seek and search for better employment. Freedom of changing employment for improving service conditions is a vital and important right of an employee - Pepsi Foods Ltd. v. Bharat Coca-Cola Holdings P. Ltd. 1999 LLR 1027 = 1999 DLT 122 (Del HC) * Ambiance India P. Ltd. v. Shri Naveen Jain 2005 LLR 837 = 2005 DLT 421 (Del HC) * American Express Bank v. Ms. Priya Puri 2006 LLR 682 (Del HC).

Of course, the employee can use his knowledge and skills in next employment. In Herbert Morris Ltd. v. Saxelby (1916) 1 AC 688, it was observed, 'An employer cannot prevent an erstwhile employee from earning his living by exercise of his skill and use of his knowledge. A man's aptitudes, skills, or manual or mental ability are not his master's property, they are his own property'.

Conference expenses [Section 115WB(2)(c)]

1.20 This entry deems conference expenses as FBE. However, fees for participation by the employee in any conference shall not be regarded as DFB. Further, for the purposes of this clause, any expenditure on conveyance, tour and travel (including foreign travel), on hotel, or boarding and lodging in connection with any conference shall be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purposes of conference.

1.20-1 Exclusion -'Conference expenses' does not include any expenditure on fee for participation by the employees in any conference. Thus, the participation fee in respect of a conference organized by an outside entity, is excluded from the purview of fringe benefit tax (external conference expense). As a logical corollary, expenses in respect of conferences organized by employer internally attract fringe benefit tax (internal conference expense).

It may be noted that, on a strict reading, 'External conference expenses', may not include expenditure incurred on conveyance, tour and travel (including foreign travel) or hotel, or boarding and lodging.

1.20-2 Taxable portion - Internal conferences could be training conferences or could be for other purposes (e.g. sales, strategy, marketing, etc.). Any expenditure on 'training conferences' could be deemed to be a 'fringe benefit' under section 115WB(2)(C), since there is a 'benefit' for the employee on account of his training. However, it could be argued that expenditure on other conferences (e.g. sales, strategy, marketing, etc.) may not be covered by this clause since there is no benefit for the employee. (See para 1.17 above)

1.20-3 General Meetings - It appears that a general meeting cannot be considered as a conference.

Wholly and exclusively

The expression ‘wholly and exclusively’ does not denote necessarily [Sassoon J. David & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)]. The word ‘wholly’ refers to quantum of expenditure. The word ‘exclusively’ refers to motive, objective or purpose with which the particular expense has been incurred [Addl. CIT v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. (2004) 137 Taxman 367 (Raj.) and Ram Bahadur Thakur Ltd. v. CIT (2003) 261 ITR 390 (Ker.)]. The word "wholly" signifies that the expenditure should be completely devoted to the business. It need not be essential, necessary or compelling; it may be optional and purely voluntary. But it must be commercially expedient and should have the aim of the continuance or furtherance of the business and an eventual augmentation or stabilization of profits [Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 156 (Mad.)]

The true test of an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of trade or business is that it is incurred by the assessee as incidental to his trade for the purpose of keeping the trade going and of making it pay and not in any other capacity than that of a trader. It has to be examined whether the expense has been incurred with the sole object of furthering the trade or business interest of the assessee unalloyed or unmixed with any other consideration. If the expense is found to bear an element other than that of the trade or business interest of the assessee, the expenditure is not an allowable one [B. K. Khanna & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 113 Taxman164 (Delhi)]

(1) Suppose the assessee incurs expenditure on advertisement in a souvenir of a labour union formed by a political party. The labour union is registered under the Trade Unions Act of 1926. Is the expenditure required to be reported by the tax auditor in the third item in clause 21(a)?

Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides that every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which it is registered, and shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire and hold both movable and immovable property and to contract, and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Thus, a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is a separate and distinct legal entity and is not part of the political party which formed it. Since the Labour union has a separate and distinct legal identity, the expenditure cannot be said to be incurred in the advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party. Therefore, the expenditure is not reportable in clause 21(a).

(2) If the advertisement is published in a newspaper published by a political party, is the expenditure thereon to be reported in clause 21(a)?

It is possible to take the view that expenditure on advertisement in a political party's newspaper is not required to be reported under this clause. A newspaper is certainly not like a brochure, tract, etc. The words 'any other like publication' occurring in clause 21(a) as well as section 37(2B) should be interpreted ejusdem generis with 'brochure', 'tract', 'pamphlet' and 'souvenir' [See para 8 of ICAI's Guidance Note on section 293A of the Companies Act and the Auditor]

Section 55(2)(a) is now being amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 to provide that in respect of trade mark or brand name associated with a business, its costs of acquisition shall be deemed to be the following amounts : Substitution of fair market value as on 1-4-1981 - In case of the aforesaid assets the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 for the original cost of acquisition is not permitted. Hence, in case of self-acquired assets, since the cost of acquisition is nil and the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 is not permitted, the indexed cost of acquisition would also be nil.

Following points need to be noted :

● Hitherto, there was a view [based on the Supreme Court decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinvasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294] that the aforesaid assets are not chargeable to capital gains tax since there is no cost of acquisition. Hence, it could be argued that the amendment clearly shows that such assets were not chargeable to tax under section 45 up to assessment year 2001-02.

● Section 55(1)(b) provides that cost of improvement (COI) in relation to a capital asset being goodwill of a business or a right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing shall be taken to be nil. Section 55(1)(b) has not been amended to provide that COI of trade mark or brand name associated with a business shall also be taken to be nil. Now, in Evans Fraser & Co. Ltd. v. CIT[1982] 137 ITR 493 (Bom.), it was held that if the cost of improvement of an asset cannot be ascertained, gains arising on its transfer is not liable to tax under section 45. Hence, if the nil cost assets roped in by the amendment to the definition of cost of acquisition can have some COI which cannot be quantified, then, applying the ratio of the aforesaid decision, it could be argued that the capital gains arising on transfer of such assets is still outside the purview of tax under section 45.

7.3-1 Application of section 50 - In case of trade marks, the amendment presently made under section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition thereof will be its purchase price or nil as the case may be. It is pertinent to note that in respect of trade marks acquired on or after 1-4-1998, an assessee is entitled to depreciation under section 32(1) of the Act.

Since capital gains in respect of assets forming part of a block of assets on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act is to be computed as per the special provisions under section 50, the question may arise as to whether capital gains on transfer of trade marks would be computed in the manner provided under section 50 or whether the capital gains would have to be computed by taking cost of acquisition as per section 55(2)(a).

Section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition of trade marks will be taken as purchase price/nil ‘for the purpose of sections 48 and 49’. Section 50, however, goes further to say that ‘in case of depreciable assets sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the modifications’ prescribed in that section.

Hence, it seems that in respect of trade mark on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act, the capital gains would have to be computed as per the provisions of section 50 since the said section clearly provides that ‘the provisions under sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the following modifications’. However, as regards trade marks on which depreciation has not been allowed under the Act (which would include self-acquired trade marks and trade marks acquired prior to 1-4-1998) the capital gains would have to be computed on the basis of cost determined as per section 55(2)(a).

7.3-1a Brand names - While trade marks have been expressly referred to as an intangible asset under section 32(1) the said section does not expressly refer to ‘brand name’. However, ‘brand name’ would also qualify for depreciation as intangible assets since it would fall within the meaning of expression ‘any other business or commercial rights of similar nature’ as referred to under section 32(1). Hence, the same position as stated above in regard to trade mark would also hold good in respect of ‘brand name’.

IT : Where assessee at time of acquiring an undertaking, paid certain amount under head 'Techno Commercial Agreement' and 'Brand Licensing Agreement', amounts so paid were deductible as it was essential for assessee to make such payments on account of nature of its business and on account of procuring knowledge for setting up systems as well as other procedures

INCOME TAX : Where assessee paid non-compete fees to a company on termination of agreement, since by paying said fees, assessee acquired rights which not only gave it enduring benefit but also protected assessee's business against competition, impugned non-compete fees paid by assessee would be capital in nature, however, it would be an intangible asset on which assessee was entitled to claim depreciation

INCOME TAX : Where in view of non-compete agreement entered into by assessee with a company from which it acquired business, non-compete fee paid by assessee would form part of initial outlay on acquisition of business, Assessing Officer was justified in treating said non-compete fee as capital expenditure and disallowing same under section 37(1)
Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under sec. 37(1): SC

IT : Where assessee made payment to its partner to ward-off competition, rights acquired by assessee under said agreement would not only give enduring benefit, but protected assessee's business against competition, and fell under expression 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' used in Explanation 3 to sub-section 32(1)(ii) and, thus, assessee was eligible for depreciation

IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee on advertisement to bring public awareness regarding change in its name, could not be said to bring into existence an advantage of enduring nature and, thus, same was to be allowed as deduction under section 37(1)
Ad exp. incurred to publicize change of name from UTI bank to Axis Bank allowable as revenue exp.
License fee for use of goodwill of another firm allowable as deduction u/s 37(1) incurred for business: HC
Non-compete fee was allowable as deduction as it facilitated earning more profit in business ; SLP dismissed
Sum paid to AE for use of its trademark couldn't be disallowed even if assessee's own trademark was well established
IT: Where assessee failed to produce any evidence to show that a company had provided training to its employees, connected expenditure could not be allowed
IT : Expenditure on training of employees would be revenue expense
Sum paid to IFA to create awareness of 'Vaish Associates' by constructing meeting hall in its name is business exp.
X. INCOME TAX : Recruitment and training expenses have to be treated as revenue expenditure and cannot be seen as leading to enduring benefit warranting any disallowance

IT : Where Holding Company and assessee demarcated their areas of business, in view of fact holding company rendered other services also and assessee paid one per cent of turnover, said payment was not just for non competition and, thus, to be allowed as revenue expenditure
Non-compete fee paid to directors to restrain them from engaging in same business was allowable deduction
IT : Training expense on new manufacturing unit which was extension of existing business were allowable as revenue expenditure

IT-I : Where assessee, engaged in manufacturing of pharmaceutical products, paid certain amount as trademark and patent registration fee, in view of fact that said expenditure was incurred for protection of its running business without generating any new asset, same was to be allowed as deduction
Employees training exp. to run an extended unit of an existing business is an allowable expenditure

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, manufacturer of sports products, claimed an expenditure towards establishing a pace foundation for giving training to pace bowlers, since assessee got huge publicity by training of bowlers through said foundation and it promoted assessee's brand thereby helping in sale of products, impugned expenditure was to be allowed under secion 37(1)
IT : Where assessee incurred expenses for brand popularity, merely because overseas owner of brand also gained some benefits, claim of expenditure as business expenditure could not be denied

INCOME TAX : Where assessee company, engaged in business of production and telecasting of TV serials, entered into non-compete agreement with two firms belonging to same person for a period of 5 years wherein it acquired copyrights of number of movies owned by two firms and paid certain amount as non-compete fee, since entire business was transferred as a going concern concept, then, nothing was left with transferee firms to carry on business and what was held by them was a copyright
IT : Expenditure incurred by assessee on coaching of its IPL team was to be allowed as deduction
HC allows business exp. as assessee was doing new business with retained employees after transfer of old business

CL : Where brand name 'Vardhaman' was already registered trade mark of respondent-company and both appellant and respondent companies were doing same business, appellant was to be directed to delete word 'Vardhaman' from its existing name
Exp. incurred by MRF on establishing foundation to give training to pace bowlers allowable as business exp.: HC

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made a payment as donation to CCI and as part of research programme under which employees of assessee would undergo training in theory of disruptive innovation, though amount was paid under head 'donation', actual nature of payment was towards research programme which would benefit assessee in long-term and, thus, same should be allowed as a deduction under section 37(1)

IT: Where for assessment year 1996-97 under an agreement, assessee transferred one of its business to other company but continued its business using its own logo, trade name, licenses and permits, no part of non-compete fee received by assessee under aforesaid agreement could be treated as considerations for goodwill and it was not taxable as income
Non-compete fee can’t be treated as intangible asset; Depreciation claim on it to be disallowed: ITAT
