The recently released (May 2013) official version of "United Nations Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries" has a unique feature that it has a separate Chapter to outline country specific transfer pricing practices followed by Brazil, China, India and South Africa. These country specific administrative practices are based on the details provided by the representatives from these countries. The MNEs would certainly refer to these country practice notes to obtain certainty on their transfer pricing issues in these countries.

Paragraphs 10.4.8.12 to 10.4.8.18 of the UN Manual contain the Indian administrative practice on transfer pricing aspects of "Marketing Intangibles". The UN Manual defines "Intangibles" as the property that has no physical existence but whose value depends on the legal rights of the owner. Further "Marketing Intangibles" are intangibles relating to marketing activities, aiding in the commercial exploitation of a product or service or with important promotional value for a product or service. Trademarks, Trade Names are marketing intangibles.

While discussing business strategies in the Chapter on Comparability Analyis, the UN Manual says–

"5.3.2.55. When an MNE enters a new market with its product or expands market share of its product in an existing market through its subsidiary, questions of the creation of marketing intangibles and increases in the value of product-related intangibles such as trademarks, trade names etc. follow closely behind. Therefore, it is important to examine and follow the process of creation of intangibles in a market, as well as the legal ownership of such intangibles and the right to share in the return from such intangibles (the notion which some countries refer to as "economic ownership"). It is recognized that market research; designing or planning products suitable to market needs, advertising, marketing and sales promotion strategies; after-sale services and networks of dealers and sales/commission agents may contribute to the creation of marketing intangibles depending on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The Indian market has witnessed substantial marketing activities by the Indian affiliates of MNE groups in the recent past and the transfer pricing aspect of marketing intangibles has been a focus area for the Indian transfer pricing administration for the last about 5 years. The India country practice note states that the marketing intangibles are generally identified on the basis of the efforts of the Indian affiliate towards:

Enhancing the value of the foreign trademark or brand that is unknown to Indian market by incurring very large advertisement, marketing and sale promotion expenditures; creation of brand and product loyalty in the minds of customers;

Creation of an efficient supply chain;

Establishing distributor networks in the country;

Developing an after-sale services and support network in the country;

Conducting customer and market research; and

Gathering customer data and establishing customer lists, etc.

The note then goes on to say that Indian affiliates (which are claimed as no risk or limited risk bearing distributors by the parent MNE in order to justify low cost plus return) incur and bear very large expenditures on the development of marketing intangibles. Consequently, the Indian affiliates generally incur very large losses or disclose very nominal profits.

The note further says-

"10.4.8.16 The Indian tax administration computes the ALP in the cases involving marketing intangibles following the concept of a "bright line" test; that is, no risk or limited risk distributor will bear the cost of only routine expenditure on advertisement, marketing and sale promotion (AMP). However, the tax administration faces the following challenges in determination of the ALP:

The issue of whether the parent MNE should reimburse the cost incurred by the Indian subsidiary or related party for the development of marketing intangibles with or without mark-up;

Lack of uniform accounting rules creates significant difficulties in identifying AMP expenditure in comparable companies and the tested party; and

The developer of marketing intangibles who has economic ownership in the intangibles is entitled to additional returns. However, the difficult question is what should be the arm's length price of such returns.

10.4.8.17. The important issue in the determination of ALP in these cases is to examine who benefits from the extraordinary AMP expenditure. Taxpayers generally claim that such extraordinary expenditure helps the business of the Indian entity in addition to the parent MNE.

However, the tax authorities in India have found that Indian distributors are claimed to be no risk or low risk bearing entities and are receiving fixed and routine return on a cost plus basis. They do not receive a share in the excess profit related to local marketing intangibles. Accordingly, extraordinary AMP expenditure does not enhance the profitability of the Indian subsidiary or related party. This conclusion of the tax authorities is further supported by the fact that these so called risk-free or limited risk distributors have disclosed very large losses even when they are entitled for fixed return on cost plus basis and should not have incurred losses.

AMP Expenses Off late there has been controversy whether an 'international transaction' in relation to brand building of foreign AE can be said to exist when some part of business expenses relating to advertisement, marketing and sales promotion (AMP) are considered by tax authorities attributable to activity of brand building of foreign AE. The expression "international transaction" is defined in section 92B in a wide manner and means a transaction between two or more associated enterprises, either or both of whom are non-residents, in the nature of purchase, sale, or lease of tangible or intangible property, or provision of services, or lending or borrowing money, or any other transaction having a bearing on the profits, income, losses or assets of such enterprises, and shall include a mutual arrangement between two or more parties for allocation of any cost or expense. It is thus clear that in order to bring the transaction within the ambit of transfer pricing regulations there must be transaction between two or more enterprises of which at least one party is non-resident. Where Indian entity incurs AMP expenses for its own business and payments are made to a resident company it is difficult to say that this would ipso facto result in "international transaction" of brand building of foreign AE unless there is some express or implied agreement or understanding between the parties in regard to sharing of such expenses. This brings us to the meaning of term "transaction" as defined in section 92F of the Act, which states that "transaction" includes an arrangement, understanding or action in concert, whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is formal or in writing or intended to be enforceable by legal proceedings. It is thus apparent that AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Company for the purposes of its business cannot be said to be related to brand building of a foreign AE unless it can be established that such expenses were incurred pursuant to some express or oral arrangement or understanding between the parties.

Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. case

The issue relating to transfer pricing of trademarks and brands created as a result of AMP expenses was first considered in case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT8. The controversy in this case related to arm's length price of transactions involving royalty payment of Rs 198.6 crores by Maruti India to its foreign associated enterprise, Suzuki Corporation, Japan, where foreign AE did not reimburse the Indian Company its share of advertisement and marketing expenditure incurred by Maruti India, which provided marketing benefit to Suzuki Corporation for using 'Suzuki' logo on products manufactured by Maruti company. The Revenue contention was that Suzuki Corporation Japan should have reimbursed part of advertisement and marketing expenses incurred by Maruti India for promotion of 'Suzuki' logo on the products manufactured and sold by Maruti company. The High Court remitted the matter to the Transfer Pricing Officer with liberty to issue fresh show cause notice and decide the matter in accordance with law. However, whilst remanding the matter the court made certain observations and gave directions to the TPO about taxability of marketing intangibles from mandatory use of the trademark by Maruti company which benefited the Suzuki Corporation and thus virtually concluded the matter. On further appeal the Supreme Court held9 that the TPO should proceed with the matter in accordance with law uninfluenced by the observations given by the High Court.

Ltd.1 involving the issue of marketing intangibles, it was held that the AMP computation (i.e. computation of advertisement, marketing and sales promotion expenses) which was based on the adoption of the Bright Line Test (BLT), would clearly not sustain in light of the judgement rendered by the Court in Sony Ericson v. On opening a soda bottle, carbon dioxide dissolved in it suddenly comes out as a fizz. This is because, there is a sudden decrease in the pressure above the drink and thus the dissolved carbon dioxide becomes less soluble resulting in fast release of CO2 with a fizzing sound. Similar to this, is the marketing intangibles or the AMP expenses issue, where the pressure is created from the excess AMP expenses, incurred by the local Indian subsidiaries, tested by BLT and if excessive, resulting into a fizzing adjustment for marketing intangibles issue. However, as per the Hon'ble HC, the BLT cannot create any fizz.

The Background

The issue of marketing intangibles or the AMP expenses as is its commonly called, is vexed and has been in litigation from a long time. Its original shape and form was designed around the BLT and inspite of being struck down very explicitly by HC, it remains in its vintage form, in the Transfer Pricing (TP) orders.

Let us dwell further on the issue and what's the history has been so far.

In many instances, the Tax Authorities in India have taken an aggressive stand by claiming that the AMP expenses or any expense incurred under the AMP account makes a valuable addition to the trademark/ brand legally owned by the foreign-related party for brand building. This thereby concludes that the local Indian subsidiary must be compensated by the legal brand owner, i.e. the overseas related party/ associated enterprise, for the benefit bestowed or the additional services rendered by the local Indian subsidiary, on an arm's length basis.

As a background, even though intellectual property (IP) is part of the definition of an 'international transaction', however in addition to this, the Indian TP regulations do not offer clear guidance on intangibles. Furthermore, there is no specific inclusion of the expenses relating to AMP in the definition of the term 'international transaction'. On the contrary, the BLT is used to state that if the AMP expenses are higher than comparables, then there is an international transaction, else not. Thus, the basic premise of being an international transaction is a non-starter to begin with. This leads to a discussion about the legitimacy of whether the AMP should be considered an international transaction in the first place. Besides, the question in this regard arises as to whether AMP expenses are allowed in the hands of the taxpayer based on the commercial justification or the legal ownership of the assets.

The Controversy

India as the new global market has its unique characteristic features that includes location advantages, market accessibility, customer necessity, etc. that have made its subsidiaries/ related parties of Multi-National-Enterprises (MNEs) spearhead different and far more extensive and faster marketing techniques seeking to gain a competitive ground in India. This has resulted in the topic of marketing intangibles becoming one of the most widely discussed TP topics in India.

As mentioned earlier, the tax authorities indicate that the issues relating to legal ownership of intangibles are pertinent to the TP regulations. However, the taxpayers argue that since the Indian subsidiary is the economic owner of such intangibles, they cannot justify that the subsidiary must recover the AMP expenses from its related parties because the subsidiary would be the direct recipient of the benefits from the incurring of such expenses.

The information is further amplified by the use of what the tax department employs to determine the arm's length price (ALP) of such other alleged international transaction: the 'BLT.' This is a concept derived from a US tax court case. As per this test, all such AMP expenses that are incurred by the taxpayer and are more than the amount of average AMP expenses, about foreign-related parties, incurred by comparable companies in India, then such fees are to be treated as non-routine expenses (expenses for creating brand value in India of the foreign related parties) and thus should be benchmarked as per the ALP.

The missing pieces

In this context, several pertinent questions arise:

-

Whether the AMP expenses can be considered an international transaction?

-

Must the Indian local subsidiary, seeing it is not a legal owner of the trademark but is an economic owner or developer of the brand/ trademark, be exonerated from the necessity to cover AMP expenses?

The department demanded service tax on sale consideration and imposed penalty. The applicant contended that it had paid sales tax on the SIM cards and since the cards were goods, provisions of the Act could not be invoked for imposition of service tax. Based on the decision of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd’s case (supra), New Delhi Bench of the Tribunal held that even if some amount was charged for SIM cards supplied to customers, SIM card of the applicant-company was clearly relatable to the services provided by it. Such SIM card could not have been used for any other service. Moreover, unless activated it was useless, which showed that it was only a part of the services provided, and it was not goods separately sold. If some company manufactures SIM cards for the purpose of selling them to a cellular service provider for its business, that may stand on the footing of SIM cards being sold as goods, which has nothing to do with cellular service. Cellular service is not to be provided by the manufacturer of such SIM cards and is to be provided by the purchaser for whom such tailor made SIM cards were manufactured. It was also urged by the assessee that it was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 12/03-ST, dated 20-6-2003. On this, the Tribunal held that, admittedly, this contention had never been raised so far. Even otherwise, prima facie this notification could not be of any help to the applicant because SIM cards were not sold as goods, independent from the services provided, but they were part and parcel of the services provided and the dominant intent was to provide services and not to sell the material, namely, SIM cards, which on its own without the service, would hardly have any value. Thus, the Tribunal did not allow waiving of any part of the amount payable under the impugned order. It is also important to note that in case of State of Uttar Pradesh v. UOI12 , the Supreme Court has held that levy of service tax on a particular service is no bar to levy trade tax on it.

Similarly, in the case of Hindustan Associated Traders v. CCE, Cochin [2007] 7 STT 81 (Bang. - CESTAT), the assessees were given marketing and distribution rights of SIM cards. The assessees had to purchase SIM cards from BSNL outright. The assessees contended that they could not be considered to have provided any service, as they had purchased SIM cards outright and were carrying an activity of distributing. Bangalore Bench of the Tribunal held that since as per agreement entered into by assessee with BSNL the assessees were required to provide services to customers also, it could not prima facie be said that they had not carried on services of business auxiliary services; therefore, the Tribunal directed the assessees to pre-deposit demand raised.

These decisions of the Tribunal are moot pointer to the aspect of tax planning by giving different colour to a simple transaction of service as sale transaction. It is settled law that the substance of a transaction is more important than the form of transaction and for this purpose the nomenclature of a transaction given by the parties cannot control the actual tax implications.

Depreciation on 'Goodwill' - A critical analysis

Kavita Kachhwaha

Introduction

1. An intangible asset can be defined as "an identifiable non-monetary asset, without physical substance, which is able to generate economic benefits to the business enterprise."1 It creates significant values for an organization beyond its tangible assets. Intangible assets (including intellectual properties), such as goodwill, know-how, customer lists, copyrights, etc., may be self-generated and, hence, an off-balance sheet item or these may be purchased. It is to be noted that expenses on development or on purchasing of such intangibles are either capitalized, or are expensed out in the profit and loss account, depending on the facts of each case. Where such intangibles are capitalized, the Income-tax Act, 1961 expressly provides for depreciation allowance.2 Depreciation is allowed on know-how, patents, copyrights, trade-marks, licences, franchises and 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature'. However, there is no express provision for depreciation in respect of other widely known intangible assets, such as, goodwill, non-compete rights, employees' contracts, vendor/customer contracts, distributorship rights, service process flows, knowledge databases, brands, etc. Thus, the key issue in respect of depreciation of such unspecified intangible assets, mentioned above, is whether they can be regarded as business or commercial rights of a 'similar' nature ?

It is to be noted that Goodwill is one of the significant intangible assets which either arises on acquisition or is internally generated. As per section 55(2)(a) of the Act, the cost of acquisition in case of goodwill is the purchase price and in case of self-generated goodwill it is nil. Thus, purchased goodwill is now specifically recognized as a capital asset. In practice, M&A transactions usually results in the transferee-company paying a consideration higher than the value of the assets taken over, which is accounted for as 'Goodwill'. Thus, since the statute is silent, a moot point from an income-tax perspective is whether such goodwill would be eligible for tax depreciation? This issue has become quite relevant in today's competitive atmosphere. Enterprises frequently expend resources, or incur liabilities on the acquisition, development, maintenance or enhancement of intangible resources such as scientific or technical knowledge, design and implementation of new processes or systems, licences, trademarks, etc. It is more significant in corporate sector with India incorporated actively pursuing mergers and acquisitions route for their expansions and valuations reaching dizzy heights, intangibles being a larger part of acquisition.

Thus, in the light of the significance of this issue, this paper takes an opportunity to examine whether goodwill, being an 'intangible asset', is eligible for depreciation under section 32 of the I.T. Act. It also takes into account the relevant provisions of the proposed Direct Taxes Code.

2. The Concept of Goodwill

2.1 Definition of goodwill - The term "goodwill" has not been defined in the Income Tax Act, 1961. Thus, in order to understand the concept recourse must be made to the judicial pronouncements.

20 STT 203 by the Supreme Court as under :

"Work done or duty performed for another or others; a serving; as, professional services, repair service, a life devoted to public service. An activity carried on to provide people with the use of something, as electric power, water, transportation, mail delivery, telephones, etc. Anything useful, as maintenance, supplies, installation, repairs, etc., provided by a dealer or manufacturer for people who have bought things from him."

Event 10. The word ‘event’ is defined in ‘Business Dictionary.com’ as follows :

"Occurrence or happening at a determinable time and place, with or without the participation of human agents. It may be a part of a chain of occurrences and effect of a preceding occurrence and as the cause of a succeeding occurrence."

There can be different kinds of events like organization of film fare awards; organization of Gujarat Vibrant Summit 2010, Navratri Festival, Kite Flying Festival, etc., promotion of Common Wealth Games, Indian Premier League (IPL), Cricket World Cup, etc. The promotion or marketing of any type of event would be a taxable service.

Endorsement of name

11. The definition of ‘taxable service’ provides for ‘endorsement of name’. The name can be endorsed by any celebrity like a film-star, sports person, etc. The name would include a trade name, logo or house mark of business entity. For example, house mark of TATA Group. The promotion of name through endorsement would be taxable.

u Trade name - It means "the name used by a trade to refer to a commodity, service, etc., the name under which a commercial enterprise operates in business". [www.thefreedictionary.com/trade+name]

u Logo - It means "a name, symbol, or trademark designed for easy and definite recognition, especially one borne on a single printing plate or piece of type". [www.thefreedictionary.com/trade+name]

u "A logo is a graphic or emblem commonly used by commercial enterprises organizations and even individuals to aid and promote instant public recognition". [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logo].

u House mark - It means "distinctive mark used in identifying products as well as professional services (such as architecture, consultancy, engineering) provided by a firm" [www.businessdictionary.com/definition/housemark.html].

The Supreme Court has, in the case of Asra Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise 1995 (75) ELT 214, explained the difference between ‘house mark’ and ‘product mark’ (brand name) by relying on Navratna’s Book on Trade Marks and Passing-Off as follows :

"677A. House mark and product mark (or brand name) - In the pharmaceutical business a distinction is made between a house mark and a product mark. The former is used on all the products of the manufacturer. It is usually a device in the form a emblem, word or both. For each product a separate mark known as a product mark or a brand name is used which is invariably a word or a combination of a word and letter or numeral by which the product is identified and asked for. In respect of all products both the product mark and house mark will appear side by side on all the labels, cartons, etc. Goods are ordered only by the product mark or brand name. The house mark serves as an emblem of the manufacturer projecting the image of the manufactured generally."

It will be evident from the above that the brand name is generally associated with the product, whereas a house mark may represent a particular corporate house or group or professional association. Normally, a house mark like Tata, Adiyta Birla, Sahara, ICAI, etc., do not represent any product but represent the entire group whereas the brand name is associated with the product.

12. As per the definition of taxable service, the manner of promotion can be either in the form of appearing in advertisements or through making appearance in promotional events or by carrying out any promotional activity for the goods or services or events.

The inter-linkage between the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion (AMP) expense by distributor of a branded/trademarked product and the value of brand/trademark, first came into prominence in the 1980s when the US Internal Revenue sought to disallow part of AMP expense incurred by a distributor on the plea that the same was incurred on behalf of the foreign trademark owner. The case was settled by the parties out of court and, therefore, not much is known about the outcome.

Later in 1994, the US Internal Revenue issued the Transfer Pricing Regulations in Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code incorporating the famous 'cheese examples'. These examples prescribed compensation for the US distributor of branded cheese, who incurred advertisement and marketing expense significantly larger than what independent distributors incurred under similar circumstances. The expenditure in excess of the level incurred by independent distributors was to be considered to be a service provided to the brand owner.

OECD Transfer pricing Guidelines issued in 1995 also made reference in paragraphs 6.36 to 6.39 to the transfer pricing issues that could arise when marketing activities were undertaken by enterprises that did not own the trademarks or trade names that they promoted (such as distributor of branded goods). The Guidelines indicated that in cases where a distributor bore extraordinary marketing expenditures beyond what an independent distributor with similar rights might incur for the benefits of its own distribution activities, it was entitled to an additional return from the owner of the trademark, perhaps through a decrease in the purchase price of the product or a reduction in the royalty rate. Unlike the US 'cheese examples', the OECD Guidelines accepted that a distributor may have the ability to obtain benefits from its investments in developing the value of a trademark from its turnover and market share where it has a long term contract of sole distribution rights for the trademarked product.

Further significant development on this front was the DHL case in US in the year 2002. DHL operated courier business inside US. Its Hong Kong affiliate DHLI (DHL International) handled courier business outside US. DHL was the legal owner of DHL trademark and DHLI was licensee of the trademark for territories outside US. DHLI developed the DHL trademark outside US and did not pay any royalty to DHL for use of the trademark. US Internal Revenue imputed trademark royalty to DHL for the use of its trademark by DHLI outside US. DHL asserted that a royalty should not be imputed from DHLI because DHLI bore the economic investment for the development of DHL trademark outside US. During the years under consideration, DHL had incurred advertisement and marketing spend of $ 150 Million in US and DHLI had incurred advertisement and marketing spend of $ 340 Million outside US. The US IRS allocated royalties which DHL should have charged to DHLI for use of DHL trademark outside US. The Tax Court upheld the allocation by saying that DHL had failed to show that DHLI had itself developed the trademark outside US because it was not demonstrated that AMP by DHLI was more than what would have been incurred by an arm's length licensee. The Tax Court observed on page 60 of its order – "Petitioners have presented evidence that, over a period of years, DHLI spent substantially more on advertising than DHL. We have no way of measuring these expenditures' effect on the value of the trademark". The Court of Appeal reversed the decision of Tax Court by observing that DHLI need not have shown the precise amount of its trademark development expenditure, since presumably at least $ 50 Million (which was undisputed value of DHL trademark for the Overseas Trademark Rights) of the $ 340 Million spent by DHLI constituted development expenses for the DHL trademark outside US.

The DHL case therefore did not throw up any exact correlation between the AMP expense and the trademark value. It only said that out of $ 340 Million AMP expense by DHLI, at least $ 50 Million was contribution to the value of the trademark. Further, the case did not elaborate on the nature of expenses that exactly constitute AMP expenses. Though the court in DHL case used the words 'arm's length licensee expenditure' test, Marc Levey in his Article in 2007 on 'A closer focus on 1marketing intangibles' in Euromoney Handbooks preferred to call the same as2 'Bright-Line' Test. The term 'Bright-Line Test' has since gained popularity in the context of AMP expense by a licensee. The 'Arm's Length Licensee Expenditure Test' or the 'Bright-Line Test', whatever one may call it, seems relevant because otherwise in most of the cases, it is almost impossible to segregate routine and non-routine AMP expenditure, or in other words, product and brand promotion AMP expenditure. What promotes product may also promote brand and vice versa.

The underlying thread seems to be that AMP, if substantive enough, creates an intangible. Numerous unanswered questions remain, however, such as how to define a company’s marketing intangibles from a tax and legal perspective, what expenses truly contribute to the building of this intangible, how to determine in tax parlance where the level of AMP transcends from routine to non-routine expenditures, what expenses qualify for these considerations, (e.g. registration costs, legal costs for routine expenses and real broad brand building expenses as such non-routine expenses), whether an analysis of each underlying accounting code requires the segregation of routine from non-routine expenditures, what allocation keys may be employed and what is the "shelf life" of the created marketing intangible, as well as any pre existing marketing intangibles that are included within the considered intangible. One further practical problem, and a significant one, is that not every taxpayer accounts for its AMP within the same accounting classifications.

While there may be merit in the DHL "bright line" test from a practical point of view, the definition of non-routine expenditures is so industry and company specific, that it may be impossible to apply in most cases. Similar companies within the same industry may have vastly different approaches to their marketing philosophies, product launches, and/or product dependence or interdependence. This could create very different levels of AMP and different "bright lines." This may even occur within the same companies and for similar product categories. These expenditures can also be influenced by, among other things, the product’s position in other countries, the timing of product launches, and the competitors and their products, each of which impacts the "bright line" benchmarking and comparability standards. Also, the legal status of the intangibles concerned may impact the expenditures differently. Even more complexity arises where the company has many product lines and the AMP expenditures are not segregated by those lines.

In the Mary Kay Holdings case,8 that was docketed in the Tax Court and later on settled the Petitioner begged the question of whether AMP are deductible under I.R.C. Section 162 when they are incurred for the development of a brand outside the United States. In the facts contained in the Petition, the U.S. parent company seemingly used the AMP spend as a vehicle to make a transfer pricing adjustment to its "limited risk" distribution under the guise that the adjustments (i.e. AMP charge backs) were made by the parent to support the development of the "Mary Kay" brand. The amounts of these expenses were approximately $16.1 million in 1997, $20.6 million in 1998 and $14.2 million in 1999. While the case was settled, and some underlying papers indicate the Government was challenging the documentation, it is not clear therefore how the Tax Court would have held on this issue. However, what is clear is that there should be a distinct delineation between how transfer pricing adjustments are made and how AMP support payments and/or charge-backs are addressed so that there is a clean line of demarcation between the two and the AMP payments can truly be tracked to brand development and enhancement expense codes.

Notwithstanding the above, the analysis that has evolved from the prior jurisprudence begs the question of what expenses are truly brand building. For example, some marketing consultants would argue that pure advertising is not a brand building cost. Instead, placements for specific events (e.g., the Super Bowl, the U.S. Open, etc.) may be considered to produce lasting brand equity. The same can be said that celebrity endorsements create more brand building and brand association than pure advertising. Similarly, market campaigns and strategic focus groups geared to market knowledge, spending habits, and market placement can be of equal value. In tax audits, the IRS and other taxing authorities have focused on flagship stores as brand builders, or another form of AMP. The premise is that these flagships are strategically positioned in locations where their presence is of greater value than the revenue, if any, generated from the store (e.g. 5th Avenue in New York City) Michigan Avenue in Chicago, Rodeo Drive in Los Angeles. The taxing authorities have often characterized the "excess rental costs" associated with flagship properties as brand builders to be borne by the brand owner.

The likelihood of attaining a consensus view on these items of brand building is nil. But what is clear is that the brand building/development costs will be company specific and will require a detailed analysis to meet the ever increasing challenges of global tax authorities in this area.

Executives of Indian subsidiaries of Multinationals ('MNE group') and tax professionals across the country should now be able to breathe easy. The Hon'ble Delhi High Court ('Delhi HC') recently pronounced its decision on the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ('AMP') controversy1 involving various Indian distributors ('Taxpayers'2) of reputed MNE groups. The amounts involved on the issue run into several crores.

In past few years, a highly debated issue in Transfer Pricing ('TP') audits/litigation involving taxpayers who incur significant AMP expenses, has been the creation of marketing intangibles. Tax authorities at ground level have typically held that excessive or non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India contribute to building of the brand legally owned by the MNE group outside India. Consequently, the taxpayers should receive an arm's length compensation on the excessive or non-routine AMP expenses alongwith a mark-up from the legal owner of the brand in the MNE group. This view was upheld by the Special Bench ('SB') of Delhi Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ('ITAT'/'Tax Tribunal') in the case of LG Electronics India Private Limited3.The ITAT in its detailed order held that AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayer towards building a brand legally owned by the MNE group constituted an 'international transaction' and the foreign entity should pay for the AMP expenses incurred beyond the amount arrived at by applying the 'bright line'.

Consequent to the SB ruling in case of LG Electronics, tax authorities proposed TP additions in many other cases on account of the AMP issue, which were later upheld by various tax Tribunals. Aggrieved taxpayers filed appeals before the Delhi High Court against the rulings of the tax Tribunal in their respective cases.

1. Core issues before the Delhi HC

The Delhi HC, in its more than 140 page order, discussed at length the following core issues with respect to AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India:

whether AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function undertaken by the taxpayers could be considered as an 'International Transaction' as per India Transfer Pricing Regulations4;

whether taxpayers could be said to be engaged in the activity of building 'Brand' in India which is legally owned by the MNE group;

whether the taxpayers could be said to be the 'Economic Owner' of the 'Marketing Intangible' purportedly developed by them for the MNE group;

whether AMP spend could be segregated into routine and non-routine expenditure in the hands of taxpayers by applying 'Bright Line Test5' in order to determine the value of so called 'Marketing Intangible'; and

how the marketing and distribution function (whether standalone or bundled with the other core transaction of import of goods) should be acknowledged and the arm's length compensation should be determined in such cases.

The Delhi HC, partly ruling in favour of the tax authorities and partly in favour of the taxpayers, gave elaborated reasons and findings on the above core issues. Some important aspects of the decision have been discussed in the following paragraphs.

2. AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function is an 'International Transaction'

The Delhi HC struck down the contention of the taxpayers that AMP expenses were paid by them to third parties in India and accordingly should not be classified as an 'International Transaction'. It confirmed the finding of the ITAT in the case of LG Electronics that AMP expenditure incurred by the taxpayers with respect to distribution and marketing function is an international transaction in terms of Indian TP regulations. The HC observed that since taxpayers themselves advanced an argument that the declared price of international transactions included a remuneration for their AMP function, the argument challenging that it is not an international transaction is incorrect.

3. Legal ownership of 'Brand' and 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers

The Delhi HC observed (and rightly so) that a reputed 'Brand' is developed (by the MNE groups) over a passage of time. Brand value of any product/service refers to intangibles like know-how, infrastructure, and would depend upon the nature and quality of products/services offered to the customers. The HC further clarified that expenditure incurred by the taxpayers on advertisement and promotion of products/services with a 'Trademark' is only for commercial exploitation of the said 'Trademark' and per se there is no substantial value addition or 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers. Reputed brands do not undertake advertisement and marketing activities with the intention to increase (already established) brand value, but to increase sales and thereby earn larger profits.

Introduction

1. The growth of international trade and corporate endeavour to capture new markets, resulted in multijurisdictional presence of companies in different forms. Often multinational groups prefer different modes of doing business ranging from undertaking direct manufacturing or appointing distributors or agents. Depending upon the nature of the model adopted, such arrangements invariably involve certain intra-group transfer of goods, products, services and intangibles with accompanying tax implications. Most jurisdictions have put in place transfer pricing regimes within their domestic tax laws to address issues evolving from intra-group transfers. Payment of royalty for the use of 'intangibles' such as brand name or trade name of the foreign company by its domestic group company or subsidiary, as the case may be, is a quite common arrangement. Of late contribution of domestic company to the benefit of overall brand name of its foreign company has attracted lot of attention from tax authorities. In other words, when Indian subsidiary incurs advertising, marketing and promotional expenses which may have incidental benefits for the overall brand name of its foreign parent does it amount to an international transaction which attracts transfer pricing provisions? If it does, what amount of benefit should be attributable to the foreign company for which the Indian counterpart requires to be compensated? Issues such as these have emerged in the recent past.

Insofar as marketable intangibles are concerned, it has been acknowledged that it involves a complicated exercise in quantifying the benefit that accrues to the foreign company. This complexity makes it particularly amenable to controversy regarding the requisite amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian company. While several countries such as the U.S, New Zealand and Australia adopt a 'bright line test' (hereinafter BLT) to ascertain the said benefit, Indian jurisdiction does not as yet statutorily recognize the BLT despite attempts by the Revenue department in computing the arms length price (hereinafter ALP) of AMP expenses based on the BLT. Several companies that either manufacture or market branded goods and products have fallen prey to the aforesaid controversy.

The recent landmark judgment from the Delhi High Court in the matter of Maruti Suzuki India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT1 (hereinafter Maruti Suzuki) adds to the existing jurisprudence with regards to tax implications of AMP expenses incurred by Indian entities that may contribute to marketing intangibles of its foreign counterparts. The issue of application of the BLT in determining arms length price of the AMP expenses in India had already been negated by the Delhi High Court judgment in Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT2 (hereinafter Sony Erricson). The said decision of the Delhi High Court overruled the decision of the Special Bench of the Income Tax Tribunal in LG Electronics India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3 (hereinafter L.G.Electronics) that had found favours with the BLT. The present judgment of Maruti Suzuki 2015 builds on the decision of Sony Ericsson to nullify reliance upon the BLT so as to deduce existence of international transaction as to then invoke transfer pricing regulations for excessive AMP expenses.

(hereinafter MUL), as a Government of India owned company. Somewhere in the year 1982, MUL entered into a composite license agreement with Suzuki Motor Corporation, Japan (hereinafter SMC) for the use of technical know-how for the manufacturing of specified cars with the co-branded trade mark 'Maruti Suzuki'. At the time of 1982 agreement, MUL and SMC were unrelated entities. It was only in 2003 that SMC acquired controlling interest in MSIL. As on 31st March 2006, SMC held 54.21% shares in MSIL. 10.27% of the shares were held by the Government of India and the balance was held by the Indian public and others. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer invoked the transfer pricing provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and referred the case to the transfer pricing officer (hereinafter TPO) for determination of ALP in relation to the international transactions undertaken by MSIL with its associated enterprise SMC. This included purchase of components, capital items, technical services, payment of royalty for technology/trademark.

KRISHAN MALHOTRA

Introduction

1. The issue of applicability of transfer pricing provisions has always been a Cause of concern for Indian companies. There are a number of Indian companies who are engaged in distribution of various branded products manufactured by their foreign affiliates. In most of the cases the Indian companies incur expenses on advertisement, marketing and promotional activities ("AMP") for the various products distributed by them. The argument of tax authorities has always been that since the brand-name/trademark/trade-name is owned by the foreign affiliate, the expenses incurred by the Indian companies on AMP activities lead to creation of brand value for the foreign affiliates for which the Indian companies should be compensated by the foreign affiliates.

The Special Bench of the Hon'ble Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("ITAT") in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.1 tried to address the above issue by segregating 'routine' and 'non-routine' AMP activities by applying the 'Bright Line Test'. As per the ITAT any expense on AMP activities beyond the 'Bright Line Test' should be treated as a separate international transaction and, accordingly, benchmarked. As per the said 'Bright Line test' expense on AMP activities in excess of similar expense incurred by comparable independent domestic companies was regarded as an expense incurred by the Indian company for brand promotion of foreign affiliate.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd.2 has disagreed with judgment of the ITAT in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra) and has held that 'Bright Line Test' cannot be applied for benchmarking of AMP expenses.

This article gives a detailed analysis of this decision, which may have a significant bearing on all Indian companies engaged in the distribution of goods manufactured by their foreign affiliates.

Rulings of the Delhi High Court

2. The 'Bright Line Test' finds its roots in the US Transfer Pricing Regulations wherein the concept has been explained by way of the following illustrations:

Example : FP, a foreign producer of cheese, markets the cheese in countries other than the United States under the trade name Fromage Frere. FP owns all the worldwide rights to this name. The name is widely known and is valuable outside the United States but is not known within the United States. In 1995, FP decides to enter the United States market and incorporates U.S. subsidiary, USSub, to be its U.S. distributor and to supervise the advertising and other marketing efforts that will be required to develop the name Fromage Frere in the United States. USSub incurs expenses that are not reimbursed by FP for developing the U.S. market for Fromage Frere. These expenses are comparable to the levels of expense incurred by independent distributors in the U.S. cheese industry when introducing a product in the U.S. market under a brand name owned by a foreign manufacturer. Since USSub would have been expected to incur these expenses if it were unrelated to FP, no allocation to USSub is made with respect to the market development activities performed by USSub.

Example : The facts are the same as in above Example, except that the expenses incurred by USSub are significantly larger than the expenses incurred by independent distributors under similar circumstances. FP does not reimburse USSub for its expenses. The district director concludes based on this evidence that an unrelated party dealing at arm's length under similar circumstances would not have engaged in the same level of activity relating to the development of FP's marketing intangibles. The expenditures in excess of the level incurred by the independent distributors therefore are considered to be a service provided to FP that adds to the value of FP's trademark for Fromage Frere. Accordingly, the district director makes an allocation under section 482 for the fair market value of the services that USSub is considered to have performed for FP.

The Hon'ble ITAT in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) had provided a legal recognition to the 'Bright Line Test' in spite of the fact that there was no such statutory mandate under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("Act").

In the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra) the Hon'ble Delhi High Court has disagreed with the applicability of 'Bright Line Test' for benchmarking expenses incurred on AMP expenses. The important principles laid down by the Hon'ble High Court are as follows:

though unenforceable as being time barred, was allowable deductions. It was so held in the following cases on—

(i) Eastern Investments Ltd. v. CIT [1951] 20 ITR 1 (SC);

(ii) Binodiram Balchand v. CIT [1963] 48 ITR 548 (MP);

(iii) Calcutta Landing & Shipping Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1967] 65 ITR 1 (Cal.); (iv) CIT v. Orient Paper Mills Ltd. [1988] 171 ITR 181 /[1987] 34 Taxman 249 (Cal.); and

In yet another case, the Supreme Court in CIT v. Chandulal Keshavlal & Co. In this case also there was in fact no cash outflow as is in the topic under consideration.

Therefore, in construing the allowability or otherwise of the ESOS/ESOP compensation expenses claimed by a company, due emphasis may be given from the point of view of businessman and not from the point of view of outsiders including taxing authorities. This was so held by the Madhya Pradesh High Court in the case of Binodiram Balchand (supra). This line of reasoning is further approved by the Supreme Court in Aluminium Corporation of India Ltd. v. CIT [1972] 86 ITR 11 ; J.K. Woollen Mfrs. v. CIT [1962] 72 ITR 612 and in the case of CIT v. Walchand & Co. (P.) Ltd. [1967] 65 ITR 381 and the Supreme Court reiterated this principle of commercial expediency, for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of business; and in adjudging the reasonableness of the expenditure from the point of view of business and not of the revenue.

Similarly, the Calcutta High Court in Calcutta Landing & Shipping Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) held that payment made to employees in the expectation of creating impetus or to encourage them to put in selfless work for the employer is a payment made of commercial consideration and commercial expediency. In the same stride, the Madras High Court in CIT v. Deccan Sugars & Abkhari & Co. Ltd. [1986] 157 ITR 467 /[1987] 33 Taxman 28 allowed the loss suffered by its employees’ cooperative stores from the taxable income of the assessee by holding that running of the stores was a welfare measure which the assessee had to undertake to keep the workmen contended and, hence, the expenditure should be taken to be "for the purpose of the assessee’s business".

again a segment of such bundled transaction need not be tested. No need for the AE to further compensate the company for the services rendered towards brand building of the AE, as the same already stood factored in the pricing adjustment of the contract goods. When segmentation or segregation of a bundled transaction is required, the question of set off and apportionment must be examined realistically and with a pragmatic approach. Each segment of a bundled transaction, should give appropriate reduction/adjustment against other segments of same transaction. Therefore, applying the TNMM, it must be stated that there is no question of TP adjustment on account of AMP expenditure.

Bright Line Test (BLT)

9. The Special Bench (majority view) of the ITAT held in case of LG's Electronics (India)(P.) Ltd. case (supra) that a Bright Line Test is required to be done in case of AMP expenses.

Bright line test draws a line between reasonable and unreasonable AMP expense. Whatever is more than reasonable, it would be treated as excessive and it would be deemed as incurred for the foreign AE. The Special Bench said that if the expense incurred by the Assessee on AMP was higher than what was incurred by an independent entity behaving in a commercially rational manner, than Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) would determine whether the said transaction required re-characterisation. A transaction cannot be recharacterized in a case where an independent enterprise behaving in a commercially rational manner would incur the expenses to the extent the assessee has incurred.

There is no statutory provision in the Act or Rules which holds that it is obligatory that the AMP expenses must and necessarily be subjected to Bright Line Test. In case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Delhi High Court said that BLT test cannot be applied for evaluating AMP expenses under Transfer Pricing provisions. In case of Whirlpool of India Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble High Court went beyond this and said that by validating the Bright Line test, the Special Bench in LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) went beyond Chapter X of the Act. Even international tax jurisprudence and commentaries do not recognise BLT for bifurcation of routine and non-routine expenses.

In nutshell, Bright line test is no more applicable. All the decisions, except LG's, have ruled out the applicability of BLT on AMP expenses.

Economic Ownership v. Legal Ownership

10. There are two types of ownership of a brand, viz., legal ownership and economic ownership. Legal ownership means who owns the brand like Trademark registered, patent owner, etc., whereas the person who gets the economic benefits due to his engagement with product, called as economic owner. Non-routine expenses on AMP should also be attributed to the economic ownership of the brand. As it is the Indian entity which acquires the economic ownership of brand and then exploits it for making more and more sales in India, those should also be allowed in its hands. A part of the AMP expenses incurred in India can be construed as leading only to the building of the economic ownership of a foreign brand, which vests solely with the Indian assessee.

Economic ownership is accepted in International Taxation in cases where contracts for goods or services are long-term. Though the assessee-company may not be legal owner of the brand but its revenue will increase in future due to AMP expenses. In other words, certainly the entity which incurs the AMP expenses will get economic benefit in future. In substance, economic ownership is existing in the world. It is up to the company who incurs the expenses that has to prove such future economic benefits.

It was also acknowledged in aforesaid Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra)that even if marketing intangible is created as a consequence of non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the Indian entity, the economic ownership of such intangibles vested in the Indian entity, which could exploit the same for furthering its business interest.

Sales Promotion (After Sales) expenses

11. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to distributors, wholesellers or retailers are not in the nature and character of brand promotion. These types of expenses are called as selling expenses & being incurred for doing high volume of sales or cash flow purposes. There is no motive of publicity or advertisement behind these types of expenses.

The expenses which are incurred after sales, are nowhere related to brand building. These cannot be part of AMP expenses. Same has been reiterated in all Judicial pronouncements, including in LG's Electronics India (P.) Ltd's case (supra). Even Special Bench of the ITAT in case of LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), agreed with that sale related expenses, i.e., trade discount, volume rebate, cash discount, commissions, etc., should be excluded while computing the T.P. Adjustment for AMP expenses. Trade discount or volume discount are related to price of product rather than brand building.

In summary, expenses which are incurred after sales, cannot be a part of AMP expenses.

Benefit to Foreign Legal Owner: Incidental or intentional

HC overrules Special Bench's ruling of ITAT on treatment of AMP expenses

Nilesh Patel

IRS (Ex), US CPA

Background

1. Consider the scenario: An Indian Company (IndCo) is Associated Enterprise (AE) of a Foreign Manufacturer. The Foreign Manufacturer manufactures branded consumer goods. Those goods - bearing the brand name, trademark or logo of the Foreign Manufacturer - are imported by IndCo and are sold in the Indian Market. Thus, IndCo acts as a Distributor of goods manufactured by its Foreign AE. In course of distributing the branded goods IndCo also markets those goods; IndCo incurs advertising, marketing and promotion (AMP) expenses, in addition to the regular selling and distribution expenses. The AMP expenses are paid to uncontrolled third parties (non-AEs) and are allowable under section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Following Transfer Pricing issues arise in this case –

(i)

Is IndCo rendering brand-building services to the Foreign Manufacturer AE, in addition to distributing goods manufactured by the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(ii)

Is IndCo creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign Manufacturer AE, by promoting the latter's brand name, trademark and logo in India?

(iii)

Does incurring of AMP expenses by IndCo give rise to an International Transaction between IndCo and the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(iv)

If the answer to question iii above is in the affirmative, then how do we determine the arm's length price of the International Transaction?

The above issues have arisen in a number of cases before the Transfer Pricing Officers. The matter has travelled to the ITAT. In January, 2013, the Special Bench of the ITAT pronounced its verdict in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi).

Later on, in the case of BMW India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 146 ITD 165/[2013] 37 taxmann.com 319 (Delhi – Trib.), the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable to licensed manufacturers but not to distributors. Then, in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Casio India Co. Ltd. [2014] 43 taxmann.com 56/62 SOT 110 (Delhi – Trib.) the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable not only to licensed manufacturers but also to distributors. Now, on the issue, the Delhi High Court has recently delivered its Judgment in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi), a judgment that has brought much needed clarity.

This article analyses and examines the Transfer Pricing issues emerging out of AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributors, in light of the Delhi High Court's Judgment in the above mentioned case. Let us take a look at what the Special Bench held in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra).

Case of L.g. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.

2. In this Case the Special Bench of the ITAT held as follows:–

Incurring of AMP expenses by an Indian AE needs to be bifurcated into routine and non-routine (excess or abnormal) AMP expenses. The routine AMP expenses are incurred for the Indian Entity's own business purposes to achieve its own sales targets and to grow its market share. But the non-routine AMP expenses are incurred for creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand, trademark, logo, embedded in the product), in India by way of brand-building or brand-promotion.

If it is found that the Indian Entity has incurred non-routine AMP expenses – in excess of routine AMP expenses – then it can be inferred that the Indian Entity has provided brand-building services to its Foreign AE. That will be an International Transaction covered by the Transfer Pricing Regulations.

The arm's length price of such an International Transaction can be worked out by Cost Plus Method, i.e., by applying an arm's length markup to the non-routine AMP expenses. That price would be the arm's length remuneration which the Indian Entity should recover from the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand) for brand-building services, or for creating marketing intangibles.

A question that arises here is: how to determine whether the Indian Entity has, or has not, incurred non-routine AMP expenses? To make such determination a Bright Line Test should be applied.

Shubham Jain

CA

Introduction

Advertisement, Marketing & Promotional (AMP) expenditure is an expenditure incurred by the company in order to increase the sales of the company by creating awareness of the company and its products/services among the numerous customers. AMP expenditure covers various components as mentioned below :—

(1)

Sales Expenditure like discounts, salesman commissions etc.

(2)

Advertisement expenditure like banners, brand ambassador expenses etc.

However, from transfer pricing perspective where AMP expenditure is incurred by associated enterprise of a foreign company, such AMP expenditure has been a matter of long time litigation as Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) considers AMP as an international transaction by invoking Section 92CA(2A) of the Income Tax Act,1961 and make adjustment on account of AMP expenditure in the hands of AE.

Cause of Litigation

AMP expenditure by AE in order to increase sales is recharacterized by TPO as amount incurred by India AE toward creation of marketing intangible (brand) of foreign company in India i.e, Indian entity has rendered services of brand creation to foreign company , therefore such Indian company shall be compensated from foreign company on Cost plus mark-up basis.

Computation of Adjustment by TPO

There are two approaches followed by TPO in order to compute adjustment amount on account of AMP expenditure :-

(1) Substantive Approach

Under substantive approach, TPO simply computes total amount of AMP expenditure and add mark-up upon that , resultant figure is the amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian AE.

(2) Protective Approach

Under protective approach, TPO applies Bright Line Test (BLT) method. Under BLT method, Indian companies belong to same industry of AE are identified and excess AMP expenditure incurred by AE is computed [ (AMP of AE/Sales of AE) – (Avg AMP of Indian comparable/Sales of Comparable). Such excess AMP expenditure along with mark-up is the adjustment amount in the hands of AE.

Adjustment amount as per substantive approach is always more in comparison to adjustment amount as per protective approach.

Contention of Taxpayer against AMP adjustment

(1)

There is no such agreement between Indian AE and foreign entity to create brand and incur AMP expenditure for foreign entity, therefore, in absence of any agreement , such transaction shall not be considered as an international transaction.

(2)

Bright Line Test method adopted by TPO is neither a permissible method under Indian Tax Laws nor prescribed under section 92C of the Income Tax Act,1961 read with Rule 10B of the Income Tax Rule, 1962.

(3)

Economic owner of such brand is AE.

(4)

AMP expenditure incurred to increase sales and therefore it is a domestic transaction and TPO has no jurisdiction over non international transaction

(5)

While computing AMP adjustment, Selling expenditure and amount reimburse from foreign AE shall be reduced from the amount of AMP expenditure incurred.

Landmark Judicial Judgements

(1) Sony Mobile Communications (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 312 (Delhi - Trib.)

The Hon'ble ITAT New Delhi Bench, I-2 in the aforementioned case held that assessee was a subsidiary of Sony Ericsson incorporated under the laws of Sweden . It was primarily engaged in business of importing, buying, selling and distribution of wide range of mobile phones in India and providing related post sale support services. During relevant year, assessee incurred huge cost on Advertisement Marketing and Sales Promotion of its mobile phones, TPO opined that expenditure on AMP incurred by assessee was exclusively to promote brand name 'Sony Ericssion' which was owned by AE, TPO thus took a view that expenditure incurred by assessee company was for advantage of its AE and it should have been suitably compensated by AE. He applied bright line test and made certain addition to assessee's ALP. It was undisputed that Sony Ericssion being a new entrant in mobile segment in year under consideration, assessee had to incur huge advertisement expenses to remind general public of its existence in domestic market. Thus, it could be concluded that AMP expenditure was incurred mainly for purpose of increase in sales of mobile phones in India and not for brand building of AE. Moreover, net profit margin declared by assessee was much higher than comparables and, looking from that angle also, there was no merit in transfer pricing adjustment.

(2) Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT (ITA 110/2014)

Amongst many controversial issues involving transfer pricing, the adjustment on account of marketing intangibles is certainly one of the most litigated and controversial, with enormous stakes involved at either side. As a brief recap, in January 2013 the Special Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("SB"), in the case of LG India Electronics (P)Ltd.1 ("LG SB Ruling") had adjudicated that the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ("AMP") expenditure incurred by the Indian AE is an international transaction, to the extent such AMP expense, as a percentage of turnover, exceeds that of the comparable companies (The concept of pegging AMP to industry standard is typically referred to as 'Bright Line Test'or "BLT"). While so concluding, the SB observed that the incurring of non-routine or excess AMP by the Indian taxpayer is in the nature of providing brand building service to the brand owners i.e. AE and consequently up-held adjustment for such excess AMP expenditure to the Indian taxpayer along with an arm's length mark-up. The LG SB ruling, was hailed as one of the most significant wins of the revenue in a transfer pricing matter, and the principles of the ruling were followed in a plethora of cases involving marketing intangibles resulting in billions of dollars of transfer pricing adjustments. Apparently, the issue, per se, travelled to the High Court against the decision of the division benches who had merely applied the ratio of the ruling of the Special Bench, being at the detriment of the appellant taxpayers.

Recently, the Delhi High Court ("Delhi HC" or "HC") in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communication Private Limited2, and several other connected matters3, adjudicated on the issue of marketing intangibles and upheld the transfer pricing officer's jurisdiction to AMP expenditure, as an international transaction. Further, ruling in favour of the taxpayer, the High Court held that the legal principles, commercial logic and methodology relied and accepted by the tribunal in LG SB Ruling (Supra) as erroneous and unacceptable. The 142 page HC ruling is a pleasure to read, as it paves its way into intricate details of various aspects of AMP adjustments and discusses the principles of brand building versus AMP, economic ownership, aggregated versus segregated approach of benchmarking, OECD guidelines, Indian law and the methodologies adopted for determination of ALP in relation to marketing intangibles. Enumerated below are some of the key findings of the Delhi HC.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the Revenue

TPO can adjudicate on international transactions which are not reported in Form 3CEB

Pursuant to retrospective amendment4 by the Finance Act, 2012, the TPO is empowered to adjudicate on the transactions which have not been reported by the taxpayer in the Form 3CEB. No specific reference by the Assessing Officer (AO) is required for the same.

AMP expense constitute an international transaction

The HC rejected the contention of the taxpayer that AMP is not an international transaction and is outside the scope of transfer pricing provisions. In this regard, the HC observed that dispute pertains to adequacy of the compensation received by the Indian taxpayer for incurring and performing marketing and 'non-routine' AMP expense in India. By virtue of application of the TP provisions, the TPO seeks to determine an arm's length compensation for the marketing and distribution functions performed by the taxpayer towards related parties. In summary, the AMP expense is an international transaction which is covered under the realms of transfer pricing.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the taxpayers

Aggregation of transactions and application of Transactional Net Margin Method

The HC held that the usage of words "an international transaction" in section 92(1) should not be read restrictively rather its interpretation should be gathered from other section and the Rules, whereby it would be amply clear that the legislative intent was to allow clubbing of closely linked transactions, which includes continuous transactions. However, close linkage of transactions is a pre-condition for aggregation. On the same logic, the HC held that distribution and marketing are intertwined and may be examined as bundled/inter-connected transactions. The HC also observed that in case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no prohibition in applying Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) on an entity wide basis, which follows that AMP function can be looked as closely linked to and a part of overall marketing and distribution activity, whereof it can be aggregated under the realms of TNMM.

Referral fees - Assessee had paid referral fee to its AEs with respect to revenue earned by assessee on property transaction referred to it by its AE, such expenditure was to be allowed [CIT v. Cushman & Wakefield India (P.) Ltd. [2015] 60 taxmann.com 168/233 Taxman 250 (Delhi)].

SEBI fees - Authorisation fee paid by assessee-bank to SEBI was allowable as business expenditure [CIT v. Vysya Bank Ltd. [2009] 313 ITR 315 (Kar.)].

Amount of registration fee paid to SEBI was allowable as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Joint Venture of MCL & MMCL (AOP) [2015] 55 taxmann.com 56/229 Taxman 527 (Guj.); CIT v. J. M. Financial Securities (P.) Ltd. [2016] 72 taxmann.com 286/241 Taxman 551 (Bom.)].

Travancore Titanium Products Ltd. [2010] 187 Taxman 81 (Ker.)].

Stock exchange membership fees - Subscription fee paid by share broking company for obtaining membership in NSE was capital expenditure [Abhipra Capital Ltd. v. DCIT [2018] 91 taxmann.com 101/254 Taxman 19 (Delhi)].

Salary/wages for training period - The salaries and wages paid to the employees for the period of the training in the courses organised by the Central Board of Workers' Education should be allowed as admissible deductions while computing the income of the employers.—Letter : F. No. 27(30)-IT/59, dated 6-7-1959.

Membership fees - The expenditure by way of membership fee of the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade can be said to be wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business of the members. Therefore, such expenditure may be allowed as admissible deduction under section 37(1) in the hands of the payers in computing their total income from business.—Letter : F. No. 9/54/64-IT(A-I), dated 2-9-1964 and Letter : F. No. 9/56/66-IT(A-I), dated 17-1-1967.

The expenditure by way of membership fee of the Indian Institute of Packaging can be said to be wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business of the members. Laga contribution - Where laga contribution is made at the customary rate prevalent in the market, such contribution should be allowed in full in the assessment of the member-contributors.—Circular : No. 5-P(XIV-I), dated 28-9-1963.

Share listing expenses - Expenses incurred by a company on getting its shares listed in a stock exchange should be considered as laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business and, therefore, admissible as business expenditure under section 37(1).—Letter : F. Professional tax - Professional tax paid by a person carrying on a business or trade can be allowed to him as a deduction under section 37(1).—Circular : No. 16, dated 18-9-1969.

Payments under profit-sharing scheme - Where the payments made under a profit-sharing scheme are bona fide and not merely a device to reduce tax liability and the sums have actually been paid to the employees, the amounts may be treated to have been expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the employer's business.—Circular : No. 64(XI-2), dated 27-10-1951.

Rebate/bonus to members by Consumer Co-operative stores - Rebate or bonus (which is in the nature of deferred discount) passed on by the consumer co-operative stores to their members on the value of the purchases made by them during a year should be allowed as a deduction in computing the business income of such a society.—Circular : No. 117, dated 22-8-1973.

Remuneration paid by company to Registrar - Reasonable remuneration paid by a company to its Registrar for performing duties in connection with the company's legal obligations to be discharged under the company law should be regarded as revenue expenditure provided the company is not itself maintaining a separate organization for the performance of such duties.—Letter : [F. No. 10/25/63-IT(A-I)], dated 18-6-1964.

Expenses allowable to Indian authors/writers - In cases of Indian authors/writers where the amount receivable from royalties/writings are less than Rs. 25,000 and where detailed accounts regarding expenses incurred are not maintained, claims of expenses to the extent of 25 per cent of such amount or Rs. 5,000, whichever is less, may be allowed in the year of publication of a book or other publication including articles. The expenses to the extent mentioned above will be allowable without calling for any evidence in support of the claim. This circular will not, however, be available in cases of such authors/writers who are included in the terms of film artistes being story writers, screen-play writers and dialogue writers if they are engaged in their professional capacity in the production of cinematograph film.—Letter : F. No. 204/42/77-IT(A-II), dated 28-9-1977.

Royalty/dead rent - Royalty and dead rent paid under the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 will have to be allowed as revenue deduction.—Circular : No. 1-D(IV-53), dated 20-1-1966.

Expenses on sales tax assessments/appeals - The expenses incurred in original proceedings for assessment to sales tax as also in appeals arising from such proceedings should be allowed as a deduction in income-tax assessments—Circular : No. 2, dated 8-3-1946.

30.5.2-3 "Ownership of assets" - Depreciation shall be allowed only on the assets owned by the assessee, partly or wholly. The following points are noteworthy:

Ownership does not mean legal ownership.

If the assessee has possession of immovable property purchased by him but sale the sale deed is not registered in the assessee's name, the assessee can be considered owner under section 32.

In a landmark judgment in Mysore Minerals Ltd. v. CIT [1999] 106 Taxman 166 (SC), the Supreme Court held that to claim de-preciation, the assessee doesn't need to be the registered owner of the assets. Exclusive possession rights, to exclude others from enjoyment of assets, right to retain possession and defend the same are some of the characteristics of ownership which would entitle the assessee to depreciation under section 32 (so long as it was used for carrying on business or profession).

In Tata Electric Companies (AOP) v. Jt. CIT [ITA No. 2330/Mum./2001] (17-10-2006) (unreported), the Tribunal consid­ered the issue of 'ownership' of asset for claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Act in the light of various Apex Court decisions on the subject and beautifully extracted the law in this regard at para 21 of the Order : "... the substantial de facto ownership of an asset is to be looked into, rather than examining the religious de jure owner­ship of the asset.......... In a case where the transfer of property was contemplated by an agreement and thereafter, the physical delivery of the property was handed over and the property was used for the business of the assessee and thereafter, even if delayed, the transaction was concluded by executing the rele­vant conveyance and documents, then in such circumstances, the ownership of the asset must be considered as having been trans­ferred from the date of actual delivery of the asset. ..... in such circumstances, where the contract has been lawfully executed, ....the validity of the registered documents go back to the date of de facto transfer of ownership of the asset. This liberal principle has been upheld by the Supreme Court ...".

Sub-stantial de facto ownership is sufficient. De jure ownership (or legal ownership) is not required. This definition of ownership perfectly accords with the accounting definition of asset which stresses on 'Control' rather than legal ownership.

Thus, depreciation is available to the lessee in respect of assets acquired under a finance lease/hire-purchase.

Where the assessee-company has made payment for acquisition of cars and qualifies as beneficial owner, it was entitled to depreciation, RTO expenses and insurance charges in respect of cars even though registered in name of directors. Training charges to customer

12.8-1 Training charges to customer will be includible if they are in connection with sale or by reason of sale. If the transaction of providing training to employees of customer is an independent transaction, it may be 'in relation to sale', but not 'in connection with sale'.

Training charges are not includible in assessable value - CCE v. Real Time Systems (2009) 237 ELT 289 (CESTAT).

Liquidated damages for late delivery or breach of contract payable/receivable

12.8-2 Liquidated damages may be either payable or receivable by assessee.

Liquidated damages payable - Some contracts make provision for liquidated damages where an amount is deducted if delivery is not effected in time or some other condition of contract is violated. 'Transaction Value' means the price actually paid or payable for goods. It includes any amount payable by buyer at the time of the sale or at any other time. Thus since the amount of 'liquidated damages' is not 'payable' by buyer to assessee at all, it can be argued that 'transaction value' should be calculated only after deducting the liquidated damages, i.e. it should be allowed as deduction. Counter argument can be that 'full amount' is 'payable' though actual amount paid is less on account of deduction by way of penalty. Thus, effectively, full amount is 'paid' and deduction has nothing to do with value of goods.

In United Telecom Ltd. v. CCE (2006) 204 ELT 626 (CESTAT), price was reduced by customer for late delivery of goods. It was held that such compensation paid to buyer is liquidated damages and not in nature of penalty. It will be allowable as deduction and duty paid in excess is refundable. It was held that ratio of decisions under old section 4 cannot be made applicable to new section 4 which has come into effect from 1-7-2000 - followed in CCE v. HFCL (2008) 231 ELT 307 (CESTAT).

This view has been confirmed in CCE v. Victory Electricals Ltd. (2014) 43 GST 649 = 42 taxmann.com 215 = 298 ELT 534 (CESTAT LB), where it was held that after such liquidated damages (even if termed as penalty), the transaction value is reduced. Excise duty is payable on such lower value only - followed in CCE v. HFCL (Wireless Division) (2014) 46 GST 664 = 47 taxmann.com 171 (CESTAT).
