Where the assessee-company had made payments to his partner to ward-off competition and to protect its existing business since said rights acquired by the assessee would not only give enduring benefit, but also protected assessee's business against competition, it could be covered under expression 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' used in Explanation 3 to section 32(1)(ii) and, thus, the assessee was eligible for depreciation.

it was held that the expression ‘similar’ is a significant expression. It does not mean identical but it means corresponding to or resembling to in many respects; somewhat like; or having a general likeness’. Hence a business or commercial right will be covered only if it is corresponding to or resembling to any one of the preceding assets in many respects. Thus, it appears that trade name is similar to trademark and hence a trade name should be considered as an intangible asset within the definition of block of assets. 2.2-10a Whether goodwill is covered by the expression of ‘Business or commercial right of similar nature’ ? - According to one view, the expression ‘Business or commercial right of similar nature’ suggests rights which are legally enforceable and separable from the business itself. However, goodwill being a right which is attached with the business and which cannot be separated from the business itself, it should not be reckoned as a business or commercial right of similar nature.

Even otherwise, it appears that having regard to the meaning of the term goodwill, it may not be covered by the expression in all cases. In R.C.Cooper v. UOI AIR 1970 SC 564, it was observed as follows :

“Goodwill is that component of the total value of the undertaking which is attributable to the ability of the concern to earn profits over a course of years or in excess of normal amounts because of its reputation, location and other features : Trego v. Hunt [1896] AC 7 (HL). Goodwill of an undertaking therefore is the value of the attraction to customers arising from the name and reputation for skill, integrity, efficient business management, or efficient service.”

In CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294 (SC), it was observed as follows (p. 298) :

“Goodwill denotes the benefit arising from connection and reputation. A variety of elements goes into its making, and its composition varies in different trades and in different business in the same trade, and while one element many preponderate in one business, another may dominate in another business.

Its value may fluctuate from one moment to another depending on changes in the reputation of the business. It is affected by everything relating to the business, the personality and business rectitude of the owners, the nature and character of the business, its name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio-economic ecology, introduction to old customers and agreed absence of competition. There can be no account in value of the factors producing it”.

In CED v. Kanta Devi Taneja [1981] 132 ITR 437(Gau.) it was held as follows:

“Broadly speaking, it is the magnetic quality of a particular trade or business which attracts customers to it as a matter of course. This quality springs from and is developed by various contributing factors that earn a reputation for honest dealing, quality and standard. Goodwill is founded on the belief and faith of the customer. It is commonly built up in relation to a particular type of manufacture or production of articles identified by a trademark which becomes widely known to the public and by which the customers take it for granted that it represents what they wish for. No trademark gains reputation overnight. Naturally, the standing of the business is necessarily one of the contributing factors. The personalities who are engaged in the business, the location in which it is carried on and the like are other features which go into the goodwill. Where a business involves no distinguishable features and deals in standard articles manufactured by someone else which one can get from anywhere, not merely from a particular dealer, there is hardly any possibility of there being a goodwill attached to such business”.

In Permanent Edition of Words and Phrases, it is mentioned that

◆ A ‘trade-mark’ symbolizes business goodwill.

◆ A ‘trade-mark’ and ‘goodwill’ are similar and analogous and indicate favour which community holds for a certain commodity.

From the above, it appears that it cannot be generalised that goodwill is similar to the other intangible assets. For example, if the predominant element of goodwill is location or contacts with customers then these elements not being similar to the preceding assets in the definition of block of assets, it may not be possible to claim that goodwill is covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’. On the other hand, if the predominant element of goodwill is trademark then it could be argued that goodwill is covered by the expression.

2.2-10b Non-compete payment-whether covered by the definition - Another type of payment made is ‘non-compete payment’, that is, payment to another person in consideration of his agreeing not to compete with the payer. Having regard to the nature of the payment, it is perhaps not in the nature of the acquisition of an asset which is a precondition for grant of depreciation. In any case it may increase the value of goodwill (see definition of ‘goodwill’ as explained in Srinivasa Setty’s case, reproduced above) and if goodwill itself cannot be considered as an intangible asset, the non-compete payment also cannot be considered so.

In CED v. Kanta Devi Taneja [1981] 132 ITR 437(Gau.) it was held as follows:

"Broadly speaking, it is the magnetic quality of a particular trade or business which attracts customers to it as a matter of course. This quality springs from and is developed by various contributing factors that earn a reputation for honest dealing, quality and standard. Goodwill is founded on the belief and faith of the customer. It is commonly built up in relation to a particular type of manufacture or production of articles identified by a trademark which becomes widely known to the public and by which the customers take it for granted that it represents what they wish for. No trademark gains reputation overnight. Naturally, the standing of the business is necessarily one of the contributing factors. The personalities who are engaged in the business, the location in which it is carried on and the like are other features which go into the goodwill. Where a business involves no distinguishable features and deals in standard articles manufactured by someone else which one can get from anywhere, not merely from a particular dealer, there is hardly any possibility of there being a goodwill attached to such business".

While the expression ‘any other business or commercial rights’ is very wide, it is qualified by the words ‘of similar nature’. Hence, all types of business or commercial rights will not be covered by the definition of block of assets but only those which are similar in nature to the preceding assets, namely know-how, patent, copyright, etc., will be covered by the expression intangible assets. In New Steel Equipment Pvt. Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise AIR 1988 SC 631 it was held that the expression ‘similar’ is a significant expression. It does not mean identical but it means corresponding to or resembling to in many respects; somewhat like; or having a general likeness’. Hence a business or commercial right will be covered only if it is corresponding to or resembling to any one of the preceding assets in many respects. Thus, it appears that trade name is similar to trademark and hence a trade name should be considered as an intangible asset within the definition of block of assets.

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

Provision to be reasonably interpreted - Since the object and purpose of granting additional depreciation is to encourage industries by permitting assessee setting up new undertaking installation of new plant and machinery, therefore, provisions are required to be interpreted reasonably and purposively as strict and literal reading would lead to an absurd result denying additional depreciation to assessee though admittedly assessee had installed new plant and machinery. In the present case, assessee has purchased the plant and machinery before 1-4-2005 but the same has been installed after 1-4-2005, additional depreciation could not be denied [PCIT v. IDMC Ltd. The provision does not state that setting up of a new machinery or plant should have any operational connectivity to article or thing that was already being manufactured by assessee. Betterment charges - Betterment charges on account of increase in the valuation of the land of the assessee should not be held as a revenue expenditure although general improvement of the area might have an impact on better running of the business [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 63 Taxman 493 (SC)].

Business expansion - The nature of the new business is not a decisive test for determining whether or not there is an expansion of an existing business. The nature of the business could be as distinct as a jewellery business and a business of cinematographic films; it could be as different as manufacture of metal alloys and manufacture of rubber products. What is of importance is that the control of both the ventures, the existing venture as well as the new venture, must be in the hands of one establishment or management or administration. The place of business of the existing business and the new business may not be in close proximity - it could be as far apart as Baroda and Bangalore. However, the funds utilised for the management of both the concerns must be common as reflected in the balance sheet of the company [Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. CIT [2008] 166 Taxman 55 (Delhi)].

Expenditure in connection with expansion of existing business would be allowed as revenue expenditure notwithstanding that same have been capitalised in the books of account [CIT v. Nirma Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 125/229 Taxman 535 (Guj.)]. However, where expenditure incurred by assessee for expansion of business had no nexus with business carried on by assessee, same held to be not allowable [United Breweries Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 8/229 Taxman 113 (Kar.)].

Business exploration expenses - Where the assessee, had paid a sum of Rs. 75 lakhs to management consultants, as professional fees for assessment of market attractiveness of assessee's business in terms of gaining global market, evaluation of assessee's business ability to compete, analysis of business's future growth trend, and development of detailed business strategies for the assessee to grow in the dynamic business environment, the said payment was fully deductible as revenue expenditure, since the assessee, with an intention of bringing about improvements in the way it did its business, had sought for and obtained reports of the consultant [CIT v. Carborandum Universal Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 347 (Mad.)].

Expenditure incurred by assessee on market survey report obtained during course of business activities of assessee for exploring further business is allowable [CIT v. Nuchem Ltd. [2015] 59 taxmann.com 455 (P&H)].

Decree to protect property/name - Payment by assessee to satisfy decree passed by the High Court against it in order to protect its property and name is allowable as business expenditure [CIT v. Hitachi Koki India Ltd. [2015] 56 taxmann.com 8/230 Taxman 643 (Kar.)].

However, the term shall not include the goodwill of a business or profession

The scope of the words "Other similar business or commercial rights" also fell for consideration before the Delhi High Court in Sharp Business System v. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 50/211 Taxman 576 (Delhi). The issue before the Court was whether non-compete fee paid to ex-JV partner under a non-compete agreement for 7 years was 'intangible asset' eligible for depreciation. The Court held that in personam rights such as non-compete fees are not depreciable intangible assets u/s 32(1)(ii). Depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) is admissible only to those intangible assets which give exclusive rights to the owner, which can be asserted against the world at large - i.e. in rem. A non-compete agreement can be asserted only in personam against the other party to the non-compete agreement. Hence, non-compete fee is not a depreciable intangible asset u/s 32(1)(ii). The Court analysed section 32(1)(ii) as under:

As would be evident from section 32(1)(ii), depreciation can be allowed in respect of intangible assets.

Par-liament has spelled out the nature of such assets by express reference to "know-how," "patents," "copyrights," "trademarks," "licenses," and "franchises."

So far as patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses and franchises are concerned, though they are intangible assets, the law recognises through various enactments that specific intellectual property rights flow from them.

Li-censes are derivative and often confer such intellectual property rights. The enjoyment of such intellectual property rights implies the exclusion of others who do not own or have a license to such rights from using them in any manner whatsoever.

Similarly, in the matter of franchises and know-how, the primary brand or intellectual process owner owns the exclusive right to produce, retail and distribute the products and the advantages flowing from such brand or intellectual process owner, but for the grant of such know-how rights or franchises.

The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the owner-ship.

In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance "in rem".

However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity.

The right can be asserted in the present instance only against ex-JV partner and in a sense, the right "in personam".

In-deed, the 7 years period spelt-out by the non-competing covenant brings the advantage within the public policy embedded in section 27 of the Contract Act, which enjoins a contract in restraint of trade would otherwise be void.

An-other way of looking at the issue is whether such rights can be treated or transferred – a proposition fully supported by the controlling object clause, i.e. intangible asset.

Every species of right spelt out expressly by the Statute—i.e., intellectual property rights and other advantages such as know-how, franchise, license, etc., and even those considered by the Courts, such as goodwill—can be said to be alienable. Such is not the case with an agreement not to compete, which is purely personal.

The words "similar business or commercial rights" necessarily have to result in an intangible asset against the entire world, which can be asserted as such to qualify for depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) of the Act.

Thus, "Other similar business or commercial rights" would not cover rights of a person's nature. The expression would cover only alienable rights in rem.

GEOGRAPHICAL REPORT - Where the assessee, involved in coal mining, purchased a geographical report and claimed depreciation on the same, since the report was highly technical and was a basic document based on which the assessee got a right to mine apart from assessing the quantity of mineral that could be exploited from said mines, formation of dyke and other technical details, Tribunal was justified to allow depreciation on the geographical report as an intangible asset and by not considering it as an expense under section 35E [CIT v. Integrated Coal Mining Ltd. [2022] 142 taxmann.com 44 (Calcutta)]

EX-PENSES INCURRED IN OBTAINING A CONCESSION AGREEMENT FROM THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION - Where the assessee entered into a concession agreement with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and incurred certain expenses towards legal, technical, and management fees to obtain the agreement, the assessee was entitled to depreciation on expenses incurred since the assessee had acquired business and commercial rights and licenses by making payments which were in the nature of intangible assets. [Bangalore International Airport Ltd. v. DCIT [2023] 146 tax-mann.com 206 (Karnataka)]

COST INCURRED TOWARDS ACQUIRING A LEASEHOLD RIGHT - Where the assessee incurred cost towards acquiring a leasehold right which constituted an intangible right, the cost incurred towards acquiring the leasehold right would be eligible for depreciation [Bangalore International Airport Ltd. v. DCIT [2023] 146 taxmann.com 206 (Karnataka)]

JCIT(OSD) [2023] 157 taxmann.com 106 (Ahmedabad - Trib.)]

Daikin Shri Ram Aircon (P.) Ltd [2023] 146 taxmann.com 465 (Delhi]

PUR-CHASE OF IP RIGHTS SUCH AS BRAND NAME, LOGO, PATENT AND TRADE-MARKS - Where the assessee purchased the business of one 'SAL' against payment which included intellectual property rights (IP rights) such as brand name, logo, patent and trademarks and claimed depreciation on IP rights, as there was no doubt raised by revenue with respect to payment of consideration to SAL, ownership of IP rights of the assessee stood proved and it was entitled to depreciation as claimed [Commissioner of Income-tax v. Daikin Shri Ram Aircon (P.) Ltd. [2023] 146 taxmann.com 465 (Delhi]

CIT [2016] 74 taxmann.com 174 (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. GE Medical Systems (I) (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 79/277 Taxman 315 (Kar.). Salary by HUF - A HUF is allowed to deduct salaries paid to members of the family, if the payment is made as a matter of commercial or business expediency; but the service must be to the family [Jitmal Bhuramal v. CIT [1962] 44 ITR 887 (SC)].

The general view expressed by commentators on Hindu law as well as in decided cases is that even the karta of a family can be paid remuneration for carrying on family business, provided it is under some agreement. If such remuneration is not excessive and is reasonable and is not a device to escape income-tax, then it will be a legitimate deduction in computing the profits of the business. If, on the other hand, the amount paid is unreasonably high and disproportionate to the service rendered by him, then it may be treated as part of the profit of the HUF distributed in a particular manner [Jugal Kishore Baldeo Sahai v. CIT [1967] 63 ITR 238 (SC)].

Salary paid to a coparcener for services rendered to assessee-HUF, where karta was not well due to old age and bad health, is an admissible deduction [Sunderlal Nanalal (HUF) v. CIT [1984] 16 Taxman 3 (Guj.)].

Salary to relatives - Where the assessee-company paid high salaries to the wife and son of its top executive, when the son and wife had neither requisite qualifications nor any experience to discharge the duties entrusted to them, and no internal evidence was produced to substantiate that they rendered services commensurate with high salaries, the said salaries were not deductible as business expenditure [Birla Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1981] 128 ITR 235 (Cal.)].

Where payment of salary to relatives was not found to be wholly or exclusively for purpose of assessee's business, same could not be allowed as deduction [Jayesh Raichand Shah v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 108 (Guj.)].

Secondment cost - Where assessee entered into an agreement with its group company for secondment of employee for management consultancy services on cost to company basis without any mark-up, since TDS was deducted by assessee on payment made with respect to employee's salary and professional fees earned by assessee on account of services rendered by seconded employees was charged to tax, assessee's claim of total secondment cost borne was to be allowed [PCIT v. KKM Management Centre (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 110 (Delhi)].

Speed money payment - Where assessee claimed expenditure towards speed money paid by it to workers on port for speedy completion of work, since payment of speed money was a trade practice which was followed by assessee and similar business concerns for speedy completion of their work, same was to be allowed [Sri Ganesh Shipping Agency v. Asstt. CIT [2021] 128 taxmann.com 106/281 Taxman 637 (Kar.)].

Others - Where it was found that the presentation of wrist watches was in the nature of an incentive to encourage the employees to attend work punctually and was incurred also to keep the employees happy and to earn their goodwill towards the company as an employer, the expenditure on account of such presentation to the employees was an expenditure wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of its business [CIT v. Hayward Waldia Refinery Ltd. [1995] 78 Taxman 558 (Cal.)].

Where assessee had given phones, etc., to its employees, dealers, etc., ownership had been transferred to employees, dealers, sales personnel and after-sales-service centres, and mobile phones were not to be returned to assessee, cost of mobile phones was held to be business expenditure [PCIT v. Nokia India (P.) Ltd. [2018] 98 taxmann.com 415 (Delhi)].

Cost of production not recovered - Where assessee had not recovered cost of its production to compute income or loss of relevant AY as per Rule 9A(3), the AO had to take into account number of days for which film was commercially exhibited and then allow deduction for cost of production of film to extent of collections made during period of exhibition only and balance cost of production was to be amortized, to be allowed as deduction in next year [CIT v. Joseph Valakuzhy [2008] 170 Taxman 196 (SC)].

28.4

Commercial Training or Coaching Service

Tax on commercial training or coaching service was introduced with effect from 1-7-2003. This service will be taxable under new provisions also.

However, in case of coaching upto Higher Secondary School, there is no requirement that such service should be recognised by any law. Hence, a clear view is possible that even private coaching for students upto HSC level is not subject to service tax (admittedly a litigation prone issue).

28.4-1 Value of taxable service of commercial training

Donations received is not consideration for service - Donations and grants-in-aid received by charitable institution received from different sources for conducting training courses is not 'consideration received' for coaching service provided - MF(DR) circular No. 127/9/2010-ST dated 16-8-2010.

Amount payable to franchisor is also part of value of service - In M Power v. CCE (2012) 35 STT 282 = 20 taxmann.com 589 (CESTAT), assessee was paying 20% of fees to franchisor and paying service tax on 80% amount retained by him. It was held that service tax is payable on entire amount.

Books supplied by the Institute - In case of commercial training and coaching institutes, deduction will be available only to the sale value of standard text books, which are priced. Any study material or written text provided by the institute will be subjected to service tax, i.e. it will not be allowable as deduction - CBE&C circular No. 59/8/2003 dated 20-6-2003.

Though this circular stands withdrawn w.e.f. 19-4-2006 vide MF(DR) circular No. B1/4/2006-TRU dated 19-4-2006, in my view, the principle is still valid.

In Soni Classes v. CCE (2013) 29 taxmann.com 308 (CESTAT), it was held that study material, test papers etc. as part of coaching services is includible in taxable value. However, sale of purchased books is not includible.

In Chate Coaching Classes P Ltd. v. CCC (2013) 58 VST 55 (CESTAT), it has been held that the material supplied need not be 'standard text book', as that expression has not been used in the exemption notification (used only in CBE&C circular). Hence, if any book is supplied, its deduction will be allowable (In this case it book was printed by another company in the same groups)- following Pinnacle v. CCE (2011) 53 VST 433 (CESTAT) * Mastermind Classes v. CCE (2016) 53 GST 398 = 65 taxmann.com 112 (CESTAT).

In Chate Coaching Classes P Ltd. v. CCC (2013) 39 STT 545 = 27 taxmann.com 160 = 58 VST 55 (CESTAT), it has been held that the material supplied need not be 'standard text book', as that expression has not been used in the exemption notification (used only in CBE&C circular). Hence, if any book is supplied, its deduction will be allowable (In this case its book was printed by another company in the same groups) - following Pinnacle v. CCE (2011) 53 VST 433 (CESTAT) - confirmed in CCE v. Pinnacle (2013) 59 VST 466 (P&H HC DB) * Mastermind Classes v. CCE (2016) 53 GST 398 = 65 taxmann.com 112 (CESTAT).

In Cerebral Learning Solutions v. CCE (2013) 43 GST 43 = 37 taxmann.com 398 (CESTAT) also, it was held that service tax is not payable on study material and text books supplied and charged separately.

No service tax on mess charges, hostel charges, laptop supplied - There is no service tax on mess charges, hostel charges, laptop supplied to students - I21T (P) Ltd. v. CCE (2013) 43 GST 232 = 38 taxmann.com 142 (CESTAT).

In Ambala Cantt Electric Supply Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1981] 7 Taxman 398/[1982] 133 ITR 343 (Punj. & Har.) the transfer of the assessee's electricity supply undertaking to the State Government had taken place but the as-sets were yet to be valued and the amount of compensation had not yet been determined. The matter of compensation could not be settled amicably and had to be referred to arbitration. The assessee, therefore, continued to retain some staff, till the issue was finally settled. The Court held that payment of compensation was a neces-sary part of the transfer of the undertaking and the maintenance of the staff was necessary to safeguard the interests of the assessee, in order to get the maximum price. Compensation as an incident of the transfer was to be received by the assessee and the expenditure so incurred on the staff was for pursuing the matters with the con-cerned authorities, including arbitration. These expenses could therefore, be deducted under section 48(i).

After closure of business and on sale of land and building the assessee paid retrenchment compensation to workers which was claimed as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer. The Court held that it was not de-ductible while computing capital gains [CIT v. Radio Talkies [1999] 238 ITR 872 (Bom.)].

Restructuring - Where assessee-company had several units engaged in different business, expenditure incurred by assessee on restructuring of said business was to be allowed as deduction [PCIT v. Akzo Noble India Ltd. [2018] 94 taxmann.com 38/256 Taxman 1 (Cal.)]. Expenditure incurred by assessee on shifting of employees to another place consequent on shifting of factory to another site due to labour unrest was allowable as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Bimetal Bearings Ltd. [1994] 210 ITR 945 (Mad.)].

Where assessee-company carrying on business of manufacturing drugs at different units had to close down one of its unit on account of statutory compulsion, expenditure incurred on shifting of manufacturing activity of said unit to other units was to be allowed as deduction [CIT v. Nicholas Piramal (India) Ltd. [2016] 69 taxmann.com 164/239 Taxman 470 (Bom.)].

Software - Payment for application software, though there is an enduring benefit, does not result in acquisition of any capital asset and it merely enhances productivity or efficiency of business of assessee and, hence, it has to be treated as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Title - Where money is paid to perfect a title or as consideration for getting rid of a defect in the title or a threat of litigation, the payment would be capital payment and not revenue payment [V. Jaganmohan Rao v. CIT [1970] 75 ITR 373 (SC)].

CIT [2015] 61 taxmann.com 121/234 Taxman 831 (Cal.)]. Also see, CIT v. Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corporation Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 275 (Bom.), SLP dismissed inCIT v. Expenditure incurred by an Indian AE of a foreign entity on AMP of its products using a foreign trademark/logo does not require any payment or compensation by the owner of the foreign trademark/logo to the domestic entity on account of use of the foreign trademark/logo in the promotion, advertising and marketing undertaken by it, so long as the expenses incurred by the domestic entity do not exceed the expenses which a similarly situated and comparable independent domestic entity would have incurred.

(6) In order to ascertain whether the expenses incurred by an Indian AE of a foreign entity on the marketing, promotion and advertising of its products using the brand trademark/logo of the foreign entity, are more than what a similarly situated and comparable independent domestic entity would have incurred or not, it would be necessary to identify appropriate comparables for the purpose of comparison of their expenditure with the expenditure incurred by the domestic entity. In case if the expenses incurred by an Indian AE are more than what a similarly situated and comparable independent domestic entity would have incurred, the foreign entity needs to suitable compensate the domestic entity in respect of the advantage obtained by it in the form of brand building and increased awareness of its brand in the domestic market. Where the foreign entity is liable to compensate, income arising from such international transaction(s) needs to be determined at ALP taking into consideration all the rights obtained and obligations incurred by the two entities, including the advantage obtained by the foreign entity.

Advertisement expenses when incurred to increase sales of products are usually treated as a revenue expenditure since the memory of purchasers or customers is short. Advertisements are issued from time to time and the expenditure is incurred periodically so that the customers remain attracted and do not forget the product and its qualities. The advertisements published/displayed may not be of relevance or significance after lapse of time in a highly competitive market, wherein the products of different companies compete and are available in abundance. Advertisements and sales promotion are conducted to increase sale and their impact is limited and felt for a short duration. No permanent character or advantage is achieved and is palpable, unless special or specific factors are brought on record. Expenses for advertising consumer products generally are a part of the process of profit earning and not in the nature of capital outlay—CIT v. Monto Motors Ltd. [2012] 206 Taxman 43/19 taxmann.com 57 (Delhi). The expenses, in the present case, were not incurred once and for all, but were a periodical expenses which had to be incurred continuously in view of the nature of the business. It was an on-going expense. Given the factual matrix, it is difficult to hold that the expenses were incurred for setting the profit earning machinery in motion or not for earning profits.

Mere fact that assessee was permitted to use brand name 'Valvoline' of its AE, it would not automatically lead to an inference that any expense incurred towards AMP was only to enhance brand 'Valvoline' particularly when there was no international transaction between assessee and its AE—Valvoline Cummins (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2017] 84 taxmann.com 191 (Delhi).

AMP expenses incurred by assessee could not be termed as an international transaction particularly when there was nothing on record to show that assessee by incurring AMP expenses wanted to promote brand of its AE and there was no agreement for sharing AMP expenses—PCIT v. Amadeus India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 145 taxmann.com 578 (Del.); PCIT v. Amadeus India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 145 taxmann.com 311/[2023] 290 Taxman 201 (Del.).

Where assessee charged royalty from foreign entity by allowing it to use its brand name, in such a case, even though assessee acquired entire shareholding of said company subsequently, yet unless at entity level there was a complete re-organization so as to result in a complete identity of two concerns, royalty arising out of use of brand name had to be treated as an 'international transaction'—Dabur India Ltd. v. PCIT [2018] 89 taxmann.com 78/253 Taxman 129 (Delhi).

10A.2-3-4 BRIGHT LINE TEST (BLT) - There is nothing in the 1961 Act or the 1962 Rules to hold that it is obligatory that the AMP expenses must and necessarily should be subjected to 'bright line test' and the non-routine AMP expenses as a separate transaction to be computed in the manner as stipulated. Applying 'bright line test' on the basis of certain prescribed parameters would be adding and writing words in the statute and the Rules and introducing a new concept which has not been recognised and accepted in any of the international commentaries or as per the general principles of international taxation accepted and applied universally—Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240/231 Taxman 113 (Delhi).

CIT [1996] 218 ITR 688 (MP)]. Also see, CIT v. Sakthi Textiles Ltd. [2002] 120 Taxman 268 (Mad.).

Expenditure incurred by assessee in respect of health and safety measures for benefit of its employees to foster a safe working environment is revenue expenditure [PCIT v. Holcim Services (South Asia) Ltd. [2018] 93 taxmann.com 270/255 Taxman 392 (Bom.)].

Quality improvement - Where assessee incurred expenditure on product development and the expenditure so incurred did not involve development of a new product or even a new technique or technology to manufacture existing product more efficiently rather it was aimed at improving quality of existing products of assessee, assessee's claim for deduction was to be allowed [CIT v. Arvind Products Ltd. [2018] 93 taxmann.com 454/255 Taxman 472 (Guj.)].

Race club - Where a race club, being open to its members only, had incurred expenses on the maintenance of club house and kiosks, it was heldthat the expenses so incurred were allowable as business expenses of club [Royal Western India Turf Club Ltd. v. CIT [1970] 78 ITR 548 (Bom.)].

Research and development - Where assessee, engaged in business of design, development, manufacture and maintenance of aircrafts and avionics systems, incurred expenditure towards R&D for manufacture of aircrafts which were to be sold, since expenditure was incurred for purpose of business of assessee and, hence, allowed as deduction [Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2021] 125 taxmann.com 80/278 Taxman 266 (Kar.)].

Research and testing - Development charges incurred on research and testing of components should be allowed as revenue expenditure [CIT v. JCB India Ltd. [2016] 71 taxmann.com 30 (Delhi)].

Software development services - Expenditure on development of software is a revenue expenditure and not a capital expenditure [CIT v. Sri Renuga Textiles Mills Ltd. [2012] 26 taxmann.com 108/210 Taxman 244 (Mag.) (Mad.)].

Expenditure incurred on software development services which were in nature of maintenance and support services providing essential backup to assessee, who had procured software for its business purpose, was to be allowed as deduction [PCIT v. Kitchen Express Overseas Ltd. [2018] 89 taxmann.com 407 (Guj.)].

Website development expenses - Where the assessee engaged in travel business developed a website in which details of the various destinations and places for which it could arrange travel/hotel booking etc, were made available to its clients, such a website might provide an enduring benefit to the assessee but nevertheless the intent and purpose behind the website was not to create an asset but only to provide a means for disseminating information about the assessee. The advance of technology and the widespread use of the internet has provided a very powerful medium to companies to publicise their activities to a larger spectrum of people at a much lower cost. Websites enable companies to do what printed brochures did earlier, but in a much more efficient manner as well as in a much shorter period of time and covering a much larger set of people worldwide. Hence expenditure incurred by the assessee on developing a website was allowable as revenue expenditure [CIT v. Indian Visit.com (P.) Ltd. [2009] 176 Taxman 164 (Delhi)].

An employer can restrain an employee from using the data or trade secrets of the employer in his next employment. However, he cannot be restrained from joining other employment - Krishnan Murgai v. Superintendence Co. of India AIR 1979 Del 232.

Conference expenses [Section 115WB(2)(c)]

1.20 This entry deems conference expenses as FBE. However, fees for participation by the employee in any conference shall not be regarded as DFB. Further, for the purposes of this clause, any expenditure on conveyance, tour and travel (including foreign travel), on hotel, or boarding and lodging in connection with any conference shall be deemed to be expenditure incurred for the purposes of conference.

1.20-1 Exclusion -'Conference expenses' does not include any expenditure on fee for participation by the employees in any conference. Thus, the participation fee in respect of a conference organized by an outside entity, is excluded from the purview of fringe benefit tax (external conference expense). As a logical corollary, expenses in respect of conferences organized by employer internally attract fringe benefit tax (internal conference expense).

It may be noted that, on a strict reading, 'External conference expenses', may not include expenditure incurred on conveyance, tour and travel (including foreign travel) or hotel, or boarding and lodging.

1.20-2 Taxable portion - Internal conferences could be training conferences or could be for other purposes (e.g. sales, strategy, marketing, etc.). Any expenditure on 'training conferences' could be deemed to be a 'fringe benefit' under section 115WB(2)(C), since there is a 'benefit' for the employee on account of his training. However, it could be argued that expenditure on other conferences (e.g. sales, strategy, marketing, etc.) may not be covered by this clause since there is no benefit for the employee. (See para 1.17 above)

1.20-3 General Meetings - It appears that a general meeting cannot be considered as a conference.

ALLOWABILITY OF EXPENDITURE

'Being', meaning of - The word 'being' used in section 35D(2)(c)(iv) is not illustrative to mean only those expenses which are specified in the statute could be allowed and nothing further [CIT v. Ennar Steel & Alloy (P.) Ltd. [2004] 137 Taxman 429 (Mad.)].

Advertisement - Advertisement expenditure is an allowable deduction [CIT v. Madras Fertilizers Ltd. [1999] 238 ITR 672 (Mad.); CIT v. Salora International Ltd. [2009] 308 ITR 199 (Delhi)].

Consultancy charges - Expenses incurred towards consultancy charges were for purposes of carrying out existing business more efficiently is not an allowable deduction [CIT v. Gillette Group India (P.) Ltd. [2008] 173 Taxman 52 (Delhi)].

Convertible notes - Expenditure incurred on convertible premium notes is an allowable deduction [CIT v. Dhampur Sugar Mills Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 94/[2014] 226 Taxman 24 (Mag.) (All.)].

Expanding production capacity - Expenditure for expanding production capacity of vehicles held to be an allowable deduction [CIT v. Ashok Leyland Ltd. [2012] 23 taxmann.com 50/ [2013] 213 Taxman 204 (Mad.)].

Incorporation expenses - Expenses incurred by assessee's holding company relating to formation of assessee-company is not an allowable deduction [Cairn Energy (India) Ltd. v. JCIT [2008] 171 Taxman 54 (Mad.)].

Interest - Where there was no inextricable link between investment and project, interest income on said investment could not be permitted to be adjusted against pre-operative expenses in respect of said project [CIT v. Indian Vaccines Corporation Ltd. [2014] 44 taxmann.com 130/222 Taxman 207 (Mag.) (Delhi)]. However, where production had not yet been started and assessee kept available funds in FDRs for obtaining letter of credit required to import machineries, in such a case, interest income was liable to be adjusted against pre-operative cost of plant and machinery [Phoenix Lamps India Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 50 taxmann.com 320/[2015] 228 Taxman 306 (Mag.) (All.)].

Lease rent - Lease rent incurred before commencement of production held not to be an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Ennar Steel & Alloy (P.) Ltd. [2004] 137 Taxman 429 (Mad.)]. Also see, GAIL India Ltd. v. JCIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 97/211 Taxman 587 (Delhi).

Loan issue expenses - Front-end fees paid to bank at the time of obtaining new loan is an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. [2019] 112 taxmann.com 356/[2020] 268 Taxman 446 (Cal.)].

Refund of oversubscription - Expenditure incurred in connection with refund of oversubscription in relation to issue of shares held to be an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Shree Synthetics Ltd. [1986] 162 ITR 819 (MP)].

ROC fees - Expenditure incurred for obtaining registration would be liable to be deducted and, consequently, fees paid to ROC for raising authorized capital of company would also be covered [CIT v. Multi Metals Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 151 (Raj.), approved inPunjab State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 93 Taxman 5 (SC)].

Fees paid for increase in share capital is not fees for registration of the company and, hence, is not amortisable u/s 35D(2)(c)(iii) [CIT v. Hindustan Insecticides Ltd. [2001] 116 Taxman 406 (Delhi)].

Share issue expenses - Expenditure in connection with issuance of Euro share which was directly relatable to expansion of capital base of company for raising of new projects held to be an allowable expenditure [EID Parry (India) Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 23 taxmann.com 348/209 Taxman 214 (Mad.); Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilisers Co. Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 49 (Guj.)].

However, the question of valuation of improvements will not arise where there could be no claim for the value of improvements at all, because, in such a case, the ascertainment of the value does not arise. Maintenance/Training expenses of mare and off springs: The word 'improve' has various shades of meaning and it includes everything, by doing which, there is an enhancement in the value of the asset, or there is a rise in its price, or the asset is made to grow better, or, it is even followed up by something better. [CIT v. V. Ramaswamy Mudaliar [1993] 66 Taxman 469 (Mad.)]. In this case a mare and its colt and filly had been subjected to training. The Court held that maintenance and training expenses by the assessee on the colt, filly and the mare would form part of cost of improvement of these assets.

Wholly and exclusively

The expression ‘wholly and exclusively’ does not denote necessarily [Sassoon J. David & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)]. The word ‘wholly’ refers to quantum of expenditure. The word ‘exclusively’ refers to motive, objective or purpose with which the particular expense has been incurred [Addl. CIT v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. (2004) 137 Taxman 367 (Raj.) and Ram Bahadur Thakur Ltd. v. CIT (2003) 261 ITR 390 (Ker.)]. The word "wholly" signifies that the expenditure should be completely devoted to the business. It need not be essential, necessary or compelling; it may be optional and purely voluntary. But it must be commercially expedient and should have the aim of the continuance or furtherance of the business and an eventual augmentation or stabilization of profits [Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 156 (Mad.)]

The true test of an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of trade or business is that it is incurred by the assessee as incidental to his trade for the purpose of keeping the trade going and of making it pay and not in any other capacity than that of a trader. It has to be examined whether the expense has been incurred with the sole object of furthering the trade or business interest of the assessee unalloyed or unmixed with any other consideration. If the expense is found to bear an element other than that of the trade or business interest of the assessee, the expenditure is not an allowable one [B. K. Khanna & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 113 Taxman164 (Delhi)]

(1) Suppose the assessee incurs expenditure on advertisement in a souvenir of a labour union formed by a political party. The labour union is registered under the Trade Unions Act of 1926. Is the expenditure required to be reported by the tax auditor in the third item in clause 21(a)?

Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides that every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which it is registered, and shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire and hold both movable and immovable property and to contract, and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Thus, a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is a separate and distinct legal entity and is not part of the political party which formed it. Since the Labour union has a separate and distinct legal identity, the expenditure cannot be said to be incurred in the advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party. Therefore, the expenditure is not reportable in clause 21(a).

(2) If the advertisement is published in a newspaper published by a political party, is the expenditure thereon to be reported in clause 21(a)?

It is possible to take the view that expenditure on advertisement in a political party's newspaper is not required to be reported under this clause. A newspaper is certainly not like a brochure, tract, etc. The words 'any other like publication' occurring in clause 21(a) as well as section 37(2B) should be interpreted ejusdem generis with 'brochure', 'tract', 'pamphlet' and 'souvenir' [See para 8 of ICAI's Guidance Note on section 293A of the Companies Act and the Auditor]

The name and the business of a company are taken as going hand in hand and any interloping is considered in Company Law as affecting the pair of credit and custom of the company registered first in point of time and existing. Each case is a question of fact as to whether the similarity or resemblance is calculated, even if not actually intended, to deceive or cause confusion between the two businesses by diverting the customers to take or mistake one for the other. However, if the company registered earlier is dissolved or amalgamated and its name is not live on the Register, whether it is a matter of agreement between the persons concerned like it seems to be in the UK or in terms of section 20 or 22 of the Act, is a moot question because it is difficult to see who can agree on behalf of a dissolved or amalgamated company which has no existence recognised in law. The Research and Statistics Division of DCA used to be the reference point with its data base that the Registrars were required to refer to in doubtful cases, but, now, with on-line entries of new company registrations, the picture should be instantaneously clear to any.

(c) colourable imitation including transliteration in English of the vernacular equivalent of a registered and existing company’s English name or its phonetic imitation by different spelling or other plagiarisation,

(d) general names like Cotton Textiles or Silk Manufacturing with no specifics prefaced like a place name,

(e) use of the word ‘co-operative’ or ‘sahakari’,

(f) names prohibited as improper under the Emblems & Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950,

(g) names suggestive of State, national or international, patronage or participation in its absence,

(h) use of the name of a National hero or a person of public eminence,

(i) Vague alphabets like DJMO Ltd.,

(j) adaptations of popular abbreviations or acronyms like Tisco or HMT though they may or not be registered as trade marks (while it is open to the existing companies concerned which are well-known by their abbreviated names or their subsidiaries to adopt such coined words as the names or part of the names to be registered or changed to, which the Registrar can himself allow, vide DCA Circular No. 27/1/87-CL III of 27th March,1988),

(o) use of proper name or surname which is not of a director’s,

(p) names containing numerals like ‘21st C’. Use of certain identified key words like ‘corporation’, ‘international’, ‘global’, ‘universal’, ‘continental’, ‘inter-continental’, ‘Asiatic’, ‘Asia’, ‘Hindustan’, ‘India’, ‘Bharat’, ‘enterprise’, ‘products’, ‘business’, ‘manufacturing’—as part of a proposed company’s name(s) or a name to be changed to, is allowed depending upon the amount of authorized share capital, on which a consultation would be necessary with the concerned Registrar of Companies.

Section 55(2)(a) is now being amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 to provide that in respect of trade mark or brand name associated with a business, its costs of acquisition shall be deemed to be the following amounts : Substitution of fair market value as on 1-4-1981 - In case of the aforesaid assets the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 for the original cost of acquisition is not permitted. Hence, in case of self-acquired assets, since the cost of acquisition is nil and the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 is not permitted, the indexed cost of acquisition would also be nil.

Following points need to be noted :

● Hitherto, there was a view [based on the Supreme Court decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinvasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294] that the aforesaid assets are not chargeable to capital gains tax since there is no cost of acquisition. Hence, it could be argued that the amendment clearly shows that such assets were not chargeable to tax under section 45 up to assessment year 2001-02.

● Section 55(1)(b) provides that cost of improvement (COI) in relation to a capital asset being goodwill of a business or a right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing shall be taken to be nil. Section 55(1)(b) has not been amended to provide that COI of trade mark or brand name associated with a business shall also be taken to be nil. Now, in Evans Fraser & Co. Ltd. v. CIT[1982] 137 ITR 493 (Bom.), it was held that if the cost of improvement of an asset cannot be ascertained, gains arising on its transfer is not liable to tax under section 45. Hence, if the nil cost assets roped in by the amendment to the definition of cost of acquisition can have some COI which cannot be quantified, then, applying the ratio of the aforesaid decision, it could be argued that the capital gains arising on transfer of such assets is still outside the purview of tax under section 45.

7.3-1 Application of section 50 - In case of trade marks, the amendment presently made under section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition thereof will be its purchase price or nil as the case may be. It is pertinent to note that in respect of trade marks acquired on or after 1-4-1998, an assessee is entitled to depreciation under section 32(1) of the Act.

Since capital gains in respect of assets forming part of a block of assets on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act is to be computed as per the special provisions under section 50, the question may arise as to whether capital gains on transfer of trade marks would be computed in the manner provided under section 50 or whether the capital gains would have to be computed by taking cost of acquisition as per section 55(2)(a).

Section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition of trade marks will be taken as purchase price/nil ‘for the purpose of sections 48 and 49’. Section 50, however, goes further to say that ‘in case of depreciable assets sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the modifications’ prescribed in that section.

Hence, it seems that in respect of trade mark on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act, the capital gains would have to be computed as per the provisions of section 50 since the said section clearly provides that ‘the provisions under sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the following modifications’. However, as regards trade marks on which depreciation has not been allowed under the Act (which would include self-acquired trade marks and trade marks acquired prior to 1-4-1998) the capital gains would have to be computed on the basis of cost determined as per section 55(2)(a).

7.3-1a Brand names - While trade marks have been expressly referred to as an intangible asset under section 32(1) the said section does not expressly refer to ‘brand name’. However, ‘brand name’ would also qualify for depreciation as intangible assets since it would fall within the meaning of expression ‘any other business or commercial rights of similar nature’ as referred to under section 32(1). Hence, the same position as stated above in regard to trade mark would also hold good in respect of ‘brand name’.

Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee-company carried on business in providing education and training for various preparatory examinations - During relevant assessment year, it paid certain amount to its two faculty members as non-compete fees for not entering into a business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005 - Assessee claimed said payment as revenue expenditure but revenue authorities held that elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to assessee and, therefore, payment amounted to capital expenditure - Whether having regard to short period of twelve months during which above two persons were prohibited from competing with assessee, payment in question was to be allowed as revenue expenditure - Held, yes [In favour of assessee]

FACT: During relevant assessment year, the assessee paid certain amount to its two faculty members, namely, 'V' and 'S' as non-compete fees for not entering into business similar to assessee's business upto 31-12-2005. The assessee claimed that the non-compete fee was paid in respect of a very short period of non-competition and, therefore, payment represented revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer, however, held that the elimination or warding off of competition over some length of time resulted in an enduring advantage to the assessee and, therefore, the payment amounted to capital expenditure. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the disallowance. On second appeal, the Tribunal allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that those payments were to be made in monthly instalments over a period of time; and that the period involved, during which 'V' and 'S' were not to compete with the assessee in any manner was only a short period of 12 months and, therefore, there could be no enduring benefit enuring to the assessee.

On the revenue's appeal:

HELD: It is necessary to keep the nature of the assessee's business in mind before judging the allowability by the payment. The assessee is engaged in the business of running learning centers for preparing/coaching students to face competitive examinations held by IIM, IIT, Institute of Information Technology, etc. In conducting the classes for the students, the assessee has to rely on faculty members of repute. 'V' and 'S' were such faculty, who were engaged by the assessee. It is also necessary for the assessee to ensure that the faculty members do not compete with its business because that would affect the business. It cannot be disputed that the popularity and success of the learning centers run by the assessee is in a large measure due to the efficiency, knowledge and reputation of the faculty members. If the faculty members leave the assessee and decide to set up their own learning centers, that is most certain to affect the assessee's business. It was, therefore, in the interest of the assessee's business that it ensured that for some period of time, such faculty members do not compete with it in the same business. It is with this end in view that the assessee made the payment to 'V' and 'S'. The period for which these persons could not compete with the assessee has been found by the Tribunal to be a short period of 12 months. This is not an irrelevant consideration taken into account by the Tribunal. The fact that the payment was made in monthly instalments is not decisive of the question; even if it had been made in a lump sum, that would have made little difference to the conclusion, having regard to the short period of 12 months during which the above two persons were prohibited from competing with the assessee business. It cannot be disputed any more that payment to ward off competition for a limited period should be held to be revenue expenditure and not capital expenditure. If that is so, the fact that the payment was made in a lump sum or in instalments hardly matters. Therefore, in coming to the conclusion that the payment in questions was a revenue expenditure, the Tribunal has not ignored any relevant material or taken into account irrelevant material. The Tribunal was certainly entitled to take note of the entire conspectus of the facts of the case and in particular the period during which the faculty members were prohibited from competing with the assessee's business. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessee's claim. [Para 48]

3. Non-compete fee paid to restrict competition held allowable as revenue expenditure under section 37(1): Supreme Court

Sharp Business System v. Commissioner of Income-tax [2025] 181 taxmann.com 657 (SC)

Assessee, a public limited company, was engaged in the business of software development, hardware sales, technical training and engineering services. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year, declaring a net loss. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) computed the assessee's total income and made several disallowances. One of the disallowances concerned the depreciation claim on the non-compete fee.

Aggrieved-assessee preferred an appeal to the CIT(A), where it contended that the non-compete fee was nothing but a license. Assessee could exclusively carry on the business of software development, training and export of technologies by restraining M/s. Pentamedia Graphics Limited is not allowed to carry out the same activities. Thus, the payment of the non-compete fee was held to be an intangible asset entitled to depreciation under Section 32(1)(ii).

The matter, after passing through the ITAT and the High Court, was carried in appeal before the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court ruled that non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. The purpose of a non-compete payment is to give the payer's business a head start. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the payer's business or enhancing its profitability by insulating it from competition.

Thus, the non-compete fee seeks only to protect or enhance the business's profitability, thereby facilitating its carrying on more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in the creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit-earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, of restricting a competitor in business is not in the capital field.

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring such expenditure.

Thus, the Supreme Court held that a payment made by the assessee as a non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Act.

In that case the Tribunal had not misdirected itself as to the true scope and meaning of the words "wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of the assessee's business." In the present case the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal had misdirected itself as to the true scope and meaning of these words. In our opinion, in the circumstances of this case, it cannot be said that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact. The question as to whether the expenses of running the school for jockeys is deductible has to be decided taking into consideration the circumstances of this case. The business of the respondent was to run race meetings on a commercial scale for which it is necessary to have races of as high an order as possible. For the popularity of the races run by the respondent and to make its business profitable it was necessary that there were jockeys of requisite skill and experience in sufficient numbers who would be available to the owners and trainers because without such efficient jockeys the running of race meeting would not be commercially profitable. It was for this purpose that the respondent started the school for training Indian jockeys. If there were not sufficient number of efficient Indian jockeys to ride horses its interest would have suffered, and it might have had to abandon its business if it did not take steps to make jockeys of the necessary calibre available. Therefore, any expenditure which was incurred for preventing the extinction of the respondent's business would, in our opinion, be expenditure wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee and would be an allowable deduction. This finds support from decided cases. In Commissioner of Income-tax v. Chandulal Keshavlal & Co [1960] 38 ITR 601. this court held that in order to justify a deduction the disbursement must be for reasons of commercial expediency; it may be voluntary but incurred for the assessee's business; and if the expense is incurred for the purpose of the business of the assessee it does not matter that the payment also ensures to the benefit of a third party. Another test laid down was that if the transaction is properly entered into as a part of the assessee's legitimate commercial undertaking in order to facilitate the carrying on of its business it is immaterial that a third party also benefits thereby. In British Insulated and Helsby Cables v. Atherton [1926] AC 205 Viscount Cave, L.C, held that a sum of money expended, not of necessity and with a view to a direct and immediate benefit to the trade, but voluntarily and on the ground of commercial expediency and in order indirectly to facilitate the carrying on of the business may yet be expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the trade. In a case more recently decided, Morgan v. Tate & Lyle Ltd. [1954] 26 ITR 195, the assessee company was engaged in sugar refining business and it incurred expenses in a propaganda campaign to oppose the threatened nationalisation of the industry. It was held by the House of Lords by a majority that the object of the expenditure being to preserve the assets of the company from seizure and so to enable it to carry on its business and earn profits, the expense was an admissible deduction being wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of the company's trade. Lord Morton of Henryton said:

"Looking simply at the words of the rule I would ask:'If money so spent is not spent for the purposes of the company's trade, for what purpose is it spent?' If the assets are seized, the company can no longer carry on the trade which has been carried on by the use of these assets. Thus the money is spent to preserve the very existence of the company's trade."

See also Strong & Co. v. Woodifield [1906] AC 448the observations of Lord Davey; and Smith v. Incorporated Council of Law Reporting [1914] 3 KB. 674.

CIT [2011] 332 ITR 531 /[2010] 194 Taxman 477 . As would be evident from Section 32(1)(ii), depreciation can be allowed in respect of intangible assets. Parliament has spelt-out the nature of such assets by express reference to 'know-how', 'patents', 'copyrights', 'trademarks', 'licenses' and 'franchises'. So far as patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses and franchises are concerned, though they are intangible assets, the law recognizes through various enactments that specific intellectual property rights flow from them. Licenses are derivative and often are the means of conferring such intellectual property rights. The enjoyment of such intellectual property right implies exclusion of others, who do not own or have license to such rights from using them in any manner whatsoever. Similarly, in the matter of franchises and know-how, the primary brand or intellectual process owner owns the exclusive right to produce, retail and distribute the products and the advantages flowing from such brand or intellectual process owner, but for the grant of such know-how rights or franchises. In other words, out of these species of intellectual property like rights or advantages lead to the definitive assertion of a right in rem. The decisions of this Court in Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd. (supra) and that of the Kerala High Court in B. Raveendran Pillai ( supra) underlined that goodwill is also a species of depreciable right which can claim the benefit of Section 32. Those decisions were based on the ruling of the Supreme Court in CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294/5 Taxman 1 and subsequent cases which have ruled that goodwill is a depreciable capital asset. So far as the decisions in Techno Shares & Stocks Ltd. (supra) is concerned, the Supreme Court clearly limited its holding that the right to membership of Stock Exchange is in the nature of "any other business or commercial right" which was an intangible asset as is evident from the following observations:

"Before concluding we wish to clarify that our present judgment is strictly confined to the right to membership conferred upon the membership under the BSE Membership Card during the relevant assessment years. We hold that the said right to membership is "business or commercial activity" which gives a non-defaulting continuing membership and right to access Exchange and to participate therein and in that sense it is a license or akin to a license, in terms of Section 32(1)(ii)."

The proprie- tary concerns have been acquired by the assessee-company as going concerns. The two proprietors, by virtue of this agreement, have transferred the respective business along with rights, assets and liabilities which included trademarks etc. In addition to the value of the assets, the assessee-company has undertaken to pay a sum of Rs. 3.5 lakhs per month to one proprietor and another sum of Rs. 2 lakhs per month to another proprietor which is clearly for eliminating competition in the same line of business for a sufficiently long period of 15 years. The user of trademark, if any, by the assessee-company is only an inseparable part of the entire arrangement. By the ‘non-compete’ clause of the agreement, the erstwhile proprietors are automatically excluded from use of such trademarks and they have bound themselves contractually not to carry on similar business activity in whatever names for a period of 15 years. As a consideration, the impugned monthly payments are to be paid by the assessee-company for a period of 15 years. This means that on the expiry of the non-compete period of 15 years, the payments would also cease to be made. We do not find much merit in the arguments of the ld. counsel for the assessee that the payments are partly attributable to the benefit acquired by the assessee-company by way of user of the tenanted premises at a nominal rent. There is no reference to this fact in the agreement. Further, the landlord or owner of such premises is not a party to the agreement and even if some benefit has accrued to the assessee-company, it is entirely on account of the Rent Control Act, which may be applicable. The business premises either owned or rented have been taken over by the assessee-company as part of the overall agreement or arrangement for purchase of proprietary business as going concern along with all assets and liabilities.

(10) It is not the law that if an enduring advantage is obtained, the expenditure for securing it must always be treated as a capital expenditure. If the advantage acquired is to get the stock-in-trade of the business, then it would be revenue expenditure. But if what is acquired is not the advantage of getting the stock-in-trade directly, but of something which facilitates the acquisition of stock, the expenditure is of capital nature.

(11) The expenditure of capital nature is not referable only to tangible assets, but also to intangible assets. The asset acquired may be of impalpable or incalculable nature.

(12) The expenditure to enhance the profit earning capacity or capital base is of capital nature notwithstanding the fact that no tangible asset has been acquired.

(13) The expenditure to ward off competition for indefinite period is also of capital nature unless the agreement can be terminated at will.

(14) Expenditure on a capital asset does not lose the character of capital expenditure and does not become revenue expenditure on the score that the capital expenditure also ensures efficient running of the business.

(15) There can be enduring advantage acquired without any addition to the value of capital assets. [Para 11]

Applying the above test to the facts of the instant case, the cumulative effect of the preamble, clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement and the statement of facts before the Commissioner (Appeals) did not leave any doubt to hold that the essence of the agreement of the assessee with ‘W’ was to avoid competition in the business. The assessee had thus got an advantage of enduring nature. In the agreement, ‘W’ had the option of taking back the business of the assessee if the assessee would fail to start the business within a period of five years from the date of execution of the agreement. However, the assessee having started the business, the said clause had been rendered redundant. Consequently, the right of ‘W’ to carry on the business of similar nature as taken over from them was relinquished for good. Though no tangible asset had come into surface as a result of takeover of the business, yet an enduring benefit had ensued to the assessee by warding off competition in the business for all the times to come. The expenditure incurred for avoiding competition was of capital nature. Thus the amount paid by the assessee to ‘W’ was of capital nature. The incidental benefit arising to the assessee, such as references and course material, etc., which ‘W’ was supposed to give to the assessee did not carry any separate price tag. The transfer of such material to the assessee might have benefited the assessee to earn more profits, but such a benefit was incidental and consequential to taking over of the business by the assessee. It would have been a different matter if a separate price tag had been fixed for the references and course material transferred to the assessee by ‘W’ in which case a question about treating the expenditure attributable to such transfer could be considered to fall within the ambit of revenue expenditure. The essence of the agreement being the taking over of the business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, the expenditure fell in the category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure. [Para 12]

The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.
