A 'patent' gives its owner an exclusive right to make and sell the subject-matter of the 'patent' for a particular period of time. The grant of a 'patent', to any individual or a firm, provides an individual or a firm competitive advantage over others within a given industrial field. [Para 24] A 'patent' is intended to protect the commercial exploitation of ideas, which are original, new and unobvious. It is a Government supported monopoly. It ensures that those who incur a cost of 'inventing' will reap its reward if users find the result worth paying for. This cannot occur if others reap where the inventor has sown. The 'patent' system is designed to stop the 'free riding' by non-patentees. [Para 24.1]

A 'copyright' means a right conferred upon its owner in respect of his literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work. It does not really mean a right to do something, but only the right to exclude others from the doing of certain specific acts and things. A 'patent' is distinguishable from a 'copyright'. The owner of the 'copyright' has a sole right and he has the right to exclude all others from reproducing his work without his permission. The 'copyright' gives protection to its owner from the necessity of having to compete with the product of his own effort. [Para 25]

A 'trade mark' is a symbol attached to goods or services that adds or creates a distinctive quality to the product by associating it in the buyer's mind with some manufacturer or distributor. Its main purpose is to eliminate 'free riding' by other manufacturers of similar goods and services. The property consists in the right of the owner to use the 'trade mark' in relation to specified goods and under certain circumstances to prevent others from using it. It ensures that the established reputation of one manufacturer is not appropriated by another by 'passing off', or misrepresentations. It is essentially part of a marketing strategy. The owner is granted excluded right to control the use of his 'trade mark' and the articles to which it is attached. [Para 26]

A person who buys a 'patent' acquires an exclusive business/commercial right, and if there is a breach, he can sue. In the instant case also, the assessee-company acquired an exclusive business/commercial right, and in the case of a breach, the assessee could sue. Therefore, the business/commercial right acquired by the assessee was of the 'same nature' as the business/commercial right of a 'patent'. [Para 27]

In the case of copyright, trade mark, license and franchisees also, the owners have exclusive business/commercial rights; and if there is a breach, they can sue. [Para 28]

Consequently, if the business/commercial right of a patent, copyright, trade mark, license and franchise, fulfils the conditions of 'being intangible asset', then surely the impugned business/commercial right acquired by the assessee also fulfilled that condition, by way of a logical corollary. [Para 29]

Therefore, the impugned 'non-compete right' acquired by the assessee-company, was eligible for depreciation under clause (ii ) of section 32(1). The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was, accordingly, upheld. [Para 31]

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(XV) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of Assessment years 1961-62 and 1962-63 - Assessee, a union of truck operators provided facilities to its member operators in matter of booking their trucks and charged commission at rate of 5 per cent on gross booking - Out of commission so received, one-half was paid to members of union whose trucks could not be booked - Whether since payment was made to eliminate competitors and to carry on business unfettered by competition, payment was of capital nature and was not permissible deduction as revenue expenditure in computing assessee's total income - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a union of truck operators in the Subzi Mandi area. It wrong found provided facilities to truck operators in the matter of booking of their trucks and charged commission at 5 per cent of gross booking. After keeping one-half of such commission the assessee used to return the balance to those members of the union whose trucks were not booked. The payment was not allowed as deduction by the ITO. On appeal the AAC decided in favour of the assessee. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the payment was in the nature of capital expenditure.

On reference :

HELD: The amount in question was paid only to those members whose trucks were not booked. But for this payment, they would have otherwise competed in the business with the assessee. The object of the payment was to eliminate those competitors and to carry on the business unfettered by competition. The assessee made the payment to acquire this right of these persons. This led to enhance the value of its existing assets to make them more profit-yielding. The expense, therefore, could not be a revenue expense but was of a capital nature. The Tribunal was therefore right, in holding that amount so paid was not a permissible deduction for the purpose of income-tax.

Note : The decision was in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1955-56 to 1958-59 - Whether in deciding question whether expenditure was in nature of capital expenditure or business expenditure laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for purpose of assessee’s business, one must not confine one selves only to agreement between parties and said question must be decided in light of facts and circumstances of each case - Held, yes - Whether where assessee-company took over business carried on by a firm and made payment of pension amount to employees of firm in consideration of their past services rendered by them to firm and to abstain them from being engaged or employed in business of kind carried on by assessee-company, it could be said that payment made was for purposes of business and has in nature of business expenditure and would not partake of nature of capital expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: By an agreement the assessee-company took over the entire business carried on by a firm. There were two persons in the employment of the firm, who put more than 25 years of service of with the firm. Under the agreement these employees remained in the service of the assessee. The assessee agreed to pay certain amount per annum as pension on termination or retirement of their services from the company to abstain from being engaged or employed in the business of the kind carried on by the company. One of the aforesaid persons retired from the service of the assessee and the amount paid by the assessee in accordance with aforesaid agreement was claimed as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim to the pension payment made on the ground that the assessee did not have any pension scheme and that it was not proved that there was an agreement between the firm and the employee to pay him pension. On appeal, the AAC held that the stipulation in the agreement by the employees to abstain from being engaged or employed in business of the kind carried on by the company ‘amounted to nothing else than a covenant not to compete with the company in its business’. He held that by buying off potential competitors the company improved the value of its goodwill and thus brought into existence an advantage for the enduring benefit of the trade and, therefore, quite apart from the fact that the payment might have been made out of non-business considerations, the payment was also of the nature of capital expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the view taken by the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: Whether the expenditure was in the nature of a capital expenditure or a business expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the assessee’s business, one must not confine oneselves only to the agreements between the parties. The question must be determined in the light of all the facts and circumstances of each case and there is no rule that if there is a written agreement between the parties the authorities and the High Court must look only to that written agreement and nothing else.

It is now settled law that the question whether the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out or spent wholly or exclusively for the purposes of the assessee's business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances of each case.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(2)(xv) of the indian income-tax act, 1922 [Corresponding to section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961]-Business expenditure-Payments to foreign companies towards royalty in the form of share of profits, technical fees and expenses on training of employees abroad-Whether revenue or capital in nature-Held, on facts, that expenditure in question is revenue in nature

FACT: The assessee entered into agreements with two foreign companies for obtaining technical knowledge and information, training of Indian employees abroad and for use of trade name. In one case, the assessee was to establish a factory for the manufacture of trucks and other automotive products. For this, the payment was to be a percentage of net sales prices and net profits of the assessee's particular products. In the other case the foreign company's assistance was sought to start the operation of assessee-company's steel foundry for bringing it into effective commission. In the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee had paid towards fees Rs. 29,59,608 as share of profits to one company and Rs. 2,99,158 as lump sum fees to the other company. The assessee also incurred Rs. 1,69,925 as expenses on training its employees abroad by the foreign companies. All the three items were claimed as revenue expenditure but the ITO treated them as capital expenditure. On appeal, the AAC accepted the assessee's claim and allowed the appeal. On Department's appeal, the Tribunal considered the terms of the two agreements and found that, under one agreement, the assessee only got technical assistance and knowledge in regard to truck manufacture and the right to use its trade name for a specific period. It was thus really a case of fees being paid for user of technical know-how and trade name. Under the other agreement, it was the right to trade for purposes of carrying on its business upon the technical knowledge of the foreign company in regard to foundry business. In both the cases, the Tribunal opined that these items of expenditure had not resulted in acquisition or bringing into existence an asset or capital of enduring nature. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the payments were deafly revenue expenditure. Similarly, the expenditure on training was for running the business more efficiently so as to earn higher profits and was revenue in nature.

On reference :

HELD: In essence, the agreements in question were for acquiring technical knowledge regarding methods of production and in addition, in the case of one company, payment was for use of trade name. Acquiring technical know-how and technical advice cannot in these days of technological and scientific development and consequent change in production technique, be treated as a capital asset. Mere length of period of agreement is not of much consequence if the nature of advice made available is such that it cannot be called a capital asset. Technical know-how made available by a party to such an agreement does not stand on the same footing as rights under a registered patent.

The expenditure incurred on training of employees was with a view to give training to persons so as to achieve maximum and efficient production. This was undoubtedly closely related to the profit earning process.

The expenditure in question was, therefore, held to be of a revenue nature deductible in computing taxable income.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1961-62 - Assessee had entered into an agreement to sell vehicles manufactured by Telco, and for purpose of ensuring compliance with agreement requiring assessee to maintain a staff of trained personnel, it secured training of its personnel from Telco and made payment, therefore to it - Amount so received by Telco was intended to meet cost of construction of hostel and hostel was to be Telco's property - Whether payment made by assessee to Telco was payment was wholly and exclusively for purpose of its business and thus, should be allowed as deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee carried on business as a dealer in motor vehicles. During the relevant period it was a dealer of Telco, under an agreement with that company, for the sale of Mercedes Benz trucks. The agreement required the assessee to maintain at its own expense an organization for the sale of vehicles, providing for maintenance of show rooms, service centers, repair shops, etc. and an adequate staff of trained salesman and a staff of trained technical service personnel. According to the agreement, the training was actually imparted by Telco which charged the assessee on that account. Under the training scheme, Telco proposed to build a hostel for the apprentices and to recover the entire cost of the hostel from its several dealers. The assessee paid Telco certain amount during the relevant accounting year and claimed that amount was a deduction from its assessable profits for the assessment year 1961-62. The ITO was of the view that the payment was made as the assessee's contribution towards the construction of the hostel, that the hostel would be the property of Telco and that, therefore, it was not a business expenditure. Accordingly, he rejected the assessee's claim.

The AAC allowed the assessee's claim on the ground that although the said amount was a contribution towards the construction of the hostel it was not an expense of a capital nature but was a revenue expense incurred in connection with the business of the assessee.

The Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO, holding that the amount was a capital expenditure.

On reference :

HELD: No doubt, the amount received by Telco was intended to meet the cost of construction of the hostel, and the hostel was to be Telco's property. And when the assessee made the payment, it was aware that it would be so applied by Telco. But so far as the assessee was concerned, it paid to Telco for the training imparted to the apprentices sent by the assessee. It paid the amount as training charge, and so far as the assessee was concerned, it remained a training charge, even though Telco applied it to the construction of the hostel and the assessee knew that it would be so applied.

The AAC had held that the amount represented payment made by the assessee to Telco in respect of the training scheme. That finding was not upset by the Tribunal. But, the Tribunal proceeded on the basis that under the training scheme the assessee was obliged to contribute towards the construction of the hostel. What the Tribunal omitted to consider was that the entire object of the scheme was the training of the assessee's apprentices and it was for that reason that payment was made by the assessee. There was no dispute that if Telco had not undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices there would have been no obligation on the assessee to pay the amount. One could not ignore that payment was made because Telco had undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices.

If expenditure is incurred for the purpose of increasing the profits while carrying on the business it must be treated as revenue expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee made payment to Telco on account of the training imparted by Telco to the assessee's apprentices. Trained personnel were necessary for the purpose of the assessee's business. It was necessary because a condition of the agency agreement with Telco required the assessee to have trained personnel. It was necessary also because the staff of trained personnel obviously induced better sales. There was no question here of the assessee acquiring any asset or advantage of an enduring nature. There was nothing to show that the personnel so trained were under bond to serve the assessee for a long term of years.

In the facts of that case, this Court held that the financial outlay under the agreement was for the better conduct and improvement of the existing business and should therefore be treated as revenue expenditure. ■ The next case that is adverted to is the case of CIT v. Madras Auto Service (P.) Ltd. [1998] 99 Taxman 575 (SC)/[1998] 233 ITR 468 (SC). In this case, the respondent assessee, a tenant, had incurred expenditure on demolition and construction of a new building which was to vest in the landlord. Assessee in lieu of incurring the actual cost of construction was entitled to use the premises for a period of 39 years at a reduced rent. The entire capital cost of construction was claimed by the assessee as revenue expenditure on the ground that the assessee had not acquired any new asset or such expenditure did not result in any enduring advantage to the assessee in the capital field. The above stand of the assessee was accepted by the ITAT and the High Court. When revenue came up in appeal before this Court, it was held that right from inception, the building was of the ownership of the lessor. Therefore, by spending this money, the assessee did not acquire any capital asset. The only advantage which the assessee derived by spending the money was that it got the lease of a new building at a low rent. From the business point of view, therefore, the assessee got the benefit of reduced rent. The High Court has, therefore, rightly considered this as obtaining a business advantage. The expenditure is, therefore, to be treated as revenue expenditure. [Para 24]

■

Having adverted to the relevant case laws, one may now examine the nature and character of non-compete fee; whether payment of non-compete fee is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure. Non-compete fee is paid by one party to another to restrain the latter from competing with the payer in the same line of business. It may be by way of a written agreement or by an oral understanding. The restriction may be limited to a specified territory or otherwise; similarly, it can be for a specified period or otherwise. Purpose of non-compete payment is to give a head start to the business of the payer. It can also be for the purpose of protecting the business of the payer or for enhancing the profitability of the business of the payer by insulating the payer from competition. [Para 25]

■

Thus non-compete fee only seeks to protect or enhance the profitability of the business, thereby facilitating the carrying on of the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment neither results in creation of any new asset nor accretion to the profit earning apparatus of the payer. The enduring advantage, if any, by restricting a competitor in business, is not in the capital field. [Para 26]

■

Following the judicial trend, it can be safely inferred that the length of time over which the enduring advantage may enure to the payer is not determinative of the nature of expenditure. As long as the enduring advantage is not in the capital field, where the advantage merely facilitates in carrying on the business more efficiently and profitably, leaving the fixed assets untouched, the payment made to secure such advantage would be an allowable business expenditure, irrespective of the period over which the advantage may accrue to the payer (assessee) by incurring of such expenditure. [Para 27]

■

The non-compete compensation from the stand point of the payer of such compensation is so paid in anticipation that absence of a competition from the other party may secure a benefit to the party paying the compensation. However, there is no certainty that such benefit would accrue. Notwithstanding such an arrangement, the payer (assesee) may still not achieve the desired result. In so far the present case is concerned, on account of payment of non-compete fee, the assessee had not acquired any new business and there is no addition to the profit making apparatus of the assessee. The assets remained the same. The expenditure incurred was essentially to keep a potential competitor out of the same business. Further, there is no complete elimination of competition. Such payment made by the appellant to L&T did not create a monopoly of the appellant over the business of electronic products/ equipments. Payment was made to L&T only to ensure that the appellant operated the business more efficiently and profitably. Such payment made to L&T cannot, therefore, be considered to be for acquisition of any capital asset or towards bringing into existence a new profit earning apparatus. [Para 28]

■

That being the position, it is opined that payment made by the appellant to L&T as non-compete fee is an allowable revenue expenditure under section 37(1). [Para 29]

■

Consequently, the impugned judgment and order of the Delhi High Court dated 5-11-2012 passed in Income Tax Appeal No. 492/2012 is hereby set aside. The question framed is thus answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 30]

However, goodwill being a right which is attached with the business and which cannot be separated from the business itself, it should not be reckoned as a business or commercial right of similar nature.

Even otherwise, it appears that having regard to the meaning of the term goodwill, it may not be covered by the expression in all cases. In R.C.Cooper v. UOI AIR 1970 SC 564, it was observed as follows :

"Goodwill is that component of the total value of the undertaking which is attributable to the ability of the concern to earn profits over a course of years or in excess of normal amounts because of its reputation, location and other features : Trego v. Hunt [1896] AC 7 (HL). Goodwill of an undertaking therefore is the value of the attraction to customers arising from the name and reputation for skill, integrity, efficient business management, or efficient service."

In CIT v. B.C. Srinivasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294 (SC), it was observed as follows (p. 298) :

"Goodwill denotes the benefit arising from connection and reputation. A variety of elements goes into its making, and its composition varies in different trades and in different business in the same trade, and while one element many preponderate in one business, another may dominate in another business.

Its value may fluctuate from one moment to another depending on changes in the reputation of the business. It is affected by everything relating to the business, the personality and business rectitude of the owners, the nature and character of the business, its name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio-economic ecology, introduction to old customers and agreed absence of competition. There can be no account in value of the factors producing it".

In CED v. Kanta Devi Taneja [1981] 132 ITR 437(Gau.) it was held as follows:

"Broadly speaking, it is the magnetic quality of a particular trade or business which attracts customers to it as a matter of course. This quality springs from and is developed by various contributing factors that earn a reputation for honest dealing, quality and standard. Goodwill is founded on the belief and faith of the customer. It is commonly built up in relation to a particular type of manufacture or production of articles identified by a trademark which becomes widely known to the public and by which the customers take it for granted that it represents what they wish for. No trademark gains reputation overnight. Naturally, the standing of the business is necessarily one of the contributing factors. The personalities who are engaged in the business, the location in which it is carried on and the like are other features which go into the goodwill. Where a business involves no distinguishable features and deals in standard articles manufactured by someone else which one can get from anywhere, not merely from a particular dealer, there is hardly any possibility of there being a goodwill attached to such business".

In Permanent Edition of Words and Phrases, it is mentioned that

A 'trade-mark' symbolizes business goodwill.

A 'trade-mark' and 'goodwill' are similar and analogous and indicate favour which community holds for a certain commodity.

From the above, it appears that it cannot be generalised that goodwill is similar to the other intangible assets. For example, if the predominant element of goodwill is location or contacts with customers then these elements not being similar to the preceding assets in the definition of block of assets, it may not be possible to claim that goodwill is covered by the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature'. On the other hand, if the predominant element of goodwill is trademark then it could be argued that goodwill is covered by the expression.

2.2-10b NON-COMPETE PAYMENT-WHETHER COVERED BY THE DEFINITION - Another type of payment made is 'non-compete payment', that is, payment to another person in consideration of his agreeing not to compete with the payer. Having regard to the nature of the payment, it is perhaps not in the nature of the acquisition of an asset which is a precondition for grant of depreciation. In any case it may increase the value of goodwill (see definition of 'goodwill' as explained in Srinivasa Setty's case, reproduced above) and if goodwill itself cannot be considered as an intangible asset, the non-compete payment also cannot be considered so.

FACT: During the year under consideration, a sum of Rs. 66,13,440 was spent by the assessee on training of its employees and the same was claimed as revenue expenditure deductible under section 37(1) on the ground that it was incurred in order to increase the efficiency of the employees in the day-to-day working. HELD: It is by now well-settled that if the expenditure incurred by the taxpayer is of revenue nature, the same is entirely deductible even if there accrues an advantage of enduring nature in favour of the taxpayer as a result of the said expenditure. This is because going by the very nature of the expenditure being revenue, it operates in the revenue field leaving the capital field untouched. The enduring benefit resulting from the said expenditure may justify the action of the taxpayer to write off the said expenditure in his books of account over a period of more than one year. However, such accounting treatment by itself is not conclusive to decide the nature of the relevant expenditure, whether capital or revenue. In the instant case, there was no dispute that the expenditure in question incurred by the assessee on training of its employees was wholly and exclusively for the purpose of its business. As regards the nature of the said expenditure, the submission of the assessee had been that the said expenditure was incurred for the purpose of imparting training to its employees in order to increase their efficiency in day-to-day working and there was nothing brought on record by the revenue to controvert/rebut that position. The expenditure incurred by the assessee was in the revenue field and that being so, keeping in view the legal position emanating from the judicial pronouncements, it was to be held that the same was entirely deductible in the year under consideration, as rightly claimed by the assessee. The impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) confirming the disallowance made by the Assessing Officer to the extent of 50 per cent on that issue was, therefore, to be reversed and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to allow the said expenditure in full. If an assessee acquires any capital asset or enduring benefit for a longer period, the expenditure may be called to be a ‘capital expenditure’. In the instant case, the assessee had purchased the shipping business from the vendor against a lumpsum consideration of Rs. 43,47,000 comprising of cost of goodwill of Rs. 5 lakhs and Rs. 38,47,000 for non-competition covenant fees for a period of 5 years. From a perusal of the non-competition clause contained in the agreement, it was clear that in lieu of receipt of a non-competition fees, the vendor was restrained from doing similar type of business in any capacity for a period of 5 years within India. This condition would not apply to a business carried on by the vendor outside the India. Period of condition was fixed up to 5 years and, thereafter, the vendor was at liberty to enter into similar type of business activity. Further from the other provisions of the agreement, it was not borne out that the vendor was permanently restrained from doing the shipping business in future. Meaning thereby, it was a temporary arrangement made with the vendor in order to settle down its new business of shipping. It has been repeatedly held by the Apex Court and various High Courts that an expenditure incurred to avoid competition, if dictated by business necessity and commercial exigencies, would be allowable as a revenue expenditure as the benefit derived out of it is directly related to the enhancement of profitability of business. In the instant case, by avoiding a main competition from the vendor, the assessee had derived the benefits out of it to enhance its profitability only and it was not a case that the competition was eliminated permanently or for a longer period. Moreover, it was not a case of the revenue that the vendor was only competitor in this line of business. There were other business constituents who were engaged in the similar type of business and a threat of competition was also there to be faced by the assessee from those business constituents. This covenant was executed only for a period of 5 years and that too only for Indian territory. If the assessee intended to do its business outside Indian territory, it had to face the competition from the vendor also. Meaning thereby, this covenant was not executed for a permanent elimination of the competition from the seller. Therefore, the benefit was derived by the assessee for a limited period of 5 years and that too only in Indian territory. Therefore, the non-competition covenant fees paid by the assessee to the vendor could not be treated as capital expenditure. The covenant was executed on account of business necessity and commercial expediencies in order to settle down the assessee in a new acquired business of shipping and the benefit derived out of it was only to enhance its profitability. As such, the expenditure incurred by the assessee was a revenue expenditure and the same was to be allowed as a business expenditure. [Para 23]

Further, since the assessee had acquired a benefit over a period of 5 years, this expenditure should be spread over for a period of 5 years and the corresponding expenditure be allowed in every year. Therefore, the impugned order was to be set aside and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to allow the total expenditure over a period of 5 years in which the non-competition covenant fees remained in force. FACT: Facts

•

The Court granted a scheme of amalgamation of some companies with the assessee-company.

•

The assessee entered into a non-compete agreement with 'U' former chairman and managing director of the amalgamating companies and paid a certain sum to 'U' by way of non-compete fee.

•

It claimed said amount as a revenue expenditure but did not write off same in its books of account.

•

The Assessing Officer found that non-compete agreement had increased the assessee's market presence and improved its potential to have better results in the market; the payment made over a period of more than five years once was for procuring an enduring benefit to the business. Consequently, he held that the expenditure was in the capital field and disallowed said claim.

•

The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the decision of the assessing authority.

•

The Tribunal, by a cryptic order, rejected the assessee's claim.

Argument of assessee

•

The agreement entered into between the assessee with 'U' would clearly show that the expenditure was only on the revenue account.

Argument of revenue

•

When the assessee had not written off the said expenditure in its accounts and the amount paid was to ward off any competition in the business of the assessee, the expenditure made was only a capital expenditure.

Issue involved

•

Whether non-compete fee paid to the ex-managing director was a revenue or a capital expenditure?

HELD: •

As far as the question as to whether an expenditure could be a capital expenditure or revenue expenditure is concerned, the concept that the expenditure yielding an advantage of enduring nature would be only a capital expenditure, has been fine-tuned, that even when expenditure is incurred for obtaining advantage of enduring benefit, nonetheless, same can be taken as one of revenue account. [Para 14]

•

It is not denied by the revenue that 'U' was the chairman and managing director of some of the companies which got merged with the assessee-company. 'U' had access to all information starting from manufacturing process, know-how to the clientele and the products, including the pricing of the products. By a process of amalgamation, the assessee had acquired the business of the amalgamating companies. However, for the fruitful exercise of its business as a business proposition, the assessee thought it fit to enter into a non-compete agreement with a person who had the knowledge of the entire operations, so as to get the full yield of the amalgamated company's business. In that context, rightly, the assessee took a commercial decision to pay non-compete fee to 'U' and going by the decision of the Apex Court, that the payment was in respect of the performing of the business of the assessee, it was to be held that the expenditure is only on revenue account and not on capital account. In the circumstances, the order of the Tribunal was set aside. [Para 19]

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: ■

Section 37 is a residuary provision. Sub-section (1) of section 37 provides that any expenditure not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession'. [Para 16]

■

This provision contemplates that any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession.' For such an expenditure to be allowed, it should fulfil the following criteria: (i) it should not be an expenditure described in sections 30 to 36; (ii) it should not be in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee. [Para 16.1]

■

It is axiomatic that such expenditure should be incurred during the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration. [Para 16.2]

■

This provision was examined by this Court in another case, where it has been explained that in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession', section 37 enables the deduction of any expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business or profession, as the case may be. The fact that an item of expenditure is wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of business by itself is not sufficient to entitle its allowance in computing the income chargeable to tax. In addition, the expenditure should not be in the nature of a capital expenditure. In the infinite variety of situational diversities in which the concept of what is capital expenditure and what is revenue expenditure arises, it is well nigh impossible to formulate any general rule, even in the generality of cases, sufficiently accurate and reasonably comprehensive, to draw any clear line of demarcation. However, some broad and general tests have been suggested from time to time to ascertain on which side of the line the outlay in any particular case might reasonably be held to fall. These tests are generally efficacious and serve as useful servants but as masters they tend to be over-exacting. [Para 17]

■

There is a classical test laid down by Lord Cave L.C. in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. (1925) 10 TC 155, where it was held: When an expenditure is made, not only once and for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, I think that there is very good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to an opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as properly attributable not to revenue but to capital. [Para 18]

■

There is another test of contemporary vintage. This test is based on the distinction between fixed and circulating capital and was propounded by Lord Haldane in John Smith and Son v. Moore (1921) 12 TC 266. This test was explained in the following manner: Fixed capital is what the owner turns to profit by keeping it in his own possession; circulating capital is what he makes profit of by parting with it and letting it change masters. [Para 19]

8. The question whether payment made for acquiring technical know-how will fall for deduction as revenue expenditure was considered in detail by the Supreme Court. In Ciba’s case that was a case where the Indian subsidiary made contributions at fixed percentages on sale in consideration of technical consultancy services, use of trade marks, etc., to the Swiss Principal. There was also an agreement to keep information confidential. The patents and trade marks were to be returned to the Swiss company on termination of the agreement. The agreement was to be in force for five years. The Supreme Court held that the amount should be allowed as business expenditure. The Indian company did not become entitled exclusively to the patents and trade marks at any time. It had merely access to the technical knowledge and experience of the Swiss Major. The Indian company was a mere licensee.

Will the present amendment supersede this ruling of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Ciba of India Ltd. [1968] 69 ITR 692 ? Obviously not. The very concept of depreciation pre-supposes at least limited ownership or title. If the collaboration agreement is drafted in the manner done by Ciba of India Ltd., obviously the entire payment will have to be allowed as revenue expenditure.

On the other hand, if the company acquires complete title over the process or patents different considerations will arise. In Alembic Chemical Works Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1989] 43 Taxman 312 (SC), the question was whether know-how obtained on ‘once for all’ payment for increasing the yield of penicillin in the existing plant with an undertaking regarding confidentiality would help the company to claim the expenditure in the revenue field.

The Supreme Court held that there was no material for the Tribunal to hold that the area of improvisation was not a part of the existing business or that the entire gamut of the existing manufacturing operations for the commercial production of penicillin in the assessee’s existing plant had become obsolete or inappropriate in relation to the exploitation of the new sub-cultures of the high yielding strains of penicillin supplied by the foreign firm and that the mere introduction of the new bio synthetic source required the erection and commissioning of a totally new and different type of plant and machinery.

The ‘once for all’ payment test was also inconclusive. What was relevant was the purpose of the outlay and its intended object and effect, considered in a commonsense way having regard to the business realities. In a given case, the test of ‘enduring benefit’ might break down. Hence, it was revenue expenditure.

Despite the provision made for allowing depreciation on know-how, patent, etc., under the latest Finance Act, the field is still open for enterprising companies to take advantage of the rulings of the courts and make claims for deduction of the entire expenditure as revenue expenditure. This will, of course, have to be decided on various circumstances of the case. The amendment is only an enabling provision. The expenditure on know-how will hereafter have to be allowed either over a period of four years or in the year of acquisition itself depending on the facts of the case.

Where a bus was purchased along with the route permit, depreciation is allowable only on the amount representing the value of the vehicle, and not on the amount representing the value of the route per-mit—CIT v. S. Sudhakar [2001] 117 Taxman 711/247 ITR 747 (Mad.).

Therefore, specified intangible assets, viz., business claims, business information, business records, contracts, employees and know-how acquired by assessee under slump sale agreement, are in nature of 'business or commercial rights of similar nature'—Areva T & D India Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 20 taxmann.com 29/208 Taxman 252 (Del.).

Applying the principle of ejusdem generis, which provides that where there are general words following particular and specific words, the meaning of the latter words shall be confined to things of the same kind, as specified for interpreting the expression 'business or commercial rights of similar nature' specified in section 32(1)(ii), it is seen that such rights need not answer the description of 'know-how, patents, trademarks, licenses or franchises' but must be of similar nature as the specified assets.

CIT v. Ingersoll Rand International Ind. Ltd. [2014] 48 taxmann.com 349/227 Taxman 176 (Mag.)(Kar.)

The word 'commercial' is defined in Black's Law Dictionary as 'related to or connected with trade and commerce in general', 'commerce' is defined as 'the exchange of goods, production or property of any kind; the buying, selling and exchanging of articles'. A right by way of non-compete is acquired essentially for trade and, commerce, and therefore it will also qualify as a commercial right. A right acquired by way of non-compete can be transferred to any other person in the sense that the acquirer gets the right to enforce the performance of the terms of agreement under which a person is restrained from competing. When a businessman pays money to another businessman for restraining the other businessman from competing with the assessee, he gets a vested right which can be enforced under law and without that, the other businessman can compete with the first businessman. When by payment of non-compete fee, the businessman gets his right what he is practically getting is kind of monopoly to run his business without bothering about the competition.

Generally, non-compete fee is paid for a definite period. The idea is that by that time, the business would stand firmly on its own footing and can sustain later on. This clearly shows that the commercial right comes into existence whenever the assessee makes payment for non-compete fee. Therefore that right which the assessee acquires on payment of non-compete fee confers in him a commercial or a business right which is held to be similar in nature to know-how, patents, copyrights, trade marks, licences, franchises. Therefore, the commercial right thus acquired by the assessee unambiguously falls in the category of an 'intangible asset'. Their right to carry on business without competition has an economic interest and money value. The words 'or any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' have to be interpreted in such a way that they would have some similarities as other assets mentioned in clause (b) of Explanation 3. Here the doctrine of ejusdem generis would come into operation and therefore the non-compete fee vests a right in the assessee to carry on business without competition which in turn confers a commercial right to carry on business smoothly.

In Permanent Edition of Words and Phrases, it is mentioned that ◆ A ‘trade-mark’ symbolizes business goodwill.

◆ A ‘trade-mark’ and ‘goodwill’ are similar and analogous and indicate favour which community holds for a certain commodity.

From the above, it appears that it cannot be generalised that goodwill is similar to the other intangible assets. For example, if the predominant element of goodwill is location or contacts with customers then these elements not being similar to the preceding assets in the definition of block of assets, it may not be possible to claim that goodwill is covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’. On the other hand, if the predominant element of goodwill is trademark then it could be argued that goodwill is covered by the expression.

2.2-10b Non-compete payment-whether covered by the definition - Another type of payment made is ‘non-compete payment’, that is, payment to another person in consideration of his agreeing not to compete with the payer. Having regard to the nature of the payment, it is perhaps not in the nature of the acquisition of an asset which is a precondition for grant of depreciation. In any case it may increase the value of goodwill (see definition of ‘goodwill’ as explained in Srinivasa Setty’s case, reproduced above) and if goodwill itself cannot be considered as an intangible asset, the non-compete payment also cannot be considered so.

2.2-10c Agency rights/Distribution rights - An agent has been defined under section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as follows :

“An ‘agent’ is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in any dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the ‘Principal’.”

While an agency is certainly not similar to trademark, know how, patent, copyright, a question that arises is that whether an agency is similar to a franchise. According to one view, an agency is similar to a franchise (as defined above) in view of the following similarities :

◆ In agency as well as in franchise, there is a permission from another to sell a product.

◆ The agent as well as a franchisee undertake to conduct a business in accordance with methods and procedures prescribed by the franchisor.

According to the other view, the terms are not similar and the fundamental difference is that while a franchisee acts on his own behalf, an agent acts on behalf of the principal. Further, a franchise is associated with a licence to use a trademark or trade name, whereas an agency can be obtained even where the principal does not have a trade mark or trade name. Again, a franchise generally involves some manufacture or production (in relation to goods) or some activity (in relation to services) at the franchisee’s level whereas an agent generally does not manufacture or produce or perform any activity except that of selling the goods / services of the principal.

So far as distribution is concerned, while the distributor does act on his own behalf, the other differences as compared to a franchise given above are still applicable and hence, both the aforesaid views could be held as to whether or not distribution rights are covered by the expression ‘business or commercial rights of similar nature’.

◆ applicability of double taxation avoidance agreement.

Provision to be reasonably interpreted - Since the object and purpose of granting additional depreciation is to encourage industries by permitting assessee setting up new undertaking installation of new plant and machinery, therefore, provisions are required to be interpreted reasonably and purposively as strict and literal reading would lead to an absurd result denying additional depreciation to assessee though admittedly assessee had installed new plant and machinery. In the present case, assessee has purchased the plant and machinery before 1-4-2005 but the same has been installed after 1-4-2005, additional depreciation could not be denied [PCIT v. IDMC Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 285/246 Taxman 6 (Guj.)].

The provision does not state that setting up of a new machinery or plant should have any operational connectivity to article or thing that was already being manufactured by assessee. Thus, where an assessee engaged in the manufacture of textile goods, acquired and installed a wind mill for generation of power, additional depreciation cannot be denied on the ground that a wind mill has absolutely no connection with the manufacture of textile goods [CIT v. VTM Ltd. [2010] 187 Taxman 319 (Mad.)].

Amendment brought into s. 32(1)(iia) by the Finance Act, 2015 with effect from 1-4-2016 is retrospective in operation. Therefore, assessee would be eligible for additional depreciation in assessment year 2015-16 [PCIT v. Deepak Industries Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 467 (Cal.)].

Betterment charges - Betterment charges on account of increase in the valuation of the land of the assessee should not be held as a revenue expenditure although general improvement of the area might have an impact on better running of the business [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1992] 63 Taxman 493 (SC)].

Business expansion - The nature of the new business is not a decisive test for determining whether or not there is an expansion of an existing business. The nature of the business could be as distinct as a jewellery business and a business of cinematographic films; it could be as different as manufacture of metal alloys and manufacture of rubber products. What is of importance is that the control of both the ventures, the existing venture as well as the new venture, must be in the hands of one establishment or management or administration. The place of business of the existing business and the new business may not be in close proximity - it could be as far apart as Baroda and Bangalore. However, the funds utilised for the management of both the concerns must be common as reflected in the balance sheet of the company [Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. CIT [2008] 166 Taxman 55 (Delhi)].

Expenditure in connection with expansion of existing business would be allowed as revenue expenditure notwithstanding that same have been capitalised in the books of account [CIT v. Nirma Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 125/229 Taxman 535 (Guj.)]. However, where expenditure incurred by assessee for expansion of business had no nexus with business carried on by assessee, same held to be not allowable [United Breweries Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 8/229 Taxman 113 (Kar.)].

Business exploration expenses - Where the assessee, had paid a sum of Rs. 75 lakhs to management consultants, as professional fees for assessment of market attractiveness of assessee's business in terms of gaining global market, evaluation of assessee's business ability to compete, analysis of business's future growth trend, and development of detailed business strategies for the assessee to grow in the dynamic business environment, the said payment was fully deductible as revenue expenditure, since the assessee, with an intention of bringing about improvements in the way it did its business, had sought for and obtained reports of the consultant [CIT v. Carborandum Universal Ltd. [2009] 177 Taxman 347 (Mad.)].

Expenditure incurred by assessee on market survey report obtained during course of business activities of assessee for exploring further business is allowable [CIT v. Nuchem Ltd. [2015] 59 taxmann.com 455 (P&H)].

Decree to protect property/name - Payment by assessee to satisfy decree passed by the High Court against it in order to protect its property and name is allowable as business expenditure [CIT v. Hitachi Koki India Ltd. [2015] 56 taxmann.com 8/230 Taxman 643 (Kar.)].

One reason is that name of a company is selected by choice and hence action of 'passing off' is possible. However, the term shall not include the goodwill of a business or profession

The scope of the words "Other similar business or commercial rights" also fell for consideration before the Delhi High Court in Sharp Business System v. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 50/211 Taxman 576 (Delhi). The issue before the Court was whether non-compete fee paid to ex-JV partner under a non-compete agreement for 7 years was 'intangible asset' eligible for depreciation. The Court held that in personam rights such as non-compete fees are not depreciable intangible assets u/s 32(1)(ii). Depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) is admissible only to those intangible assets which give exclusive rights to the owner, which can be asserted against the world at large - i.e. in rem. A non-compete agreement can be asserted only in personam against the other party to the non-compete agreement. Hence, non-compete fee is not a depreciable intangible asset u/s 32(1)(ii). The Court analysed section 32(1)(ii) as under:

As would be evident from section 32(1)(ii), depreciation can be allowed in respect of intangible assets.

Par-liament has spelled out the nature of such assets by express reference to "know-how," "patents," "copyrights," "trademarks," "licenses," and "franchises."

So far as patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses and franchises are concerned, though they are intangible assets, the law recognises through various enactments that specific intellectual property rights flow from them.

Li-censes are derivative and often confer such intellectual property rights. The enjoyment of such intellectual property rights implies the exclusion of others who do not own or have a license to such rights from using them in any manner whatsoever.

Similarly, in the matter of franchises and know-how, the primary brand or intellectual process owner owns the exclusive right to produce, retail and distribute the products and the advantages flowing from such brand or intellectual process owner, but for the grant of such know-how rights or franchises.

The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the owner-ship.

In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance "in rem".

However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity.

The right can be asserted in the present instance only against ex-JV partner and in a sense, the right "in personam".

In-deed, the 7 years period spelt-out by the non-competing covenant brings the advantage within the public policy embedded in section 27 of the Contract Act, which enjoins a contract in restraint of trade would otherwise be void.

An-other way of looking at the issue is whether such rights can be treated or transferred – a proposition fully supported by the controlling object clause, i.e. intangible asset.

Every species of right spelt out expressly by the Statute—i.e., intellectual property rights and other advantages such as know-how, franchise, license, etc., and even those considered by the Courts, such as goodwill—can be said to be alienable. Such is not the case with an agreement not to compete, which is purely personal.

The words "similar business or commercial rights" necessarily have to result in an intangible asset against the entire world, which can be asserted as such to qualify for depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) of the Act.

Thus, "Other similar business or commercial rights" would not cover rights of a person's nature. The expression would cover only alienable rights in rem.

The other aspects relevant for comparability of transactions are nature of transaction (license or assignment); type of property; duration of the agreement; degree of protection and expected benefits likely to accrue from use of intangible property. The terms of agreement between parties for transfer of intangibles are also relevant consideration to compare transactions; and where these are not defined properly they can be culled from conduct of the parties and surrounding circumstances.

3. Benefit Test Benefit test is important aspect of valuation of marketing intangible. It indicates the measure of benefits derived by an associated enterprise from use of intangible property. The payer of royalty may benefit from intangible property in various forms such as, increase in sales volume, market share or profitability of associated enterprise for which proper documentation should be maintained. The tax authorities normally require taxpayers to satisfy the benefit test, where internal comparables are not available and intangible used is unique for which uncontrolled transactions do not exist.

4. Marketing Intangibles

Marketing intangibles mean an intangible asset such as a trade-mark or brand name that may enable a company to commercially exploit a product or service because of their interface and recognition by markets. Determining arm's length royalty rate of marketing intangible is complicated as one cannot easily determine market value of licensing such an asset.

As per OECD Guidelines3, in a case involving transfer of marketing intangibles, such as, trade mark the comparability analysis should consider the value added by the trademark, taking into account the consumer acceptability, geographic significance, market shares, sales volume and other relevant factors. But if international transaction involves trade intangibles the analysis should take into consideration the value attributable to such intangibles like patent protection or exclusivity of the use of intangible.

In Hyatt Group Holdings v. Commissioner4 the US Court held that since brand name was a valuable intangible right that provided high credit rating to the hotel the royalty at arm's length rate of 0.4% was payable for grant of right to use trademark. In another case of DHL Corporation and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner5 the US Court again held that transfer price regulations applied to value of trade-mark rights so determined by the Court and therefore, arm's length rate of royalty was payable by Hong Kong subsidiary DHLI to its US parent DHL Corporation even though the two companies had entered into a MOU in 1974 agreeing to do business without any payment of royalty.

In a Danish case6 the Tax Tribunal held that royalty paid by foreign AE at 6% of turnover for use of standard software developed by the parent company could not be treated excessive and subject to transfer pricing adjustment when the subsidiary company had agreed to use standard software of the parent company to avoid increased cost of developing more advanced software and there was no material to show that any unrelated enterprise could have obtained more favourable terms than the taxpayer.

5. Brand Royalty

Brand name is a distinctive name which is identified with a particular product or goods; it can be arbitrary, fanciful, suggestive, descriptive or generic depending upon the underlying product. When manufacture or processing of certain goods or business of an enterprise mainly depends upon value of a particular brand owned by the associated enterprise the royalty paid for the use of the brand must satisfy the arm's length test.

EKL Appliances Ltd. case

The Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. EKL Appliances Ltd7 examined the issue of arm's length payment of royalty to foreign AE for use of 'brand' by Indian company. The assessee was engaged in manufacturing of refrigerators, washing machines, compressors and spare parts. It paid brand fee of 1% of net sales to its Swedish AE (AB Electrolux) even though assessee company was incurring losses every year except in FY 1999-2000. The assessee's contention was that royalty payment was justified under CUP method as AE received similar payment from uncontrolled company Fisher Paykel Industries Ltd. The transaction was also certified by M/s Ernst Young which opined that fee paid was lower than uncontrolled brand fees. The High Court confirming the order of Tribunal held that payment of royalty was justified under CUP method and the company had benefited from use of technology of the foreign AE even though it suffered losses. The Court further observed that Rule 10B(1) does not authorise disallowance of any expenditure on the ground it was not necessary or prudent for the assessee; or because the company had incurred losses. The issue was accordingly decided in favour of the assessee.

The accounting of such training costs can be debatable and often companies have treated specific training costs as a part of the contract cost.

Under Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 2015, Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers sets forth the following guidance for contract fulfilment costs:

95 If the costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer are not within the scope of another Standard (for example, Ind AS 2, Inventories, Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment or Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets), an entity shall recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract only if those costs meet all of the following criteria:

(a)

the costs relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that the entity can specifically identify (for example, costs relating to services to be provided under renewal of an existing contract or costs of designing an asset to be transferred under a specific contract that has not yet been approved);

(b)

the costs generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying (or in continuing to satisfy) performance obligations in the future;

and

(c)

the costs are expected to be recovered.

96 For costs incurred in fulfilling a contract with a customer that are within the scope of another Standard, an entity shall account for those costs in accordance with those other Standards.

97 Costs that relate directly to a contract (or a specific anticipated contract) include any of the following:

(a)

direct labour (for example, salaries and wages of employees who provide the promised services directly to the customer);

(b)

direct materials (for example, supplies used in providing the promised services to a customer);

(c)

allocations of costs that relate directly to the contract or to contract activities (for example, costs of contract management and supervision, insurance and depreciation of tools and equipment used in fulfilling the contract);

(d)

costs that are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract; and

(e)

other costs that are incurred only because an entity entered into the contract (for example, payments to subcontractors).

98 An entity shall recognise the following costs as expenses when incurred:

(a)

general and administrative costs (unless those costs are explicitly chargeable to the customer under the contract, in which case an entity shall evaluate those costs in accordance with paragraph 97);

(b)

costs of wasted materials, labour or other resources to fulfil the contract that were not reflected in the price of the contract;

(c)

costs that relate to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations) in the contract (ie costs that relate to past performance);

and

(d)

costs for which an entity cannot distinguish whether the costs relate to unsatisfied performance obligations or to satisfied performance obligations (or partially satisfied performance obligations).

Therefore, based on the above guidance, if an entity incurs costs for training its staff specifically in order to execute a revenue contract with customers or as a requirement of the customer contracts, the cost may fit into a contract fulfilment cost. This is because, the training costs would relate directly to a contract or to an anticipated contract that can be specifically identified and would generate or enhance resources of the entity that will be used in satisfying performance obligations towards the customers in the future.

However, the conflict arises in Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets, which states as follows:

5 This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (eg a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, ie the knowledge embodied in it.

Ind AS 38 acknowledges that an entity usually has insufficient control over the future economic benefits arising from an assembled workforce (i.e. a team of skilled workers, or specific management or technical talent) or from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset.

Therefore, this guidance would require specific training costs to be recognised as expense as incurred.

A question, therefore, arises as to whether such training costs can be capitalised under Ind AS 115 since they would fulfil the definition of fulfilment costs.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

Brands and goodwill

9. The current financial year has seen a rush for amortisation of Brands and Goodwill. Brand valuation is now the buzz word in the corporate world. Both Goodwill and Brands are intangible. It is not easy to value the same in the balance sheet. Companies can capitalise brands in the balance sheet and reduce taxable income by claiming depreciation against such capitalised value. Accounting Standard 14 (AS 14) issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India provide for writing off goodwill in the books of the transferee company. This is mandatory since April 1, 1995. AS 14 deals with accounting for amalgamations only. It makes a distinction between amalgamation in the nature of a merger and amalgamation in the nature of a purchase. Goodwill is to be written off generally over a period of five years. It is only when brands and goodwill are acquired for a price that the question of allowing depreciation will arise. Brands built-up over a period of years like goodwill which is sui generis may not fall under the category of intangible assets eligible for depreciation under the new provision. This can give rise to avoidable tax mitigation devices like selling a company’s brand and then re-purchasing it in order to boost the balance sheet and claim depreciation. This again calls for amendment of the law in order to avoid litigation.

Though brands, goodwill and trade marks appear some what synonimous, there is a certain distinction between the three concepts. Trade marks are of several kinds, descriptive, suggestive or fanciful. Suggestive trade marks require the buyer to use thought, imagination or perception to connect the mark with the goods. Descriptive terms directly convey to the buyer, the ingredients or qualities that are characteristic of the product. The trade mark consisting of a made up or a coined word, is said to be fanciful. Such marks are considered inherently distinctive and are protected by law. A brand is a word, a mark, a symbol or a design or a term used for the purpose of identification of some product or service. It may be visual or oral. Goodwill is generally recognised as the custom of patronage of any established trade or business. The excess of cost of an acquired firm or operating unit over the current or fair market value of net assets of the acquired unit may generally be taken as the approximate value of goodwill.

The amended law is innovative and opens up infinite possibilities for rearranging the balance sheet for purpose of company law and also for the purpose of the tax law.

On this basis the Tribunal held that these advantages accrued by the assessee were nothing but various intangible assets. All the rights similar to the rights mentioned in section 32 were acquired by the assessee. Thus, in this case goodwill was a business or commercial right of similar nature and the assessee was benefited by amalgamation by acquiring that commercial value, being intangible assets for which the assessee had paid on amalgamation. CIT31 the Tribunal observed that "goodwill is nothing but positive reputation built by a person /company/ business-house over a period of time which is not manufactured or produced overnight but is brought into existence by experience and reputation." It held that the goodwill will fall under the category of 'business or commercial right of similar nature' under the definition of intangible asset.' • In B. Raveendran Pillai32 the assessee purchased a hospital with its land, building, equipments, staff, name, trademark and goodwill as a going concern. In the subsequent years, depreciation on goodwill was claimed on the written down value. When the case was taken for scrutiny assessment, AO held that goodwill was not covered by section 32(1)(ii) and the assessee was not entitled to depreciation, even though depreciation claimed on goodwill had been allowed in the earlier years. This prima facie appeals to any person as though it is gratuitous but the intendement ex facie behind it is only in recognition of the long-standing services of employees in a graded manner and also to keep the work force of the company more efficient by creating an affable environment so as to enable them to increase productivity and profitability of a company.

3.1.9 Economic Ownership of Brand:The Special Bench had rejected the concept of economic ownership of brand, in the context of Transfer Pricing. That concept has been now appreciated by the High Court. The High Court has held that the economic ownership of a brand name or trademark is accepted in international taxation as one of the components of determining the transfer price of goods.

Economic ownership when pleaded can be accepted if it is proved by the assessee. The burden is on the assessee. It cannot be assumed.

Economic ownership of a brand is an intangible asset, just as legal ownership is. On this point we may draw an inference from the High Court's observation, that in long-term distribution-cum-marketing arrangements, with the Foreign AE, the Indian Distributor (the purchasing AE) may acquire economic ownership of the brand – such ownership, however, has to be proved by the Indian Distributor. In that case the Indian Distributor does acquire the right to exploit the intangible property, like trademark or logo, embedded or affixed on the distributed goods. Therefore, in such a case we may assert that the AMP expenses are incurred by the Indian Distributor for its own benefit, as economic owner of the trademark or the logo. So, no separate AMP remuneration is due from the Foreign AE.

But what would be the appropriate remuneration in such a case, for AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributor? The appropriate remuneration would be the premium profits realised from exploitation of the brand. Such premium profits would be reflected in higher Gross Profit margins or higher Net Profit margins realised by the Indian Distributor, as compared to comparable distributors.

3.1.10 Direct Marketing Expenses:The High Court has rejected the Revenue's contention that direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, would form part of the AMP expenses.

Distribution and marketing exercise in case of tangible goods requires transfer or sale of goods to third parties, be it sub-distributors or retailers. That transaction is in the nature of sale of goods for consideration. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to sub-distributors or retailers are not in the nature and character of 'brand promotion'. They are not directly or immediately related to 'brand building' exercise, but have a live link and direct connection with marketing and increased volume of sales or turnover. The 'brand building' connect is too remote and faint.

To include and treat the direct marketing expenses, like trade discount or volume discount or incentive, as 'brand building' exercise would be contrary to common sense and would be highly exaggerated. The expenses being in the nature of selling expenses have an immediate connect with price or consideration payable for the goods sold. They are not incurred for publicity or advertisement.

Based on the above reasoning, the High Court has held that the direct marketing and sale related expenses, or discounts and concessions, should not form part of the AMP expenses.

3. Appropriate Funding This point get to the heart of the marketing intangible issue that India, as well as other countries, are grappling with. The U.S. Tax Court case of DHL set the bar for this issue noting that the "non-routine" or brand building expenses constituted the investment for the economic right to its trademark. Cases since, as well as taxing authorities, have in a rudimentary fashion interpreted this to generally mean an advertising, marketing and promotion expenses, (AMP). This is wrong. The recent India case, LG India addressed this issue and refined the Courts prior analysis in the Maruti-Suzuki case. Here, for the first time, the Court acknowledge the "non-routine" expense issue raised in DHL as the critical element. However, the Court carefully noted that the taxpayer failed in its burden of proof to identify these company specific expenses and acknowledged that the transfer pricing officer had to resort to outside benchmarks to address the issue. However, having not been convinced that the transfer pricing officer achieved a reasonable level of comparability, the case was remanded for further development.

Implicit in LG India is the notion that brand building expenses are company specific and that the affiliates have the burden of establishing this fact, if such exists. That is the correct approach. It is these brand building expenses that creates the funding for a marketing intangible that can be compensable. One pitfall however is not to confuse these expenses with the intellectual property concepts of quality control and goodwill that are attached to the trademark, cannot be separated from the trademark, nor are separately compensable. Absent these items of quality control and goodwill, a trademark is not enforceable.

The intention behind the expense is required to be known for allowability of a particular expense in the hands of the person who incurs it. The provisions under Chapter X of the Act, do envisage a 'separate entity concept'. In other words, there cannot be a presumption that all the activities of a subsidiary company are, in fact, dictated by the parent company (foreign AE). Merely because a parent company has a financial interest, it cannot be presumed that AMP expenses incurred by subsidiary company are at the instance or on behalf of the parent company. The initial onus is on the Income Tax department to demonstrate through some tangible material that the two parties acted in concert and further, that there should be an agreement to enter into an international transaction concerning AMP expenses.

If a subsidiary or other associate company entered into an agreement with foreign AE (parent co.) and such agreement prescribes for doing brand building activity by Indian entity for parent company's brand, through incurring of AMP expenses, in that case certainly a transaction emerges from Indian entity's such activity.

But if an Indian entity is under no obligation to incur an extent of AMP expense for brand building of parent company then a presumption should not be drawn that parent company might get an incidental benefit and a proportion of the AMP expenses incurred must be attributed to it. This view is upheld by the Delhi High Court in case of Whirlpool of India Ltd. (supra).

Even in case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra), the High Court acknowledges that an expenditure cannot be disallowed wholly or partly because it incidentally benefits the third party. It holds that "the issue of arm's length price per se does not arise when deduction under section 37(1) is claimed." Further the decision of an assessee, whether or not to incur an expenditure cannot be substituted and disallowed by the Assessing Officer. In the context of the AMP expenses incurred by manufacturer exclusively for its own business, it is arguable that once such expense is allowed under section 37(1) of the Act, it cannot be disallowed for the purpose of Chapter X by attributing some part of the said expenditure to promoting the brand of the foreign AE.

The Supreme Court in case ofSassoon J David & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261/1 Taxman 485, emphasised on that the expression 'wholly and exclusively' used in section 10(2)(xv) of the Act did not mean 'necessarily'. It said: "The fact that somebody other than the Assessee is also benefitted by the expenditure, should not come in the way of an expenditure being allowed by way of a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act if it satisfies otherwise the tests laid down by the law." section 37 of the 1961 Act is corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act.

The OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines also emphasises on that there should not be any automatic inference about an AE receiving an entity group service only because it gets an incidental benefit for being part of a larger concern and not to any specific activity performed.
