4.3 Analysis of the case of CIT v. Coca Cola Beverages Ltd. - In the recent case of CIT v. Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd.34 decided on January 14, 2011 by the Delhi High Court, the question was: "whether learned ITAT erred in setting aside the order of the CIT under section 263 ignoring the fact that the goodwill generated in a business cannot be described as an "asset" so as to be entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the depreciation on goodwill was not admissible?"

The facts of the case are: Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd. (the "Taxpayer") was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of non-alcoholic beverages. It acquired a business for a slump price on a going concern basis and allocated a part of the price towards goodwill in its books of account. The price was paid for marketing and trading reputation, trading style and name, territory know-how, customer database, distribution network, contracts and other commercial rights. The taxpayer claimed depreciation on the understanding that the consideration was paid to acquire certain commercial rights which were in the nature of intangible capital assets. Such intangible assets were termed as goodwill by the taxpayer in its books of account. The Assessing Officer accepted the depreciation claim of the taxpayer. However, the CIT directed the AO to revise the assessment on the following grounds:

(a) goodwill is not covered within the meaning of intangible assets under Section 32,

(b) the assessee considered goodwill to be a valuable commercial asset similar to other intangible asset mentioned in the definition of block of assets which was contrary to the Explanation 3 to section 32 and, hence, the same was not justified.

The assessee appealed to the ITAT, Delhi. The Tribunal noted that the allocation of amount paid as a slump price was not in dispute and the fact that a part of consideration represented consideration for rights, as detailed in the audit report notes was also not in dispute. The Tribunal held that goodwill is not specifically excluded from the intangible assets eligible for depreciation, and, therefore, even if an asset is described as goodwill but it fits in the description of section 32(1)(ii), depreciation is to be granted on the same. The true basis of depreciation allowance is the character of the asset not its description.

The Department appealed to the High Court. The Court held that goodwill in this case was in substance similar to tangible assets. It included industrial information like database of the territory relating to customer preferences, distribution networks, etc. Hence, in effect, it was know-how. The Court held that non-monetary assets could not be seen or touched or physically measured, but were created. Such assets assumed diverse forms like copyrights, patents, trademarks, etc., which arose on acquisition or were internally generated. The Court based its decision on the following grounds:

(a) the nomenclature given to the entries in the books of account was not relevant for ascertaining the real nature of the transaction. The accounting treatment of a payment per se could not govern its treatment in income-tax proceedings.

(b) the meaning of business or commercial rights of similar nature has to be understood in the backdrop of section 32(1)(ii) of the Act. Commercial rights are such rights which are obtained for effectively carrying on the business and commerce. Commerce, as is understood, is a wider term which encompasses in its fold many facets.

The question whether such restrictive covenants are allowed or is it violative of provisions of any law or may be prohibited under any Act is to be examined carefully. Further, in terms of the Competition Act, every restraint or every restrictive covenant in an agreement does not restrict competition. The agreements which impose restriction of Trade or the Agreements in Restraint of Trade are covered by section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 states that "Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is to that extent void."

But there are some exceptions to the aforesaid rule. For example, a person who sells the total business may agree with the buyer that he will not carry on a similar business, may be, within a specified local limits till such time the buyer carries on a like business therein, provided such limits appear to the Court reasonable, having regard to the nature and operations of the business. So, in other words, all agreements in restraint of trade will be valid, provided they are reasonable having regard to the nature of business and also reasonable in the interests of the parties and in public interest.

The Supreme Court in the matter of Gujarat Bottling Co. Ltd. v. Coca Cola Co. [1994] 84 Comp. Cas. 618, has in detail analysed the scope of section 27 of the Indian Contract Act and given the judgment reads as under :—

". . . A covenant in restraint of trade must be reasonable with reference to the public policy and it must also be reasonably necessary for the protection of the interest of the covenantee and regard must be had to the interests of the covenantor. Contracts in restraint of trade are prima facie void and the onus of proof is on the party supporting the contract to show that the restraint goes no further than is reasonably necessary to protect the interest of the covenantee and if this onus is discharged the onus of showing that the restraint is nevertheless injurious to the public is on the party attacking the contract. The Court has to decide, as a matter of law, (i) whether a contract is or is not in restraint of trade, and (ii) whether, if in restraint of trade, it is reasonable. . . ." (p. 642)

Thus, in the aforesaid case, the Supreme Court ruled that a negative stipulation contained in a Franchise Agreement restraining the franchisee from dealing with competing goods was to facilitate the distribution of the goods of the franchiser and could not be regarded as a restraint of a right to trade. However, in yet another case, where the defendant and the plaintiff used to carry on the business of ferrying boats and arrived at a business sale settlement, wherein the defendant had to pay a certain amount to the plaintiff in order that the plaintiff should abstain from carrying on his business of boat ferrying for a period of three years, the Court held that the agreement was void as the restraining covenant was a vital part of the agreement itself and did not fall under the ‘goodwill exception’ as mentioned in section 27 of the Indian Contract Act. Thus, while drafting an agreement, care should be taken to see that the restrictive covenants, if at all to be included, should convey correct meaning and fit into the exception module.

Benefits of framing guidelines on Competition Law by Corporates

13. Certain benefits of framing guidelines on Competition Law are :—

(i) Commitment to compliance with Competition Law - Compliance with the law is part of corporate image and an organisation grows only with sound ethical practices combined with adherence to various provisions of laws, which would take it to next league in achieving success. Further, it will earn a better brand image and goodwill in the market. By complying with the requirement of Competition Law, the company can avoid penalties that may be imposed for activities that may curb anti-competitive practices in the Indian market.

(ii) Detection - With the introduction of proper guidelines, education and training, an organisation can carve out appropriate and inappro-priate conduct which will help in early detection of violations. This is because, by this method, the employees are well-informed about the signs of illegal conduct by co-employees and, thus, pave the way for clear and safe ways for reporting suspected violations. Further, the employees would get an indirect message that the company will not tolerate anti-competitive behaviours or conduct.

(iii) Responsibilities - The responsibility for observing the rules and regulations of the Competition Act lies with every employee who encounters issues relating to Competition Law and particularly applies to senior management and managers involved in the department of sales, procurement and merger and acquisition projects. Each and every employee is required to acquire necessary knowledge in order to assess such issues and, in this regard, to consult the legal department/in-house counsel/external law firms, if necessary. The Senior Management Executive must select, instruct and train their employees to ensure that they observe the rules and regulations of the Act.

(iv) Litigation - The adherence to the guidelines of Competition Laws and proper training will alert the unpleasant situation, if any, of being caught for violation of laws of competition. Thus, proper training of the concerned employees and sticking to the guidelines on competition law will help in identifying potential risk in the conduct and would avoid unnecessary litigation costs.

It must be noted here that IAS 38 and IFRS 15 are similar to Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 115 in this respect.

Internationally, the IFRS Interpretations Committee had received a request in 2019 about training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. In the fact pattern described in the request:

a. an entity enters into a contract with a customer that is within the scope of IFRS 15. The contract is for the supply of outsourced services.

b.

to be able to provide the services to the customer, the entity incurs costs to train its employees (as described in paragraph 15 of IAS 38 Intangible Assets) so that they understand the customer's equipment and processes. Applying IFRS 15, the entity does not identify the training activities as a performance obligation.

c.

the contract permits the entity to charge to the customer the costs of training (i) the entity's employees at the beginning of the contract, and (ii) new employees that the entity hires as a result of any expansion of the customer's operations.

The request asked whether the entity recognises the training costs as an asset or an expense when incurred.

Which IFRS Standard applies to the training costs?

Paragraph 95 of IFRS 15 requires an entity to recognise an asset from the costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer not within the scope of another IFRS Standard, only if those costs meet all three criteria specified in paragraph 95. Consequently, before assessing the criteria in paragraph 95, the entity first considers whether the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract are within the scope of another IFRS Standard.

Paragraph 5 of IAS 38 states that 'this Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities'. Accordingly, the Committee concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity applies IAS 38 in accounting for the training costs incurred to fulfil the contract with the customer.

Application of IAS 38

Paragraph 69(b) of IAS 38 lists 'expenditure on training activities' as an example of expenditure that an entity recognises as an expense when incurred. Paragraph 15 of IAS 38 explains that 'an entity usually has insufficient control over the expected future economic benefits arising from a team of skilled staff and from training for these items to meet the definition of an intangible asset'.

In addition, in explaining the requirements in IFRS 15 regarding costs to fulfil a contract, paragraph BC307 of IFRS 15 states that 'if the other Standards preclude the recognition of any asset arising from a particular cost, an asset cannot then be recognised under IFRS 15'.

Accordingly, the Committee, in its September 2019 meeting, concluded that, in the fact pattern described in the request, the entity recognises as an expense when incurred the training costs to fulfil the contract with the customer.

The Committee concluded that the principles and requirements in IFRS 15 and IAS 38 provide an adequate basis for an entity to determine its accounting for training costs incurred to fulfil a contract with a customer. Consequently, the Committee decided not to add this matter to its standard-setting agenda.

According to the assessee, said firm had developed reliable business relationships with foreign principals and had earned a goodwill and trade name in the line of business. Therefore, while acquiring said goodwill and name of said firm, assessee had paid amount for trade name, goodwill and for all other business and commercial rights. He contended that what was acquired by him was an intangible asset and, therefore, was entitled to depreciation under provisions of section 32. Therefore, it is very obvious that all intangible assets are not eligible for depreciation allowance. Amount paid by assessee towards acquisition of goodwill does not come under either category." Aggregation or bundling of transactions, use of TNMM and intentional set-off Delhi HC held that in situations where separate transactions are so intertwined and linked or are continuous so that they cannot be evaluated adequately on separate basis, aggregation of transactions is both desirable and permissible. The verdict of Delhi HC was based on Organisation for Economic Cooperation & Development (OECD) Transfer Pricing Guidelines and the United Nations (UN) Transfer Pricing Manual, which, according to the HC, supplement the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and constitute a valuable commentary on the subject matter.

The Indian legislature in Rule 10A(d) clearly expounds that the term 'transaction' includes a number of closely linked transactions and hence, envisages a situation where aggregation of closely connected transaction may be necessary. Para 3.9 of OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines iterates that though ideally the arm's length principles should be applied on a transaction by transaction basis, there are often situations where separate transactions are so closely linked or continuous that they cannot be evaluated adequately on a separate basis. OECD provides a number of illustrations to substantiate 'closely linked or continuous' test.

The Delhi HC also has analysed whether in situations requiring aggregation, TNMM can be applied reliably? It has examined the strengths and weaknesses of this method. It eventually concludes that once a composite set of transactions have been benchmarked collectively under TNMM, it would not be appropriate to segregate AMP expenses as a separate international transaction without providing an appropriate set-off of the composite profits earned. However, the HC cautions aggregating dissimilar activities like manufacturing and distribution and benchmarking them using a single TNMM would not be correct.

Para 3.13 of OECD Commentary deals with the topic of Intentional set offs. Intentional set-offs generally occur between AEs in respect of controlled transactions wherein when one enterprise provides benefit to another enterprise within the group that is balanced to some degree by different benefits received from that enterprise in return. Similar comments on both 'closely linked and continuous transactions and intentional set-offs are covered in U.N. Transfer Pricing Manual2. The HC held that the concept of set-off is or adjustment is well recognized and accepted internationally and the Indian law does not preclude it.

Brightline test not obligatory

Upholding the bright line test was one of the most contentious prescriptions emanating from the SB ruling of Delhi ITAT in case of LG Electronics. The HC has correctly dismissed the use of this method to identify excess AMP expenditure. The HC observed that this is not a method prescribed under Indian transfer pricing law and has also not been recognised and accepted in any of the international commentaries or principles of taxation. The Delhi HC further held that direct marketing expenses like discounts, rebates and incentives as well as selling expenses cannot be considered to be incurred for the purpose of brand building and thus should not form part of AMP expenditure.

The bright line test was propounded by a US Tax Court in the matter of DHL.3 In the aforesaid case, AMP expenditure incurred to the tune of what uncontrolled comparable distributors incurred was characterized as falling within 'Bright Line Limit' of routine expenses. Any AMP spent beyond the Bright Line Limit constituted non-routine expenditure, resulting in creation of market intangibles belonging to the foreign brand owner. While the Developer-Assister rules forming part of US Transfer Pricing regulations does mention 'routine' and 'non-routine' expenses (through 'cheese' examples in order to decipher the share of AMP expense to be reimbursed), the aforesaid US Transfer Pricing Rules do not advocate 'Bright Line Test' in particular.

Economic ownership of brand

The SB ruling had held that only legal ownership is recognized under Indian income tax laws and economic ownership exists only in commercial sense. The Delhi HC has on the contrary, help that economic ownership of a brand is an intangible asset, just as legal ownership and valuation of economic ownership of a brand is not done from time to time but only at the time of termination or transfer at which point of time a transfer pricing valuation may be undertaken.

Application of mark-up

In respect of the mark-up on the portion determined to be a service, the Delhi HC held that the prime lending rate cannot be the basis for computing mark-up since the mark-up has to be benchmarked with comparable uncontrolled transactions or transactions for providing similar services/product.

Present & Future

The HC judgment reaches an all-important conclusion that if a taxpayer (being a distributor) has earned an appropriate arm's length compensation established using a set of comparable uncontrolled distributors, any excessive AMP expenditure incurred by the taxpayer is subsumed in the distribution net margin and no separate compensation is warranted. This fortifies taxpayers' who have always believed this to be the foundation of their transfer pricing policy. The HC judgment has also validated the stand of the various tribunals that not all expenditure constitutes brand building and selling expenses should be kept out of the ambit of AMP expenditure.

The amount referred to in (b) above has been paid for certain contracts, rights, etc., owned by the seller. In the valuation report these contracts, rights, etc., have not been assigned any value. Therefore, the difference between the total consideration and the value of the tangible assets has been accounted for as goodwill. Goodwill in the assessee's case is in substance similar to the tangible assets." In the above case, it is hinted that Goodwill is a special value addition which is difficult to be grouped under one of those well known intangibles such as patent, copyright, etc., which have legal backing. The High Court has gone further in making a pausing remark by equating Goodwill with tangible asset to stress on the significant role of Goodwill in Business and not to be construed literally. In fact, it is mentioned that in the business valuation report no value has been placed upon certain contracts, rights, etc. It is only such unidentified items which can be found on paper, that have been reckoned to make up a part of the difference between total consideration and value of tangible assets. Such items are indeed of evidential value of certain competitive advantages accruing to the possessor.

Also, interestingly, it has made references to a classical judgment. It drew reference from a very old case, named, IRC v. Muller & Co.'s Margarine Ltd. [1901] A.C. 217 (HL) in UK and recited "In a progressing business goodwill tends to show progressive increase. And in a failing business it may begin to wane. Its value may fluctuate from one moment to another, depending on changes in the reputation of the business. It is affected by everything relating to the business, the personality and business rectitude of the owners, the nature and character of the business, its name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio-economic ecology, introduction to old customers and agreed absence of competition. There can be no account in value of the factors producing it.."

The above classical judgment took us through the other invisible facets of the intangibles called as Goodwill and also educated us on that it needs to be reviewed regularly in relation to the business reputation, being a subjective thing. This is in addition to a view available from the previous paragraph that Goodwill may even exist in visible forms, such as contracts and special commercial rights.

3.2 B. Raveendran Pillai v. CIT [2010] 194 Taxman 477 (Ker.) - The assessee purchased a hospital as a going concern. The value of the goodwill was included in the name of the hospital and its logo and trademark. The assessee claimed depreciation on the goodwill. The Assessing Officer and the Tribunal disallowed the claim. However, on appeal by the assessee, the Kerala High Court reversed the decision of the Tribunal. In doing so it made the following significant point:

"(ii) Admittedly the hospital was run in the same building, in the same town, in the same name for several years prior to the purchase by the assessee. By transferring the right to use the name of the hospital itself, the previous owner had transferred the goodwill to the assessee and the benefit derived by the assessee was retention of continued trust of the patients who were patients of the previous owners."

The essence of this judgment is supplementary that when a going concern is transferred as such, depreciation on Goodwill, will be admissible subject to existence of other factors, such as right to use the name of transferor, etc., which can justify the exploitation of such Goodwill.

3.3 Asstt. v. Smt. Sangeeta Wij [2012] 24 taxmann.com 128 (Delhi) - In both the above cases, a value was already assigned to Goodwill in their respective sale deeds. In this case where there was a slump sale involving no value assignment to any of the individual assets including Goodwill. The seller, being a sole proprietary concern (civil engineer), was taken over as a going concern by a newly formed company in which the erstwhile proprietor was to serve as a whole-time Director for about 5 years as per the agreement on salary basis. The net worth of the concern was only Rs. 473,725 while the compensation on sale of the business was a huge Rs. 12,000,000. The assessee (proprietor) claimed the difference of Rs. 11,526,275 as long-term capital gain and claimed exemption from capital gains taxation by resorting to section 54F. The AO, however, rejected that the difference was chargeable as business income.

The ITAT agreed with fact that the difference was a self-generated goodwill and taxable as long-term Capital Gains by recognizing the following facts, namely,

1. The assessee had been in business for about 11 years and carried over 500 projects in India and abroad (Being a sole proprietor the entire Goodwill was created by a single person's effort).

2. The business had been transferred as a going concern and not discontinued.

3. The assessee was a whole-time director earning salary in the newly formed company for a stipulated period of 5 years as per the agreement.

ALLOWABILITY OF EXPENDITURE

'Being', meaning of - The word 'being' used in section 35D(2)(c)(iv) is not illustrative to mean only those expenses which are specified in the statute could be allowed and nothing further [CIT v. Ennar Steel & Alloy (P.) Ltd. [2004] 137 Taxman 429 (Mad.)].

Advertisement - Advertisement expenditure is an allowable deduction [CIT v. Madras Fertilizers Ltd. [1999] 238 ITR 672 (Mad.); CIT v. Salora International Ltd. [2009] 308 ITR 199 (Delhi)].

Consultancy charges - Expenses incurred towards consultancy charges were for purposes of carrying out existing business more efficiently is not an allowable deduction [CIT v. Gillette Group India (P.) Ltd. [2008] 173 Taxman 52 (Delhi)].

Convertible notes - Expenditure incurred on convertible premium notes is an allowable deduction [CIT v. Dhampur Sugar Mills Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 94/[2014] 226 Taxman 24 (Mag.) (All.)].

Expanding production capacity - Expenditure for expanding production capacity of vehicles held to be an allowable deduction [CIT v. Ashok Leyland Ltd. [2012] 23 taxmann.com 50/ [2013] 213 Taxman 204 (Mad.)].

Incorporation expenses - Expenses incurred by assessee's holding company relating to formation of assessee-company is not an allowable deduction [Cairn Energy (India) Ltd. v. JCIT [2008] 171 Taxman 54 (Mad.)].

Interest - Where there was no inextricable link between investment and project, interest income on said investment could not be permitted to be adjusted against pre-operative expenses in respect of said project [CIT v. Indian Vaccines Corporation Ltd. [2014] 44 taxmann.com 130/222 Taxman 207 (Mag.) (Delhi)]. However, where production had not yet been started and assessee kept available funds in FDRs for obtaining letter of credit required to import machineries, in such a case, interest income was liable to be adjusted against pre-operative cost of plant and machinery [Phoenix Lamps India Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 50 taxmann.com 320/[2015] 228 Taxman 306 (Mag.) (All.)].

Lease rent - Lease rent incurred before commencement of production held not to be an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Ennar Steel & Alloy (P.) Ltd. [2004] 137 Taxman 429 (Mad.)]. Also see, GAIL India Ltd. v. JCIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 97/211 Taxman 587 (Delhi).

Loan issue expenses - Front-end fees paid to bank at the time of obtaining new loan is an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Kesoram Industries Ltd. [2019] 112 taxmann.com 356/[2020] 268 Taxman 446 (Cal.)].

Refund of oversubscription - Expenditure incurred in connection with refund of oversubscription in relation to issue of shares held to be an allowable expenditure [CIT v. Shree Synthetics Ltd. [1986] 162 ITR 819 (MP)].

ROC fees - Expenditure incurred for obtaining registration would be liable to be deducted and, consequently, fees paid to ROC for raising authorized capital of company would also be covered [CIT v. Multi Metals Ltd. [1991] 188 ITR 151 (Raj.), approved inPunjab State Industrial Development Corporation Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 93 Taxman 5 (SC)].

Fees paid for increase in share capital is not fees for registration of the company and, hence, is not amortisable u/s 35D(2)(c)(iii) [CIT v. Hindustan Insecticides Ltd. [2001] 116 Taxman 406 (Delhi)].

Share issue expenses - Expenditure in connection with issuance of Euro share which was directly relatable to expansion of capital base of company for raising of new projects held to be an allowable expenditure [EID Parry (India) Ltd. v. DCIT [2012] 23 taxmann.com 348/209 Taxman 214 (Mad.); Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilisers Co. Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 49 (Guj.)].

service tax as these have been specifically excluded from definition of ‘commercial training or coaching services’. As regards management consultancy service (if provided directly by IIM), the service will be taxable w.e.f. May 1, 2006 since this service is taxable if provided by ‘any person’. IIM can certainly fall within the meaning of ‘any person’ (I believe it is registered as Society).

Hence, possible controversy is only in respect of remaining two activities.

Charges for campus interviews 1. IIM arranges campus interviews for students studying for final examination. IIM collects fees from companies which visit IIM for selecting candidates through campus interviews. It seems this activity is said to be falling under ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’s service.

As per section 65(105)( k), any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a manpower recruitment or supply agency in relation to the recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, in any manner, is a ‘taxable service’.

As per section 65(68) (amended w.e.f. June 16, 2005), ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ means any person (earlier, the words were ‘commercial concern’ up to May 1, 2006) engaged in providing any service, directly or indirectly, in any manner for recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, to a client.

Till May 1, 2006, IIM could not fall within the definition since it is not a ‘commercial concern’. However, since May 1, 2006, the words ‘commercial concern’ have been replaced by ‘any person’. Hence, the earlier defence has gone.

The definition of ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ is very wide. The service can be provided directly or indirectly in any manner for recruitment of manpower. Service is taxable if provided by ‘any person’. In view of this, in my view, the campus interview activity of IIM will be held as taxable w.e.f. May 1, 2006.

Even if it is not covered under this head, it can get covered under ‘Business Support Service’, since as per section 65(104c), ‘Support services of business or commerce’ means services provided in relation to business or commerce. That service is taxable if provided by any person to any person.

Short-term courses to executives and managers

2. IIM arranges short-term residential courses for executives and managers in companies, PSUs and corporations.

As per section 65(105)( zzc), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a commercial training or coaching centre in relation to commercial training or coaching, is a ‘taxable service’.

‘Commercial training or coaching’ means any training or coaching provided by a commercial training or coaching centre [Section 65(26)].

‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ means any institute or establishment providing commercial training or coaching for imparting skill or knowledge or lessons on any subject or field other than sports, with or without issuance of a certificate and includes coaching or tutorial classes but does not include pre-school coaching and training centre or any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force [Section 65(27 )].

2.1 IIM short-term courses are ‘education’ - not training or coaching - Education is different from training or coaching. The word ‘education’ is much broader than ‘train’ or ‘coach’. ‘Train’ means train in a particular skill like computer repairs, machine operation etc. ‘Coach’ means special or personal tuition. Giving education in a particular subject is not ‘training’ or ‘coaching’.

Train - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘train’ means to teach (a person, animal, oneself etc.) a specified skill especially by practice. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘train’ means cause or grow in particular way; educate, instruct, exercise.

Coach - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘coach’ means an instructor trainer in sport, a private tutor. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘coach’ means tutor, instructor.

Educate - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘educate’ means give an intellectual, moral and social instruction to (a pupil, especially a child) as a formal and prolonged process. If followed by in or to plus infinitive, it means train or instruct for a particular purpose. ‘Education’ means the act or process of educating or being educated, systematic instruction. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘educate’ means bring up, train mentally and morally; provide schooling for.

Education denotes training of mind, in contradistinction to training in manual skills - Barry v. Hughes [1973] 1 All ER 537 (Ch. D).

Education is the systematic instruction, schooling or training given to the young in preparation for the work of life. It also connotes the whole course of scholastic instruction which a person had received. Education is the process of training and developing the knowledge, skill, mind and character of students by formal schooling - Sole Trustee Loka Shikshana Trust v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 10.

Thus, IIM courses cannot be said to be ‘training’ or ‘coaching’. It is education.

Wholly and exclusively

The expression ‘wholly and exclusively’ does not denote necessarily [Sassoon J. David & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)]. The word ‘wholly’ refers to quantum of expenditure. The word ‘exclusively’ refers to motive, objective or purpose with which the particular expense has been incurred [Addl. CIT v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. (2004) 137 Taxman 367 (Raj.) and Ram Bahadur Thakur Ltd. v. CIT (2003) 261 ITR 390 (Ker.)]. The word "wholly" signifies that the expenditure should be completely devoted to the business. It need not be essential, necessary or compelling; it may be optional and purely voluntary. But it must be commercially expedient and should have the aim of the continuance or furtherance of the business and an eventual augmentation or stabilization of profits [Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 156 (Mad.)]

The true test of an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of trade or business is that it is incurred by the assessee as incidental to his trade for the purpose of keeping the trade going and of making it pay and not in any other capacity than that of a trader. It has to be examined whether the expense has been incurred with the sole object of furthering the trade or business interest of the assessee unalloyed or unmixed with any other consideration. If the expense is found to bear an element other than that of the trade or business interest of the assessee, the expenditure is not an allowable one [B. K. Khanna & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 113 Taxman164 (Delhi)]

(1) Suppose the assessee incurs expenditure on advertisement in a souvenir of a labour union formed by a political party. The labour union is registered under the Trade Unions Act of 1926. Is the expenditure required to be reported by the tax auditor in the third item in clause 21(a)?

Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides that every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which it is registered, and shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire and hold both movable and immovable property and to contract, and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Thus, a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is a separate and distinct legal entity and is not part of the political party which formed it. Since the Labour union has a separate and distinct legal identity, the expenditure cannot be said to be incurred in the advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party. Therefore, the expenditure is not reportable in clause 21(a).

(2) If the advertisement is published in a newspaper published by a political party, is the expenditure thereon to be reported in clause 21(a)?

It is possible to take the view that expenditure on advertisement in a political party's newspaper is not required to be reported under this clause. A newspaper is certainly not like a brochure, tract, etc. The words 'any other like publication' occurring in clause 21(a) as well as section 37(2B) should be interpreted ejusdem generis with 'brochure', 'tract', 'pamphlet' and 'souvenir' [See para 8 of ICAI's Guidance Note on section 293A of the Companies Act and the Auditor]

The recently released (May 2013) official version of "United Nations Practical Manual on Transfer Pricing for Developing Countries" has a unique feature that it has a separate Chapter to outline country specific transfer pricing practices followed by Brazil, China, India and South Africa. These country specific administrative practices are based on the details provided by the representatives from these countries. The MNEs would certainly refer to these country practice notes to obtain certainty on their transfer pricing issues in these countries.

Paragraphs 10.4.8.12 to 10.4.8.18 of the UN Manual contain the Indian administrative practice on transfer pricing aspects of "Marketing Intangibles". The UN Manual defines "Intangibles" as the property that has no physical existence but whose value depends on the legal rights of the owner. Further "Marketing Intangibles" are intangibles relating to marketing activities, aiding in the commercial exploitation of a product or service or with important promotional value for a product or service. Trademarks, Trade Names are marketing intangibles.

While discussing business strategies in the Chapter on Comparability Analyis, the UN Manual says–

"5.3.2.55. When an MNE enters a new market with its product or expands market share of its product in an existing market through its subsidiary, questions of the creation of marketing intangibles and increases in the value of product-related intangibles such as trademarks, trade names etc. follow closely behind. Therefore, it is important to examine and follow the process of creation of intangibles in a market, as well as the legal ownership of such intangibles and the right to share in the return from such intangibles (the notion which some countries refer to as "economic ownership"). It is recognized that market research; designing or planning products suitable to market needs, advertising, marketing and sales promotion strategies; after-sale services and networks of dealers and sales/commission agents may contribute to the creation of marketing intangibles depending on the facts and circumstances of each case.

The Indian market has witnessed substantial marketing activities by the Indian affiliates of MNE groups in the recent past and the transfer pricing aspect of marketing intangibles has been a focus area for the Indian transfer pricing administration for the last about 5 years. The India country practice note states that the marketing intangibles are generally identified on the basis of the efforts of the Indian affiliate towards:

Enhancing the value of the foreign trademark or brand that is unknown to Indian market by incurring very large advertisement, marketing and sale promotion expenditures; creation of brand and product loyalty in the minds of customers;

Creation of an efficient supply chain;

Establishing distributor networks in the country;

Developing an after-sale services and support network in the country;

Conducting customer and market research; and

Gathering customer data and establishing customer lists, etc.

The note then goes on to say that Indian affiliates (which are claimed as no risk or limited risk bearing distributors by the parent MNE in order to justify low cost plus return) incur and bear very large expenditures on the development of marketing intangibles. Consequently, the Indian affiliates generally incur very large losses or disclose very nominal profits.

The note further says-

"10.4.8.16 The Indian tax administration computes the ALP in the cases involving marketing intangibles following the concept of a "bright line" test; that is, no risk or limited risk distributor will bear the cost of only routine expenditure on advertisement, marketing and sale promotion (AMP). However, the tax administration faces the following challenges in determination of the ALP:

The issue of whether the parent MNE should reimburse the cost incurred by the Indian subsidiary or related party for the development of marketing intangibles with or without mark-up;

Lack of uniform accounting rules creates significant difficulties in identifying AMP expenditure in comparable companies and the tested party; and

The developer of marketing intangibles who has economic ownership in the intangibles is entitled to additional returns. However, the difficult question is what should be the arm's length price of such returns.

10.4.8.17. The important issue in the determination of ALP in these cases is to examine who benefits from the extraordinary AMP expenditure. Taxpayers generally claim that such extraordinary expenditure helps the business of the Indian entity in addition to the parent MNE.

However, the tax authorities in India have found that Indian distributors are claimed to be no risk or low risk bearing entities and are receiving fixed and routine return on a cost plus basis. They do not receive a share in the excess profit related to local marketing intangibles. Accordingly, extraordinary AMP expenditure does not enhance the profitability of the Indian subsidiary or related party. This conclusion of the tax authorities is further supported by the fact that these so called risk-free or limited risk distributors have disclosed very large losses even when they are entitled for fixed return on cost plus basis and should not have incurred losses.

Thus, it was held that goodwill simpliciter cannot be considered for allowance of depreciation.

4.2 Cases ruling in favour of the motion

• In Skyline Caterers (P.) Ltd. v. ITO 27 the assessee entered into an agreement with a contractor who was rendering catering and house keeping services to principal contractor, for taking over business of catering, and paid consideration for acquiring rights under catering contract and non-compete fee. He reflected the total sum paid to contractor in the balance sheet as goodwill and claimed depreciation thereon. In appeal, the Tribunal observed that the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' as appearing in section 32(1)(ii) itself would include all kinds of commercial rights. But for the words 'similar nature' the rule of ejusdem generis would apply.28 It observed that the specific words in section 32 reveal the similarity in the sense that all the intangible assets specified are tools of the trade which facilitate the assessee in carrying on the business. Therefore, the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' would include such rights which can be used as a tool to carry on the business. The Tribunal opined that sum paid by assessee to contractor was for acquiring all rights under catering contract between contractor and the main contractee, as well as all articles and paraphernalia belonging to the contractor. Therefore, it could not be said that sum paid was on account of goodwill. Applying the above test, it was held that the rights acquired by the assessee under the agreement would fall within the expression mentioned above, since catering business at HLL canteen could be carried on only with the help of such rights under the contract, and consequently, the assessee would be entitled to depreciation. Merely because assessee showed the total sum paid to contractor on account of goodwill in books, no adverse inference was to be drawn against the assessee.

6. AMP Expenses Off late there has been controversy whether an 'international transaction' in relation to brand building of foreign AE can be said to exist when some part of business expenses relating to advertisement, marketing and sales promotion (AMP) are considered by tax authorities attributable to activity of brand building of foreign AE. The expression "international transaction" is defined in section 92B in a wide manner and means a transaction between two or more associated enterprises, either or both of whom are non-residents, in the nature of purchase, sale, or lease of tangible or intangible property, or provision of services, or lending or borrowing money, or any other transaction having a bearing on the profits, income, losses or assets of such enterprises, and shall include a mutual arrangement between two or more parties for allocation of any cost or expense. It is thus clear that in order to bring the transaction within the ambit of transfer pricing regulations there must be transaction between two or more enterprises of which at least one party is non-resident. Where Indian entity incurs AMP expenses for its own business and payments are made to a resident company it is difficult to say that this would ipso facto result in "international transaction" of brand building of foreign AE unless there is some express or implied agreement or understanding between the parties in regard to sharing of such expenses. This brings us to the meaning of term "transaction" as defined in section 92F of the Act, which states that "transaction" includes an arrangement, understanding or action in concert, whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is formal or in writing or intended to be enforceable by legal proceedings. It is thus apparent that AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Company for the purposes of its business cannot be said to be related to brand building of a foreign AE unless it can be established that such expenses were incurred pursuant to some express or oral arrangement or understanding between the parties.

Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. case

The issue relating to transfer pricing of trademarks and brands created as a result of AMP expenses was first considered in case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT8. The controversy in this case related to arm's length price of transactions involving royalty payment of Rs 198.6 crores by Maruti India to its foreign associated enterprise, Suzuki Corporation, Japan, where foreign AE did not reimburse the Indian Company its share of advertisement and marketing expenditure incurred by Maruti India, which provided marketing benefit to Suzuki Corporation for using 'Suzuki' logo on products manufactured by Maruti company. The Revenue contention was that Suzuki Corporation Japan should have reimbursed part of advertisement and marketing expenses incurred by Maruti India for promotion of 'Suzuki' logo on the products manufactured and sold by Maruti company. The High Court remitted the matter to the Transfer Pricing Officer with liberty to issue fresh show cause notice and decide the matter in accordance with law. However, whilst remanding the matter the court made certain observations and gave directions to the TPO about taxability of marketing intangibles from mandatory use of the trademark by Maruti company which benefited the Suzuki Corporation and thus virtually concluded the matter. On further appeal the Supreme Court held9 that the TPO should proceed with the matter in accordance with law uninfluenced by the observations given by the High Court.

L.G. Electronics India (P) Ltd. case

In a recent case of L.G. Electronics India (P) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT Circle 3, Noida10 the Special Bench of Tribunal examined the justification of transfer pricing adjustment in relation to advertisement, marketing and sales promotion expenses alleged to have been incurred for and on behalf of AE. The brief facts are that on 1st July, 2001, the assessee company (LGI) and its foreign AE (LGK), entered into a technical assistance and royalty agreement as per which LGI in the capacity of a licensee, obtained the right to use the technical information, designs, drawings, brand name, trademark etc. on payment of royalty at 1%. According to TPO the Indian company was promoting LG brand owned by the foreign AE and hence should have been compensated by the foreign AE for AMP expenses. Applying the 'bright line test' the TPO held that out of total AMP expenses of 3.85% of sales the expenses up to 1.39% of sales should be considered to have been incurred for assessee's own business and remaining 2.46% of sales on brand building of the foreign AE. Pursuant to the directions given by DRP the Assessing Officer passed the order making addition of Rs. 182.71 crores (inclusive of mark-up of 13%) towards AMP expenses on brand building incurred for and on behalf of its AE.

Section 55(2)(a) is now being amended with effect from assessment year 2002-03 to provide that in respect of trade mark or brand name associated with a business, its costs of acquisition shall be deemed to be the following amounts : Substitution of fair market value as on 1-4-1981 - In case of the aforesaid assets the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 for the original cost of acquisition is not permitted. Hence, in case of self-acquired assets, since the cost of acquisition is nil and the substitution of fair market value on 1-4-1981 is not permitted, the indexed cost of acquisition would also be nil.

Following points need to be noted :

● Hitherto, there was a view [based on the Supreme Court decision in CIT v. B.C. Srinvasa Setty [1981] 128 ITR 294] that the aforesaid assets are not chargeable to capital gains tax since there is no cost of acquisition. Hence, it could be argued that the amendment clearly shows that such assets were not chargeable to tax under section 45 up to assessment year 2001-02.

● Section 55(1)(b) provides that cost of improvement (COI) in relation to a capital asset being goodwill of a business or a right to manufacture, produce or process any article or thing shall be taken to be nil. Section 55(1)(b) has not been amended to provide that COI of trade mark or brand name associated with a business shall also be taken to be nil. Now, in Evans Fraser & Co. Ltd. v. CIT[1982] 137 ITR 493 (Bom.), it was held that if the cost of improvement of an asset cannot be ascertained, gains arising on its transfer is not liable to tax under section 45. Hence, if the nil cost assets roped in by the amendment to the definition of cost of acquisition can have some COI which cannot be quantified, then, applying the ratio of the aforesaid decision, it could be argued that the capital gains arising on transfer of such assets is still outside the purview of tax under section 45.

7.3-1 Application of section 50 - In case of trade marks, the amendment presently made under section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition thereof will be its purchase price or nil as the case may be. It is pertinent to note that in respect of trade marks acquired on or after 1-4-1998, an assessee is entitled to depreciation under section 32(1) of the Act.

Since capital gains in respect of assets forming part of a block of assets on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act is to be computed as per the special provisions under section 50, the question may arise as to whether capital gains on transfer of trade marks would be computed in the manner provided under section 50 or whether the capital gains would have to be computed by taking cost of acquisition as per section 55(2)(a).

Section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition of trade marks will be taken as purchase price/nil ‘for the purpose of sections 48 and 49’. Section 50, however, goes further to say that ‘in case of depreciable assets sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the modifications’ prescribed in that section.

Hence, it seems that in respect of trade mark on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act, the capital gains would have to be computed as per the provisions of section 50 since the said section clearly provides that ‘the provisions under sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the following modifications’. However, as regards trade marks on which depreciation has not been allowed under the Act (which would include self-acquired trade marks and trade marks acquired prior to 1-4-1998) the capital gains would have to be computed on the basis of cost determined as per section 55(2)(a).

7.3-1a Brand names - While trade marks have been expressly referred to as an intangible asset under section 32(1) the said section does not expressly refer to ‘brand name’. However, ‘brand name’ would also qualify for depreciation as intangible assets since it would fall within the meaning of expression ‘any other business or commercial rights of similar nature’ as referred to under section 32(1). Hence, the same position as stated above in regard to trade mark would also hold good in respect of ‘brand name’.

In the recent ruling of Hon'ble Delhi High Court (HC) in the case of Pr. CIT v. Pepsico India Holding Pvt. Ltd.1 involving the issue of marketing intangibles, it was held that the AMP computation (i.e. computation of advertisement, marketing and sales promotion expenses) which was based on the adoption of the Bright Line Test (BLT), would clearly not sustain in light of the judgement rendered by the Court in Sony Ericson v. CIT2. Thus, the case did not find any merits and same was dismissed.

On opening a soda bottle, carbon dioxide dissolved in it suddenly comes out as a fizz. This is because, there is a sudden decrease in the pressure above the drink and thus the dissolved carbon dioxide becomes less soluble resulting in fast release of CO2 with a fizzing sound. Similar to this, is the marketing intangibles or the AMP expenses issue, where the pressure is created from the excess AMP expenses, incurred by the local Indian subsidiaries, tested by BLT and if excessive, resulting into a fizzing adjustment for marketing intangibles issue. However, as per the Hon'ble HC, the BLT cannot create any fizz.

The Background

The issue of marketing intangibles or the AMP expenses as is its commonly called, is vexed and has been in litigation from a long time. Its original shape and form was designed around the BLT and inspite of being struck down very explicitly by HC, it remains in its vintage form, in the Transfer Pricing (TP) orders.

Let us dwell further on the issue and what's the history has been so far.

In many instances, the Tax Authorities in India have taken an aggressive stand by claiming that the AMP expenses or any expense incurred under the AMP account makes a valuable addition to the trademark/ brand legally owned by the foreign-related party for brand building. This thereby concludes that the local Indian subsidiary must be compensated by the legal brand owner, i.e. the overseas related party/ associated enterprise, for the benefit bestowed or the additional services rendered by the local Indian subsidiary, on an arm's length basis.

As a background, even though intellectual property (IP) is part of the definition of an 'international transaction', however in addition to this, the Indian TP regulations do not offer clear guidance on intangibles. Furthermore, there is no specific inclusion of the expenses relating to AMP in the definition of the term 'international transaction'. On the contrary, the BLT is used to state that if the AMP expenses are higher than comparables, then there is an international transaction, else not. Thus, the basic premise of being an international transaction is a non-starter to begin with. This leads to a discussion about the legitimacy of whether the AMP should be considered an international transaction in the first place. Besides, the question in this regard arises as to whether AMP expenses are allowed in the hands of the taxpayer based on the commercial justification or the legal ownership of the assets.

The Controversy

India as the new global market has its unique characteristic features that includes location advantages, market accessibility, customer necessity, etc. that have made its subsidiaries/ related parties of Multi-National-Enterprises (MNEs) spearhead different and far more extensive and faster marketing techniques seeking to gain a competitive ground in India. This has resulted in the topic of marketing intangibles becoming one of the most widely discussed TP topics in India.

As mentioned earlier, the tax authorities indicate that the issues relating to legal ownership of intangibles are pertinent to the TP regulations. However, the taxpayers argue that since the Indian subsidiary is the economic owner of such intangibles, they cannot justify that the subsidiary must recover the AMP expenses from its related parties because the subsidiary would be the direct recipient of the benefits from the incurring of such expenses.

The information is further amplified by the use of what the tax department employs to determine the arm's length price (ALP) of such other alleged international transaction: the 'BLT.' This is a concept derived from a US tax court case. As per this test, all such AMP expenses that are incurred by the taxpayer and are more than the amount of average AMP expenses, about foreign-related parties, incurred by comparable companies in India, then such fees are to be treated as non-routine expenses (expenses for creating brand value in India of the foreign related parties) and thus should be benchmarked as per the ALP.

The missing pieces

In this context, several pertinent questions arise:

-

Whether the AMP expenses can be considered an international transaction?

-

Must the Indian local subsidiary, seeing it is not a legal owner of the trademark but is an economic owner or developer of the brand/ trademark, be exonerated from the necessity to cover AMP expenses?

If the parties intend that the SIM card should be treated as a separate object of sale, it would be open to the sales tax authorities to levy sales tax thereon. However, if the sale of a SIM card is merely incidental to the service being provided and only facilitates the identification of the subscribers, their credit and other details, it would not be assessable to sales tax. In the case of Bharati Hexacom Ltd. v. CCE, Jaipur, [2007] 7 STT 242 (Delhi - CESTAT) the assessee provided cellular services and as a part of its services SIM cards were supplied and shown to have been sold. The department demanded service tax on sale consideration and imposed penalty. The applicant contended that it had paid sales tax on the SIM cards and since the cards were goods, provisions of the Act could not be invoked for imposition of service tax. Based on the decision of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd’s case (supra), New Delhi Bench of the Tribunal held that even if some amount was charged for SIM cards supplied to customers, SIM card of the applicant-company was clearly relatable to the services provided by it. Such SIM card could not have been used for any other service. Moreover, unless activated it was useless, which showed that it was only a part of the services provided, and it was not goods separately sold. If some company manufactures SIM cards for the purpose of selling them to a cellular service provider for its business, that may stand on the footing of SIM cards being sold as goods, which has nothing to do with cellular service. Cellular service is not to be provided by the manufacturer of such SIM cards and is to be provided by the purchaser for whom such tailor made SIM cards were manufactured. It was also urged by the assessee that it was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 12/03-ST, dated 20-6-2003. On this, the Tribunal held that, admittedly, this contention had never been raised so far. Even otherwise, prima facie this notification could not be of any help to the applicant because SIM cards were not sold as goods, independent from the services provided, but they were part and parcel of the services provided and the dominant intent was to provide services and not to sell the material, namely, SIM cards, which on its own without the service, would hardly have any value. Thus, the Tribunal did not allow waiving of any part of the amount payable under the impugned order. It is also important to note that in case of State of Uttar Pradesh v. UOI12 , the Supreme Court has held that levy of service tax on a particular service is no bar to levy trade tax on it.

Similarly, in the case of Hindustan Associated Traders v. CCE, Cochin [2007] 7 STT 81 (Bang. - CESTAT), the assessees were given marketing and distribution rights of SIM cards. The assessees had to purchase SIM cards from BSNL outright. The assessees contended that they could not be considered to have provided any service, as they had purchased SIM cards outright and were carrying an activity of distributing. Bangalore Bench of the Tribunal held that since as per agreement entered into by assessee with BSNL the assessees were required to provide services to customers also, it could not prima facie be said that they had not carried on services of business auxiliary services; therefore, the Tribunal directed the assessees to pre-deposit demand raised.

These decisions of the Tribunal are moot pointer to the aspect of tax planning by giving different colour to a simple transaction of service as sale transaction. It is settled law that the substance of a transaction is more important than the form of transaction and for this purpose the nomenclature of a transaction given by the parties cannot control the actual tax implications.

In this connection, it would be relevant to make mention of the Delhi High Court ruling dated 1 July 2010 in case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. The ruling was later set aside by the Supreme Court on technicalities of power of High Court to give such a ruling in a writ petition but the Supreme Court did not comment on merits of the observations made by the High Court. The High Court had observed:

"If the domestic entity which is an Associate Enterprise of the foreign entity within the meaning of Section 92A of the Income-tax Act is mandatorily required to use the foreign trademark and/or logo on its products and/or their containers, packaging, etc., appropriate payment in this regard should be made by the foreign entity to the domestic entity, on account of the benefit it derives in the form of marketing intangibles, obtained by it from such mandatory use of its trademark and/or logo."

To sum up: The Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not contain any guidance on compensation by the foreign licensor of brand/trademark for the excess AMP spend by the licensee in India. But the India Practice Note in the UN Manual clarifies that the Indian Transfer Pricing Administration would make adjustment on account of excess AMP spend (along with a mark up for the functions undertaken) by the Indian licensee. The India Practice Note seems to indicate relevance of AMP issue only in cases of 'No Risk' or 'Limited Risk' distributors but the ground reality is that even Full Risk Distributors and Full Fledged Manufacturers are benchmarked for the AMP spend. The Tax Tribunal Special Bench has also ruled that brand advertisement by the Indian licensee of brand, coupled with excess AMP spend, constitutes an international transaction. The Special Bench has laid down a 14 Point criteria for proper selection of comparables for AMP spend. The taxpayers in India would have to evaluate the level of their marketing activities in the light of above.

Depreciation on 'Goodwill' - A critical analysis

Kavita Kachhwaha

Introduction

1. An intangible asset can be defined as "an identifiable non-monetary asset, without physical substance, which is able to generate economic benefits to the business enterprise."1 It creates significant values for an organization beyond its tangible assets. Intangible assets (including intellectual properties), such as goodwill, know-how, customer lists, copyrights, etc., may be self-generated and, hence, an off-balance sheet item or these may be purchased. It is to be noted that expenses on development or on purchasing of such intangibles are either capitalized, or are expensed out in the profit and loss account, depending on the facts of each case. Where such intangibles are capitalized, the Income-tax Act, 1961 expressly provides for depreciation allowance.2 Depreciation is allowed on know-how, patents, copyrights, trade-marks, licences, franchises and 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature'. However, there is no express provision for depreciation in respect of other widely known intangible assets, such as, goodwill, non-compete rights, employees' contracts, vendor/customer contracts, distributorship rights, service process flows, knowledge databases, brands, etc. Thus, the key issue in respect of depreciation of such unspecified intangible assets, mentioned above, is whether they can be regarded as business or commercial rights of a 'similar' nature ?

It is to be noted that Goodwill is one of the significant intangible assets which either arises on acquisition or is internally generated. As per section 55(2)(a) of the Act, the cost of acquisition in case of goodwill is the purchase price and in case of self-generated goodwill it is nil. Thus, purchased goodwill is now specifically recognized as a capital asset. In practice, M&A transactions usually results in the transferee-company paying a consideration higher than the value of the assets taken over, which is accounted for as 'Goodwill'. Thus, since the statute is silent, a moot point from an income-tax perspective is whether such goodwill would be eligible for tax depreciation? This issue has become quite relevant in today's competitive atmosphere. Enterprises frequently expend resources, or incur liabilities on the acquisition, development, maintenance or enhancement of intangible resources such as scientific or technical knowledge, design and implementation of new processes or systems, licences, trademarks, etc. It is more significant in corporate sector with India incorporated actively pursuing mergers and acquisitions route for their expansions and valuations reaching dizzy heights, intangibles being a larger part of acquisition.

Thus, in the light of the significance of this issue, this paper takes an opportunity to examine whether goodwill, being an 'intangible asset', is eligible for depreciation under section 32 of the I.T. Act. It also takes into account the relevant provisions of the proposed Direct Taxes Code.

2. The Concept of Goodwill

2.1 Definition of goodwill - The term "goodwill" has not been defined in the Income Tax Act, 1961. Thus, in order to understand the concept recourse must be made to the judicial pronouncements.

u Logo - It means "a name, symbol, or trademark designed for easy and definite recognition, especially one borne on a single printing plate or piece of type". [www.thefreedictionary.com/trade+name]

u "A logo is a graphic or emblem commonly used by commercial enterprises organizations and even individuals to aid and promote instant public recognition". [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logo].

The Supreme Court has, in the case of Asra Pharmaceuticals (P.) Ltd. v. Collector of Central Excise 1995 (75) ELT 214, explained the difference between ‘house mark’ and ‘product mark’ (brand name) by relying on Navratna’s Book on Trade Marks and Passing-Off as follows :

"677A. House mark and product mark (or brand name) - In the pharmaceutical business a distinction is made between a house mark and a product mark. The former is used on all the products of the manufacturer. It is usually a device in the form a emblem, word or both. For each product a separate mark known as a product mark or a brand name is used which is invariably a word or a combination of a word and letter or numeral by which the product is identified and asked for. In respect of all products both the product mark and house mark will appear side by side on all the labels, cartons, etc. Goods are ordered only by the product mark or brand name. The house mark serves as an emblem of the manufacturer projecting the image of the manufactured generally."

It will be evident from the above that the brand name is generally associated with the product, whereas a house mark may represent a particular corporate house or group or professional association. Normally, a house mark like Tata, Adiyta Birla, Sahara, ICAI, etc., do not represent any product but represent the entire group whereas the brand name is associated with the product.

Manner of promotion

12. As per the definition of taxable service, the manner of promotion can be either in the form of appearing in advertisements or through making appearance in promotional events or by carrying out any promotional activity for the goods or services or events.

Departmental clarification on the scope of taxable services

13. As regards scope of services rendered in relation to promotion of a ‘brand’ of goods, services, business entity, etc., Circular Letter DOF No. 334/1/2010-TRU, dated February 26, 2010 states as under :

The inter-linkage between the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion (AMP) expense by distributor of a branded/trademarked product and the value of brand/trademark, first came into prominence in the 1980s when the US Internal Revenue sought to disallow part of AMP expense incurred by a distributor on the plea that the same was incurred on behalf of the foreign trademark owner. The case was settled by the parties out of court and, therefore, not much is known about the outcome.

Later in 1994, the US Internal Revenue issued the Transfer Pricing Regulations in Section 482 of the Internal Revenue Code incorporating the famous 'cheese examples'. These examples prescribed compensation for the US distributor of branded cheese, who incurred advertisement and marketing expense significantly larger than what independent distributors incurred under similar circumstances. The expenditure in excess of the level incurred by independent distributors was to be considered to be a service provided to the brand owner.

OECD Transfer pricing Guidelines issued in 1995 also made reference in paragraphs 6.36 to 6.39 to the transfer pricing issues that could arise when marketing activities were undertaken by enterprises that did not own the trademarks or trade names that they promoted (such as distributor of branded goods). The Guidelines indicated that in cases where a distributor bore extraordinary marketing expenditures beyond what an independent distributor with similar rights might incur for the benefits of its own distribution activities, it was entitled to an additional return from the owner of the trademark, perhaps through a decrease in the purchase price of the product or a reduction in the royalty rate. Unlike the US 'cheese examples', the OECD Guidelines accepted that a distributor may have the ability to obtain benefits from its investments in developing the value of a trademark from its turnover and market share where it has a long term contract of sole distribution rights for the trademarked product.

Further significant development on this front was the DHL case in US in the year 2002. DHL operated courier business inside US. Its Hong Kong affiliate DHLI (DHL International) handled courier business outside US. DHL was the legal owner of DHL trademark and DHLI was licensee of the trademark for territories outside US. DHLI developed the DHL trademark outside US and did not pay any royalty to DHL for use of the trademark. US Internal Revenue imputed trademark royalty to DHL for the use of its trademark by DHLI outside US. DHL asserted that a royalty should not be imputed from DHLI because DHLI bore the economic investment for the development of DHL trademark outside US. During the years under consideration, DHL had incurred advertisement and marketing spend of $ 150 Million in US and DHLI had incurred advertisement and marketing spend of $ 340 Million outside US. The US IRS allocated royalties which DHL should have charged to DHLI for use of DHL trademark outside US. The Tax Court upheld the allocation by saying that DHL had failed to show that DHLI had itself developed the trademark outside US because it was not demonstrated that AMP by DHLI was more than what would have been incurred by an arm's length licensee. The Tax Court observed on page 60 of its order – "Petitioners have presented evidence that, over a period of years, DHLI spent substantially more on advertising than DHL. We have no way of measuring these expenditures' effect on the value of the trademark". The Court of Appeal reversed the decision of Tax Court by observing that DHLI need not have shown the precise amount of its trademark development expenditure, since presumably at least $ 50 Million (which was undisputed value of DHL trademark for the Overseas Trademark Rights) of the $ 340 Million spent by DHLI constituted development expenses for the DHL trademark outside US.

The DHL case therefore did not throw up any exact correlation between the AMP expense and the trademark value. It only said that out of $ 340 Million AMP expense by DHLI, at least $ 50 Million was contribution to the value of the trademark. Further, the case did not elaborate on the nature of expenses that exactly constitute AMP expenses. Though the court in DHL case used the words 'arm's length licensee expenditure' test, Marc Levey in his Article in 2007 on 'A closer focus on 1marketing intangibles' in Euromoney Handbooks preferred to call the same as2 'Bright-Line' Test. The term 'Bright-Line Test' has since gained popularity in the context of AMP expense by a licensee. The 'Arm's Length Licensee Expenditure Test' or the 'Bright-Line Test', whatever one may call it, seems relevant because otherwise in most of the cases, it is almost impossible to segregate routine and non-routine AMP expenditure, or in other words, product and brand promotion AMP expenditure. What promotes product may also promote brand and vice versa.

RAJESH DHAWAN*

Whether expenses incurred on ‘market research’ for the client by the advertising agency fall under advertising services?

No. The Government in its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that if the ‘market research’ relates to advertisement then the ‘market research’ forms part of the service in relation to advertisement and all expenses charged from the client on this account are includible in the value of taxable services. For instance, the expenses incurred to find out the time slot on T.V. for giving advertisement, studying consumers buying preference, etc., may be treated as expenses in respect of market research.

Whether services provided by co-loaders fall under courier services?

No. The Government in its Circular F. No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that as such co-loaders provide services to the ‘courier agency’ and not directly to the customers and, therefore, in this case, services provided by the co-loaders to the ‘courier agency’ are not chargeable to service tax.

In the case of On Time Couriers v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 615/[2007] 7 STT 194 (Kol. - CEGAT), the Tribunal remanded the matter to the original adjudicating authority to look into the claim that the business between the two courier agencies is not covered by the rules and no service tax is leviable on the same.

Whether training falls under consulting engineer services?

No. The Tribunal in the case of Bharat Fritz Werner Ltd. v. Dy. CCE [2007] 6 STT 382 (Bang. - CESTAT) accepted the plea of the appellants that they were not collecting any fee and they were not providing consulting services but they were only giving training to the employees of the purchasers, which did not come within the ambit of ‘Consulting Engineer’ Services.

Whether transportation of fly ash falls under clearing and forward agent services?

No. The Tribunal in the case of Sharma Roadlines v. CST [2007] 8 STT 97 (New Delhi - CESTAT) while granting the interim stay of recovery of demand observed that transportation of fly ash is essentially rendering service of transportation and not covered under clearing and forward agent services.

Whether educational institutes conducting campus interview falls under manpower recruitment or supply agency services?

Yes. The Government in its Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated 23-8-2007 has clarified that educational institutes such as IITs and IIMs fall within the definition of ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’, and service tax is leviable on services provided by such institutions in relation to campus recruitment under section 65(105)( k).

Whether convention services are also charged as mandap keeper services?

No. The Government in its Circular F. No. B. 11/1/2001-TRU, dated 9-7-2001 has clarified that the intention is not to charge the service tax twice on the same service. If a service provider is already registered as a mandap keeper and paying service tax, he is not liable to pay service tax again under the category of ‘convention services’.

Whether ambulance services fall under rent-a-cab service ?

No. The Government in its letter D.O.F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-8-2007 has clarified that ambulances are not meant for carrying passengers for hire or reward. Hence, the question of levy does not arise.

Whether services rendered for issue of compliance certificate fall under practising Company Secretary services?

Yes. The Government has withdrawn exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated 16-10-1998 with effect from 1-3-2006 vide Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006. However, even earlier also, if a practising Company Secretary rendered the services for issue of compliance certificate under provisions to section 383A of the Companies Act, 1956 it was taxable service as covered under clause (vii) of the aforesaid Notification No. 59/98 as the same was required to be submitted with the Registrar of Companies along with the report of board of directors. However, if a compliance certificate is voluntarily obtained by a company from a practising Company Secretary, then said clause of the aforesaid Notification is not attracted, as the same is not mandatorily required to be submitted under Companies Act. But the same may be covered under audit and, hence, service becomes taxable accordingly.
