However, the Cheese Examples in the early regulations and the global attention given the Glaxo case has alerted many other tax authorities to this evolving issue and as they look for additional ways to raise revenue, a potentially attractive vehicle to raise revenue.7 The theories described above continue to be raised in most global tax audits and Advance Pricing Agreement proceedings, and are presently under consideration by the U.S. Tax Court in current pending cases. The underlying thread seems to be that AMP, if substantive enough, creates an intangible. Numerous unanswered questions remain, however, such as how to define a company’s marketing intangibles from a tax and legal perspective, what expenses truly contribute to the building of this intangible, how to determine in tax parlance where the level of AMP transcends from routine to non-routine expenditures, what expenses qualify for these considerations, (e.g. registration costs, legal costs for routine expenses and real broad brand building expenses as such non-routine expenses), whether an analysis of each underlying accounting code requires the segregation of routine from non-routine expenditures, what allocation keys may be employed and what is the "shelf life" of the created marketing intangible, as well as any pre existing marketing intangibles that are included within the considered intangible. One further practical problem, and a significant one, is that not every taxpayer accounts for its AMP within the same accounting classifications.

While there may be merit in the DHL "bright line" test from a practical point of view, the definition of non-routine expenditures is so industry and company specific, that it may be impossible to apply in most cases. Similar companies within the same industry may have vastly different approaches to their marketing philosophies, product launches, and/or product dependence or interdependence. This could create very different levels of AMP and different "bright lines." This may even occur within the same companies and for similar product categories. These expenditures can also be influenced by, among other things, the product’s position in other countries, the timing of product launches, and the competitors and their products, each of which impacts the "bright line" benchmarking and comparability standards. Also, the legal status of the intangibles concerned may impact the expenditures differently. Even more complexity arises where the company has many product lines and the AMP expenditures are not segregated by those lines.

In the Mary Kay Holdings case,8 that was docketed in the Tax Court and later on settled the Petitioner begged the question of whether AMP are deductible under I.R.C. Section 162 when they are incurred for the development of a brand outside the United States. In the facts contained in the Petition, the U.S. parent company seemingly used the AMP spend as a vehicle to make a transfer pricing adjustment to its "limited risk" distribution under the guise that the adjustments (i.e. AMP charge backs) were made by the parent to support the development of the "Mary Kay" brand. The amounts of these expenses were approximately $16.1 million in 1997, $20.6 million in 1998 and $14.2 million in 1999. While the case was settled, and some underlying papers indicate the Government was challenging the documentation, it is not clear therefore how the Tax Court would have held on this issue. However, what is clear is that there should be a distinct delineation between how transfer pricing adjustments are made and how AMP support payments and/or charge-backs are addressed so that there is a clean line of demarcation between the two and the AMP payments can truly be tracked to brand development and enhancement expense codes.

Notwithstanding the above, the analysis that has evolved from the prior jurisprudence begs the question of what expenses are truly brand building. For example, some marketing consultants would argue that pure advertising is not a brand building cost. Instead, placements for specific events (e.g., the Super Bowl, the U.S. Open, etc.) may be considered to produce lasting brand equity. The same can be said that celebrity endorsements create more brand building and brand association than pure advertising. Similarly, market campaigns and strategic focus groups geared to market knowledge, spending habits, and market placement can be of equal value. In tax audits, the IRS and other taxing authorities have focused on flagship stores as brand builders, or another form of AMP. The premise is that these flagships are strategically positioned in locations where their presence is of greater value than the revenue, if any, generated from the store (e.g. 5th Avenue in New York City) Michigan Avenue in Chicago, Rodeo Drive in Los Angeles. The taxing authorities have often characterized the "excess rental costs" associated with flagship properties as brand builders to be borne by the brand owner.

The likelihood of attaining a consensus view on these items of brand building is nil. But what is clear is that the brand building/development costs will be company specific and will require a detailed analysis to meet the ever increasing challenges of global tax authorities in this area.

Executives of Indian subsidiaries of Multinationals ('MNE group') and tax professionals across the country should now be able to breathe easy. The Hon'ble Delhi High Court ('Delhi HC') recently pronounced its decision on the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ('AMP') controversy1 involving various Indian distributors ('Taxpayers'2) of reputed MNE groups. The amounts involved on the issue run into several crores.

In past few years, a highly debated issue in Transfer Pricing ('TP') audits/litigation involving taxpayers who incur significant AMP expenses, has been the creation of marketing intangibles. Tax authorities at ground level have typically held that excessive or non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India contribute to building of the brand legally owned by the MNE group outside India. Consequently, the taxpayers should receive an arm's length compensation on the excessive or non-routine AMP expenses alongwith a mark-up from the legal owner of the brand in the MNE group. This view was upheld by the Special Bench ('SB') of Delhi Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ('ITAT'/'Tax Tribunal') in the case of LG Electronics India Private Limited3.The ITAT in its detailed order held that AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayer towards building a brand legally owned by the MNE group constituted an 'international transaction' and the foreign entity should pay for the AMP expenses incurred beyond the amount arrived at by applying the 'bright line'.

Consequent to the SB ruling in case of LG Electronics, tax authorities proposed TP additions in many other cases on account of the AMP issue, which were later upheld by various tax Tribunals. Aggrieved taxpayers filed appeals before the Delhi High Court against the rulings of the tax Tribunal in their respective cases.

1. Core issues before the Delhi HC

The Delhi HC, in its more than 140 page order, discussed at length the following core issues with respect to AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India:

whether AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function undertaken by the taxpayers could be considered as an 'International Transaction' as per India Transfer Pricing Regulations4;

whether taxpayers could be said to be engaged in the activity of building 'Brand' in India which is legally owned by the MNE group;

whether the taxpayers could be said to be the 'Economic Owner' of the 'Marketing Intangible' purportedly developed by them for the MNE group;

whether AMP spend could be segregated into routine and non-routine expenditure in the hands of taxpayers by applying 'Bright Line Test5' in order to determine the value of so called 'Marketing Intangible'; and

how the marketing and distribution function (whether standalone or bundled with the other core transaction of import of goods) should be acknowledged and the arm's length compensation should be determined in such cases.

The Delhi HC, partly ruling in favour of the tax authorities and partly in favour of the taxpayers, gave elaborated reasons and findings on the above core issues. Some important aspects of the decision have been discussed in the following paragraphs.

2. AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function is an 'International Transaction'

The Delhi HC struck down the contention of the taxpayers that AMP expenses were paid by them to third parties in India and accordingly should not be classified as an 'International Transaction'. It confirmed the finding of the ITAT in the case of LG Electronics that AMP expenditure incurred by the taxpayers with respect to distribution and marketing function is an international transaction in terms of Indian TP regulations. The HC observed that since taxpayers themselves advanced an argument that the declared price of international transactions included a remuneration for their AMP function, the argument challenging that it is not an international transaction is incorrect.

3. Legal ownership of 'Brand' and 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers

The Delhi HC observed (and rightly so) that a reputed 'Brand' is developed (by the MNE groups) over a passage of time. Brand value of any product/service refers to intangibles like know-how, infrastructure, and would depend upon the nature and quality of products/services offered to the customers. The HC further clarified that expenditure incurred by the taxpayers on advertisement and promotion of products/services with a 'Trademark' is only for commercial exploitation of the said 'Trademark' and per se there is no substantial value addition or 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers. Reputed brands do not undertake advertisement and marketing activities with the intention to increase (already established) brand value, but to increase sales and thereby earn larger profits.

appears that under the law as it stands and also as per the view taken by the Courts, the ground reality that sales is a pre-condition to manufacture or produce things is recognized as a reality. Even in the absence of specific provisions in this regard, such expenses should be considered as wholly and exclusively incurred for the related business. The words ‘sales promotion’, should not be considered as limited to activity of sale, but they should be considered as promotion of manufacture and production also.

The bureaucracy must recognize reality 4. Conceptually what is applicable in the context of CENVAT in case of manufacture of excisable goods is equally applicable in case of providing taxable services. In era of intense competition, service providers have also to adopt marketing, sales promotion, advertisement and publicity of their services. With the changes in time, the bureaucracy has to recognize realities. There was a time that in the Income-tax Act, 1961 we found specific provisions for disallowance of such expenses. Those provisions were omitted long ago. However, still revenue authorities have some pre-notions and prejudices that such expenses are unproductive and wasteful expenses having no connection with or remote connection with business. The mindset need to be changed. It is expected that the revenue shall accept the judgment of Bombay High Court and will not appeal against the same. And will also not bring in the amendment to nullify the judgment.

Conclusion

5. It can be said that sales and sales promotion are essential pre-conditions to manufacture or production of any product. Therefore, creation and maintenance of market share of any product should be considered as a part and parcel of any business and in case of manufacture or production of any product, an essential pre-condition. Viewed from this angle, it cannot be denied that the sales promotion, advertisement and marketing are integral part and essentials of any activity of manufacturing or producing any type of goods or rendering of services. In case of branded products, or products manufactured under brand or license of brand or patent owner, which are manufactured and/or marketed through others, the brand or patent owner advertises the product and brands, and the benefit is derived by the brand owner as well as the licensed manufacturer of such brand and patent holder. If the brand owner or patent holder also sales, certain crucial material to licensees, then sale of such crucial products is also promoted by advertisement of end products in which such crucial products are used. Therefore, a brand owner or a patent holder also promotes his business by advertising his brands though the end-products may be manufactured by others.

DR. NEHA PATHAKJI

Asstt. Professor, Nalsar University of Law

Introduction

1. The growth of international trade and corporate endeavour to capture new markets, resulted in multijurisdictional presence of companies in different forms. Often multinational groups prefer different modes of doing business ranging from undertaking direct manufacturing or appointing distributors or agents. Depending upon the nature of the model adopted, such arrangements invariably involve certain intra-group transfer of goods, products, services and intangibles with accompanying tax implications. Most jurisdictions have put in place transfer pricing regimes within their domestic tax laws to address issues evolving from intra-group transfers. Payment of royalty for the use of 'intangibles' such as brand name or trade name of the foreign company by its domestic group company or subsidiary, as the case may be, is a quite common arrangement. Of late contribution of domestic company to the benefit of overall brand name of its foreign company has attracted lot of attention from tax authorities. In other words, when Indian subsidiary incurs advertising, marketing and promotional expenses which may have incidental benefits for the overall brand name of its foreign parent does it amount to an international transaction which attracts transfer pricing provisions? If it does, what amount of benefit should be attributable to the foreign company for which the Indian counterpart requires to be compensated? Issues such as these have emerged in the recent past.

Insofar as marketable intangibles are concerned, it has been acknowledged that it involves a complicated exercise in quantifying the benefit that accrues to the foreign company. This complexity makes it particularly amenable to controversy regarding the requisite amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian company. While several countries such as the U.S, New Zealand and Australia adopt a 'bright line test' (hereinafter BLT) to ascertain the said benefit, Indian jurisdiction does not as yet statutorily recognize the BLT despite attempts by the Revenue department in computing the arms length price (hereinafter ALP) of AMP expenses based on the BLT. Several companies that either manufacture or market branded goods and products have fallen prey to the aforesaid controversy.

The recent landmark judgment from the Delhi High Court in the matter of Maruti Suzuki India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT1 (hereinafter Maruti Suzuki) adds to the existing jurisprudence with regards to tax implications of AMP expenses incurred by Indian entities that may contribute to marketing intangibles of its foreign counterparts. The issue of application of the BLT in determining arms length price of the AMP expenses in India had already been negated by the Delhi High Court judgment in Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT2 (hereinafter Sony Erricson). The said decision of the Delhi High Court overruled the decision of the Special Bench of the Income Tax Tribunal in LG Electronics India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT3 (hereinafter L.G.Electronics) that had found favours with the BLT. The present judgment of Maruti Suzuki 2015 builds on the decision of Sony Ericsson to nullify reliance upon the BLT so as to deduce existence of international transaction as to then invoke transfer pricing regulations for excessive AMP expenses.

Factual Background

2. Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. (hereinafter MSIL) is engaged in the manufacture of passenger cars in India. MSIL started its business in 1982 as Maruti Udyog Ltd. (hereinafter MUL), as a Government of India owned company. Somewhere in the year 1982, MUL entered into a composite license agreement with Suzuki Motor Corporation, Japan (hereinafter SMC) for the use of technical know-how for the manufacturing of specified cars with the co-branded trade mark 'Maruti Suzuki'. At the time of 1982 agreement, MUL and SMC were unrelated entities. It was only in 2003 that SMC acquired controlling interest in MSIL. As on 31st March 2006, SMC held 54.21% shares in MSIL. 10.27% of the shares were held by the Government of India and the balance was held by the Indian public and others. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer invoked the transfer pricing provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and referred the case to the transfer pricing officer (hereinafter TPO) for determination of ALP in relation to the international transactions undertaken by MSIL with its associated enterprise SMC. This included purchase of components, capital items, technical services, payment of royalty for technology/trademark.

Cargo handling services and Manpower recruitment agency service

1.1 The revenue demanded service tax from the assessee under the categories of ‘Cargo handling service’ and ‘Manpower recruitment agency service’ for supply of labour and handling of goods inside factory for the period prior to 16-6-2005. The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order had clearly brought out that only for the service of supply of labour and handling of the goods inside the factory, the assessee was brought to charge under the categories of ‘Manpower recruitment agency’ and ‘Cargo handling service’. The fact that authority had noticed that the gross value received to the tune of Rs. 15,66,569 relating to supply of manpower related to the period prior to 16-6-2005. The Tribunal held that when it was noticed that supply of manpower was taxed for a period when the law did not provide a levy for the same, the assessee could not be asked to pay taxes under such category of ‘Manpower recruitment agency’. So far as the cargo handling was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had applied his mind. While doing so, he had examined the case record. When both the authorities were in quarrel as to realization of the service tax by one or the other, the invoice copies were examined. None of these pages was reflecting that there was realization of service tax. As the service tax was not realized, the assessee was not directed to deposit the same. Further, activity carried out by the labourers was found to be loading and unloading of the raw material/semi-finished goods and final products inside factory. Those were not proved to be carried out beyond the factory by the revenue. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had discharged the assessee from the charge of taxability under the ‘Cargo handling service’. There was no other evidence available on record to hold otherwise. In absence of any cogent evidence and aforesaid observations, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be impeached. Commercial training or coaching centre

1.2 The assessee-company provided induction-training programme covering ERP (SAP), its software products, quality software products, quality software engineering and personality development topics to its prospective employees. It collected certain amount as ‘joining fee’ from recruits who gain opportunity for on-site implementation experience and programming skills in SAP related development. The revenue treated said activity of the assessee as ‘Commercial training or coaching service’ and demanded service tax from the assessee. IVL being a well-established brand in software market, the SAP training programme conducted by the assessee by collecting amount from the trainees as joining fee, though it was essentially a training fee, attracts a large number of job seekers and the activity undertaken by the assessee could be rightly classified as noticed from the appointment letter that the assessee was offering the person an employment with the company. The payment clause would indicate that it was nothing but a kind of bond taken from the employee. On appeal , it could be revenue’s contention that paragraph 5 of the appointment letter indicated that the assessee had given training, was also mis-construed and mis-directed inasmuch as, the said paragraph specifically started with the words ‘on joining the company they will be given training’. This would mean that the person who was joining the company was being trained on the particular programme. The counsel stated that the definition of ‘Commercial Training or Coaching Centre’ under section 65(105)( zzc) of the Finance Act, 1994 means any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a Commercial Training or Coaching Centre in relation to commercial training or coaching. Further, from the ratio laid down in ICFAI v. CC&CE [2008] 17 STT 501 (Bang. - CESTAT), it was very clear that the activities undertaken by the assessee were nothing but giving training to its own employees and, hence, the same could not get covered under the definition of ‘Commercial training or coaching services’. For the foregoing reasons, the Tribunal held that the impugned order which considered the assessee as a ‘Commercial Training or Coaching Centre’ was unsustainable and was to be set aside and the appeal was allowed with consequential relief, if any.

Introduction

1. The issue of applicability of transfer pricing provisions has always been a Cause of concern for Indian companies. There are a number of Indian companies who are engaged in distribution of various branded products manufactured by their foreign affiliates. In most of the cases the Indian companies incur expenses on advertisement, marketing and promotional activities ("AMP") for the various products distributed by them. The argument of tax authorities has always been that since the brand-name/trademark/trade-name is owned by the foreign affiliate, the expenses incurred by the Indian companies on AMP activities lead to creation of brand value for the foreign affiliates for which the Indian companies should be compensated by the foreign affiliates.

The Special Bench of the Hon'ble Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("ITAT") in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.1 tried to address the above issue by segregating 'routine' and 'non-routine' AMP activities by applying the 'Bright Line Test'. As per the ITAT any expense on AMP activities beyond the 'Bright Line Test' should be treated as a separate international transaction and, accordingly, benchmarked. As per the said 'Bright Line test' expense on AMP activities in excess of similar expense incurred by comparable independent domestic companies was regarded as an expense incurred by the Indian company for brand promotion of foreign affiliate.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd.2 has disagreed with judgment of the ITAT in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra) and has held that 'Bright Line Test' cannot be applied for benchmarking of AMP expenses.

This article gives a detailed analysis of this decision, which may have a significant bearing on all Indian companies engaged in the distribution of goods manufactured by their foreign affiliates.

Rulings of the Delhi High Court

2. The 'Bright Line Test' finds its roots in the US Transfer Pricing Regulations wherein the concept has been explained by way of the following illustrations:

Example : FP, a foreign producer of cheese, markets the cheese in countries other than the United States under the trade name Fromage Frere. FP owns all the worldwide rights to this name. The name is widely known and is valuable outside the United States but is not known within the United States. In 1995, FP decides to enter the United States market and incorporates U.S. subsidiary, USSub, to be its U.S. distributor and to supervise the advertising and other marketing efforts that will be required to develop the name Fromage Frere in the United States. USSub incurs expenses that are not reimbursed by FP for developing the U.S. market for Fromage Frere. These expenses are comparable to the levels of expense incurred by independent distributors in the U.S. cheese industry when introducing a product in the U.S. market under a brand name owned by a foreign manufacturer. Since USSub would have been expected to incur these expenses if it were unrelated to FP, no allocation to USSub is made with respect to the market development activities performed by USSub.

Example : The facts are the same as in above Example, except that the expenses incurred by USSub are significantly larger than the expenses incurred by independent distributors under similar circumstances. FP does not reimburse USSub for its expenses. The district director concludes based on this evidence that an unrelated party dealing at arm's length under similar circumstances would not have engaged in the same level of activity relating to the development of FP's marketing intangibles. The expenditures in excess of the level incurred by the independent distributors therefore are considered to be a service provided to FP that adds to the value of FP's trademark for Fromage Frere. Accordingly, the district director makes an allocation under section 482 for the fair market value of the services that USSub is considered to have performed for FP.

The Hon'ble ITAT in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) had provided a legal recognition to the 'Bright Line Test' in spite of the fact that there was no such statutory mandate under the Income-tax Act, 1961 ("Act").

In the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra) the Hon'ble Delhi High Court has disagreed with the applicability of 'Bright Line Test' for benchmarking expenses incurred on AMP expenses. The important principles laid down by the Hon'ble High Court are as follows:

Similarly, the Calcutta High Court in Calcutta Landing & Shipping Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) held that payment made to employees in the expectation of creating impetus or to encourage them to put in selfless work for the employer is a payment made of commercial consideration and commercial expediency. In the same stride, the Madras High Court in CIT v. Deccan Sugars & Abkhari & Co. Ltd. When segmentation or segregation of a bundled transaction is required, the question of set off and apportionment must be examined realistically and with a pragmatic approach. Bright Line Test (BLT)

9. The Special Bench (majority view) of the ITAT held in case of LG's Electronics (India)(P.) Ltd. case (supra) that a Bright Line Test is required to be done in case of AMP expenses.

Bright line test draws a line between reasonable and unreasonable AMP expense. Whatever is more than reasonable, it would be treated as excessive and it would be deemed as incurred for the foreign AE. The Special Bench said that if the expense incurred by the Assessee on AMP was higher than what was incurred by an independent entity behaving in a commercially rational manner, than Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) would determine whether the said transaction required re-characterisation. A transaction cannot be recharacterized in a case where an independent enterprise behaving in a commercially rational manner would incur the expenses to the extent the assessee has incurred.

There is no statutory provision in the Act or Rules which holds that it is obligatory that the AMP expenses must and necessarily be subjected to Bright Line Test. In case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Delhi High Court said that BLT test cannot be applied for evaluating AMP expenses under Transfer Pricing provisions. In case of Whirlpool of India Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble High Court went beyond this and said that by validating the Bright Line test, the Special Bench in LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) went beyond Chapter X of the Act. Even international tax jurisprudence and commentaries do not recognise BLT for bifurcation of routine and non-routine expenses.

In nutshell, Bright line test is no more applicable. All the decisions, except LG's, have ruled out the applicability of BLT on AMP expenses.

Economic Ownership v. Legal Ownership

10. There are two types of ownership of a brand, viz., legal ownership and economic ownership. Legal ownership means who owns the brand like Trademark registered, patent owner, etc., whereas the person who gets the economic benefits due to his engagement with product, called as economic owner. Non-routine expenses on AMP should also be attributed to the economic ownership of the brand. As it is the Indian entity which acquires the economic ownership of brand and then exploits it for making more and more sales in India, those should also be allowed in its hands. A part of the AMP expenses incurred in India can be construed as leading only to the building of the economic ownership of a foreign brand, which vests solely with the Indian assessee.

Economic ownership is accepted in International Taxation in cases where contracts for goods or services are long-term. Though the assessee-company may not be legal owner of the brand but its revenue will increase in future due to AMP expenses. In other words, certainly the entity which incurs the AMP expenses will get economic benefit in future. In substance, economic ownership is existing in the world. It is up to the company who incurs the expenses that has to prove such future economic benefits.

It was also acknowledged in aforesaid Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra)that even if marketing intangible is created as a consequence of non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the Indian entity, the economic ownership of such intangibles vested in the Indian entity, which could exploit the same for furthering its business interest.

Sales Promotion (After Sales) expenses

11. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to distributors, wholesellers or retailers are not in the nature and character of brand promotion. These types of expenses are called as selling expenses & being incurred for doing high volume of sales or cash flow purposes. There is no motive of publicity or advertisement behind these types of expenses.

The expenses which are incurred after sales, are nowhere related to brand building. These cannot be part of AMP expenses. Same has been reiterated in all Judicial pronouncements, including in LG's Electronics India (P.) Ltd's case (supra). Even Special Bench of the ITAT in case of LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), agreed with that sale related expenses, i.e., trade discount, volume rebate, cash discount, commissions, etc., should be excluded while computing the T.P. Adjustment for AMP expenses. Trade discount or volume discount are related to price of product rather than brand building.

In summary, expenses which are incurred after sales, cannot be a part of AMP expenses.

Benefit to Foreign Legal Owner: Incidental or intentional

HC overrules Special Bench's ruling of ITAT on treatment of AMP expenses

Nilesh Patel

IRS (Ex), US CPA

Background

1. Consider the scenario: An Indian Company (IndCo) is Associated Enterprise (AE) of a Foreign Manufacturer. The Foreign Manufacturer manufactures branded consumer goods. Those goods - bearing the brand name, trademark or logo of the Foreign Manufacturer - are imported by IndCo and are sold in the Indian Market. Thus, IndCo acts as a Distributor of goods manufactured by its Foreign AE. In course of distributing the branded goods IndCo also markets those goods; IndCo incurs advertising, marketing and promotion (AMP) expenses, in addition to the regular selling and distribution expenses. The AMP expenses are paid to uncontrolled third parties (non-AEs) and are allowable under section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Following Transfer Pricing issues arise in this case –

(i)

Is IndCo rendering brand-building services to the Foreign Manufacturer AE, in addition to distributing goods manufactured by the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(ii)

Is IndCo creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign Manufacturer AE, by promoting the latter's brand name, trademark and logo in India?

(iii)

Does incurring of AMP expenses by IndCo give rise to an International Transaction between IndCo and the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(iv)

If the answer to question iii above is in the affirmative, then how do we determine the arm's length price of the International Transaction?

The above issues have arisen in a number of cases before the Transfer Pricing Officers. The matter has travelled to the ITAT. In January, 2013, the Special Bench of the ITAT pronounced its verdict in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi).

Later on, in the case of BMW India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 146 ITD 165/[2013] 37 taxmann.com 319 (Delhi – Trib.), the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable to licensed manufacturers but not to distributors. Then, in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Casio India Co. Ltd. [2014] 43 taxmann.com 56/62 SOT 110 (Delhi – Trib.) the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable not only to licensed manufacturers but also to distributors. Now, on the issue, the Delhi High Court has recently delivered its Judgment in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi), a judgment that has brought much needed clarity.

This article analyses and examines the Transfer Pricing issues emerging out of AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributors, in light of the Delhi High Court's Judgment in the above mentioned case. Let us take a look at what the Special Bench held in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra).

Case of L.g. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.

2. In this Case the Special Bench of the ITAT held as follows:–

Incurring of AMP expenses by an Indian AE needs to be bifurcated into routine and non-routine (excess or abnormal) AMP expenses. The routine AMP expenses are incurred for the Indian Entity's own business purposes to achieve its own sales targets and to grow its market share. But the non-routine AMP expenses are incurred for creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand, trademark, logo, embedded in the product), in India by way of brand-building or brand-promotion.

If it is found that the Indian Entity has incurred non-routine AMP expenses – in excess of routine AMP expenses – then it can be inferred that the Indian Entity has provided brand-building services to its Foreign AE. That will be an International Transaction covered by the Transfer Pricing Regulations.

The arm's length price of such an International Transaction can be worked out by Cost Plus Method, i.e., by applying an arm's length markup to the non-routine AMP expenses. That price would be the arm's length remuneration which the Indian Entity should recover from the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand) for brand-building services, or for creating marketing intangibles.

A question that arises here is: how to determine whether the Indian Entity has, or has not, incurred non-routine AMP expenses? To make such determination a Bright Line Test should be applied.

(2)

Advertisement expenditure like banners, brand ambassador expenses etc.

However, from transfer pricing perspective where AMP expenditure is incurred by associated enterprise of a foreign company, such AMP expenditure has been a matter of long time litigation as Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) considers AMP as an international transaction by invoking Section 92CA(2A) of the Income Tax Act,1961 and make adjustment on account of AMP expenditure in the hands of AE.

Cause of Litigation

AMP expenditure by AE in order to increase sales is recharacterized by TPO as amount incurred by India AE toward creation of marketing intangible (brand) of foreign company in India i.e, Indian entity has rendered services of brand creation to foreign company , therefore such Indian company shall be compensated from foreign company on Cost plus mark-up basis.

Computation of Adjustment by TPO

There are two approaches followed by TPO in order to compute adjustment amount on account of AMP expenditure :-

(1) Substantive Approach

Under substantive approach, TPO simply computes total amount of AMP expenditure and add mark-up upon that , resultant figure is the amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian AE.

(2) Protective Approach

Under protective approach, TPO applies Bright Line Test (BLT) method. Under BLT method, Indian companies belong to same industry of AE are identified and excess AMP expenditure incurred by AE is computed [ (AMP of AE/Sales of AE) – (Avg AMP of Indian comparable/Sales of Comparable). Such excess AMP expenditure along with mark-up is the adjustment amount in the hands of AE.

Adjustment amount as per substantive approach is always more in comparison to adjustment amount as per protective approach.

Contention of Taxpayer against AMP adjustment

(1)

There is no such agreement between Indian AE and foreign entity to create brand and incur AMP expenditure for foreign entity, therefore, in absence of any agreement , such transaction shall not be considered as an international transaction.

(2)

Bright Line Test method adopted by TPO is neither a permissible method under Indian Tax Laws nor prescribed under section 92C of the Income Tax Act,1961 read with Rule 10B of the Income Tax Rule, 1962.

(3)

Economic owner of such brand is AE.

(4)

AMP expenditure incurred to increase sales and therefore it is a domestic transaction and TPO has no jurisdiction over non international transaction

(5)

While computing AMP adjustment, Selling expenditure and amount reimburse from foreign AE shall be reduced from the amount of AMP expenditure incurred.

Landmark Judicial Judgements

(1) Sony Mobile Communications (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 312 (Delhi - Trib.)

The Hon'ble ITAT New Delhi Bench, I-2 in the aforementioned case held that assessee was a subsidiary of Sony Ericsson incorporated under the laws of Sweden . It was primarily engaged in business of importing, buying, selling and distribution of wide range of mobile phones in India and providing related post sale support services. During relevant year, assessee incurred huge cost on Advertisement Marketing and Sales Promotion of its mobile phones, TPO opined that expenditure on AMP incurred by assessee was exclusively to promote brand name 'Sony Ericssion' which was owned by AE, TPO thus took a view that expenditure incurred by assessee company was for advantage of its AE and it should have been suitably compensated by AE. He applied bright line test and made certain addition to assessee's ALP. It was undisputed that Sony Ericssion being a new entrant in mobile segment in year under consideration, assessee had to incur huge advertisement expenses to remind general public of its existence in domestic market. Thus, it could be concluded that AMP expenditure was incurred mainly for purpose of increase in sales of mobile phones in India and not for brand building of AE. Moreover, net profit margin declared by assessee was much higher than comparables and, looking from that angle also, there was no merit in transfer pricing adjustment.

(2) Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT (ITA 110/2014)

Amongst many controversial issues involving transfer pricing, the adjustment on account of marketing intangibles is certainly one of the most litigated and controversial, with enormous stakes involved at either side. As a brief recap, in January 2013 the Special Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("SB"), in the case of LG India Electronics (P)Ltd.1 ("LG SB Ruling") had adjudicated that the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ("AMP") expenditure incurred by the Indian AE is an international transaction, to the extent such AMP expense, as a percentage of turnover, exceeds that of the comparable companies (The concept of pegging AMP to industry standard is typically referred to as 'Bright Line Test'or "BLT"). While so concluding, the SB observed that the incurring of non-routine or excess AMP by the Indian taxpayer is in the nature of providing brand building service to the brand owners i.e. AE and consequently up-held adjustment for such excess AMP expenditure to the Indian taxpayer along with an arm's length mark-up. The LG SB ruling, was hailed as one of the most significant wins of the revenue in a transfer pricing matter, and the principles of the ruling were followed in a plethora of cases involving marketing intangibles resulting in billions of dollars of transfer pricing adjustments. Apparently, the issue, per se, travelled to the High Court against the decision of the division benches who had merely applied the ratio of the ruling of the Special Bench, being at the detriment of the appellant taxpayers.

Recently, the Delhi High Court ("Delhi HC" or "HC") in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communication Private Limited2, and several other connected matters3, adjudicated on the issue of marketing intangibles and upheld the transfer pricing officer's jurisdiction to AMP expenditure, as an international transaction. Further, ruling in favour of the taxpayer, the High Court held that the legal principles, commercial logic and methodology relied and accepted by the tribunal in LG SB Ruling (Supra) as erroneous and unacceptable. The 142 page HC ruling is a pleasure to read, as it paves its way into intricate details of various aspects of AMP adjustments and discusses the principles of brand building versus AMP, economic ownership, aggregated versus segregated approach of benchmarking, OECD guidelines, Indian law and the methodologies adopted for determination of ALP in relation to marketing intangibles. Enumerated below are some of the key findings of the Delhi HC.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the Revenue

TPO can adjudicate on international transactions which are not reported in Form 3CEB

Pursuant to retrospective amendment4 by the Finance Act, 2012, the TPO is empowered to adjudicate on the transactions which have not been reported by the taxpayer in the Form 3CEB. No specific reference by the Assessing Officer (AO) is required for the same.

AMP expense constitute an international transaction

The HC rejected the contention of the taxpayer that AMP is not an international transaction and is outside the scope of transfer pricing provisions. In this regard, the HC observed that dispute pertains to adequacy of the compensation received by the Indian taxpayer for incurring and performing marketing and 'non-routine' AMP expense in India. By virtue of application of the TP provisions, the TPO seeks to determine an arm's length compensation for the marketing and distribution functions performed by the taxpayer towards related parties. In summary, the AMP expense is an international transaction which is covered under the realms of transfer pricing.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the taxpayers

Aggregation of transactions and application of Transactional Net Margin Method

The HC held that the usage of words "an international transaction" in section 92(1) should not be read restrictively rather its interpretation should be gathered from other section and the Rules, whereby it would be amply clear that the legislative intent was to allow clubbing of closely linked transactions, which includes continuous transactions. However, close linkage of transactions is a pre-condition for aggregation. On the same logic, the HC held that distribution and marketing are intertwined and may be examined as bundled/inter-connected transactions. The HC also observed that in case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no prohibition in applying Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) on an entity wide basis, which follows that AMP function can be looked as closely linked to and a part of overall marketing and distribution activity, whereof it can be aggregated under the realms of TNMM.

Recognition of an Expense

55. Expenditure on an intangible item should be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it forms part of the cost of an intangible asset that meets the recognition criteria (see paragraphs 19-54); or

(b)

the item is acquired in an amalgamation in the nature of purchase and cannot be recognised as an intangible asset. If this is the case, this expenditure (included in the cost of acquisition) should form part of the amount attributed to goodwill (capital reserve) at the date of acquisition (see AS 14, Accounting for Amalgamations).

56. In some cases, expenditure is incurred to provide future economic benefits to an enterprise, but no intangible asset or other asset is acquired or created that can be recognised. In these cases, the expenditure is recognised as an expense when it is incurred. For example, expenditure on research is always recognised as an expense when it is incurred (see paragraph 41). Examples of other expenditure that is recognised as an expense when it is incurred include:

(a)

expenditure on start-up activities (start-up costs), unless this expenditure is included in the cost of an item of fixed asset under AS 10. Start-up costs may consist of preliminary expenses incurred in establishing a legal entity such as legal and secretarial costs, expenditure to open a new facility or business (pre-opening costs) or expenditures for commencing new operations or launching new products or processes (pre-operating costs);

(b)

expenditure on training activities;

(c)

expenditure on advertising and promotional activities; and

(d)

expenditure on relocating or re-organising part or all of an enterprise.

57. Paragraph 55 does not apply to payments for the delivery of goods or services made in advance of the delivery of goods or the rendering of services. Such pre-payments are recognised as assets.

Past Expenses not to be Recognised as an Asset

58. Expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognised as an expense by a reporting enterprise in previous annual financial statements or interim financial reports should not be recognised as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date.

Subsequent Expenditure

59. Subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after its purchase or its completion should be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it is probable that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standard of performance; and

(b)

the expenditure can be measured and attributed to the asset reliably.

If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the cost of the intangible asset

60. Subsequent expenditure on a recognised intangible asset is recognised as an expense if this expenditure is required to maintain the asset at its originally assessed standard of performance. The nature of intangible assets is such that, in many cases, it is not possible to determine whether subsequent expenditure is likely to enhance or maintain the economic benefits that will flow to the enterprise from those assets. In addition, it is often difficult to attribute such expenditure directly to a particular intangible asset rather than the business as a whole. Therefore, only rarely will expenditure incurred after the initial recognition of a purchased intangible asset or after completion of an internally generated intangible asset result in additions to the cost of the intangible asset.

68. Expenditure on an intangible item shall be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

expenditure on training activities.

(c)

expenditure on advertising and promotional activities (including mail order catalogues).

expenditure on relocating or reorganising part or all of an entity.

INDIAN ACCOUNTING STANDARD (IND AS) 38 :

INTANGIBLE ASSETS

(This Indian Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold type indicate the main principles.)

Objective

1. The objective of this Standard is to prescribe the accounting treatment for intangible assets that are not dealt with specifically in another Standard. This Standard requires an entity to recognise an intangible asset if, and only if, specified criteria are met. The Standard also specifies how to measure the carrying amount of intangible assets and requires specified disclosures about intangible assets.

Scope

2. This Standard shall be applied in accounting for intangible assets, except:

(a)

intangible assets that are within the scope of another Standard;

(b)

financial assets, as defined in Ind AS 32, Financial Instruments: Presentation;

(c)

the recognition and measurement of exploration and evaluation assets (see Ind AS 106, Exploration for and Evaluation of Mineral Resources); and

(d)

expenditure on the development and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources.

3. If another Standard prescribes the accounting for a specific type of intangible asset, an entity applies that Standard instead of this Standard. For example, this Standard does not apply to:

1[(a)

intangible assets held by an entity for sale in the ordinary course of business (see Ind AS 2, Inventories).]

(b)

deferred tax assets (see Ind AS 12, Income Taxes).

2[(c)

leases of intangible assets accounted for in accordance with Ind AS 116, Leases.]

(d)

assets arising from employee benefits (see Ind AS 19, Employee Benefits).

(e)

financial assets as defined in Ind AS 32. The recognition and measurement of some financial assets are covered by Ind AS 110, Consolidated Financial Statements, Ind AS 27, Separate Financial Statements, and Ind AS 28, Investments in Associates and Joint Ventures.

(f)

goodwill acquired in a business combination (see Ind AS 103, Business Combinations).

2a[(g)

contracts within the scope of Ind AS 117, Insurance Contracts, and any assets for insurance acquisition cash flows as defined in Ind AS 117.]

(h)

non-current intangible assets classified as held for sale (or included in a disposal group that is classified as held for sale) in accordance with Ind AS 105, Non-current Assets Held for Sale and Discontinued Operations.

3[(i)

assets arising from contracts with customers that are recognised in accordance with Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers.]

4. Some intangible assets may be contained in or on a physical substance such as a compact disc (in the case of computer software), legal documentation (in the case of a licence or patent) or film. In determining whether an asset that incorporates both intangible and tangible elements should be treated under Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment, or as an intangible asset under this Standard, an entity uses judgment to assess which element is more significant. For example, computer software for a computer-controlled machine tool that cannot operate without that specific software is an integral part of the related hardware and it is treated as property, plant and equipment. The same applies to the operating system of a computer. When the software is not an integral part of the related hardware, computer software is treated as an intangible asset.

5. This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (e.g. a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, i.e. the knowledge embodied in it.

4[6. Rights held by a lease under licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights are within the scope of this Standard and are excluded from the scope of Ind AS 116.]

7. Exclusions from the scope of a Standard may occur if activities or transactions are so specialised that they give rise to accounting issues that may need to be dealt with in a different way. Such issues arise in the accounting for expenditure on the exploration for, or development and extraction of, oil, gas and mineral deposits in extractive industries and in the case of insurance contracts. Therefore, this Standard does not apply to expenditure on such activities and contracts. However, this Standard applies to other intangible assets used (such as computer software), and other expenditure incurred (such as start-up costs), in extractive industries or by insurers.

47. To demonstrate how an intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits, an enterprise assesses the future economic benefits to be received from the asset using the principles in Accounting Standard on Impairment of Assets4. If the asset will generate economic benefits only in combination with other assets, the enterprise applies the concept of cash generating units as set out in Accounting Standard on Impairment of Assets. 48. In certain cases, an enterprise demonstrates the availability of external finance by obtaining a lender's indication of its willingness to fund the plan.

49. An enterprise's costing systems can often measure reliably the cost of generating an intangible asset internally, such as salary and other expenditure incurred in securing copyrights or licences or developing computer software.

50. Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance should not be recognised as intangible assets.

51. This Standard takes the view that expenditure on internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. Therefore, such items are not recognised as intangible assets.

Cost of an Internally Generated Intangible Asset

52. The cost of an internally generated intangible asset for the purpose of paragraph 23 is the sum of expenditure incurred from the time when the intangible asset first meets the recognition criteria in paragraphs 20-21 and 44. Paragraph 58 prohibits reinstatement of expenditure recognised as an expense in previous annual financial statements or interim financial reports.

53. The cost of an internally generated intangible asset comprises all expenditure that can be directly attributed, or allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis, to creating, producing and making the asset ready for its intended use. The cost includes, if applicable:

(a)

expenditure on materials and services used or consumed in generating the intangible asset;

(b)

the salaries, wages and other employment related costs of personnel directly engaged in generating the asset;

(c)

any expenditure that is directly attributable to generating the asset, such as fees to register a legal right and the amortisation of patents and licences that are used to generate the asset; and

(d)

overheads that are necessary to generate the asset and that can be allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis to the asset (for example, an allocation of the depreciation of fixed assets, insurance premium and rent). Allocations of overheads are made on basis similar to those used in allocating overheads to inventories (see AS 2, Valuation of Inventories). AS 16, Borrowing Costs, establishes criteria for the recognition of interest as a component of the cost of a qualifying asset. These criteria are also applied for the recognition of interest as a component of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset.

54. The following are not components of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset:

(a)

selling, administrative and other general overhead expenditure unless this expenditure can be directly attributed to making the asset ready for use;

(b)

clearly identified inefficiencies and initial operating losses incurred before an asset achieves planned performance; and

(c)

expenditure on training the staff to operate the asset.

Example Illustrating Paragraph 52

An enterprise is developing a new production process. During the year 20x1, expenditure incurred was Rs. 10 lakhs, of which Rs. 9 lakhs was incurred before 1st December, 20x1 and 1 lakh was incurred between 1st December, 20x1 and 31st December, 20x1. The enterprise is able to demonstrate that, at 1st December, 20x1, the production process met the criteria for recognition as an intangible asset. The recoverable amount of the know-how embodied in the process (including future cash outflows to complete the process before it is available for use) is estimated to be Rs. 5 lakhs.

Accounting Standards (AS) 26

Intangible Assets

(This Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold italic type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold italic type indicate the main principles. This Accounting Standard should be read in the context of its objective and the General Instructions contained in part A of the Annexure to the Notification.)

Objective

The objective of this Standard is to prescribe the accounting treatment for intangible assets that are not dealt with specifically in another Accounting Standard. This Standard requires an enterprise to recognise an intangible asset if, and only if, certain criteria are met. The Standard also specifies how to measure the carrying amount of intangible assets and requires certain disclosures about intangible assets.

Scope

1. This Standard should be applied by all enterprises in accounting for intangible assets, except:

(a)

intangible assets that are covered by another Accounting Standard;

(b)

financial assets1;

(c)

mineral rights and expenditure on the exploration for, or development and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources; and

(d)

intangible assets arising in insurance enterprises from contracts with policyholders.

This Standard should not be applied to expenditure in respect of termination benefits2 also.

2. If another Accounting Standard deals with a specific type of intangible asset, an enterprise applies that Accounting Standard instead of this Standard. For example, this Statement does not apply to:

(a)

intangible assets held by an enterprise for sale in the ordinary course of business (see AS 2, Valuation of Inventories and AS 7, Construction Contracts);

(b)

deferred tax assets (see AS 22, Accounting for Taxes on Income);

(c)

leases that fall within the scope of AS 19, Leases; and

(d)

goodwill arising on an amalgamation (see AS 14, Accounting for Amalgamations) and goodwill arising on consolidation (see AS 21, Consolidated Financial Statements).

3. This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (for example, a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, that is the knowledge embodied in it. This Standard also applies to rights under licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights. These items are excluded from the scope of AS 19.

4. In the case of a finance lease, the underlying asset may be either tangible or intangible. After initial recognition, a lessee deals with an intangible asset held under a finance lease under this Standard.

5. Exclusions from the scope of an Accounting Standard may occur if certain activities or transactions are so specialised that they give rise to accounting issues that may need to be dealt with in a different way. Such issues arise in the expenditure on the exploration for, or development and extraction of, oil, gas and mineral deposits in extractive industries and in the case of contracts between insurance enterprises and their policyholders. Therefore, this Standard does not apply to expenditure on such activities. However, this Standard applies to other intangible assets used (such as computer software), and other expenditure (such as start-up costs), in extractive industries or by insurance enterprises. Accounting issues of specialised nature also arise in respect of accounting for discount or premium relating to borrowings and ancillary costs incurred in connection with the arrangement of borrowings, share issue expenses and discount allowed on the issue of shares. Accordingly, this Standard does not apply to such items also.

Definitions

6. The following terms are used in this Standard with the meanings specified:

6.1 An intangible asset is an identifiable non-monetary asset, without physical substance, held for use in the production or supply of goods or services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes.

6.2 An asset is a resource:

(a)

controlled by an enterprise as a result of past events; and

(b)

from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.

6.3 Monetary assets are money held and assets to be received in fixed or determinable amounts of money.

6.4 Non-monetary assets are assets other than monetary assets.

6.5 Research is original and planned investigation undertaken with the prospect of gaining new scientific or technical knowledge and understanding.

6.6 Development is the application of research findings or other knowledge to a plan or design for the production of new or substantially improved materials, devices, products, processes, systems or services prior to the commencement of commercial production or use.

6.7 Amortisation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an intangible asset over its useful life.

6.8 Depreciable amount is the cost of an asset less its residual value.

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee-company offering training courses in field of financial services took over business of ‘W’, who was also carrying on similar activities, for a consideration which was claimed by assessee-company as revenue expenditure - Revenue, however, treated it as of capital nature - Whether essence of agreement being taking over of business of ‘W’ and warding off competition in business, said expenditure fell in category of capital expenditure and did not qualify for deduction as revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was incorporated with the prime purpose of specializing in offering of training courses in the field of financial services and other academic activities relating to financial services, such as offering of distance education courses, organizing conferences in and outside India, developing training facilities and classrooms, etc. ‘W’ was also in the business of carrying on similar activities as that of the assessee- company. The assessee-company took over the business of ‘W’ after payment of consideration amount for such acquisition, and claimed the said payment as revenue expenditure. The Assessing Officer held that the amount paid by the assessee for taking over the business of ‘W’ was of capital nature, as the business activity of that company was taken over for an indefinite period. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee-company took over the training courses and educational activities, for a consideration, of a company belonging to the same group and that ‘W’ stopped the activities following the takeover of their business by the assessee-company. It was, thus, held that the consider- ation amount paid by the assessee was for initiation of business to set up profit making apparatus in motion. Accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer. On second appeal to the Tribunal, the Accountant Member took the view that the said payment was in the nature of revenue expenditure because none of the components of the consideration could be said to be in the nature of creation of any asset, which was of the nature of capital assets. However, the Judicial Member was of the opinion that the amount was paid for taking over the business of imparting and conducting training courses in the field of leasing and hire-purchase of related areas, and that by taking over the business the assessee acquired the right to conduct the commercial activities of another company for an indefinite period and that acquisition of such right was of capital nature. As a result of difference of opinion between the two Members, the matter was referred to the Third Member for his opinion.

HELD (PER THIRD MEMBER)

It is well-settled principle of law that in order to interpret an agreement, one has to consider the substance of the agreement rather than its form. The agreement should be read as a whole and not in piecemeals. It was observed from the preamble and clauses 4, 5 and 6 of the agreement that the essence of the agreement was to takeover all the business activities of ‘W’. The transfer of training courses, materials, references, etc., as per clause 4 was incidental to takeover of the business. There was hardly any scope for doubt that the assessee had paid the consideration amount for taking over the activity of Affiliate Company with the specific purpose of carrying on the business on the condition that the affiliate company would cease to carry on the same business.

Profits and gains of business are required to be computed in accordance with the provisions of sections 30 to 43D as provided under section 29. Sections 30 to 36 deal with specific deductions. It was nobody’s case that the expenditure in dispute fell within the ambit of any of these sections viz., sections 30 to 36. Section 37 is a residuary section. From section 37, it is clear that any expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure is not allowable as a deduction in computing the profits and gains of business. Certain principles for determining whether an expenditure is of revenue nature or capital nature may be summarised as follows:

(1) If the expenditure is for the initial outlay or for acquiring or bringing into existence an asset or advantage of an enduring benefit to the business that is being carried on, or for extension of the business that is going on, or for a substantial replacement of an existing business assets, it would be capital expenditure.

(2) If, on the other hand, the expenditure, although for the purpose of acquiring an asset or advantage, is for running of the business or for working out that asset with a view to produce profit, it would be revenue expenditure.

The assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business, under an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that the assessee would pay to the vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages as also the value of assets over the liabilities taken over. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee-firm paid certain amount to the vendors under the said agreement and claimed deduction of the same as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground of the payment being a capital expenditure. On appeals, both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1976-77 - Assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business by an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that assessee would pay vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages - Whether aforesaid payment made by assessee to vendors could be claimed as a revenue expenditure - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a partnership firm, took over certain running business, under an agreement which stipulated, inter alia, that the assessee would pay to the vendors certain sum annually for three years for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages as also the value of assets over the liabilities taken over. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1976-77, the assessee-firm paid certain amount to the vendors under the said agreement and claimed deduction of the same as business expenditure. The ITO disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground of the payment being a capital expenditure. On appeals, both the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference:

HELD: No test of universal application can be laid down to determine the question whether an expenditure made by the assessee is revenue expenditure or capital expenditure. The question whether an expenditure is on account of revenue or capital has to be decided by looking at the facts and circumstances of the case from the point of view of a practical and prudent businessman rather than from the viewpoint of a tax-gatherer upon strict juristic classification of the legal rights, if any, secured in the proceeds. In order to arrive at a just and proper conclusion one must look at the true nature and character of advantage in a commercial sense without giving undue emphasis to the form thereof or the terminology used in the light of the surrounding circumstances and in the larger context of necessity and expediency. If the expenditure is so related to the carrying on or conduct of the business that it may be regarded as an integral part of the profit-making process and not for acquisition of an asset, or a right of permanent character, the expenditure may be regarded as revenue expenditure even though the advantage may endure for an indefinite future.

Admittedly, in the instant case, the said payment was made for use and utilisation of the trade name, pending import licences, contracts and other trading benefits and advantages. These rights so acquired evidently facilitated the day-to-day trading operations of the assessee and were intended to increase profits. No asset or right of permanent nature was acquired thereby. It was not even a case where the advantage would endure for indefinite future. Considering the nature and advantages flowing from obtaining the user of the rights in question in the commercial sense, the aforesaid payment was a revenue expenditure, and allowable as a deduction in computing taxable income of the assessee.

He therefore submitted that amount of Rs. 40 lakhs should be spread over a period of ten years and 1/10 each should be allowed for ten years starting from 1997-98. In support of this ground, he has relied on the decision of Supreme Court in the case of Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802 2. 17. Shri Ajay, ld. SR DR appearing for the revenue defended the order passed by the lower authorities on this point. He argued that the assessee has acquired a new product with its brand name and other rights from M/s. DIL. It is the product of Lacto Calomine which has been acquired to expand and boost the business carried on by the assessee-company. The product acquired by the assessee-company is a patented product. It is a fast moving product. Therefore, any direct expenditure incurred by the assessee-company for acquiring the said brand name is a capital expenditure. The non-compete fee of Rs. 40 lakhs paid by the assessee-company is not for any temporary benefit. The assessee want to exploit the business opportunities coming out of the new brand product to its full swing. Therefore, the assessee-company has to see that M/s. DIL is not competing in any way with the assessee-company inasmuch as the production and marketing of Lacto Calomine are concerned. By paying the amount of Rs. 40 lakhs, the assessee-company is keeping away M/s. DIL from the field for a long period of 10 years. Any future business made by the assessee-company would be directly related to the initial market stand held by it.
