Executives of Indian subsidiaries of Multinationals ('MNE group') and tax professionals across the country should now be able to breathe easy. The Hon'ble Delhi High Court ('Delhi HC') recently pronounced its decision on the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ('AMP') controversy1 involving various Indian distributors ('Taxpayers'2) of reputed MNE groups. The amounts involved on the issue run into several crores.

In past few years, a highly debated issue in Transfer Pricing ('TP') audits/litigation involving taxpayers who incur significant AMP expenses, has been the creation of marketing intangibles. Tax authorities at ground level have typically held that excessive or non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India contribute to building of the brand legally owned by the MNE group outside India. Consequently, the taxpayers should receive an arm's length compensation on the excessive or non-routine AMP expenses alongwith a mark-up from the legal owner of the brand in the MNE group. This view was upheld by the Special Bench ('SB') of Delhi Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ('ITAT'/'Tax Tribunal') in the case of LG Electronics India Private Limited3.The ITAT in its detailed order held that AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayer towards building a brand legally owned by the MNE group constituted an 'international transaction' and the foreign entity should pay for the AMP expenses incurred beyond the amount arrived at by applying the 'bright line'.

Consequent to the SB ruling in case of LG Electronics, tax authorities proposed TP additions in many other cases on account of the AMP issue, which were later upheld by various tax Tribunals. Aggrieved taxpayers filed appeals before the Delhi High Court against the rulings of the tax Tribunal in their respective cases.

1. Core issues before the Delhi HC

The Delhi HC, in its more than 140 page order, discussed at length the following core issues with respect to AMP expenses incurred by the taxpayers in India:

whether AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function undertaken by the taxpayers could be considered as an 'International Transaction' as per India Transfer Pricing Regulations4;

whether taxpayers could be said to be engaged in the activity of building 'Brand' in India which is legally owned by the MNE group;

whether the taxpayers could be said to be the 'Economic Owner' of the 'Marketing Intangible' purportedly developed by them for the MNE group;

whether AMP spend could be segregated into routine and non-routine expenditure in the hands of taxpayers by applying 'Bright Line Test5' in order to determine the value of so called 'Marketing Intangible'; and

how the marketing and distribution function (whether standalone or bundled with the other core transaction of import of goods) should be acknowledged and the arm's length compensation should be determined in such cases.

The Delhi HC, partly ruling in favour of the tax authorities and partly in favour of the taxpayers, gave elaborated reasons and findings on the above core issues. Some important aspects of the decision have been discussed in the following paragraphs.

2. AMP expenditure/distribution and marketing function is an 'International Transaction'

The Delhi HC struck down the contention of the taxpayers that AMP expenses were paid by them to third parties in India and accordingly should not be classified as an 'International Transaction'. It confirmed the finding of the ITAT in the case of LG Electronics that AMP expenditure incurred by the taxpayers with respect to distribution and marketing function is an international transaction in terms of Indian TP regulations. The HC observed that since taxpayers themselves advanced an argument that the declared price of international transactions included a remuneration for their AMP function, the argument challenging that it is not an international transaction is incorrect.

3. Legal ownership of 'Brand' and 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers

The Delhi HC observed (and rightly so) that a reputed 'Brand' is developed (by the MNE groups) over a passage of time. Brand value of any product/service refers to intangibles like know-how, infrastructure, and would depend upon the nature and quality of products/services offered to the customers. The HC further clarified that expenditure incurred by the taxpayers on advertisement and promotion of products/services with a 'Trademark' is only for commercial exploitation of the said 'Trademark' and per se there is no substantial value addition or 'Brand Building' by the taxpayers. Reputed brands do not undertake advertisement and marketing activities with the intention to increase (already established) brand value, but to increase sales and thereby earn larger profits.

4. AMP functions entail development of 'Marketing Intangibles' only in long-term contracts

Ownership does not mean legal ownership.

In a landmark judgment in Mysore Minerals Ltd. v. In a case where the transfer of property was contemplated by an agreement and thereafter, the physical delivery of the property was handed over and the property was used for the business of the assessee and thereafter, even if delayed, the transaction was concluded by executing the rele­vant conveyance and documents, then in such circumstances, the ownership of the asset must be considered as having been trans­ferred from the date of actual delivery of the asset. ..... in such circumstances, where the contract has been lawfully executed, ....the validity of the registered documents go back to the date of de facto transfer of ownership of the asset. This liberal principle has been upheld by the Supreme Court ...".

Sub-stantial de facto ownership is sufficient. De jure ownership (or legal ownership) is not required. This definition of ownership perfectly accords with the accounting definition of asset which stresses on 'Control' rather than legal ownership.

A 'patent' gives its owner an exclusive right to make and sell the subject-matter of the 'patent' for a particular period of time. The grant of a 'patent', to any individual or a firm, provides an individual or a firm competitive advantage over others within a given industrial field. [Para 24] A 'patent' is intended to protect the commercial exploitation of ideas, which are original, new and unobvious. It is a Government supported monopoly. It ensures that those who incur a cost of 'inventing' will reap its reward if users find the result worth paying for. This cannot occur if others reap where the inventor has sown. The 'patent' system is designed to stop the 'free riding' by non-patentees. [Para 24.1]

A 'copyright' means a right conferred upon its owner in respect of his literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work. It does not really mean a right to do something, but only the right to exclude others from the doing of certain specific acts and things. A 'patent' is distinguishable from a 'copyright'. The owner of the 'copyright' has a sole right and he has the right to exclude all others from reproducing his work without his permission. The 'copyright' gives protection to its owner from the necessity of having to compete with the product of his own effort. [Para 25]

A 'trade mark' is a symbol attached to goods or services that adds or creates a distinctive quality to the product by associating it in the buyer's mind with some manufacturer or distributor. Its main purpose is to eliminate 'free riding' by other manufacturers of similar goods and services. The property consists in the right of the owner to use the 'trade mark' in relation to specified goods and under certain circumstances to prevent others from using it. It ensures that the established reputation of one manufacturer is not appropriated by another by 'passing off', or misrepresentations. It is essentially part of a marketing strategy. The owner is granted excluded right to control the use of his 'trade mark' and the articles to which it is attached. [Para 26]

A person who buys a 'patent' acquires an exclusive business/commercial right, and if there is a breach, he can sue. In the instant case also, the assessee-company acquired an exclusive business/commercial right, and in the case of a breach, the assessee could sue. Therefore, the business/commercial right acquired by the assessee was of the 'same nature' as the business/commercial right of a 'patent'. [Para 27]

In the case of copyright, trade mark, license and franchisees also, the owners have exclusive business/commercial rights; and if there is a breach, they can sue. [Para 28]

Consequently, if the business/commercial right of a patent, copyright, trade mark, license and franchise, fulfils the conditions of 'being intangible asset', then surely the impugned business/commercial right acquired by the assessee also fulfilled that condition, by way of a logical corollary. [Para 29]

Therefore, the impugned 'non-compete right' acquired by the assessee-company, was eligible for depreciation under clause (ii ) of section 32(1). The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was, accordingly, upheld. [Para 31]

Recognition of an Expense

55. Expenditure on an intangible item should be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it forms part of the cost of an intangible asset that meets the recognition criteria (see paragraphs 19-54); or

(b)

the item is acquired in an amalgamation in the nature of purchase and cannot be recognised as an intangible asset. If this is the case, this expenditure (included in the cost of acquisition) should form part of the amount attributed to goodwill (capital reserve) at the date of acquisition (see AS 14, Accounting for Amalgamations).

56. In some cases, expenditure is incurred to provide future economic benefits to an enterprise, but no intangible asset or other asset is acquired or created that can be recognised. In these cases, the expenditure is recognised as an expense when it is incurred. For example, expenditure on research is always recognised as an expense when it is incurred (see paragraph 41). Examples of other expenditure that is recognised as an expense when it is incurred include:

(a)

expenditure on start-up activities (start-up costs), unless this expenditure is included in the cost of an item of fixed asset under AS 10. Start-up costs may consist of preliminary expenses incurred in establishing a legal entity such as legal and secretarial costs, expenditure to open a new facility or business (pre-opening costs) or expenditures for commencing new operations or launching new products or processes (pre-operating costs);

(b)

expenditure on training activities;

(c)

expenditure on advertising and promotional activities; and

(d)

expenditure on relocating or re-organising part or all of an enterprise.

57. Paragraph 55 does not apply to payments for the delivery of goods or services made in advance of the delivery of goods or the rendering of services. Such pre-payments are recognised as assets.

Past Expenses not to be Recognised as an Asset

58. Expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognised as an expense by a reporting enterprise in previous annual financial statements or interim financial reports should not be recognised as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date.

Subsequent Expenditure

59. Subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after its purchase or its completion should be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it is probable that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standard of performance; and

(b)

the expenditure can be measured and attributed to the asset reliably.

If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the cost of the intangible asset

60. Subsequent expenditure on a recognised intangible asset is recognised as an expense if this expenditure is required to maintain the asset at its originally assessed standard of performance. The nature of intangible assets is such that, in many cases, it is not possible to determine whether subsequent expenditure is likely to enhance or maintain the economic benefits that will flow to the enterprise from those assets. In addition, it is often difficult to attribute such expenditure directly to a particular intangible asset rather than the business as a whole. The other aspects relevant for comparability of transactions are nature of transaction (license or assignment); type of property; duration of the agreement; degree of protection and expected benefits likely to accrue from use of intangible property. The terms of agreement between parties for transfer of intangibles are also relevant consideration to compare transactions; and where these are not defined properly they can be culled from conduct of the parties and surrounding circumstances.

3. Benefit Test Benefit test is important aspect of valuation of marketing intangible. It indicates the measure of benefits derived by an associated enterprise from use of intangible property. The payer of royalty may benefit from intangible property in various forms such as, increase in sales volume, market share or profitability of associated enterprise for which proper documentation should be maintained. The tax authorities normally require taxpayers to satisfy the benefit test, where internal comparables are not available and intangible used is unique for which uncontrolled transactions do not exist.

4. Marketing Intangibles

Marketing intangibles mean an intangible asset such as a trade-mark or brand name that may enable a company to commercially exploit a product or service because of their interface and recognition by markets. Determining arm's length royalty rate of marketing intangible is complicated as one cannot easily determine market value of licensing such an asset.

As per OECD Guidelines3, in a case involving transfer of marketing intangibles, such as, trade mark the comparability analysis should consider the value added by the trademark, taking into account the consumer acceptability, geographic significance, market shares, sales volume and other relevant factors. But if international transaction involves trade intangibles the analysis should take into consideration the value attributable to such intangibles like patent protection or exclusivity of the use of intangible.

In Hyatt Group Holdings v. Commissioner4 the US Court held that since brand name was a valuable intangible right that provided high credit rating to the hotel the royalty at arm's length rate of 0.4% was payable for grant of right to use trademark. In another case of DHL Corporation and Subsidiaries v. Commissioner5 the US Court again held that transfer price regulations applied to value of trade-mark rights so determined by the Court and therefore, arm's length rate of royalty was payable by Hong Kong subsidiary DHLI to its US parent DHL Corporation even though the two companies had entered into a MOU in 1974 agreeing to do business without any payment of royalty.

In a Danish case6 the Tax Tribunal held that royalty paid by foreign AE at 6% of turnover for use of standard software developed by the parent company could not be treated excessive and subject to transfer pricing adjustment when the subsidiary company had agreed to use standard software of the parent company to avoid increased cost of developing more advanced software and there was no material to show that any unrelated enterprise could have obtained more favourable terms than the taxpayer.

5. Brand Royalty

Brand name is a distinctive name which is identified with a particular product or goods; it can be arbitrary, fanciful, suggestive, descriptive or generic depending upon the underlying product. When manufacture or processing of certain goods or business of an enterprise mainly depends upon value of a particular brand owned by the associated enterprise the royalty paid for the use of the brand must satisfy the arm's length test.

EKL Appliances Ltd. case

The Delhi High Court in the case of CIT v. EKL Appliances Ltd7 examined the issue of arm's length payment of royalty to foreign AE for use of 'brand' by Indian company. The assessee was engaged in manufacturing of refrigerators, washing machines, compressors and spare parts. It paid brand fee of 1% of net sales to its Swedish AE (AB Electrolux) even though assessee company was incurring losses every year except in FY 1999-2000. The assessee's contention was that royalty payment was justified under CUP method as AE received similar payment from uncontrolled company Fisher Paykel Industries Ltd. The transaction was also certified by M/s Ernst Young which opined that fee paid was lower than uncontrolled brand fees. The High Court confirming the order of Tribunal held that payment of royalty was justified under CUP method and the company had benefited from use of technology of the foreign AE even though it suffered losses. The Court further observed that Rule 10B(1) does not authorise disallowance of any expenditure on the ground it was not necessary or prudent for the assessee; or because the company had incurred losses. The issue was accordingly decided in favour of the assessee.

68. Expenditure on an intangible item shall be recognised as an expense when it is incurred unless:

(a)

it forms part of the cost of an intangible asset that meets the recognition criteria (see paragraphs 18-67); or

(b)

the item is acquired in a business combination and cannot be recognised as an intangible asset. If this is the case, it forms part of the amount recognised as goodwill at the acquisition date (see Ind AS 103).

69. In some cases, expenditure is incurred to provide future economic benefits to an entity, but no intangible asset or other asset is acquired or created that can be recognised. In the case of the supply of goods, the entity recognises such expenditure as an expense when it has a right to access those goods. In the case of the supply of services, the entity recognises the expenditure as an expense when it receives the services. For example, expenditure on research is recognised as an expense when it is incurred (see paragraph 54), except when it is acquired as part of a business combination. Other examples of expenditure that is recognised as an expense when it is incurred include:

(a)

expenditure on start-up activities (i.e. start-up costs), unless this expenditure is included in the cost of an item of property, plant and equipment in accordance with Ind AS 16. Start-up costs may consist of establishment costs such as legal and secretarial costs incurred in establishing a legal entity, expenditure to open a new facility or business (i.e. pre-opening costs) or expenditures for starting new operations or launching new products or processes (i.e. pre-operating costs).

(b)

expenditure on training activities.

(c)

expenditure on advertising and promotional activities (including mail order catalogues).

(d)

expenditure on relocating or reorganising part or all of an entity.

69A. An entity has a right to access goods when it owns them. Similarly, it has a right to access goods when they have been constructed by a supplier in accordance with the terms of a supply contract and the entity could demand delivery of them in return for payment. Services are received when they are performed by a supplier in accordance with a contract to deliver them to the entity and not when the entity uses them to deliver another service, for example, to deliver an advertisement to customers.

70. Paragraph 68 does not preclude an entity from recognising a prepayment as an asset when payment for goods has been made in advance of the entity obtaining a right to access those goods. Similarly, paragraph 68 does not preclude an entity from recognising a prepayment as an asset when payment for services has been made in advance of the entity receiving those services.

Betterment charges - Betterment charges on account of increase in the valuation of the land of the assessee should not be held as a revenue expenditure although general improvement of the area might have an impact on better running of the business [Arvind Mills Ltd. v. Business expansion - The nature of the new business is not a decisive test for determining whether or not there is an expansion of an existing business. The nature of the business could be as distinct as a jewellery business and a business of cinematographic films; it could be as different as manufacture of metal alloys and manufacture of rubber products. What is of importance is that the control of both the ventures, the existing venture as well as the new venture, must be in the hands of one establishment or management or administration. The place of business of the existing business and the new business may not be in close proximity - it could be as far apart as Baroda and Bangalore. However, the funds utilised for the management of both the concerns must be common as reflected in the balance sheet of the company [Jay Engineering Works Ltd. v. CIT [2008] 166 Taxman 55 (Delhi)].

Expenditure in connection with expansion of existing business would be allowed as revenue expenditure notwithstanding that same have been capitalised in the books of account [CIT v. Nirma Ltd. However, the Cheese Examples in the early regulations and the global attention given the Glaxo case has alerted many other tax authorities to this evolving issue and as they look for additional ways to raise revenue, a potentially attractive vehicle to raise revenue.7 The theories described above continue to be raised in most global tax audits and Advance Pricing Agreement proceedings, and are presently under consideration by the U.S. Tax Court in current pending cases. The underlying thread seems to be that AMP, if substantive enough, creates an intangible. Numerous unanswered questions remain, however, such as how to define a company’s marketing intangibles from a tax and legal perspective, what expenses truly contribute to the building of this intangible, how to determine in tax parlance where the level of AMP transcends from routine to non-routine expenditures, what expenses qualify for these considerations, (e.g. registration costs, legal costs for routine expenses and real broad brand building expenses as such non-routine expenses), whether an analysis of each underlying accounting code requires the segregation of routine from non-routine expenditures, what allocation keys may be employed and what is the "shelf life" of the created marketing intangible, as well as any pre existing marketing intangibles that are included within the considered intangible. One further practical problem, and a significant one, is that not every taxpayer accounts for its AMP within the same accounting classifications.

While there may be merit in the DHL "bright line" test from a practical point of view, the definition of non-routine expenditures is so industry and company specific, that it may be impossible to apply in most cases. Similar companies within the same industry may have vastly different approaches to their marketing philosophies, product launches, and/or product dependence or interdependence. This could create very different levels of AMP and different "bright lines." This may even occur within the same companies and for similar product categories. These expenditures can also be influenced by, among other things, the product’s position in other countries, the timing of product launches, and the competitors and their products, each of which impacts the "bright line" benchmarking and comparability standards. Also, the legal status of the intangibles concerned may impact the expenditures differently. Even more complexity arises where the company has many product lines and the AMP expenditures are not segregated by those lines.

In the Mary Kay Holdings case,8 that was docketed in the Tax Court and later on settled the Petitioner begged the question of whether AMP are deductible under I.R.C. Section 162 when they are incurred for the development of a brand outside the United States. In the facts contained in the Petition, the U.S. parent company seemingly used the AMP spend as a vehicle to make a transfer pricing adjustment to its "limited risk" distribution under the guise that the adjustments (i.e. AMP charge backs) were made by the parent to support the development of the "Mary Kay" brand. The amounts of these expenses were approximately $16.1 million in 1997, $20.6 million in 1998 and $14.2 million in 1999. While the case was settled, and some underlying papers indicate the Government was challenging the documentation, it is not clear therefore how the Tax Court would have held on this issue. However, what is clear is that there should be a distinct delineation between how transfer pricing adjustments are made and how AMP support payments and/or charge-backs are addressed so that there is a clean line of demarcation between the two and the AMP payments can truly be tracked to brand development and enhancement expense codes.

Notwithstanding the above, the analysis that has evolved from the prior jurisprudence begs the question of what expenses are truly brand building. For example, some marketing consultants would argue that pure advertising is not a brand building cost. Instead, placements for specific events (e.g., the Super Bowl, the U.S. Open, etc.) may be considered to produce lasting brand equity. The same can be said that celebrity endorsements create more brand building and brand association than pure advertising. Similarly, market campaigns and strategic focus groups geared to market knowledge, spending habits, and market placement can be of equal value. In tax audits, the IRS and other taxing authorities have focused on flagship stores as brand builders, or another form of AMP. The premise is that these flagships are strategically positioned in locations where their presence is of greater value than the revenue, if any, generated from the store (e.g. 5th Avenue in New York City) Michigan Avenue in Chicago, Rodeo Drive in Los Angeles. The taxing authorities have often characterized the "excess rental costs" associated with flagship properties as brand builders to be borne by the brand owner.

The likelihood of attaining a consensus view on these items of brand building is nil. But what is clear is that the brand building/development costs will be company specific and will require a detailed analysis to meet the ever increasing challenges of global tax authorities in this area.

Section 55(2)(a) provides that the cost of acquisition of trade marks will be taken as purchase price/nil ‘for the purpose of sections 48 and 49’. Section 50, however, goes further to say that ‘in case of depreciable assets sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the modifications’ prescribed in that section.

Hence, it seems that in respect of trade mark on which depreciation has been allowed under the Act, the capital gains would have to be computed as per the provisions of section 50 since the said section clearly provides that ‘the provisions under sections 48 and 49 shall be subject to the following modifications’. However, as regards trade marks on which depreciation has not been allowed under the Act (which would include self-acquired trade marks and trade marks acquired prior to 1-4-1998) the capital gains would have to be computed on the basis of cost determined as per section 55(2)(a).

Accounting Standards (AS) 26

Intangible Assets

(This Accounting Standard includes paragraphs set in bold italic type and plain type, which have equal authority. Paragraphs in bold italic type indicate the main principles. This Accounting Standard should be read in the context of its objective and the General Instructions contained in part A of the Annexure to the Notification.)

Objective

The objective of this Standard is to prescribe the accounting treatment for intangible assets that are not dealt with specifically in another Accounting Standard. This Standard requires an enterprise to recognise an intangible asset if, and only if, certain criteria are met. The Standard also specifies how to measure the carrying amount of intangible assets and requires certain disclosures about intangible assets.

Scope

1. This Standard should be applied by all enterprises in accounting for intangible assets, except:

(a)

intangible assets that are covered by another Accounting Standard;

(b)

financial assets1;

(c)

mineral rights and expenditure on the exploration for, or development and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources; and

(d)

intangible assets arising in insurance enterprises from contracts with policyholders.

This Standard should not be applied to expenditure in respect of termination benefits2 also.

2. If another Accounting Standard deals with a specific type of intangible asset, an enterprise applies that Accounting Standard instead of this Standard. For example, this Statement does not apply to:

(a)

intangible assets held by an enterprise for sale in the ordinary course of business (see AS 2, Valuation of Inventories and AS 7, Construction Contracts);

(b)

deferred tax assets (see AS 22, Accounting for Taxes on Income);

(c)

leases that fall within the scope of AS 19, Leases; and

(d)

goodwill arising on an amalgamation (see AS 14, Accounting for Amalgamations) and goodwill arising on consolidation (see AS 21, Consolidated Financial Statements).

3. This Standard applies to, among other things, expenditure on advertising, training, start-up, research and development activities. Research and development activities are directed to the development of knowledge. Therefore, although these activities may result in an asset with physical substance (for example, a prototype), the physical element of the asset is secondary to its intangible component, that is the knowledge embodied in it. This Standard also applies to rights under licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights. These items are excluded from the scope of AS 19.

4. In the case of a finance lease, the underlying asset may be either tangible or intangible. After initial recognition, a lessee deals with an intangible asset held under a finance lease under this Standard.

5. Exclusions from the scope of an Accounting Standard may occur if certain activities or transactions are so specialised that they give rise to accounting issues that may need to be dealt with in a different way. Such issues arise in the expenditure on the exploration for, or development and extraction of, oil, gas and mineral deposits in extractive industries and in the case of contracts between insurance enterprises and their policyholders. Therefore, this Standard does not apply to expenditure on such activities. However, this Standard applies to other intangible assets used (such as computer software), and other expenditure (such as start-up costs), in extractive industries or by insurance enterprises. Accounting issues of specialised nature also arise in respect of accounting for discount or premium relating to borrowings and ancillary costs incurred in connection with the arrangement of borrowings, share issue expenses and discount allowed on the issue of shares. Accordingly, this Standard does not apply to such items also.

Definitions

6. The following terms are used in this Standard with the meanings specified:

6.1 An intangible asset is an identifiable non-monetary asset, without physical substance, held for use in the production or supply of goods or services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes.

6.2 An asset is a resource:

(a)

controlled by an enterprise as a result of past events; and

(b)

from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.

6.3 Monetary assets are money held and assets to be received in fixed or determinable amounts of money.

6.4 Non-monetary assets are assets other than monetary assets.

6.5 Research is original and planned investigation undertaken with the prospect of gaining new scientific or technical knowledge and understanding.

6.6 Development is the application of research findings or other knowledge to a plan or design for the production of new or substantially improved materials, devices, products, processes, systems or services prior to the commencement of commercial production or use.

6.7 Amortisation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an intangible asset over its useful life.

6.8 Depreciable amount is the cost of an asset less its residual value.

Depreciation on 'Goodwill' - A critical analysis

Kavita Kachhwaha

Introduction

1. An intangible asset can be defined as "an identifiable non-monetary asset, without physical substance, which is able to generate economic benefits to the business enterprise."1 It creates significant values for an organization beyond its tangible assets. Intangible assets (including intellectual properties), such as goodwill, know-how, customer lists, copyrights, etc., may be self-generated and, hence, an off-balance sheet item or these may be purchased. It is to be noted that expenses on development or on purchasing of such intangibles are either capitalized, or are expensed out in the profit and loss account, depending on the facts of each case. Where such intangibles are capitalized, the Income-tax Act, 1961 expressly provides for depreciation allowance.2 Depreciation is allowed on know-how, patents, copyrights, trade-marks, licences, franchises and 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature'. However, there is no express provision for depreciation in respect of other widely known intangible assets, such as, goodwill, non-compete rights, employees' contracts, vendor/customer contracts, distributorship rights, service process flows, knowledge databases, brands, etc. Thus, the key issue in respect of depreciation of such unspecified intangible assets, mentioned above, is whether they can be regarded as business or commercial rights of a 'similar' nature ?

It is to be noted that Goodwill is one of the significant intangible assets which either arises on acquisition or is internally generated. As per section 55(2)(a) of the Act, the cost of acquisition in case of goodwill is the purchase price and in case of self-generated goodwill it is nil. Thus, purchased goodwill is now specifically recognized as a capital asset. In practice, M&A transactions usually results in the transferee-company paying a consideration higher than the value of the assets taken over, which is accounted for as 'Goodwill'. Thus, since the statute is silent, a moot point from an income-tax perspective is whether such goodwill would be eligible for tax depreciation? This issue has become quite relevant in today's competitive atmosphere. Enterprises frequently expend resources, or incur liabilities on the acquisition, development, maintenance or enhancement of intangible resources such as scientific or technical knowledge, design and implementation of new processes or systems, licences, trademarks, etc. It is more significant in corporate sector with India incorporated actively pursuing mergers and acquisitions route for their expansions and valuations reaching dizzy heights, intangibles being a larger part of acquisition.

Thus, in the light of the significance of this issue, this paper takes an opportunity to examine whether goodwill, being an 'intangible asset', is eligible for depreciation under section 32 of the I.T. Act. It also takes into account the relevant provisions of the proposed Direct Taxes Code.

2. The Concept of Goodwill

2.1 Definition of goodwill - The term "goodwill" has not been defined in the Income Tax Act, 1961. Thus, in order to understand the concept recourse must be made to the judicial pronouncements.

Amongst many controversial issues involving transfer pricing, the adjustment on account of marketing intangibles is certainly one of the most litigated and controversial, with enormous stakes involved at either side. As a brief recap, in January 2013 the Special Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ("SB"), in the case of LG India Electronics (P)Ltd.1 ("LG SB Ruling") had adjudicated that the Advertisement, Marketing and Promotion ("AMP") expenditure incurred by the Indian AE is an international transaction, to the extent such AMP expense, as a percentage of turnover, exceeds that of the comparable companies (The concept of pegging AMP to industry standard is typically referred to as 'Bright Line Test'or "BLT"). While so concluding, the SB observed that the incurring of non-routine or excess AMP by the Indian taxpayer is in the nature of providing brand building service to the brand owners i.e. AE and consequently up-held adjustment for such excess AMP expenditure to the Indian taxpayer along with an arm's length mark-up. The LG SB ruling, was hailed as one of the most significant wins of the revenue in a transfer pricing matter, and the principles of the ruling were followed in a plethora of cases involving marketing intangibles resulting in billions of dollars of transfer pricing adjustments. Apparently, the issue, per se, travelled to the High Court against the decision of the division benches who had merely applied the ratio of the ruling of the Special Bench, being at the detriment of the appellant taxpayers.

Recently, the Delhi High Court ("Delhi HC" or "HC") in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communication Private Limited2, and several other connected matters3, adjudicated on the issue of marketing intangibles and upheld the transfer pricing officer's jurisdiction to AMP expenditure, as an international transaction. Further, ruling in favour of the taxpayer, the High Court held that the legal principles, commercial logic and methodology relied and accepted by the tribunal in LG SB Ruling (Supra) as erroneous and unacceptable. The 142 page HC ruling is a pleasure to read, as it paves its way into intricate details of various aspects of AMP adjustments and discusses the principles of brand building versus AMP, economic ownership, aggregated versus segregated approach of benchmarking, OECD guidelines, Indian law and the methodologies adopted for determination of ALP in relation to marketing intangibles. Enumerated below are some of the key findings of the Delhi HC.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the Revenue

TPO can adjudicate on international transactions which are not reported in Form 3CEB

Pursuant to retrospective amendment4 by the Finance Act, 2012, the TPO is empowered to adjudicate on the transactions which have not been reported by the taxpayer in the Form 3CEB. No specific reference by the Assessing Officer (AO) is required for the same.

AMP expense constitute an international transaction

The HC rejected the contention of the taxpayer that AMP is not an international transaction and is outside the scope of transfer pricing provisions. In this regard, the HC observed that dispute pertains to adequacy of the compensation received by the Indian taxpayer for incurring and performing marketing and 'non-routine' AMP expense in India. By virtue of application of the TP provisions, the TPO seeks to determine an arm's length compensation for the marketing and distribution functions performed by the taxpayer towards related parties. In summary, the AMP expense is an international transaction which is covered under the realms of transfer pricing.

Issues wherein the HC has ruled in favour of the taxpayers

Aggregation of transactions and application of Transactional Net Margin Method

The HC held that the usage of words "an international transaction" in section 92(1) should not be read restrictively rather its interpretation should be gathered from other section and the Rules, whereby it would be amply clear that the legislative intent was to allow clubbing of closely linked transactions, which includes continuous transactions. However, close linkage of transactions is a pre-condition for aggregation. On the same logic, the HC held that distribution and marketing are intertwined and may be examined as bundled/inter-connected transactions. The HC also observed that in case the tested party is engaged in single line of business, there is no prohibition in applying Transactional Net Margin Method (TNMM) on an entity wide basis, which follows that AMP function can be looked as closely linked to and a part of overall marketing and distribution activity, whereof it can be aggregated under the realms of TNMM.

Bright line test draws a line between reasonable and unreasonable AMP expense. Whatever is more than reasonable, it would be treated as excessive and it would be deemed as incurred for the foreign AE. The Special Bench said that if the expense incurred by the Assessee on AMP was higher than what was incurred by an independent entity behaving in a commercially rational manner, than Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) would determine whether the said transaction required re-characterisation. A transaction cannot be recharacterized in a case where an independent enterprise behaving in a commercially rational manner would incur the expenses to the extent the assessee has incurred.

There is no statutory provision in the Act or Rules which holds that it is obligatory that the AMP expenses must and necessarily be subjected to Bright Line Test. In case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. (supra), the Delhi High Court said that BLT test cannot be applied for evaluating AMP expenses under Transfer Pricing provisions. In case of Whirlpool of India Ltd. (supra), the Hon'ble High Court went beyond this and said that by validating the Bright Line test, the Special Bench in LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra) went beyond Chapter X of the Act. Even international tax jurisprudence and commentaries do not recognise BLT for bifurcation of routine and non-routine expenses.

In nutshell, Bright line test is no more applicable. All the decisions, except LG's, have ruled out the applicability of BLT on AMP expenses.

Economic Ownership v. Legal Ownership

10. There are two types of ownership of a brand, viz., legal ownership and economic ownership. Legal ownership means who owns the brand like Trademark registered, patent owner, etc., whereas the person who gets the economic benefits due to his engagement with product, called as economic owner. Non-routine expenses on AMP should also be attributed to the economic ownership of the brand. As it is the Indian entity which acquires the economic ownership of brand and then exploits it for making more and more sales in India, those should also be allowed in its hands. A part of the AMP expenses incurred in India can be construed as leading only to the building of the economic ownership of a foreign brand, which vests solely with the Indian assessee.

Economic ownership is accepted in International Taxation in cases where contracts for goods or services are long-term. Though the assessee-company may not be legal owner of the brand but its revenue will increase in future due to AMP expenses. In other words, certainly the entity which incurs the AMP expenses will get economic benefit in future. In substance, economic ownership is existing in the world. It is up to the company who incurs the expenses that has to prove such future economic benefits.

It was also acknowledged in aforesaid Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd.'s case (supra)that even if marketing intangible is created as a consequence of non-routine AMP expenses incurred by the Indian entity, the economic ownership of such intangibles vested in the Indian entity, which could exploit the same for furthering its business interest.

Sales Promotion (After Sales) expenses

11. The marketing or selling expenses like trade discounts, volume discounts, etc., offered to distributors, wholesellers or retailers are not in the nature and character of brand promotion. These types of expenses are called as selling expenses & being incurred for doing high volume of sales or cash flow purposes. There is no motive of publicity or advertisement behind these types of expenses.

The expenses which are incurred after sales, are nowhere related to brand building. These cannot be part of AMP expenses. Same has been reiterated in all Judicial pronouncements, including in LG's Electronics India (P.) Ltd's case (supra). Even Special Bench of the ITAT in case of LG Electronics (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), agreed with that sale related expenses, i.e., trade discount, volume rebate, cash discount, commissions, etc., should be excluded while computing the T.P. Adjustment for AMP expenses. Trade discount or volume discount are related to price of product rather than brand building.

In summary, expenses which are incurred after sales, cannot be a part of AMP expenses.

Benefit to Foreign Legal Owner: Incidental or intentional

There was no doubt about the fact that the assessee was already engaged in the business of manufacture of cars and the production had commenced about three years before. The new model of the car related to the same line of business which the assessee had been carrying on. The assessee had not set up a separate and independent unit to manufacture new model of the car. From the details of the expenses given, it was clear that the expenses related to travelling, training and seminar and advertisement, technical guidance fee, etc., of the on going business. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in sustaining the disallowance of the impugned expenditure.

6AAF. (1) A skill development project shall be considered for notification if it is undertaken by an eligible company and the project is undertaken in separate facilities in a training institute.

(2) The eligible company, before undertaking any skill development project, shall make an application for notification of such project under sub-section (1) of section 35CCD, in duplicate, in Form No. 3CQ, to the National Skill Development Agency (hereinafter referred to as the NSDA).

(3) The eligible company shall also send a copy of the application in Form No. 3CQ to the Commissioner of Income-tax or the Director of Income-tax, as the case may be, having jurisdiction over the case, accompanied by the acknowledgement receipt as evidence of having furnished the application form in duplicate to the NSDA.

(4) The application shall be accompanied by the following, namely :—

(a)

detailed note on the skill development project to be undertaken by the eligible company;

(b)

details of the expenditure expected to be incurred on the project and expected date of completion of the project; and

(c)

a letter of concurrence from the training institute in which the skill development project is to be undertaken.

(5) If any defect is noticed in the application referred to in sub-rule (2) or if any relevant document is not attached thereto, the NSDA shall, before the expiry of one month from the date of receipt of the application in its office, intimate the defect to the applicant for its rectification.

(6) The applicant shall remove the defect within a period of fifteen days from the date of such intimation or within such further period as, on an application made in this behalf, may be extended by the NSDA, so however, that the total period for removal of the defect does not exceed thirty days, and if the applicant fails to remove the defect within such period so allowed, the NSDA shall send its recommendation for treating the application as invalid to the CBDT.

(7) On receipt of recommendation of the NSDA under sub-rule (6), the CBDT, if satisfied, may pass an order treating the application as invalid.

(8) If the application form is complete in all respects, the NSDA may make such inquiry or call for such documents from the eligible company or the training institute as it may consider necessary for satisfying itself regarding the genuineness of the current and proposed activity of the applicant and send its recommendation to the CBDT for grant of approval or rejection of the application before the expiry of the period of two months to be reckoned from the end of the month in which the application form complete in all respects was received in its office.

To demonstrate how an intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits, an enterprise assesses the future economic benefits to be received from the asset using the principles in Accounting Standard on Impairment of Assets4. If the asset will generate economic benefits only in combination with other assets, the enterprise applies the concept of cash generating units as set out in Accounting Standard on Impairment of Assets. 48. Availability of resources to complete, use and obtain the benefits from an intangible asset can be demonstrated by, for example, a business plan showing the technical, financial and other resources needed and the enterprise's ability to secure those resources. In certain cases, an enterprise demonstrates the availability of external finance by obtaining a lender's indication of its willingness to fund the plan.

49. An enterprise's costing systems can often measure reliably the cost of generating an intangible asset internally, such as salary and other expenditure incurred in securing copyrights or licences or developing computer software.

50. Internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance should not be recognised as intangible assets.

51. This Standard takes the view that expenditure on internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing titles, customer lists and items similar in substance cannot be distinguished from the cost of developing the business as a whole. Therefore, such items are not recognised as intangible assets.

Cost of an Internally Generated Intangible Asset

52. The cost of an internally generated intangible asset for the purpose of paragraph 23 is the sum of expenditure incurred from the time when the intangible asset first meets the recognition criteria in paragraphs 20-21 and 44. Paragraph 58 prohibits reinstatement of expenditure recognised as an expense in previous annual financial statements or interim financial reports.

53. The cost of an internally generated intangible asset comprises all expenditure that can be directly attributed, or allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis, to creating, producing and making the asset ready for its intended use. The cost includes, if applicable:

(a)

expenditure on materials and services used or consumed in generating the intangible asset;

(b)

the salaries, wages and other employment related costs of personnel directly engaged in generating the asset;

(c)

any expenditure that is directly attributable to generating the asset, such as fees to register a legal right and the amortisation of patents and licences that are used to generate the asset; and

(d)

overheads that are necessary to generate the asset and that can be allocated on a reasonable and consistent basis to the asset (for example, an allocation of the depreciation of fixed assets, insurance premium and rent). Allocations of overheads are made on basis similar to those used in allocating overheads to inventories (see AS 2, Valuation of Inventories). AS 16, Borrowing Costs, establishes criteria for the recognition of interest as a component of the cost of a qualifying asset. These criteria are also applied for the recognition of interest as a component of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset.

54. The following are not components of the cost of an internally generated intangible asset:

(a)

selling, administrative and other general overhead expenditure unless this expenditure can be directly attributed to making the asset ready for use;

(b)

clearly identified inefficiencies and initial operating losses incurred before an asset achieves planned performance; and

(c)

expenditure on training the staff to operate the asset.

Example Illustrating Paragraph 52

An enterprise is developing a new production process. During the year 20x1, expenditure incurred was Rs. 10 lakhs, of which Rs. 9 lakhs was incurred before 1st December, 20x1 and 1 lakh was incurred between 1st December, 20x1 and 31st December, 20x1. The enterprise is able to demonstrate that, at 1st December, 20x1, the production process met the criteria for recognition as an intangible asset. The recoverable amount of the know-how embodied in the process (including future cash outflows to complete the process before it is available for use) is estimated to be Rs. 5 lakhs.

Held that the assessee ensured for itself services of a better qualified partner to atleast for a period of 5 years. No doubt, the amount received by Telco was intended to meet the cost of construction of the hostel, and the hostel was to be Telco's property. And when the assessee made the payment, it was aware that it would be so applied by Telco. But so far as the assessee was concerned, it paid to Telco for the training imparted to the apprentices sent by the assessee. It paid the amount as training charge, and so far as the assessee was concerned, it remained a training charge, even though Telco applied it to the construction of the hostel and the assessee knew that it would be so applied.

The AAC had held that the amount represented payment made by the assessee to Telco in respect of the training scheme. That finding was not upset by the Tribunal. But, the Tribunal proceeded on the basis that under the training scheme the assessee was obliged to contribute towards the construction of the hostel. What the Tribunal omitted to consider was that the entire object of the scheme was the training of the assessee's apprentices and it was for that reason that payment was made by the assessee. There was no dispute that if Telco had not undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices there would have been no obligation on the assessee to pay the amount. One could not ignore that payment was made because Telco had undertaken to train the assessee's apprentices.

If expenditure is incurred for the purpose of increasing the profits while carrying on the business it must be treated as revenue expenditure. In the instant case, the assessee made payment to Telco on account of the training imparted by Telco to the assessee's apprentices. Trained personnel were necessary for the purpose of the assessee's business. It was necessary because a condition of the agency agreement with Telco required the assessee to have trained personnel. It was necessary also because the staff of trained personnel obviously induced better sales. There was no question here of the assessee acquiring any asset or advantage of an enduring nature. There was nothing to show that the personnel so trained were under bond to serve the assessee for a long term of years.

There was no question of the assessee acquiring any "know-how" from Telco which would become it property subsequently. The assessee had entered into an agreement to sell vehicles manufactured by Telco, and for the purpose of ensuring compliance with the agreement requiring the assessee to maintain a staff of trained personnel, it secured the training of its personnel form Telco and made payment thereof to it. HELD: ■

Section 37 is a residuary provision. Sub-section (1) of section 37 provides that any expenditure not being expenditure of the nature described in sections 30 to 36 and not being in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession'. [Para 16]

■

This provision contemplates that any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business shall be allowed in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession.' For such an expenditure to be allowed, it should fulfil the following criteria: (i) it should not be an expenditure described in sections 30 to 36; (ii) it should not be in the nature of capital expenditure or personal expenses of the assessee. [Para 16.1]

■

It is axiomatic that such expenditure should be incurred during the previous year relevant to the assessment year under consideration. [Para 16.2]

■

This provision was examined by this Court in another case, where it has been explained that in computing the income chargeable under the head 'profits and gains of business or profession', section 37 enables the deduction of any expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business or profession, as the case may be. The fact that an item of expenditure is wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose of business by itself is not sufficient to entitle its allowance in computing the income chargeable to tax. In addition, the expenditure should not be in the nature of a capital expenditure. In the infinite variety of situational diversities in which the concept of what is capital expenditure and what is revenue expenditure arises, it is well nigh impossible to formulate any general rule, even in the generality of cases, sufficiently accurate and reasonably comprehensive, to draw any clear line of demarcation. However, some broad and general tests have been suggested from time to time to ascertain on which side of the line the outlay in any particular case might reasonably be held to fall. These tests are generally efficacious and serve as useful servants but as masters they tend to be over-exacting. [Para 17]

■

There is a classical test laid down by Lord Cave L.C. in Atherton v. British Insulated and Helsby Cables Ltd. (1925) 10 TC 155, where it was held: When an expenditure is made, not only once and for all, but with a view to bringing into existence an asset or an advantage for the enduring benefit of a trade, I think that there is very good reason (in the absence of special circumstances leading to an opposite conclusion) for treating such an expenditure as properly attributable not to revenue but to capital. [Para 18]

■

There is another test of contemporary vintage. This test is based on the distinction between fixed and circulating capital and was propounded by Lord Haldane in John Smith and Son v. Moore (1921) 12 TC 266. This test was explained in the following manner: Fixed capital is what the owner turns to profit by keeping it in his own possession; circulating capital is what he makes profit of by parting with it and letting it change masters. [Para 19]

HC overrules Special Bench's ruling of ITAT on treatment of AMP expenses

Nilesh Patel

IRS (Ex), US CPA

Background

1. Consider the scenario: An Indian Company (IndCo) is Associated Enterprise (AE) of a Foreign Manufacturer. The Foreign Manufacturer manufactures branded consumer goods. Those goods - bearing the brand name, trademark or logo of the Foreign Manufacturer - are imported by IndCo and are sold in the Indian Market. Thus, IndCo acts as a Distributor of goods manufactured by its Foreign AE. In course of distributing the branded goods IndCo also markets those goods; IndCo incurs advertising, marketing and promotion (AMP) expenses, in addition to the regular selling and distribution expenses. The AMP expenses are paid to uncontrolled third parties (non-AEs) and are allowable under section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Following Transfer Pricing issues arise in this case –

(i)

Is IndCo rendering brand-building services to the Foreign Manufacturer AE, in addition to distributing goods manufactured by the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(ii)

Is IndCo creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign Manufacturer AE, by promoting the latter's brand name, trademark and logo in India?

(iii)

Does incurring of AMP expenses by IndCo give rise to an International Transaction between IndCo and the Foreign Manufacturer AE?

(iv)

If the answer to question iii above is in the affirmative, then how do we determine the arm's length price of the International Transaction?

The above issues have arisen in a number of cases before the Transfer Pricing Officers. The matter has travelled to the ITAT. In January, 2013, the Special Bench of the ITAT pronounced its verdict in the case of L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi).

Later on, in the case of BMW India (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2014] 146 ITD 165/[2013] 37 taxmann.com 319 (Delhi – Trib.), the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable to licensed manufacturers but not to distributors. Then, in the case of Asstt. CIT v. Casio India Co. Ltd. [2014] 43 taxmann.com 56/62 SOT 110 (Delhi – Trib.) the ITAT held that the verdict of the Special Bench in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra) was applicable not only to licensed manufacturers but also to distributors. Now, on the issue, the Delhi High Court has recently delivered its Judgment in the case of Sony Ericsson Mobile Communications India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2015] 55 taxmann.com 240 (Delhi), a judgment that has brought much needed clarity.

This article analyses and examines the Transfer Pricing issues emerging out of AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Distributors, in light of the Delhi High Court's Judgment in the above mentioned case. Let us take a look at what the Special Bench held in L.G. Electronics India (P.) Ltd. (supra).

Case of L.g. Electronics India (P.) Ltd.

2. In this Case the Special Bench of the ITAT held as follows:–

Incurring of AMP expenses by an Indian AE needs to be bifurcated into routine and non-routine (excess or abnormal) AMP expenses. The routine AMP expenses are incurred for the Indian Entity's own business purposes to achieve its own sales targets and to grow its market share. But the non-routine AMP expenses are incurred for creating marketing intangibles for the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand, trademark, logo, embedded in the product), in India by way of brand-building or brand-promotion.

If it is found that the Indian Entity has incurred non-routine AMP expenses – in excess of routine AMP expenses – then it can be inferred that the Indian Entity has provided brand-building services to its Foreign AE. That will be an International Transaction covered by the Transfer Pricing Regulations.

The arm's length price of such an International Transaction can be worked out by Cost Plus Method, i.e., by applying an arm's length markup to the non-routine AMP expenses. That price would be the arm's length remuneration which the Indian Entity should recover from the Foreign AE (the legal owner of the brand) for brand-building services, or for creating marketing intangibles.

A question that arises here is: how to determine whether the Indian Entity has, or has not, incurred non-routine AMP expenses? To make such determination a Bright Line Test should be applied.

in the erstwhile sub-sec. (3B) of sec. 37, all the judgments rendered in the context of sub-sec. (3A) & (3B) of sec. 37 will squarely apply to the interpretation of the scope of AMP expenses. We, therefore, hold that the expenses in connection with the sales which do not lead to brand promotion cannot be brought within the ambit of advertisement, marketing and promotion expenses for determining the cost/value of the international transaction." It would be important to note that Marketing Intangible is generated not only through AMP expenditure but also through the use of trademark/logo of the foreign brand owner on the products of the Indian licensee. In this connection, it would be relevant to make mention of the Delhi High Court ruling dated 1 July 2010 in case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. The ruling was later set aside by the Supreme Court on technicalities of power of High Court to give such a ruling in a writ petition but the Supreme Court did not comment on merits of the observations made by the High Court. The High Court had observed:

"If the domestic entity which is an Associate Enterprise of the foreign entity within the meaning of Section 92A of the Income-tax Act is mandatorily required to use the foreign trademark and/or logo on its products and/or their containers, packaging, etc., appropriate payment in this regard should be made by the foreign entity to the domestic entity, on account of the benefit it derives in the form of marketing intangibles, obtained by it from such mandatory use of its trademark and/or logo."

To sum up: The Indian Transfer Pricing Regulations do not contain any guidance on compensation by the foreign licensor of brand/trademark for the excess AMP spend by the licensee in India. But the India Practice Note in the UN Manual clarifies that the Indian Transfer Pricing Administration would make adjustment on account of excess AMP spend (along with a mark up for the functions undertaken) by the Indian licensee. The India Practice Note seems to indicate relevance of AMP issue only in cases of 'No Risk' or 'Limited Risk' distributors but the ground reality is that even Full Risk Distributors and Full Fledged Manufacturers are benchmarked for the AMP spend. The Tax Tribunal Special Bench has also ruled that brand advertisement by the Indian licensee of brand, coupled with excess AMP spend, constitutes an international transaction. The Special Bench has laid down a 14 Point criteria for proper selection of comparables for AMP spend. The taxpayers in India would have to evaluate the level of their marketing activities in the light of above.

Wholly and exclusively

The expression ‘wholly and exclusively’ does not denote necessarily [Sassoon J. David & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 118 ITR 261 (SC)]. The word ‘wholly’ refers to quantum of expenditure. The word ‘exclusively’ refers to motive, objective or purpose with which the particular expense has been incurred [Addl. CIT v. Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. (2004) 137 Taxman 367 (Raj.) and Ram Bahadur Thakur Ltd. v. CIT (2003) 261 ITR 390 (Ker.)]. The word "wholly" signifies that the expenditure should be completely devoted to the business. It need not be essential, necessary or compelling; it may be optional and purely voluntary. But it must be commercially expedient and should have the aim of the continuance or furtherance of the business and an eventual augmentation or stabilization of profits [Sree Meenakshi Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 156 (Mad.)]

The true test of an expenditure laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of trade or business is that it is incurred by the assessee as incidental to his trade for the purpose of keeping the trade going and of making it pay and not in any other capacity than that of a trader. It has to be examined whether the expense has been incurred with the sole object of furthering the trade or business interest of the assessee unalloyed or unmixed with any other consideration. If the expense is found to bear an element other than that of the trade or business interest of the assessee, the expenditure is not an allowable one [B. K. Khanna & Co. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 113 Taxman164 (Delhi)]

AMP Expenses Off late there has been controversy whether an 'international transaction' in relation to brand building of foreign AE can be said to exist when some part of business expenses relating to advertisement, marketing and sales promotion (AMP) are considered by tax authorities attributable to activity of brand building of foreign AE. The expression "international transaction" is defined in section 92B in a wide manner and means a transaction between two or more associated enterprises, either or both of whom are non-residents, in the nature of purchase, sale, or lease of tangible or intangible property, or provision of services, or lending or borrowing money, or any other transaction having a bearing on the profits, income, losses or assets of such enterprises, and shall include a mutual arrangement between two or more parties for allocation of any cost or expense. It is thus clear that in order to bring the transaction within the ambit of transfer pricing regulations there must be transaction between two or more enterprises of which at least one party is non-resident. Where Indian entity incurs AMP expenses for its own business and payments are made to a resident company it is difficult to say that this would ipso facto result in "international transaction" of brand building of foreign AE unless there is some express or implied agreement or understanding between the parties in regard to sharing of such expenses. This brings us to the meaning of term "transaction" as defined in section 92F of the Act, which states that "transaction" includes an arrangement, understanding or action in concert, whether or not such arrangement, understanding or action is formal or in writing or intended to be enforceable by legal proceedings. It is thus apparent that AMP expenses incurred by the Indian Company for the purposes of its business cannot be said to be related to brand building of a foreign AE unless it can be established that such expenses were incurred pursuant to some express or oral arrangement or understanding between the parties.

Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. case

The issue relating to transfer pricing of trademarks and brands created as a result of AMP expenses was first considered in case of Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT8. The controversy in this case related to arm's length price of transactions involving royalty payment of Rs 198.6 crores by Maruti India to its foreign associated enterprise, Suzuki Corporation, Japan, where foreign AE did not reimburse the Indian Company its share of advertisement and marketing expenditure incurred by Maruti India, which provided marketing benefit to Suzuki Corporation for using 'Suzuki' logo on products manufactured by Maruti company. The Revenue contention was that Suzuki Corporation Japan should have reimbursed part of advertisement and marketing expenses incurred by Maruti India for promotion of 'Suzuki' logo on the products manufactured and sold by Maruti company. The High Court remitted the matter to the Transfer Pricing Officer with liberty to issue fresh show cause notice and decide the matter in accordance with law. However, whilst remanding the matter the court made certain observations and gave directions to the TPO about taxability of marketing intangibles from mandatory use of the trademark by Maruti company which benefited the Suzuki Corporation and thus virtually concluded the matter. On further appeal the Supreme Court held9 that the TPO should proceed with the matter in accordance with law uninfluenced by the observations given by the High Court.

L.G. Electronics India (P) Ltd. case

In a recent case of L.G. Electronics India (P) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT Circle 3, Noida10 the Special Bench of Tribunal examined the justification of transfer pricing adjustment in relation to advertisement, marketing and sales promotion expenses alleged to have been incurred for and on behalf of AE. The brief facts are that on 1st July, 2001, the assessee company (LGI) and its foreign AE (LGK), entered into a technical assistance and royalty agreement as per which LGI in the capacity of a licensee, obtained the right to use the technical information, designs, drawings, brand name, trademark etc. on payment of royalty at 1%. According to TPO the Indian company was promoting LG brand owned by the foreign AE and hence should have been compensated by the foreign AE for AMP expenses. Applying the 'bright line test' the TPO held that out of total AMP expenses of 3.85% of sales the expenses up to 1.39% of sales should be considered to have been incurred for assessee's own business and remaining 2.46% of sales on brand building of the foreign AE. Pursuant to the directions given by DRP the Assessing Officer passed the order making addition of Rs. 182.71 crores (inclusive of mark-up of 13%) towards AMP expenses on brand building incurred for and on behalf of its AE.

(1) Suppose the assessee incurs expenditure on advertisement in a souvenir of a labour union formed by a political party. The labour union is registered under the Trade Unions Act of 1926. Is the expenditure required to be reported by the tax auditor in the third item in clause 21(a)?

Section 13 of the Trade Unions Act, 1926 provides that every registered Trade Union shall be a body corporate by the name under which it is registered, and shall have perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire and hold both movable and immovable property and to contract, and shall by the said name sue and be sued. Thus, a trade union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 is a separate and distinct legal entity and is not part of the political party which formed it. Since the Labour union has a separate and distinct legal identity, the expenditure cannot be said to be incurred in the advertisement in a souvenir published by a political party. Therefore, the expenditure is not reportable in clause 21(a).

(2) If the advertisement is published in a newspaper published by a political party, is the expenditure thereon to be reported in clause 21(a)?

It is possible to take the view that expenditure on advertisement in a political party's newspaper is not required to be reported under this clause. A newspaper is certainly not like a brochure, tract, etc. The words 'any other like publication' occurring in clause 21(a) as well as section 37(2B) should be interpreted ejusdem generis with 'brochure', 'tract', 'pamphlet' and 'souvenir' [See para 8 of ICAI's Guidance Note on section 293A of the Companies Act and the Auditor]

appears that under the law as it stands and also as per the view taken by the Courts, the ground reality that sales is a pre-condition to manufacture or produce things is recognized as a reality. Even in the absence of specific provisions in this regard, such expenses should be considered as wholly and exclusively incurred for the related business. The words ‘sales promotion’, should not be considered as limited to activity of sale, but they should be considered as promotion of manufacture and production also.

The bureaucracy must recognize reality 4. Conceptually what is applicable in the context of CENVAT in case of manufacture of excisable goods is equally applicable in case of providing taxable services. In era of intense competition, service providers have also to adopt marketing, sales promotion, advertisement and publicity of their services. With the changes in time, the bureaucracy has to recognize realities. There was a time that in the Income-tax Act, 1961 we found specific provisions for disallowance of such expenses. Those provisions were omitted long ago. However, still revenue authorities have some pre-notions and prejudices that such expenses are unproductive and wasteful expenses having no connection with or remote connection with business. The mindset need to be changed. It is expected that the revenue shall accept the judgment of Bombay High Court and will not appeal against the same. And will also not bring in the amendment to nullify the judgment.

Conclusion

5. It can be said that sales and sales promotion are essential pre-conditions to manufacture or production of any product. Therefore, creation and maintenance of market share of any product should be considered as a part and parcel of any business and in case of manufacture or production of any product, an essential pre-condition. Viewed from this angle, it cannot be denied that the sales promotion, advertisement and marketing are integral part and essentials of any activity of manufacturing or producing any type of goods or rendering of services. In case of branded products, or products manufactured under brand or license of brand or patent owner, which are manufactured and/or marketed through others, the brand or patent owner advertises the product and brands, and the benefit is derived by the brand owner as well as the licensed manufacturer of such brand and patent holder. If the brand owner or patent holder also sales, certain crucial material to licensees, then sale of such crucial products is also promoted by advertisement of end products in which such crucial products are used. Therefore, a brand owner or a patent holder also promotes his business by advertising his brands though the end-products may be manufactured by others.

In the instant case, the assessee was making the payment to RPGEL group for use of the logo. RPGEL was providing, in addition to the use of the logo, the following services which were developed as group services and which were utilized by other licensees given in the group : (i) training of executives, (ii) recruitment of senior personnel, (iii) negotiation with financial institutions and banks, (iv) availing of the services of RPGEL personnel, and (v) formulation of market strategies for the assessee's products, etc. [Para 19]

The lower authorities below had not disputed the terms of the agreement but it appeared from the reasons given by the Commissioner (Appeals) that the said payment was not required at all. The concept of business is changing due to globalization. The market strategies of the corporate organizations are also changing fast. If any business house is required to stand in the market, then it has to improve the quality of the products and improvement of the quality of the products as well as the market strategies which depends on lot of supporting infrastructure. The contention of the assessee was that RPGEL was one of the logo having goodwill in the market and use of goodwill gave an indication to the buyers and consumers that the assessee-company was having the back-up of excellence with code of conduct and quality. In the changing scenario of globalization, one cannot go with the conservative concept of the early fifties. As far as HRD is concerned, it has gained importance in the industrial and business world. There was force in the argument of the assessee that RPGEL was having the infrastructure which was used by the assessee-company for the development of its business. Whether any particular payment is on account of business expediency or not is to be considered for allowing the same under section 37. [Para 20]

Another aspect to be considered is that section 37 provides that any expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business, but it does not mean that the said expression contemplates that the said expenditure must be incurred necessarily for the purpose of business. [Para 21]

The payments made by the assessee to RPGEL was an allowable expenditure under section 37(1). Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be set aside on this issue in all the assessment years and the Assessing Officer was directed to delete the additions. [Para 22]

The High Court has gone further in making a pausing remark by equating Goodwill with tangible asset to stress on the significant role of Goodwill in Business and not to be construed literally.
