Also, interestingly, it has made references to a classical judgment. It drew reference from a very old case, named, IRC v. Muller & Co.'s Margarine Ltd. [1901] A.C. 217 (HL) in UK and recited "In a progressing business goodwill tends to show progressive increase. And in a failing business it may begin to wane. Its value may fluctuate from one moment to another, depending on changes in the reputation of the business. It is affected by everything relating to the business, the personality and business rectitude of the owners, the nature and character of the business, its name and reputation, its location, its impact on the contemporary market, the prevailing socio-economic ecology, introduction to old customers and agreed absence of competition. There can be no account in value of the factors producing it.."

The above classical judgment took us through the other invisible facets of the intangibles called as Goodwill and also educated us on that it needs to be reviewed regularly in relation to the business reputation, being a subjective thing. This is in addition to a view available from the previous paragraph that Goodwill may even exist in visible forms, such as contracts and special commercial rights.

3.2 B. Raveendran Pillai v. CIT [2010] 194 Taxman 477 (Ker.) - The assessee purchased a hospital as a going concern. The value of the goodwill was included in the name of the hospital and its logo and trademark. The assessee claimed depreciation on the goodwill. The Assessing Officer and the Tribunal disallowed the claim. However, on appeal by the assessee, the Kerala High Court reversed the decision of the Tribunal. In doing so it made the following significant point:

"(ii) Admittedly the hospital was run in the same building, in the same town, in the same name for several years prior to the purchase by the assessee. By transferring the right to use the name of the hospital itself, the previous owner had transferred the goodwill to the assessee and the benefit derived by the assessee was retention of continued trust of the patients who were patients of the previous owners."

The essence of this judgment is supplementary that when a going concern is transferred as such, depreciation on Goodwill, will be admissible subject to existence of other factors, such as right to use the name of transferor, etc., which can justify the exploitation of such Goodwill.

3.3 Asstt. v. Smt. Sangeeta Wij [2012] 24 taxmann.com 128 (Delhi) - In both the above cases, a value was already assigned to Goodwill in their respective sale deeds. In this case where there was a slump sale involving no value assignment to any of the individual assets including Goodwill. The seller, being a sole proprietary concern (civil engineer), was taken over as a going concern by a newly formed company in which the erstwhile proprietor was to serve as a whole-time Director for about 5 years as per the agreement on salary basis. The net worth of the concern was only Rs. 473,725 while the compensation on sale of the business was a huge Rs. 12,000,000. The assessee (proprietor) claimed the difference of Rs. 11,526,275 as long-term capital gain and claimed exemption from capital gains taxation by resorting to section 54F. The AO, however, rejected that the difference was chargeable as business income.

The ITAT agreed with fact that the difference was a self-generated goodwill and taxable as long-term Capital Gains by recognizing the following facts, namely,

1. The assessee had been in business for about 11 years and carried over 500 projects in India and abroad (Being a sole proprietor the entire Goodwill was created by a single person's effort).

2. The business had been transferred as a going concern and not discontinued.

3. The assessee was a whole-time director earning salary in the newly formed company for a stipulated period of 5 years as per the agreement.

• In Godrej Agrovet Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT 29 it was reiterated, by relying on decision in ACIT v. CLC Global Ltd. [ITA No. 2288(Del.) 2008] for the proposition that once the Assessing Officer, on exactly similar facts, had allowed depreciation on goodwill in the immediately preceding year, there was no reason to take a different stand for the year under consideration and to disallow the depreciation claimed. • In AP Paper Mills Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT30 the Tribunal held that "goodwill basically is reputation. There can be no sale of goodwill without the business associated with that goodwill or the name. From that point of view, goodwill has no separate existence apart from business. One cannot sell the goodwill and retain the business that the goodwill represented, nor can one sell the business and retain the goodwill. Goodwill has no independent existence, it cannot subsist by itself. It must be attached to business." It observed that in the present case consequent upon amalgamation of CPL with APPM, the market share of the assessee-company increased substantially. Further, the brands of the CPL became the brands of the assessee-company. The assessee got the loyal domestic customers. The assessee also got various licenses on account of amalgamation like Factory License, Boiler Operating License, pollution disposal permission, etc. Further, the assessee got various infrastructural advantages since CPL had almost all infrastructure capabilities. On this basis the Tribunal held that these advantages accrued by the assessee were nothing but various intangible assets. All the rights similar to the rights mentioned in section 32 were acquired by the assessee. Thus, in this case goodwill was a business or commercial right of similar nature and the assessee was benefited by amalgamation by acquiring that commercial value, being intangible assets for which the assessee had paid on amalgamation. Hence, entitled to depreciation.

• In Kotak Forex Brokerage Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT31 the Tribunal observed that "goodwill is nothing but positive reputation built by a person /company/ business-house over a period of time which is not manufactured or produced overnight but is brought into existence by experience and reputation." It held that the goodwill will fall under the category of 'business or commercial right of similar nature' under the definition of intangible asset.' Accordingly, the taxpayer was entitled to the depreciation on that under section 32. The Tribunal observed that 'business or commercial rights' are rights obtained for effectively carrying on the business or commerce. "Commerce is a wider term, which encompasses business in its fold. Therefore, any right which is obtained for carrying on the business effectively and profitably has to fall within the meaning of intangible asset." It further observed that since in the instant case, the taxpayer formerly known as Kohanmaz Financial Services Ltd. acquired the business of Mr. Uday S. Kotak and was going to use the name 'Kotak' in its name, the taxpayer was to be benefited by the usage of the said name. Accordingly, it was to be considered as 'business or commercial right of similar nature' under the definition of intangible asset.

• In B. Raveendran Pillai32 the assessee purchased a hospital with its land, building, equipments, staff, name, trademark and goodwill as a going concern. In the income-tax returns filed subsequent to purchase, assessee claimed depreciation on goodwill on the value shown in the sale deed. In the subsequent years, depreciation on goodwill was claimed on the written down value. When the case was taken for scrutiny assessment, AO held that goodwill was not covered by section 32(1)(ii) and the assessee was not entitled to depreciation, even though depreciation claimed on goodwill had been allowed in the earlier years. In appeal, the Kerala High Court observed that, admittedly, the hospital was run in the same building, in the same town, in the same name for several years prior to purchase by the assessee. It obviously had the name of a successful hospital and that is why the assessee chose to continue the same business with the same name. It is the reputation of the Hospital that brings patients to it and the same may involve the quality of doctors, staff, equipments and other facilities available in the hospital. Even after purchase of the hospital by the assessee all the facilities and name continued to be the same and, therefore, patients might not have even known the change of management of the hospital when they went for treatment in the Hospital after its purchase by the assessee. The Court further observed that the purpose of purchasing a business concern, be it hospital or hotel, is to ensure continuity of business with the same reputation. Similarly, the purpose of paying a huge amount for goodwill was for maintenance of the continued reputation of the hospital which was run in the same name for several years.

The Court held that by transferring the right to use the name of the hospital itself the previous owner had transferred the goodwill to the assessee and the benefit derived by the assessee was retention of continued trust of the patients who were patients of the previous owners. When the goodwill paid is for ensuring retention and continued business in the hospital, it is certainly for acquiring a business and commercial rights and it is certainly comparable with trademark, franchise, copyright, etc., referred to in first part of sub-clause (ii) of section 32(1). Thus, the assessee was entitled to depreciation.

However, the term shall not include the goodwill of a business or profession

The scope of the words "Other similar business or commercial rights" also fell for consideration before the Delhi High Court in Sharp Business System v. CIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 50/211 Taxman 576 (Delhi). The issue before the Court was whether non-compete fee paid to ex-JV partner under a non-compete agreement for 7 years was 'intangible asset' eligible for depreciation. The Court held that in personam rights such as non-compete fees are not depreciable intangible assets u/s 32(1)(ii). Depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) is admissible only to those intangible assets which give exclusive rights to the owner, which can be asserted against the world at large - i.e. in rem. A non-compete agreement can be asserted only in personam against the other party to the non-compete agreement. Hence, non-compete fee is not a depreciable intangible asset u/s 32(1)(ii). The Court analysed section 32(1)(ii) as under:

As would be evident from section 32(1)(ii), depreciation can be allowed in respect of intangible assets.

Par-liament has spelled out the nature of such assets by express reference to "know-how," "patents," "copyrights," "trademarks," "licenses," and "franchises."

So far as patents, copyrights, trademarks, licenses and franchises are concerned, though they are intangible assets, the law recognises through various enactments that specific intellectual property rights flow from them.

Li-censes are derivative and often confer such intellectual property rights. The enjoyment of such intellectual property rights implies the exclusion of others who do not own or have a license to such rights from using them in any manner whatsoever.

Similarly, in the matter of franchises and know-how, the primary brand or intellectual process owner owns the exclusive right to produce, retail and distribute the products and the advantages flowing from such brand or intellectual process owner, but for the grant of such know-how rights or franchises.

The nature of these rights mentioned clearly spell-out an element of exclusivity which enures to the assessee as a sequel to the owner-ship.

In other words, but for the ownership of the intellectual property or know-how or license or franchise, it would be unable to either access the advantage or assert the right and the nature of the right mentioned or spelt-out in the provision as against the world at large or in legal parlance "in rem".

However, in the case of a non-competition agreement or covenant, the advantage is a restricted one, in point of time. It does not necessarily - and not in the facts of this case, confer any exclusive right to carry-on the primary business activity.

The right can be asserted in the present instance only against ex-JV partner and in a sense, the right "in personam".

In-deed, the 7 years period spelt-out by the non-competing covenant brings the advantage within the public policy embedded in section 27 of the Contract Act, which enjoins a contract in restraint of trade would otherwise be void.

An-other way of looking at the issue is whether such rights can be treated or transferred – a proposition fully supported by the controlling object clause, i.e. intangible asset.

Every species of right spelt out expressly by the Statute—i.e., intellectual property rights and other advantages such as know-how, franchise, license, etc., and even those considered by the Courts, such as goodwill—can be said to be alienable. Such is not the case with an agreement not to compete, which is purely personal.

The words "similar business or commercial rights" necessarily have to result in an intangible asset against the entire world, which can be asserted as such to qualify for depreciation under section 32(1)(ii) of the Act.

Thus, "Other similar business or commercial rights" would not cover rights of a person's nature. The expression would cover only alienable rights in rem.

Whether expenses incurred on ‘market research’ for the client by the advertising agency fall under advertising services?

No. The Government in its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that if the ‘market research’ relates to advertisement then the ‘market research’ forms part of the service in relation to advertisement and all expenses charged from the client on this account are includible in the value of taxable services. For instance, the expenses incurred to find out the time slot on T.V. for giving advertisement, studying consumers buying preference, etc., may be treated as expenses in respect of market research.

Whether services provided by co-loaders fall under courier services?

No. The Government in its Circular F. No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that as such co-loaders provide services to the ‘courier agency’ and not directly to the customers and, therefore, in this case, services provided by the co-loaders to the ‘courier agency’ are not chargeable to service tax.

In the case of On Time Couriers v. CCE 2003 (156) ELT 615/[2007] 7 STT 194 (Kol. - CEGAT), the Tribunal remanded the matter to the original adjudicating authority to look into the claim that the business between the two courier agencies is not covered by the rules and no service tax is leviable on the same.

Whether training falls under consulting engineer services?

No. The Tribunal in the case of Bharat Fritz Werner Ltd. v. Dy. CCE [2007] 6 STT 382 (Bang. - CESTAT) accepted the plea of the appellants that they were not collecting any fee and they were not providing consulting services but they were only giving training to the employees of the purchasers, which did not come within the ambit of ‘Consulting Engineer’ Services.

Whether transportation of fly ash falls under clearing and forward agent services?

No. The Tribunal in the case of Sharma Roadlines v. CST [2007] 8 STT 97 (New Delhi - CESTAT) while granting the interim stay of recovery of demand observed that transportation of fly ash is essentially rendering service of transportation and not covered under clearing and forward agent services.

Whether educational institutes conducting campus interview falls under manpower recruitment or supply agency services?

Yes. The Government in its Circular No. 96/7/2007, dated 23-8-2007 has clarified that educational institutes such as IITs and IIMs fall within the definition of ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’, and service tax is leviable on services provided by such institutions in relation to campus recruitment under section 65(105)( k).

Whether convention services are also charged as mandap keeper services?

No. The Government in its Circular F. No. B. 11/1/2001-TRU, dated 9-7-2001 has clarified that the intention is not to charge the service tax twice on the same service. If a service provider is already registered as a mandap keeper and paying service tax, he is not liable to pay service tax again under the category of ‘convention services’.

Whether ambulance services fall under rent-a-cab service ?

No. The Government in its letter D.O.F. No. 334/1/2007-TRU, dated 28-8-2007 has clarified that ambulances are not meant for carrying passengers for hire or reward. Hence, the question of levy does not arise.

Whether services rendered for issue of compliance certificate fall under practising Company Secretary services?

Yes. The Government has withdrawn exemption Notification No. 59/98, dated 16-10-1998 with effect from 1-3-2006 vide Notification No. 2/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006. However, even earlier also, if a practising Company Secretary rendered the services for issue of compliance certificate under provisions to section 383A of the Companies Act, 1956 it was taxable service as covered under clause (vii) of the aforesaid Notification No. 59/98 as the same was required to be submitted with the Registrar of Companies along with the report of board of directors. However, if a compliance certificate is voluntarily obtained by a company from a practising Company Secretary, then said clause of the aforesaid Notification is not attracted, as the same is not mandatorily required to be submitted under Companies Act. But the same may be covered under audit and, hence, service becomes taxable accordingly.

4.3 Analysis of the case of CIT v. Coca Cola Beverages Ltd. - In the recent case of CIT v. Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd.34 decided on January 14, 2011 by the Delhi High Court, the question was: "whether learned ITAT erred in setting aside the order of the CIT under section 263 ignoring the fact that the goodwill generated in a business cannot be described as an "asset" so as to be entitled to depreciation under section 32 and, therefore, the depreciation on goodwill was not admissible?"

The facts of the case are: Hindustan Coca Cola Beverages (P.) Ltd. (the "Taxpayer") was engaged in the business of manufacturing and trading of non-alcoholic beverages. It acquired a business for a slump price on a going concern basis and allocated a part of the price towards goodwill in its books of account. The price was paid for marketing and trading reputation, trading style and name, territory know-how, customer database, distribution network, contracts and other commercial rights. The taxpayer claimed depreciation on the understanding that the consideration was paid to acquire certain commercial rights which were in the nature of intangible capital assets. Such intangible assets were termed as goodwill by the taxpayer in its books of account. The Assessing Officer accepted the depreciation claim of the taxpayer. However, the CIT directed the AO to revise the assessment on the following grounds:

(a) goodwill is not covered within the meaning of intangible assets under Section 32,

(b) the assessee considered goodwill to be a valuable commercial asset similar to other intangible asset mentioned in the definition of block of assets which was contrary to the Explanation 3 to section 32 and, hence, the same was not justified.

The assessee appealed to the ITAT, Delhi. The Tribunal noted that the allocation of amount paid as a slump price was not in dispute and the fact that a part of consideration represented consideration for rights, as detailed in the audit report notes was also not in dispute. The Tribunal held that goodwill is not specifically excluded from the intangible assets eligible for depreciation, and, therefore, even if an asset is described as goodwill but it fits in the description of section 32(1)(ii), depreciation is to be granted on the same. The true basis of depreciation allowance is the character of the asset not its description.

The Department appealed to the High Court. The Court held that goodwill in this case was in substance similar to tangible assets. It included industrial information like database of the territory relating to customer preferences, distribution networks, etc. Hence, in effect, it was know-how. The Court held that non-monetary assets could not be seen or touched or physically measured, but were created. Such assets assumed diverse forms like copyrights, patents, trademarks, etc., which arose on acquisition or were internally generated. The Court based its decision on the following grounds:

(a) the nomenclature given to the entries in the books of account was not relevant for ascertaining the real nature of the transaction. The accounting treatment of a payment per se could not govern its treatment in income-tax proceedings.

(b) the meaning of business or commercial rights of similar nature has to be understood in the backdrop of section 32(1)(ii) of the Act. Commercial rights are such rights which are obtained for effectively carrying on the business and commerce. Commerce, as is understood, is a wider term which encompasses in its fold many facets.

1. SECTION 65 OF THE FINANCE ACT, 1994 - TAXABLE SERVICES - SCOPE OF

Cargo handling services and Manpower recruitment agency service

1.1 The revenue demanded service tax from the assessee under the categories of ‘Cargo handling service’ and ‘Manpower recruitment agency service’ for supply of labour and handling of goods inside factory for the period prior to 16-6-2005. The adjudicating authority confirmed the demand. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) in his order had clearly brought out that only for the service of supply of labour and handling of the goods inside the factory, the assessee was brought to charge under the categories of ‘Manpower recruitment agency’ and ‘Cargo handling service’. The fact that authority had noticed that the gross value received to the tune of Rs. 15,66,569 relating to supply of manpower related to the period prior to 16-6-2005. The Tribunal held that when it was noticed that supply of manpower was taxed for a period when the law did not provide a levy for the same, the assessee could not be asked to pay taxes under such category of ‘Manpower recruitment agency’. So far as the cargo handling was concerned, the Commissioner (Appeals) had applied his mind. While doing so, he had examined the case record. When both the authorities were in quarrel as to realization of the service tax by one or the other, the invoice copies were examined. None of these pages was reflecting that there was realization of service tax. As the service tax was not realized, the assessee was not directed to deposit the same. Further, activity carried out by the labourers was found to be loading and unloading of the raw material/semi-finished goods and final products inside factory. Those were not proved to be carried out beyond the factory by the revenue. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had discharged the assessee from the charge of taxability under the ‘Cargo handling service’. There was no other evidence available on record to hold otherwise. In absence of any cogent evidence and aforesaid observations, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) could not be impeached. Accordingly, the revenue’s appeal was dismissed by the Tribunal.

CCE v. Kumar Engg. & Contractors [2009] 23 STT 52 (New Delhi - CESTAT)

Commercial training or coaching centre

1.2 The assessee-company provided induction-training programme covering ERP (SAP), its software products, quality software products, quality software engineering and personality development topics to its prospective employees. It collected certain amount as ‘joining fee’ from recruits who gain opportunity for on-site implementation experience and programming skills in SAP related development. The revenue treated said activity of the assessee as ‘Commercial training or coaching service’ and demanded service tax from the assessee. IVL being a well-established brand in software market, the SAP training programme conducted by the assessee by collecting amount from the trainees as joining fee, though it was essentially a training fee, attracts a large number of job seekers and the activity undertaken by the assessee could be rightly classified as noticed from the appointment letter that the assessee was offering the person an employment with the company. The payment clause would indicate that it was nothing but a kind of bond taken from the employee. On appeal , it could be revenue’s contention that paragraph 5 of the appointment letter indicated that the assessee had given training, was also mis-construed and mis-directed inasmuch as, the said paragraph specifically started with the words ‘on joining the company they will be given training’. This would mean that the person who was joining the company was being trained on the particular programme. The counsel stated that the definition of ‘Commercial Training or Coaching Centre’ under section 65(105)( zzc) of the Finance Act, 1994 means any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a Commercial Training or Coaching Centre in relation to commercial training or coaching. Further, from the ratio laid down in ICFAI v. CC&CE [2008] 17 STT 501 (Bang. - CESTAT), it was very clear that the activities undertaken by the assessee were nothing but giving training to its own employees and, hence, the same could not get covered under the definition of ‘Commercial training or coaching services’. Introduction

Advertisement, Marketing & Promotional (AMP) expenditure is an expenditure incurred by the company in order to increase the sales of the company by creating awareness of the company and its products/services among the numerous customers. AMP expenditure covers various components as mentioned below :—

(1)

Sales Expenditure like discounts, salesman commissions etc.

(2)

Advertisement expenditure like banners, brand ambassador expenses etc.

However, from transfer pricing perspective where AMP expenditure is incurred by associated enterprise of a foreign company, such AMP expenditure has been a matter of long time litigation as Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO) considers AMP as an international transaction by invoking Section 92CA(2A) of the Income Tax Act,1961 and make adjustment on account of AMP expenditure in the hands of AE.

Cause of Litigation

AMP expenditure by AE in order to increase sales is recharacterized by TPO as amount incurred by India AE toward creation of marketing intangible (brand) of foreign company in India i.e, Indian entity has rendered services of brand creation to foreign company , therefore such Indian company shall be compensated from foreign company on Cost plus mark-up basis.

Computation of Adjustment by TPO

There are two approaches followed by TPO in order to compute adjustment amount on account of AMP expenditure :-

(1) Substantive Approach

Under substantive approach, TPO simply computes total amount of AMP expenditure and add mark-up upon that , resultant figure is the amount of adjustment in the hands of Indian AE.

(2) Protective Approach

Under protective approach, TPO applies Bright Line Test (BLT) method. Under BLT method, Indian companies belong to same industry of AE are identified and excess AMP expenditure incurred by AE is computed [ (AMP of AE/Sales of AE) – (Avg AMP of Indian comparable/Sales of Comparable). Such excess AMP expenditure along with mark-up is the adjustment amount in the hands of AE.

Adjustment amount as per substantive approach is always more in comparison to adjustment amount as per protective approach.

Contention of Taxpayer against AMP adjustment

(1)

There is no such agreement between Indian AE and foreign entity to create brand and incur AMP expenditure for foreign entity, therefore, in absence of any agreement , such transaction shall not be considered as an international transaction.

(2)

Bright Line Test method adopted by TPO is neither a permissible method under Indian Tax Laws nor prescribed under section 92C of the Income Tax Act,1961 read with Rule 10B of the Income Tax Rule, 1962.

(3)

Economic owner of such brand is AE.

(4)

AMP expenditure incurred to increase sales and therefore it is a domestic transaction and TPO has no jurisdiction over non international transaction

(5)

While computing AMP adjustment, Selling expenditure and amount reimburse from foreign AE shall be reduced from the amount of AMP expenditure incurred.

Landmark Judicial Judgements

(1) Sony Mobile Communications (India) (P.) Ltd. v. Addl. CIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 312 (Delhi - Trib.)

The Hon'ble ITAT New Delhi Bench, I-2 in the aforementioned case held that assessee was a subsidiary of Sony Ericsson incorporated under the laws of Sweden . It was primarily engaged in business of importing, buying, selling and distribution of wide range of mobile phones in India and providing related post sale support services. During relevant year, assessee incurred huge cost on Advertisement Marketing and Sales Promotion of its mobile phones, TPO opined that expenditure on AMP incurred by assessee was exclusively to promote brand name 'Sony Ericssion' which was owned by AE, TPO thus took a view that expenditure incurred by assessee company was for advantage of its AE and it should have been suitably compensated by AE. He applied bright line test and made certain addition to assessee's ALP. It was undisputed that Sony Ericssion being a new entrant in mobile segment in year under consideration, assessee had to incur huge advertisement expenses to remind general public of its existence in domestic market. Thus, it could be concluded that AMP expenditure was incurred mainly for purpose of increase in sales of mobile phones in India and not for brand building of AE. Moreover, net profit margin declared by assessee was much higher than comparables and, looking from that angle also, there was no merit in transfer pricing adjustment.

(2) Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. CIT (ITA 110/2014)

According to the HC, the dispute was whether the Indian company got adequately compensated for performing the marketing function and incurring non routine expenditure related to it. The HC also held that a separate reference to the TPO was not required once the primary international transaction related to the distribution activity was referred.

Aggregation or bundling of transactions, use of TNMM and intentional set-off Delhi HC held that in situations where separate transactions are so intertwined and linked or are continuous so that they cannot be evaluated adequately on separate basis, aggregation of transactions is both desirable and permissible. The verdict of Delhi HC was based on Organisation for Economic Cooperation & Development (OECD) Transfer Pricing Guidelines and the United Nations (UN) Transfer Pricing Manual, which, according to the HC, supplement the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and constitute a valuable commentary on the subject matter.

The Indian legislature in Rule 10A(d) clearly expounds that the term 'transaction' includes a number of closely linked transactions and hence, envisages a situation where aggregation of closely connected transaction may be necessary. Para 3.9 of OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines iterates that though ideally the arm's length principles should be applied on a transaction by transaction basis, there are often situations where separate transactions are so closely linked or continuous that they cannot be evaluated adequately on a separate basis. OECD provides a number of illustrations to substantiate 'closely linked or continuous' test.

The Delhi HC also has analysed whether in situations requiring aggregation, TNMM can be applied reliably? It has examined the strengths and weaknesses of this method. It eventually concludes that once a composite set of transactions have been benchmarked collectively under TNMM, it would not be appropriate to segregate AMP expenses as a separate international transaction without providing an appropriate set-off of the composite profits earned. However, the HC cautions aggregating dissimilar activities like manufacturing and distribution and benchmarking them using a single TNMM would not be correct.

Para 3.13 of OECD Commentary deals with the topic of Intentional set offs. Intentional set-offs generally occur between AEs in respect of controlled transactions wherein when one enterprise provides benefit to another enterprise within the group that is balanced to some degree by different benefits received from that enterprise in return. Similar comments on both 'closely linked and continuous transactions and intentional set-offs are covered in U.N. Transfer Pricing Manual2. The HC held that the concept of set-off is or adjustment is well recognized and accepted internationally and the Indian law does not preclude it.

Brightline test not obligatory

Upholding the bright line test was one of the most contentious prescriptions emanating from the SB ruling of Delhi ITAT in case of LG Electronics. The HC has correctly dismissed the use of this method to identify excess AMP expenditure. The HC observed that this is not a method prescribed under Indian transfer pricing law and has also not been recognised and accepted in any of the international commentaries or principles of taxation. The Delhi HC further held that direct marketing expenses like discounts, rebates and incentives as well as selling expenses cannot be considered to be incurred for the purpose of brand building and thus should not form part of AMP expenditure.

The bright line test was propounded by a US Tax Court in the matter of DHL.3 In the aforesaid case, AMP expenditure incurred to the tune of what uncontrolled comparable distributors incurred was characterized as falling within 'Bright Line Limit' of routine expenses. Any AMP spent beyond the Bright Line Limit constituted non-routine expenditure, resulting in creation of market intangibles belonging to the foreign brand owner. While the Developer-Assister rules forming part of US Transfer Pricing regulations does mention 'routine' and 'non-routine' expenses (through 'cheese' examples in order to decipher the share of AMP expense to be reimbursed), the aforesaid US Transfer Pricing Rules do not advocate 'Bright Line Test' in particular.

Economic ownership of brand

The SB ruling had held that only legal ownership is recognized under Indian income tax laws and economic ownership exists only in commercial sense. The Delhi HC has on the contrary, help that economic ownership of a brand is an intangible asset, just as legal ownership and valuation of economic ownership of a brand is not done from time to time but only at the time of termination or transfer at which point of time a transfer pricing valuation may be undertaken.

Application of mark-up

In respect of the mark-up on the portion determined to be a service, the Delhi HC held that the prime lending rate cannot be the basis for computing mark-up since the mark-up has to be benchmarked with comparable uncontrolled transactions or transactions for providing similar services/product.

Present & Future

The HC judgment reaches an all-important conclusion that if a taxpayer (being a distributor) has earned an appropriate arm's length compensation established using a set of comparable uncontrolled distributors, any excessive AMP expenditure incurred by the taxpayer is subsumed in the distribution net margin and no separate compensation is warranted. This fortifies taxpayers' who have always believed this to be the foundation of their transfer pricing policy. The HC judgment has also validated the stand of the various tribunals that not all expenditure constitutes brand building and selling expenses should be kept out of the ambit of AMP expenditure.

The A.O. was of the view that the Act does not explicitly mention that goodwill is eligible for depreciation. The A.O. held that the goodwill in this case was self generated and the assessee's contentions regarding goodwill and Accounting Standards were not applicable to the facts of the case in claiming the depreciation on goodwill. The CIT(A) upheld the order of the A.O. On further appeal, the Tribunal observed that the assessee had failed to establish that it had acquired any rights of either commercial or business nature while valuing the goodwill. This goodwill was not purchased from any other person. It was a balancing figure at the time of amalgamation and the focus of the entire valuation report was on fair exchange ratio for merger and allotment of shares of the amalgamated company to the shareholders of the amalgamating companies. The Tribunal held that since no commercial rights were acquired by the assessee-company under the scheme of amalgamation, goodwill being a capital asset cannot be considered for the purpose of depreciation. It further observed that in section 32(1)(ii) the Legislature has specifically excluded the word 'goodwill', because it cannot be considered as a commercial or business right. Thus, it was held that goodwill simpliciter cannot be considered for allowance of depreciation.

• In Chowgule & Co. (P) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT26 the facts of the case were similar to the previous one. In appeal, the Tribunal observed that the assessee had failed to establish that it had acquired any rights of either commercial or business nature while valuing the goodwill. This goodwill was not purchased from any other person, but self-created. Hence, not entitled to depreciation.

4.2 Cases ruling in favour of the motion

• In Skyline Caterers (P.) Ltd. v. ITO 27 the assessee entered into an agreement with a contractor who was rendering catering and house keeping services to principal contractor, for taking over business of catering, and paid consideration for acquiring rights under catering contract and non-compete fee. He reflected the total sum paid to contractor in the balance sheet as goodwill and claimed depreciation thereon. In appeal, the Tribunal observed that the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' as appearing in section 32(1)(ii) itself would include all kinds of commercial rights. But for the words 'similar nature' the rule of ejusdem generis would apply.28 It observed that the specific words in section 32 reveal the similarity in the sense that all the intangible assets specified are tools of the trade which facilitate the assessee in carrying on the business. Therefore, the expression 'any other business or commercial rights of similar nature' would include such rights which can be used as a tool to carry on the business. The Tribunal opined that sum paid by assessee to contractor was for acquiring all rights under catering contract between contractor and the main contractee, as well as all articles and paraphernalia belonging to the contractor. Therefore, it could not be said that sum paid was on account of goodwill. Applying the above test, it was held that the rights acquired by the assessee under the agreement would fall within the expression mentioned above, since catering business at HLL canteen could be carried on only with the help of such rights under the contract, and consequently, the assessee would be entitled to depreciation. Merely because assessee showed the total sum paid to contractor on account of goodwill in books, no adverse inference was to be drawn against the assessee.

Charges for campus interviews 1. IIM arranges campus interviews for students studying for final examination. IIM collects fees from companies which visit IIM for selecting candidates through campus interviews. It seems this activity is said to be falling under ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’s service.

As per section 65(105)( k), any service provided or to be provided to a client, by a manpower recruitment or supply agency in relation to the recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, in any manner, is a ‘taxable service’.

As per section 65(68) (amended w.e.f. June 16, 2005), ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ means any person (earlier, the words were ‘commercial concern’ up to May 1, 2006) engaged in providing any service, directly or indirectly, in any manner for recruitment or supply of manpower, temporarily or otherwise, to a client.

Till May 1, 2006, IIM could not fall within the definition since it is not a ‘commercial concern’. However, since May 1, 2006, the words ‘commercial concern’ have been replaced by ‘any person’. Hence, the earlier defence has gone.

The definition of ‘manpower recruitment or supply agency’ is very wide. The service can be provided directly or indirectly in any manner for recruitment of manpower. Service is taxable if provided by ‘any person’. In view of this, in my view, the campus interview activity of IIM will be held as taxable w.e.f. May 1, 2006.

Even if it is not covered under this head, it can get covered under ‘Business Support Service’, since as per section 65(104c), ‘Support services of business or commerce’ means services provided in relation to business or commerce. That service is taxable if provided by any person to any person.

Short-term courses to executives and managers

2. IIM arranges short-term residential courses for executives and managers in companies, PSUs and corporations.

As per section 65(105)( zzc), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a commercial training or coaching centre in relation to commercial training or coaching, is a ‘taxable service’.

‘Commercial training or coaching’ means any training or coaching provided by a commercial training or coaching centre [Section 65(26)].

‘Commercial training or coaching centre’ means any institute or establishment providing commercial training or coaching for imparting skill or knowledge or lessons on any subject or field other than sports, with or without issuance of a certificate and includes coaching or tutorial classes but does not include pre-school coaching and training centre or any institute or establishment which issues any certificate or diploma or degree or any educational qualification recognised by law for the time being in force [Section 65(27 )].

2.1 IIM short-term courses are ‘education’ - not training or coaching - Education is different from training or coaching. The word ‘education’ is much broader than ‘train’ or ‘coach’. ‘Train’ means train in a particular skill like computer repairs, machine operation etc. ‘Coach’ means special or personal tuition. Giving education in a particular subject is not ‘training’ or ‘coaching’.

Train - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘train’ means to teach (a person, animal, oneself etc.) a specified skill especially by practice. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘train’ means cause or grow in particular way; educate, instruct, exercise.

Coach - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘coach’ means an instructor trainer in sport, a private tutor. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘coach’ means tutor, instructor.

Educate - As per Concise Oxford Dictionary, ‘educate’ means give an intellectual, moral and social instruction to (a pupil, especially a child) as a formal and prolonged process. If followed by in or to plus infinitive, it means train or instruct for a particular purpose. ‘Education’ means the act or process of educating or being educated, systematic instruction. As per Collins English Gem Dictionary, ‘educate’ means bring up, train mentally and morally; provide schooling for.

Education denotes training of mind, in contradistinction to training in manual skills - Barry v. Hughes [1973] 1 All ER 537 (Ch. D).

Education is the systematic instruction, schooling or training given to the young in preparation for the work of life. It also connotes the whole course of scholastic instruction which a person had received. Education is the process of training and developing the knowledge, skill, mind and character of students by formal schooling - Sole Trustee Loka Shikshana Trust v. CIT AIR 1976 SC 10.

Thus, IIM courses cannot be said to be ‘training’ or ‘coaching’. It is education.

The value of taxable service under section 67 can only be the amount assigned to the taxable services rendered and this can be the value received for conversion of input into final product. If the parties intend that the SIM card should be treated as a separate object of sale, it would be open to the sales tax authorities to levy sales tax thereon. However, if the sale of a SIM card is merely incidental to the service being provided and only facilitates the identification of the subscribers, their credit and other details, it would not be assessable to sales tax. In the case of Bharati Hexacom Ltd. v. CCE, Jaipur, [2007] 7 STT 242 (Delhi - CESTAT) the assessee provided cellular services and as a part of its services SIM cards were supplied and shown to have been sold. The department demanded service tax on sale consideration and imposed penalty. The applicant contended that it had paid sales tax on the SIM cards and since the cards were goods, provisions of the Act could not be invoked for imposition of service tax. Based on the decision of Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd’s case (supra), New Delhi Bench of the Tribunal held that even if some amount was charged for SIM cards supplied to customers, SIM card of the applicant-company was clearly relatable to the services provided by it. Such SIM card could not have been used for any other service. Moreover, unless activated it was useless, which showed that it was only a part of the services provided, and it was not goods separately sold. If some company manufactures SIM cards for the purpose of selling them to a cellular service provider for its business, that may stand on the footing of SIM cards being sold as goods, which has nothing to do with cellular service. Cellular service is not to be provided by the manufacturer of such SIM cards and is to be provided by the purchaser for whom such tailor made SIM cards were manufactured. It was also urged by the assessee that it was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 12/03-ST, dated 20-6-2003. On this, the Tribunal held that, admittedly, this contention had never been raised so far. Even otherwise, prima facie this notification could not be of any help to the applicant because SIM cards were not sold as goods, independent from the services provided, but they were part and parcel of the services provided and the dominant intent was to provide services and not to sell the material, namely, SIM cards, which on its own without the service, would hardly have any value. Thus, the Tribunal did not allow waiving of any part of the amount payable under the impugned order. It is also important to note that in case of State of Uttar Pradesh v. UOI12 , the Supreme Court has held that levy of service tax on a particular service is no bar to levy trade tax on it.

Similarly, in the case of Hindustan Associated Traders v. CCE, Cochin [2007] 7 STT 81 (Bang. - CESTAT), the assessees were given marketing and distribution rights of SIM cards. The assessees had to purchase SIM cards from BSNL outright. The assessees contended that they could not be considered to have provided any service, as they had purchased SIM cards outright and were carrying an activity of distributing. Bangalore Bench of the Tribunal held that since as per agreement entered into by assessee with BSNL the assessees were required to provide services to customers also, it could not prima facie be said that they had not carried on services of business auxiliary services; therefore, the Tribunal directed the assessees to pre-deposit demand raised.

These decisions of the Tribunal are moot pointer to the aspect of tax planning by giving different colour to a simple transaction of service as sale transaction. It is settled law that the substance of a transaction is more important than the form of transaction and for this purpose the nomenclature of a transaction given by the parties cannot control the actual tax implications.

the aforesaid section, place of supply by the way of lodging accommodation by a hotel will be the location of such hotel, i.e. Amritsar (Punjab), consequently, hotel will charge CGST & SGST on the amount of tariff charges charged by them. Since, ABC Ltd. is registered in the state of Delhi, will not be entitled to avail Input Tax Credit of the amount of taxes charged by such hotel, therefore it will directly result into increase in cost. Lets take another case of place of supply of services, suppose ABC Ltd. is a registered taxable person in Delhi. This company is engaged in manufacturing/production of electronics goods. To enhance technical skills of its core technical staff about a latest development in their field, ABC Ltd. proposes to send its technical team to a conference/Seminar, which is going to be held in Mumbai, Maharashtra. Ltd. has paid certain amount as Admission Fee and the applicable taxes thereon to the organizers of such Conference/Seminar. As per section-12(6) of the IGST Act 2017, for services provided by way of admission to a cultural, artistic, sporting, scientific, educational and entertainment events, place of supply shall be the place at which such event is actually held. Now, irrespective of status of the person receiving such service, the organizer of such seminar will be charging CGST/SGST at applicable rates. Though this service is directly related with their manufacturing/services, even then ABC Ltd., registered in Delhi will not be entitled to avail Input Tax Credit of such taxes paid to the organizers; hence it will result in increase in cost.

Now, if we see in both of the above conditions, CGST portion will go to the Central Government and the Central Government itself is not allowing to take input tax credit in one state on the amount paid to it in the other state.

Under the existing provisions of Service Tax, a provider of output service or a manufacturer of excisable goods is eligible to avail the CENVAT Credit of amount of Service Tax paid on 'Input Services'. The definition of 'inputs services' as prescribed in Rule-2(l) of CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004 specifically includes the service of Market Research, Advertisement and Sales Promotion, Coaching and Training, hence, in both of the above examples, presently the provider of taxable output service or manufacturer of excisable goods is entitled to avail the amount of service tax paid as CENVAT Credit and can adjust the same against his output tax liabilities.

Concluding Remarks

In both of the cases as referred above, if the Input Tax Credit of input services is not made available to the registered person, the basic principle of GST will be completely defying. It seems that lawmakers have completely erred to take into consideration such simple business practices. If not addressed properly, it will have cascading effect resulting into a increase in cost, directly affecting the bottom-line of business in GST era, therefore, for the sake of ensuring justification to the industry at large, these issues must be properly addressed.
